text:
Transcript

SCOTT SIMON, HOST:

Possibly no state's politics will change more next year than Texas. For nearly three decades, Republicans won every single statewide race there. But this year, Democrats swept those statewide races, including one with huge national implications for the federal courts - Texas attorney general. Stephen Vladeck is a constitutional law expert and a professor at Georgetown University's Law Center, and he formerly taught at the University of Texas School of Law in Austin. Professor, thanks so much for being with us.

STEPHEN VLADECK: Thanks for having me, Scott.

SIMON: How did it come to be that the Texas attorney general's office has such a - I think I can refer to what is an outsized role in shaping national policy?

VLADECK: Yeah. It really was the brainchild of then-Attorney General Greg Abbott about 13 or 14 years ago, where he really viewed his job, as he put it, as waking up in the morning, going to work and suing the Obama administration. And that started this trend of the Texas attorney general basically becoming the lawyer general for right-wing litigants - for red states - either to challenge Democratic presidents or to challenge blue-state policies they didn't like. And that attracted many, many cases to Texas. So it really is an outsized role that Texas has been playing for more than a decade now.

SIMON: What high-profile cases would you point to in particular?

VLADECK: Well, you know, Texas has been the plaintiff in some of the biggest challenges to Obama- and Biden-era immigration policies. The DACA case started in Texas, the Remain in Mexico case. You know, it's not just that the attorney general of Texas has been spearheading these cases. It's also that this has basically brought other parties - private parties, other states - to try bringing their cases in Texas. Even the Trump administration has brought a series of cases about nationwide policies in Texas because the Texas attorney general's office has shown itself to be so solicitous. It's going to be a pretty radical shift come January.

SIMON: How so? How do you foresee that?

VLADECK: The new incoming attorney general, Nathan Johnson, has already said he's going to abandon Texas' position in some of these cases. I suspect he'll drop some of the cases that Texas is currently bringing, including, just to take one example, efforts to challenge telehealth provider shield laws in blue states and to try to prevent doctors from prescribing mifepristone, an abortion-related drug, to folks in states where it's not legal. Texas might drop its litigation continuing to object to any kind of residual status for DACA recipients, the Obama-era immigration program.

And we might even see Texas use the powers that Republican attorneys general have harnessed over the last 13 years in the other direction, perhaps to go after private entities - Elon Musk obviously has a huge corporate home in Texas - and maybe even to sue Republican presidents. I mean, it would be, I think, not beyond the realm of possibility to have a Texas-versus-United States lawsuit that's now blue Texas against the Trump administration.

SIMON: Aren't federal courts in Texas in the Fifth Judicial Circuit still very friendly to conservative viewpoints?

VLADECK: They are. And so, you know, I think it won't be quite a mirror image of what we saw under Attorney General Abbott and Attorney General Paxton because you still have the reality that the federal appeals court in Texas is deeply conservative, probably more conservative than the U.S. Supreme Court. But I think just the fact that you no longer have Texas leading the way in sort of right-coded nationwide litigation - I think it's going to create something of a vacuum. And it's not clear that there are other states that have the same political structure, that have the same interests, that have the same resources to fill the gap that losing the Texas attorney general's office will create.

SIMON: Louisiana? Mississippi?

VLADECK: Mississippi, of course, already has slightly more complicated politics, as we saw, having just elected Senator-elect Colom. Louisiana's politics have always been a little more complicated in this space. I don't doubt that they'll try in some cases. But, you know, everything's bigger in Texas. And I think it's really hard to see from the outside just how much that particular office staffed up and, you know, was given resources to basically bring nationwide litigation on a regular basis. It's hard to imagine another red state, at least, that's going to have similar capacity without a substantial investment that would have to start, you know, right away.

SIMON: Let me ask you a Washington, D.C. question, if I might. It's the first time President Trump will face Democrats in control of both chambers of Congress. Democrats made a campaign pledge to investigate alleged corruption. Are they going to face roadblocks?

VLADECK: Well, I think there's no question that we'll see roadblocks. I mean, the Trump administration has already been putting out these memoranda by the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel, trying to identify new grounds on which executive privilege could be asserted to resist those kinds of investigations and inquiries from Congress - even perhaps for third parties to resist those kinds of investigations.

You know, we've seen already this week letters from the White House counsel and from the U.S. attorney in the Southern District of Texas, basically sort of lecturing members of Congress about the limits on their constitutional investigative powers. So I think there's no question, Scott, that, you know, whatever role Texas is going to play, whatever role Congress is going to play, the administration is going to be subject to a lot more litigation and oversight in the next two years. How much of that succeeds, I think, is going to be very much up to the courts and to the Supreme Court in the final analysis.

SIMON: Stephen Vladeck, professor at Georgetown University's Law Center. Thanks so much for being with us.

VLADECK: Thank you.

title: The migrant caravan crossing Mexico that has triggered Trump's new tariff threat
description:
On September 6, in Tecún Umán, at the border with Mexico, he joined others like him.
At that time, the president of the United States published nothing, much less threatened the Mexican government with doubling tariffs if the caravan was not stopped.
Facing a crisis, the Republican has lashed out at two of his usual scapegoats: Mexico and migrants.
“Many of the people in these Caravans are those that various countries don’t want,” the president shouted online: “MEXICO MUST STOP THEM, NOW!
“They are in Arriaga and now fewer than 100 remain,” the Mexican president said.
text:
As millions of Americans voted in the November 3 midterm elections, Álvaro Vanega was once again leaving Nicaragua. The 31-year-old left his two daughters in El Viejo and set out on what has been his only concern since they were born: to leave them something so they do not have to live the life he has lived — without a home of his own, without an education, working hard for low pay in the fields. He slept in Tegucigalpa, the Honduran capital, while, to the north, a powerful president suffered an electoral defeat. He reached Guatemala and walked until his feet gave out. On September 6, in Tecún Umán, at the border with Mexico, he joined others like him. There are about 1,500 of them walking together. So far they have only advanced as far as the Mexican town of Huixtla (about 80 kilometers or 50 miles from the border), but they already represent the migrant caravan that has sparked Donald Trump’s latest bout of ire.

In two years of Claudia Sheinbaum’s administration, this is the 24th caravan that has departed from the southern state of Chiapas, according to activist Luis Villagrán’s count, and the 10th, according to the federal government. It is the largest one this year, although a few months ago nearly 1,200 migrants gathered to travel the same route. At that time, the president of the United States published nothing, much less threatened the Mexican government with doubling tariffs if the caravan was not stopped. But between that episode and now, the midterms took place and Trump lost control of both chambers of Congress. Facing a crisis, the Republican has lashed out at two of his usual scapegoats: Mexico and migrants.

“The INVASION of our Country is taking place again,” Trump wrote Thursday on his social network Truth, where he blamed the Democratic Party for the migrants’ attempt to arrive (even though the elected officials have not yet taken office and therefore have not been able to change a single comma of current immigration policy). “Many of the people in these Caravans are those that various countries don’t want,” the president shouted online: “MEXICO MUST STOP THEM, NOW! and if they do not do so, the Tariffs on Mexico will be IMMEDIATELY DOUBLED.”

The message was received at the Mexican National Palace, where Sheinbaum calmly explained that “since President Trump took office no migrant caravan has reached the northern border.” And that is true. Human rights defender Villagrán notes that almost all the caravans have crossed Chiapas to the town of Arriaga, adjacent to the state of Oaxaca, and from there migrants have been moved to Tuxtla Gutiérrez or to the city of Oaxaca itself, where they are normally given a 30-day free transit permit.

“We inform people in the caravan that if their goal is to reach the United States, they will not be able to achieve it because that possibility does not exist,” Sheinbaum said, adding they are being offered the option to return “safely” or to stay in Mexico under “certain conditions.” “But the vast majority return to their countries of origin once they learn they will not be able to cross into the United States.” That happened with the caravan that left a few days ago with about 600 people. “They are in Arriaga and now fewer than 100 remain,” the Mexican president said. The remaining group has stayed behind waiting for the larger one that is now coming, Álvaro Vanega’s caravan.

Trump’s message on Thursday also reached the caravan. Vanega learned of it early (“I watch all the news programs”) and he admits to feeling fear. “There are 1,500 of us and we walk and contribute a little to the Mexican economy,” he says, alluding to purchases of water and some food and paying to use restrooms. He knows that this cannot compare to the trade between Mexico and the United States, its main commercial partner. “If the [U.S.] government doubles tariffs, it could be pressure on Mexico’s president and she might take action and say, ‘Well, it’s not in my interest to have tariffs raised; I’ll have to send those caravans back.’ That is the real terror,” he reasons.

The caravan is mostly made up of Hondurans, but there are also several dozen Nicaraguans, about 100 Guatemalans, and also Haitians, Venezuelans, Cubans, and Ecuadorians: “Oh, and a Turk too!,” Vanega adds. He learned about the group through social media, especially TikTok, Instagram, and WhatsApp channels: “There are no organizers.” For now, the migrants have decided to rest in Huixtla, where they are receiving care from several medical brigades. They were planning to continue the journey Friday afternoon. Meanwhile, another caravan is forming in Honduras, which Villagrán estimates has about 2,000 more people. “We are risking our lives on this road, but we are definitely giving it our all,” Álvaro says: “We tell Mexico’s president: ‘We are here honestly.’”

No change yet in migration policy

After his return to the White House in 2025, Trump rescinded all of his predecessor Joe Biden’s border policies that allowed migrants to request asylum in the United States. He also declared an emergency across the southern border and with that effectively halted nearly all entry of immigrants from Mexico. The president additionally launched accelerated deportation procedures for anyone who crossed at unauthorized points. That has kept arrests at the border at historically low levels since February 2025. Those measures will remain, at least until 2028, when a new president is elected. Although some Democratic lawmakers have already called for immigration reform, so far nothing has changed as a result of the midterms.

At the local level, attention is focused on Texas, which shares the longest stretch of border with Mexico and has historically had the largest number of migrant crossings. After Democrat Gina Hinojosa’s midterm victory for governor of Texas, it is expected that the state’s cooperation with the federal government on immigration could be reduced. But it is not an issue that the newly elected politician has yet addressed in detail.

After 12 consecutive years in office, the Republican governor Greg Abbott has implemented — either by decree or with the consent of the Republican-controlled state assembly — multimillion-dollar measures to fortify the border with military forces on land, river, and air. He also issued and renewed disaster declarations (about 69 times) to freely mobilize resources and impose criminal penalties on migrants who crossed, and even announced that the state has financed almost 100 miles of border wall. On the campaign trail, Hinojosa called these measures “political grandstanding” that do not increase security in border communities. She promised to review their effectiveness, but so far she has not firmly committed to rescinding these measures.

Under threat of losing essential funding, Abbott also forced local authorities to cooperate with federal agents in detaining and deporting migrants across the state. This was one of the issues that motivated the shift from Republican to Democratic control in Texas, especially in border communities that voted for Trump in 2024.

Abbott’s handling of immigration has been harshly criticized by rights organizations, members of Congress, and analysts, who say he overstepped his authority by deciding on matters that are the exclusive competence of the federal government, such as immigration policy. On Thursday, Trump said everyone involved had been warned: “MEXICO, THE GOVERNOR OF TEXAS, THE VERY LIBERAL NEW GOVERNOR OF TEXAS, OUR GREAT BORDER PATROL, & ICE, HAVE BEEN SO INFORMED. There will be no leniency!,” he wrote. Any major changes in Texas will be seen starting January 19; they will not affect this particular caravan.

title: Fuel crisis and protests pressure Chile's far-right president | NPR & Houston Public Media
description:
SANTIAGO, Chile — Chile's ultraconservative president finds himself on the back foot after just eight months in power.
In July, Kast's government chose not to apply an anti-inflation tool available to the Chilean state to ease the rise in fuel prices brought about by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
This week, Chile's formidable truckers' unions blockaded two major highways in an effort to exert pressure on the government and address high fuel prices.
Protests are likely to grow in Santiago if the government fails to address the rising cost of living.
President Kast has shown little sign of doing so.
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile — Chile's ultraconservative president finds himself on the back foot after just eight months in power.

José Antonio Kast, a politician who spent a career railing against progressive issues, reproductive rights and welfare policies from the extreme fringes of right-wing politics, now finds himself with just 24% approval in the polls.

It is less than a year since Kast stormed to the presidency in December 2025 by avoiding all mention of his hardline stances on social matters, focusing instead on two hot-button issues whipped up in the national media: illegal immigration and public security.

But rather than pressing ahead with those at the top of his agenda, he has floundered. And as elsewhere around the Americas and worldwide, rising costs of living have come to hit him hard.

"Our salaries are maybe 20% of a European income, but with a similar cost of living – it's terrible," said Simón Echavarría, a 30-year-old architect, at a march in Santiago on Friday evening.

"We want to protest against the measures that have set us back on environmental issues, on human rights, even reducing the sentences of pedophiles – they are implementing things that nobody asked for," he said.

Behind him, heavily armed police blocked the streets and fired water cannons at protesters chanting and waving flags in the square.

Much of the recent ire stems from the revelation last month that Kast's government had signed decrees to cut the sentences of 56 prisoners whose crimes range from the rape of children to dictatorship-era human rights violations.

Kast has since admitted that this was an "error", but came out in support of the undersecretary who signed the decrees nonetheless.

But beneath the more egregious moves Kast has made in his first year in power is simmering discontent over affordability.

In July, Kast's government chose not to apply an anti-inflation tool available to the Chilean state to ease the rise in fuel prices brought about by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

Protests exploded as prices shot up overnight and motorists joined long queues at gas stations to fill their tanks before the rise came into effect.

This week, Chile's formidable truckers' unions blockaded two major highways in an effort to exert pressure on the government and address high fuel prices.

On Friday, the strike was broken after the government backed down, sending a bill to Chile's congress which will reverse planned fuel price rises.

It is expected to be approved this month, but public anger continues to grow over the cost of living.

Politicians across the Americas who have enthusiastically aligned themselves with President Donald Trump are facing challenges similar to those confronting the U.S. administration, as rising fuel prices and the cost of everyday goods fuel public discontent.

In Argentina, far-right libertarian Javier Milei faces reelection in less than a year, with 60% of the country disapproving of his leadership amid spiraling inflation. In Peru, President Keiko Fujimori is also facing growing discontent, with 53% disapproving of her government, according to a recent Ipsos poll. In Brazil, Flávio Bolsonaro lost to leftist incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva before fleeing to Miami.

At the march in Santiago on Friday, 30-year-old veterinarian Patricia Pereira said that she was concerned about cuts to science funding, but that her discontent ran deeper.

"Here in Chile, it was a hard-won victory for children to have free education, achieved through protests, and now even that's also being called into question," she said.

Protests are likely to grow in Santiago if the government fails to address the rising cost of living. President Kast has shown little sign of doing so.

title: FAA Crisis Sparks Questions Over Billions Allocated to ICE - Newsweek
description:
The transportation secretary called for $50 billion in emergency funding to replace air traffic control hardware, software, telecommunications equipment and facilities.
Could ICE Funding Be Redirected?
The executive branch could not simply move ICE funding from the Department of Homeland Security to the Department of Transportation.
ICE and the FAA are in different departments, and the 2025 law designated the ICE funding for immigration detention and enforcement.
The outage comes as the FAA works to replace outdated air traffic control technology, with lawmakers calling for faster modernization.
text:
A nationwide air traffic control outage that grounded flights across the United States has prompted questions about federal spending priorities after Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called on Congress to provide $50 billion to overhaul the system, while critics pointed to tens of billions of dollars allocated to immigration enforcement.

The transportation secretary called for $50 billion in emergency funding to replace air traffic control hardware, software, telecommunications equipment and facilities. He did not provide a detailed breakdown of that figure during Friday’s briefing.

Several Democrats have called for ICE funding to be redirected toward the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and other infrastructure, including Senator Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, who said some of the additional funding provided to ICE should instead go toward the aviation system.

Read More on News

"There is a pot of 60 billion extra dollars on top of the regularly appropriated amount for ICE and we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA," Schatz wrote in a post on X. "We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars."

Congress provided ICE with $74.85 billion in supplemental funding in 2025, including $45 billion for detention and $29.85 billion for enforcement and related operations. About $61 billion remained unobligated as of June 30, according to Democratic staff on the Senate Budget Committee.

Democrats also won control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections and could seek to rescind unobligated ICE funding after the new Congress takes office in January. Any effort to redirect that money to the FAA would require congressional authorization because agencies cannot simply transfer appropriated funds between accounts.

Newsweek has contacted DHS, DOT and Schatz’s office for comment.

Critics Point to ICE Funding

Richard Ojeda, the Democratic representative-elect for North Carolina’s 9th Congressional District, also called for immigration enforcement money to be used for infrastructure.

“How about we take $50 BILLION from DHS and ICE and put it toward rebuilding America?” Ojeda wrote on X.

David J. Bier of the libertarian Cato Institute wrote that Congress had “wasted the money on ICE,” while author and commentator Hemant Mehta wrote: “Take it from the ICE budget.”

National security analyst Juliette Kayyem criticized Duffy’s presentation of the request and said the White House had already received substantial funding for immigration enforcement.

“This press conference is not assuring the public that the system is safe,” Kayyem wrote on X. “Duffy has lost his plot line. He seems to be holding the public hostage to his money ask. The White House got plenty for ICE. This isn’t Congress fault.”

FAA Funding and the Outage

Duffy said outdated switches and routers became overloaded with data, resulting in inconsistent information. He said the agency did not completely lose radar or communications and was able to bring aircraft down safely.

The immediate problem was repaired and flying was safe, Duffy said, but he warned that similar breakdowns could occur unless aging equipment was replaced.

“This is an emergency,” Duffy said at a press conference on Friday. “What’s more important than having an air traffic control system that actually works?”

The Secretary of Homeland Security said in a press release, “This is a national security risk because our air traffic control system is outdated and it hasn’t been a priority from Congress. This is what happens when Congress kicks the can down the road.”

Earlier Friday, before the outage, Duffy and White House budget director Russell Vought asked lawmakers for $30.1 billion for aviation infrastructure, including $10.1 billion for air traffic control modernization and $18 billion for airport projects.

Congress previously approved $12.5 billion over five years for air traffic control improvements as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, a reconciliation law signed by President Donald Trump on July 4, 2025. The funding, available through September 2029, was designated for replacing aging telecommunications and radar systems, constructing and modernizing air traffic control facilities, improving runway safety technology, and upgrading weather and controller training systems.

Could ICE Funding Be Redirected?

The executive branch could not simply move ICE funding from the Department of Homeland Security to the Department of Transportation.

A 2023 Congressional Research Service report says transfers between appropriations accounts are prohibited without specific statutory authority. ICE and the FAA are in different departments, and the 2025 law designated the ICE funding for immigration detention and enforcement.

“Transfers are prohibited unless an agency has specific statutory authorization to do so,” the report says. The restriction is designed to prevent agencies from moving money in ways that conflict with the purposes for which Congress provided it.

Congress could, however, pass legislation rescinding unobligated ICE funds and appropriating the money to the FAA, enact specific transfer authority or provide new aviation funding without offsetting it against ICE’s budget.

The outage comes as the FAA works to replace outdated air traffic control technology, with lawmakers calling for faster modernization.

text:
Democrats who won in the midterms, including those in places previously considered off the blue map and those in Democratic strongholds, crafted their campaigns around economic populism and accountability.

Lawmakers in the anti-establishment incoming congressional class have more in common with each other than divisions, even across ideological factions. Voters sent a resounding message to work on affordability and rein in the Trump administration, and Democrats across the party have many more shared goals than Republicans, who face a more existential level of discord.

The challenge comes when this class of newcomers meets a Washington machine that they view as stuck to the status quo, and as they confront institutional barriers – and a president with a veto pen at the ready – that could prevent them from installing the tangible changes voters demanded.

But, political operatives and officials said, the shared agenda is clear, and Democrats need to stay focused on it, lest they lose the seats they just won in parts of the country where they previously weren’t getting traction.

“They got to just keep being who they are,” said Joe Maxwell, president of Farm Action Fund, a non-profit focused on building back rural communities. “There’s a whole different rhythm and politics and narrative to be able to be effective in Washington DC.”

Before the new lawmakers take their oath of office, they will have to decide whether to keep their party’s leaders. In the US Senate, Chris Van Hollen announced a challenge to longtime leader Chuck Schumer. On the House side, Hakeem Jeffries so far appears to have the speaker job.

In a speech at the Democrats’ meetup in Denver on Friday, Van Hollen said his bid was a response to voters’ calls for a political system that serves them.

“We should not be preserving our institutions if they are not delivering for the American people,” he continued. “And we should be making delivering for the American people the single mission of our government, even when that means shaking things up.”

Disagreements over a leader don’t mean there are deep disagreements on the path forward, though, Democrats insist.

“There’s a very small set of consultants and self-interested commentators and donor-aligned op-ed writers who are crashing out on the internet right now,” said Maurice Mitchell, the leader of the Working Families party. “I think it would be a distraction to focus on a factional fight that they are so thirsty for, when Tuesday suggested that you should be past the narrow politics of factionalism inside the Democratic party.”

This month’s wins present a “generational opportunity” to deliver results for the American people, Mitchell said, and trying to fit that into a “narrow framework” that pits moderates versus progressives misses the point.

“We just want to get things done, and we think that there’s a big terrain to get things done,” he said.

The Democratic party once again becomes a big tent, full of people from different parts of the country with varying life experiences. Because so many different Democrats got elected, there is an “interesting mix of basically a slice of America governing”, said Jane Kleeb, the chair of the Nebraska Democratic party.

“For me, that means we’re going to have a much more durable party,” she said. “It’s not going to be a one-note party.”

As former CBS News journalist John Dickerson put it: “A party big enough to win everywhere has to hold people who disagree. The tension comes with winning. When coverage treats that tension as a crack-up or a flaw, it mistakes how the game works for a threat to the game. Tackling isn’t an obstacle to football. Tackling is football.”

Newly elected Democratic lawmakers have expressed a willingness to talk to anyone. They’ve highlighted speaking with voters who disagreed with them on the campaign trail and ran against how both parties do politics. Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive who won the US Senate race in Michigan, has said Trump can call Medicare for All “Trumpcare for All” if he wants, as long as it makes it into law.

Some new members will join multiple Democratic caucuses that may seem to have competing ideologies. Indeed, the various caucuses announced big increases in membership after the election, from the progressive to the centrist New Democrats. Sam Forstag, a smoke jumper who flipped a congressional district in Montana, joined both the Progressive and Blue Dog caucuses, saying he would be one of few Democrats sitting in both. Being in both rooms would give him “a chance to fight for populist economic policies that are actually going to help working people and finally put us all back at the front of the line”, he said.

“What you realize once you get elected is that you now are the establishment,” Kleeb said. “So I think you’ll see a reopening of what the establishment means, and I do think it’s really good that the DC traditional establishment does get shook up.”

The shared agenda

Affordability, affordability, affordability: the campaign’s theme will become the clear frontrunner on a shared Democratic agenda.

That includes working to end the war in Iran to lower gas prices, rolling back tariffs, restoring subsidies on the health insurance exchanges that have pummeled people with massive cost increases, and reversing upcoming cuts to social services.

“I haven’t heard any Democrat with a different position on those,” said Glenn Ivey, a Democratic representative from Maryland. “Everybody wants to end the war. Everybody wants to roll back the tariffs. Everybody wants gas and grocery prices to go down. Everybody wants to help expand healthcare tax credits and restore Medicaid and the like.”

Other bills are more niche, but could be simple ways to respond to affordability. Maxwell, of the Farm Action Fund, said there’s already a bipartisan bill filed to address consolidation in the meatpacking industry, which would help lower meat prices.

The second-most-frequent refrain from voters was to bring accountability to the Trump administration. Amanda Litman, the founder of progressive candidate pipeline Run for Something, said it would be a mistake for Democrats to forgo any oversight in the name of putting the past behind them. This doesn’t mean a revenge or retribution campaign like Trump undertook in his second term, but an effort to show voters that there needs to be respect for the law, she said.

“At the very least, we’ve killed how many people in fishing boats off the shore?” she said. “It would be useful to have some hearings.”

There’s also consistent support for institutional reforms that would help restore public trust in Congress. A group of 50 incoming freshmen sent a letter to Democratic leadership to call for a stock trading ban, a frequent campaign promise for Democrats – and some Republicans – this year.

“A stock trading ban alone will not fix Washington, but it is the fastest way to show voters we heard them,” the group wrote in its letter. “This rule would be a down payment on much-needed reform to prevent elected and appointed government officials and their spouses from trading stocks. We promised our communities we would clean up this place. In January, we should do just that.”

At the post-election Democratic confab in Denver this week, Jeffries said banning congressional stock trading was on the menu. He also said he supported new rules that would limit how long members of Congress can serve as leaders on committees in an effort to give new, younger lawmakers a chance at leading.

Procedurally, Maxwell, of the Farm Action Fund, said Democrats should work on single-issue or pared-down bills rather than weighty omnibus measures that obscure the work that lawmakers do. People need to see movement, he said.

This also sets up Republicans to vote up or down on specific issues, then Trump to have to veto, or, possibly, not. Mitchell, of the Working Families party, said lawmakers shouldn’t hedge their bills against whether Trump will veto them.

“They voted people in to fight for them,” Mitchell said. “It’s their job to pass the legislation in line with what the voters want, and dare the president not to sign that legislation.”

Democrats flipped state legislatures in several states and now have new governing trifectas that make policy wins much more possible at the state level, which could serve as a balm to the partisan gridlock common in Washington. When these states pass new laws, “we need to communicate governing wins”, said Kleeb, the Nebraska party chair.

High pressure to deliver

Communication will be key, Democrats said. If a piece of legislation meets a roadblock in Congress, name it, said the Minnesota senator-elect Peggy Flanagan. If Trump vetoes a bill, make it clear that he’s responsible for that.

Voters understood that this election was not “business as usual”, Flanagan said, and they demanded change. Some people in power may now “sort of be kicking and screaming along the way with this change”, but Flanagan said her job is to represent the Minnesotans who shared their deeply personal struggles.

The social media prowess of the incoming class means that each lawmaker functions as their own small media entity, Litman said. They can use this massive reach to show the work they are doing to fight for the agendas they ran on, she added.

“I do think it is really, really important for Democrats in Congress to get caught trying,” Litman said.

The stakes are high for Democrats to show the cross-partisan group of voters who elected them that they can govern, or they will face the same rebuke Republicans got this year, Mitchell said.

“They will not be kind to Democrats,” Mitchell said of the voters who are sick of the status quo. “On the flip side, if Democrats actually deliver, we could be talking about the beginnings of a realignment in this country.”

Shrai Popat and Ariana Baio contributed reporting

title: How ICE raids in Kansas meatpacking country sparked fury – and turned voters against Trump
description:
Del Real, an army veteran who served two tours in Iraq, hadn’t voted in a decade.
Here in Kansas, late September raids ignited a maelstrom of rage, turning many who had been apathetic, like Del Real, into determined voters.
The resistance came not only from Democrats or the Latino population, which has grown to about two-thirds of Dodge City.
But, from rural Kansas, immigration raids in places like Minneapolis and Chicago felt abstract.
“And so I thank Donald Trump for sending immigration here.” Answers about the immigration raids never came No one knew immigration officers were coming.
text:
José Del Real looked over the crowd from the stage in a park, at hundreds of his neighbors with furious signs tucked under their arms, voicing their anger at immigration agents who had descended on their town and started rounding up their friends and family. His daughters, in the front row, were crying.

Del Real, an army veteran who served two tours in Iraq, hadn’t voted in a decade. He thought it would not matter in this ruby red corner of Kansas. But the midterm election was weeks away. He draped an American flag over his shoulders, put on his Iraq veteran cap and ended his speech with a message: “None of this matters if you do not vote. Let’s go vote.”

They did. This county and two of its neighbors in south-western Kansas, Republican strongholds where a steady stream of immigrants have settled over the decades to work at feedlots and slaughterhouses, swung wildly to the left. The shift helped elect a Democratic US Senator from Kansas for the first time in nearly a century, signaling the limits of Donald Trump’s aggressive deportation agenda.

Since Democrats won back control of Congress in a decisive rebuke to Republicans, Trump has sent mixed messages about how he plans to handle immigration enforcement going forward. He suggested that his approach to deportations was too harsh but also named hardliner Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff. Both parties will be recalibrating their approach ahead of the next presidential campaign.

Here in Kansas, late September raids ignited a maelstrom of rage, turning many who had been apathetic, like Del Real, into determined voters.

Masked officers in tactical gear banged on doors before dawn. They stopped cars in the middle of intersections. Businesses shuttered. Families feared leaving their houses. Children stopped going to school. Some live-streamed themselves being detained. One man pleaded “God help me” in Spanish, his hands shaking, as he asked anyone watching to let his family know.

The resistance came not only from Democrats or the Latino population, which has grown to about two-thirds of Dodge City. Kansas’s embattled Republican senator, Roger Marshall, who would lose his reelection bid to Adam Hamilton, issued a statement pleading with the administration to consult local officials before launching raids.

Del Real regrets he didn’t vote in 2024, when Trump roared back into office pledging mass deportations.

“We had to see it in front of us,” Del Real said. “I had to see it in the flesh.”

This corner of Kansas is responsible for much of the country’s beef. The gates leading into Dodge City boast that it’s the “Queen of the Cowtowns” Its main street is named after the classic western set here, Gunsmoke. Murals celebrating cowboy history mix with evidence of a changing culture: storefronts showcasing quinceañera dresses, Mexican bakeries, city signs printed in both Spanish and English.

Del Real’s family came from Mexico when he was a kindergartner. Like most here, they came to work. The area – Dodge City and the region’s other hubs, Garden City and Liberal – is known as the Golden Triangle of Meatpacking, responsible for about a quarter of the US beef supply.

Some here thought their importance to the nation’s food might spare them from the administration’s deportation campaigns, said Amy Soberanes, a 25-year-old local organizer.

Soberanes, the daughter of Mexican immigrants, said she and others tried for years to get people – particularly their young, Latino neighbors – engaged.

But, from rural Kansas, immigration raids in places like Minneapolis and Chicago felt abstract.

Then they saw their own streets in social media videos.

People were furious, said Soberanes, who worried the daily protests could get out of hand. They told people not to slash tires or break windows, to store up their anger and take it out on election day.

“We’ll see them at the ballot box,” she recalls repeating.

Her phone rang and rang. People she’d hassled to vote for years asked: how do I register?

“If ICE hadn’t come, we would still be red, 100%,” she said. “And so I thank Donald Trump for sending immigration here.”

Answers about the immigration raids never came

No one knew immigration officers were coming.

Dodge City commissioner Rick Sowers said he and other city officials found out just like everyone else, through social media or masses of unmarked trucks on their neighbors’ lawns.

They scrambled to get answers from the federal government – who they were looking for, who was in charge, how long they would stay – and never did.

The Trump administration issued statements naming five “heinous criminals” they said had been arrested. But the Wichita Eagle dug into that claim and found none of those people were actually apprehended during the surge: Four had been deported months before and the fifth was already in prison, the newspaper found.

The agency said it detained 104 people from south-west Kansas.

Local officials have still never seen a list, Sowers said.

Local Republican chairman Scott Fischer, who describes himself as a supporter of strong borders, was surprised by the operation’s intensity.

“There was a little showmanship,” he said. “I don’t know why it was like that.”

He said he still considers the county red – it voted, narrowly, for Republican gubernatorial candidate Ty Masterson. The Associated Press called that race on Thursday: Masterson lost to Democrat Cindy Holscher .

But some Dodge City Republicans abandoned the party in the US Senate race.

Russell Arben Fox, political science professor at Friends University in Wichita, said swings as dramatic as that one couldn’t have happened without some white, moderate Republicans changing their minds.

More than half of Kansas voters in the Senate race disapprove of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is handling its job, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters. That’s consistent with the 61% of voters who say this nationally.

Most of the Latino immigrants here are hard-working, family-oriented, faithful people – a perfect fit for conservative Kansas values, Fischer said, so local Republicans tend to have a nuanced view on immigration.

Some public officials have for years begged the federal government for reforms to provide a pathway for these workers who run the region’s economy.

“In general terms, mass deportation is not practical,” Fischer said. “When we say send them all home, what does that mean? Who is them?”

Dodge City residents came together to help during the raids

To many here, “them” this time meant relatives and friends. In this small town, nearly everybody is connected to everybody else, so they did what they could to help.

Oscar Soto delivered food to people afraid to leave home during the deportation raids.

He started calling it “the black week” after the black plague. That’s what it felt like to him, a pestilence that arrived suddenly.

His mother came here from Mexico, he said, and though she is here legally, she was terrified.

“It seemed unreal,” he said. “It was stuff that’s never been seen here, and it was day after day after day.”

He works at a family-owned grocery, and strung a garland of flags from around the world above the counter when it opened. Most customers are from Mexico and Guatemala, he said, but he wanted to signal that the store was for everyone.

Then he hung a big American flag from the ceiling. It means to him that anyone, from anywhere, can come here, work hard and build a life, free from fear.

That belief in the American dream was shaken for him when ICE arrived.

So he registered to vote for the first time aged 39.

He stood in line to cast his ballot, amazed by how many young, Latino voters were waiting along with him.

title: Judge Blocks ICE From Searching Immigration Lawyer's Phone - Newsweek

The judge said Lattarulo’s public statements opposing the government’s immigration policies and his representation of people in immigration proceedings were protected by the First Amendment.
Lattarulo and his law firm partner, Audai Cote, traveled from Boston to Aruba for a weekend trip later that month.
Fourth Amendment Question Left Open Burroughs declined to rule on whether the phone seizure violated the Fourth Amendment.
Government Barred From Reviewing Data The phone data includes confidential information and attorney-client communications, according to the ruling.
text:
A federal judge has blocked the Trump administration from searching data copied from an immigration lawyer’s cellphone, finding that he is likely to succeed on his claim that the government seized the device in retaliation for his First Amendment-protected speech.

U.S. District Judge Allison D. Burroughs, an Obama apointee, granted attorney Andrew Lattarulo a preliminary injunction Thursday, finding that evidence currently before the court suggested he “would not have been searched except for his protected speech.”

The ruling prevents federal authorities from accessing data copied from Lattarulo’s phone after Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents and an officer with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) stopped him as he returned to Boston from Aruba in September. HSI is the investigative arm within Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Read More on News

Lattarulo, a part owner of the law firm Georges Cote LLP, represents clients in immigration proceedings and runs a popular Instagram account where he posts “know-your-rights” information about U.S. immigration matters. His videos regularly receive hundreds of thousands of views, according to the ruling.

Newsweek has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security, ICE, CBP and Lattarulo's legal team for comment, outside of normal working hours.

The judge said Lattarulo’s public statements opposing the government’s immigration policies and his representation of people in immigration proceedings were protected by the First Amendment.

The government denied targeting Lattarulo because of his speech. It argued that the seizure was connected to an HSI inquiry into whether his law firm employed people who were not legally authorized to work in the United States.

The firm was served with a Notice of Inspection on September 8, 2025, and received a Notice of Suspect Documents on September 25, according to the ruling.

Lattarulo and his law firm partner, Audai Cote, traveled from Boston to Aruba for a weekend trip later that month. Cote returned to Boston on September 27 without incident. When Lattarulo returned the following day, three CBP agents and an HSI officer stopped him as he got off the plane at Boston Logan International Airport, according to the ruling.

Agents seized his cellphone without a warrant and downloaded a complete copy of the data stored on it. Authorities returned the phone eight days later.

The copied data remains in a format that cannot currently be read or reviewed, but the administration said it intended to convert the information into an accessible format and search it if permitted by the court.

Judge Finds Evidence Supporting Retaliation Claim

Burroughs said several factors supported an inference of retaliation, including the unusual use of a cellphone search and its timing. Agents seized Lattarulo’s phone just three days after his firm received a Notice of Suspect Documents, despite an HSI policy that generally gives employers 10 business days to address questions about employees’ work authorization.

“That aggressive deviation from protocol strongly suggests that the seizure did not arise from an ordinary investigative motive,” Burroughs wrote.

The judge also pointed to the treatment of Lattarulo’s law firm partner, Audai Cote, who had the same or greater access to employment records but had not publicly spoken about immigrant rights. Cote was not subjected to a similar search.

Burroughs said Cote “would have been a more logical target” if authorities were seeking evidence at the earliest opportunity. Instead, she wrote, “the government opted to wait until Lattarulo touched down in Boston the next day and subject only him to an intrusive cell phone search.”

Burroughs concluded that the current record suggested Lattarulo was likely to establish that he would not have been searched but for his protected speech. The government said it had additional evidence supporting the search but declined to disclose it publicly because of the ongoing investigation, according to court filings.

Fourth Amendment Question Left Open

Burroughs declined to rule on whether the phone seizure violated the Fourth Amendment. The government argued it was allowed to search the phone at the border, but the judge questioned that reasoning because the investigation concerned alleged employment violations unrelated to Lattarulo’s trip.

“Rather, it appears that the government seized on a fortuitous border crossing following a weekend vacation as an opportunity to search for evidence of a domestic crime it was already investigating,” Burroughs wrote.

Government Barred From Reviewing Data

The phone data includes confidential information and attorney-client communications, according to the ruling. The government said it would use a “taint team” to protect privileged material if a search is eventually permitted.

Burroughs ordered the government to preserve the copied data in its current unreadable and unreviewable format until the case concludes, finding that allowing a search now could cause Lattarulo an irreparable loss of privacy.

She declined to order the data destroyed.

text:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court agreed Friday to consider President Donald Trump's ban on asylum at the southern border, a pillar of the Republican president's far-reaching crackdown on immigration.

The Trump administration wants to overturn lower court decisions that found the executive order banning asylum applications is illegal.

Federal law gives people the right to seek asylum if they fear persecution in their home countries, no matter how they arrived in the U.S.

At the same time, it also allows the executive branch to decide whether people are granted asylum. The Trump administration argues it can categorically deny asylum to migrants covered by the order and should not have to accept applications destined to be rejected.

Federal attorneys say long yearslong processing times had previously contributed to a major influx of migrants at the southern border as many were released into the country while awaiting a decision.

But immigration attorneys at the American Civil Liberties Union and National Immigrant Justice Center counter that border crossings were already falling before Trump took office.

They say his executive order is an attempt to unilaterally "eviscerate" legal protections aimed at protecting people fleeing danger in their home countries.

The executive branch does decide whether to grant asylum, which allows people to live and work legally in the U.S. But those decisions are supposed to be made on an individual basis and the law doesn't allow the president to unilaterally stop people from even applying, those attorneys argue.

The asylum ban was one of a series of immigration restrictions Trump rolled out upon his return to office in 2025. It has remained in place during the litigation.

title: Trump 'whiplash' on deportations putting Afghans in turmoil: 'People already survived a war'
description:

It’s whiplash inflicted on people who already survived a war,” he said.
The US supreme court in June allowed the Trump administration to strip such protections, including from Afghans.
Human Rights First, the US-based human rights group, has warned about “grave, systematic dangers” for Afghans returned to Afghanistan.
text:
Dozens of Afghans who are currently in the US but fear being deported back to Afghanistan along with a larger group and possibly killed by the Taliban are experiencing “fragile relief” this weekend after it appeared that the Trump administration had put on hold plans to remove them within days.

Members of Congress and advocates have repeatedly warned that the deportations could effectively be a death sentence.

A flight originally scheduled to transport the group out of the US on election day earlier this month had stayed grounded after a federal judge issued a court order temporarily blocking its departure to Afghanistan or neighboring Pakistan. The whole group numbers more than 150 Afghans, the New York Times reported. And the AP previously reported that the federal government intends to route these detainees to their home country via Pakistan.

Then, as the temporary court order expired last weekend, immigration advocates battling to prevent the deportations talked of dreading that the detainees could be forced to leave the US during the week of 16 November . This prospect was based on a rescheduled removal date given for at least one Afghan man currently in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention who was due to be on the flight.

As that date loomed, suddenly there was another development amid frantic advocacy efforts.

Late on Tuesday, it was learned that that detainee, along with a handful of other detained Afghans on the original flight manifest, now no longer had a specified departure date issued by the US government.

Some immigration lawyers also reported that their Afghan clients had been moved from staging facilities to long-term detention facilities, suggesting they would not be forced onto a deportation flight in the coming days after all.

Amid some confusion and often few details from the administration, Shawn VanDiver, founder and president of the US non-profit coalition #AfghanEvac, said that a sensation of “fragile relief” had descended on the people involved.

Some of the Afghans in the targeted group have relatives who assisted the US war on Afghanistan after the terrorist attacks on the US on 11 September 2001 that drove out the Taliban, VanDiver said. He had already called Donald Trump’s efforts to remove Afghans from the US cruel and being done in “a heinous matter” as a scare tactic against others.

“In a matter of days, these allies were told they were being sent through Pakistan into the hands of the Taliban, then told they were safe, then told that nobody knows. That isn’t immigration policy. It’s whiplash inflicted on people who already survived a war,” he said. “These men and women kept their promise to America, and it’s time we kept ours by ending these removals for good.”

VanDiver has slammed any option to use Pakistan as a conduit for “forced rendition”.

Immigration advocates are hoping continued pressure will result in further delays and the ultimate cancellation of that flight and any others planned for the coming weeks. In the meantime, #AfghanEvac is pushing what will become the newly Democratic-controlled Congress in January to pass a bipartisan bill that has been drafted and would give Afghans who are already in the US temporary protected status (TPS) through July 2029, with a vetting process. The US supreme court in June allowed the Trump administration to strip such protections, including from Afghans.

Such legislation would “keep people we already vetted and brought here from being sent back to the Taliban while their cases are decided”, VanDiver said.

Among the passengers reported to be on the blocked flight were Afghans whose relatives helped American troops, women, at least one gay man and members of the minority ethnic Hazara group – some who have said they were previously beaten by the Taliban.

Human Rights First, the US-based human rights group, has warned about “grave, systematic dangers” for Afghans returned to Afghanistan. That includes “arbitrary detentions, executions, public flogging, and retaliatory violence”, as well as restrictions on basic freedoms for women and girls.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in response to questions and a request for comment that the agency complies with all lawful court orders and that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) does not comment on or confirm prospective removal operations, for operational security reasons, and the safety of its officers.

Sari Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First, said that the Trump administration’s targeting of Afghans reflects a broader trend of creating arrangements with other governments to send people back to war zones, security crises and countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with the US.

The US suspended relations with Afghanistan after the Taliban government took over in 2021, forcing a scrambled US evacuation.

The Trump administration has held secret talks with Iran about deporting Iranians via a third country, and last Sunday an attorney reported that the US deportation flight of Iranian nationals headed to Iran via Pakistan was abruptly canceled, according to the AP.

The Trump administration also is increasingly deporting immigrants to such “third countries”. The supreme court is still litigating in what circumstances the federal government can deport people to regions they have no connection to, though in late September, the court ruled on an emergency basis, allowing Trump to continue this practice.

Federal law is designed to prevent the US government from forcing someone to return to a country where they are likely to face torture.

The DHS said in a statement that immigrants sent to a third country “receive notice and an opportunity to challenge their removal unless the Department of State is given diplomatic assurances from destination countries” that they would be safe upon return.

More than 60 concerned lawmakers in Congress signed a letter to the DHS and the state department, citing relevant law and also calling for the cancellation of any deportation flights of Afghans or Iranians to their home countries, either directly or through any other country. “The United States is also bound not to return anyone to a country where they would face torture, and that obligation does not disappear because a flight makes a stop along the way,” the letter stated.

In another letter, New York congressman Gregory Meeks and US senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, both Democrats, wrote to Pakistan’s ambassador to the US, urging the Pakistani government not to collaborate in any operation to fly Afghans to Pakistan and then expel them over the border to Afghanistan. The Pakistani embassy did not respond to a request for comment.

The Afghans targeted are believed to have final removal orders, which means the US can legally deport them. But the fact that an immigrant failed to get asylum or prove to the Trump administration that they have a credible fear about returning to their home country does not mean they don’t face serious risks in their native country, critics argue.

The US state department advises Americans: “Do not travel to Afghanistan for any reason,” warning of “civil unrest, crime, terrorism, risk of wrongful detention, kidnapping, natural disasters, and limited health facilities”. The risks for returning Afghans are seen as much greater.

“We are talking about people who’ve already been tortured, people who came with evidence – some of the most compelling claims – and the idea that they could find themselves on this flight is pretty horrifying,” said Sarah Mehta, deputy director of immigration policy at the ACLU. “Why would we send Iranians to a war zone or Afghans to one of the most repressive regimes in the world knowing, indeed, that they are going to be targeted because of the very vulnerabilities that led them to flee in the first place?”

One Afghan national expected to be on any deportation flight, who has been detained in ICE custody since late 2024, fears returning because his wife is a former member of Afghanistan’s military before the Taliban took over, according to court documents. He is also part of the Hazara Shia group and said he has previously been severely beaten by the Taliban while they searched for his wife.

Shaw Drake, assistant professor of law at the University of New Mexico School of Law and co-counsel for the man, said the immigration judge’s not being swayed by these risk factors was “absolutely absurd”. Drake argues that his client had no notice or opportunity to present a claim of fear of persecution or torture in Pakistan.

The man’s mental health deteriorated when he was transferred to detention in El Paso, Texas, so much so that a federal court in New Mexico issued a stay for 14 days to ensure the government had enacted safeguards to protect him from the risk of suicide.

Another Afghan who could be put on a flight is a Hazara man who testified to immigration officials that he worried about being killed by the Taliban because he reported them to the police when they killed his father, according to US government documents. He said that a few years ago, he was captured, detained, tortured and threatened with death by the Taliban, whose members electrocuted him and beat him with sticks. US federal asylum officers acknowledged the detainee’s testimony but concluded there was insufficient evidence to show the Taliban would inflict severe mental or physical harm towards him if he were sent back.

Madhavi Narayanan, a lawyer at Human Rights First, who represents him, said: “It’s another confirmation that our immigration system is not equipped to help those who are fleeing persecution and genuinely seeking safety.”

title: Voters of Color, 'Backbone' of Democratic Midterm Sweep, Now Expect Results | ACoM
description:
“People of color were the backbone of the massive Democratic success,” said Henry Fernandez, CEO of the African American Research Collaborative.
Latino voters backed Democrats 67% to 31%, AAPI voters 64% to 33% and Native American voters 57% to 41%, while White voters shifted toward Democrats compared to 2024 but stayed Republican, 53% to 44%.
“After a 2024 cycle with a lot of talk about erosion of the support of Democrats by Black voters, Black voters delivered the Democratic Party’s strongest numbers once again in 2026,” said Fernandez.
“These are folks’ everyday bills, and that’s where Black voters are certainly feeling the squeeze,” said Fernandez.
As with Black voters, AAPI voters’ top five concerns were affordability-related.
text:
Voters of color helped give Democrats sweeping majorities in the midterm elections, largely driven by dissatisfaction with the cost of living and immigration enforcement under the Trump administration.

But a new national poll suggests that rather than unconditionally endorsing the Democratic Party, these voters expect concrete improvements on these issues, and the party remains vulnerable if its new congressional majorities fail to deliver.

Compared with the 2024 presidential vote, “every group of voters of color shifted toward Democrats in House races by significant margins: Latino voters by 14 points, AAPI voters by 9, Black voters by 8, and Native American voters by 6, compared with 4 points among White voters,” finds the 2026 Midterm Election Voter Poll — a survey of more than 10,000 voters conducted between Oct. 19 and Election Day, Nov. 3, with large samples of Black, Latino, Native American and Asian American, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander voters.

Every group named affordability as its top reason for the shift.

Supermajorities of each group also opposed the administration’s immigration crackdown, civil rights leaders and researchers said at a Nov. 6 American Community Media briefing about the poll. BSP Research conducted the survey with 14 partners including the National Immigration Law Center, UnidosUS, the African American Research Collaborative, Asian Americans Advancing Justice | AAJC and First Nations Development Institute.

Immigration policy took on particular urgency the day of the briefing, when President Donald Trump announced that deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, the architect of the administration’s immigration policy, would replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff starting Nov. 9.

The appointment signaled that the White House intends to double down on its immigration enforcement, even as the new Democratic majorities consider rescinding the more than $200 billion that congressional Republicans have steered to immigration enforcement since July 2025.

‘A once-in-a-generation opportunity’

Kica Matos, President, National Immigration Law Center, shares her thoughts on Trump’s appointment of Stephen Miller as White House Chief of Staff.

Most poll respondents support redirecting that money, said Kica Matos, president of the National Immigration Law Center: “They want that money to be clawed back and given instead to programs that benefit people and communities, including SNAP and Medicaid.”

This support is highest among Black voters (78%), followed by Latino (68%), AAPI (66%) and Native American voters (64%). Most white voters (59%) also support it.

“Folks have delivered an epic smackdown of the Trump administration’s handling of immigration, and chart a clear path forward for how Congress needs to move on this issue,” said Matos.

But with Miller now chief of staff, she continued, “Congress will really need to step it up because my own opinion is that they have been asleep at the wheel in the last two years when it comes to immigration, and now things are about to get worse.”

“We have a once-in-a-generation opportunity to make real change,” Matos added. “Our new congressional majorities must not waste it, and we intend to hold their feet to the fire.”

Across groups, 89% of respondents — including more than nine in 10 Black and Latino voters — agreed that “we need a balanced and orderly immigration system that has an earned path to citizenship for long-term residents; focuses enforcement inside the country on keeping communities safe, with clear accountability; offers legal ways to immigrate that help our economy and families; and keeps the border secure,” per the poll.

‘A resounding rebuke’

Clarissa Martínez De Castro, Vice President, Latino Vote Initiative, UnidosUS, discusses what Democrats need to do with their new-found majority in order to stay in power.

Latino voters particularly “delivered a resounding rebuke of current economic and immigration policies, and that rebuke led to unprecedented Democratic wins,” said Clarissa Martínez De Castro, vice president of the Latino Vote Initiative at UnidosUS.

But she rejected the idea that Democrats won Latinos back for good.

Roughly 38% of Latino voters entered the election as “part of a movable middle, independents, undecideds — people who, in 2024, crossed party lines, and/or voted for a third party,” Martínez De Castro said. “That should put both parties on notice.”

Retaining their support, she added, “will hinge on delivering solutions to the issues that are squeezing working families beyond the breaking point and stopping the abuse that many of our communities are experiencing.”

Only 15% of Latino respondents described themselves as financially comfortable, and 80% were working class.

‘What checked this administration was the voters’

Henry Fernandez, Chief Executive Officer, African American Research Collaborative, says that the recent elections Black candidates in states that have long resisted Black leadership must be credited, in part, to previous Black candidates whose campaigns and efforts to court voters set the groundwork for Black electoral success.

“People of color were the backbone of the massive Democratic success,” said Henry Fernandez, CEO of the African American Research Collaborative.

Black voters backed Democratic House candidates by the widest margin of any group in the poll, 85% to 13%. Latino voters backed Democrats 67% to 31%, AAPI voters 64% to 33% and Native American voters 57% to 41%, while White voters shifted toward Democrats compared to 2024 but stayed Republican, 53% to 44%.

“After a 2024 cycle with a lot of talk about erosion of the support of Democrats by Black voters, Black voters delivered the Democratic Party’s strongest numbers once again in 2026,” said Fernandez.

Among all 2024 Trump voters, 9% backed Democrats for the House this year, but among Black Trump voters, that number was 35%.

All five of Black voters’ top concerns were affordability-related: cost of living and inflation (60%), jobs and the economy (37%), affordable housing (35%), health care costs (32%) and gas prices (31%).

“These are folks’ everyday bills, and that’s where Black voters are certainly feeling the squeeze,” said Fernandez. “Many of us had hoped Congress would step up, or that the courts, which have done some important work, would really check this administration. What checked this administration was the voters.”

‘A movable community’

John C. Yang, President and Executive Director of Asian Americans Advancing Justice | AAJC, discusses AAPI views on the Voting Rights Act and what needs to be done to protect the right to vote.

AAPI voters backed Democrats by about 2-to-1 in Senate, House and gubernatorial races.

John C. Yang, president and executive director of Asian Americans Advancing Justice | AAJC, called the swing “a reversion” after a five-point shift toward Trump in 2024, according to the NBC News exit poll.

As with Black voters, AAPI voters’ top five concerns were affordability-related.

“Our community is a movable community when it comes to their view of the different parties,” said Yang.

Nearly two-thirds of AAPI respondents said the country is headed in the wrong direction, while 79% worried that Congress is failing to exercise its constitutional checks and balances, and 80% supported passing “a new voting rights act to ensure that all eligible American citizens can vote without barriers.”

“Oftentimes, people try to use the Asian American community as a wedge, or somehow suggest that we are white-adjacent,” said Yang. “What this survey demonstrates is that we have the same concern around immigration, discrimination, voting, representation that all of the other communities of color do.”

Outreach also made a difference, he added: “Fifty-four percent of the Asian American community heard from someone in the Democratic Party in the course of this election cycle, whereas only 38% heard from Republicans.”

‘The kind of future that people want’

Annalise Guthrie (Cherokee Nation), Senior Research Officer, Research and Advocacy at First Nations Development Institute, discusses the issues Native American voters are facing and how they would like to see them addressed.

Of the poll’s roughly 1,400 Native American respondents, 49% said no party, campaign or organization contacted them about voting.

“Native voters were making these choices, but that doesn’t mean that they’re giving either party their unconditional support,” said Annalise Guthrie, senior research officer at First Nations Development Institute. “Native voters expect to see their priorities reflected in policy, and not just acknowledged during the election season.”

While affordability issues constituted Native voters’ top five concerns, 89% also said a candidate’s position on tribal sovereignty, treaty rights and federal trust responsibilities “are important in deciding who they’re going to support,” she continued.

“We’re talking about whether families can afford to stay in their communities, support their children, care for their elders and actually build financial stability for the future,” added Guthrie. “I really don’t think that this election was just about political preference. I think it was really about the kind of future that people want for their families and their communities.”

SELEN OZTURK

ACoM editor and research director Selen Ozturk was born in Istanbul and raised in the Bay Area. She holds a philosophy degree from UC Berkeley. Her work has been published in the San Francisco Chronicle, SFGATE, Bay City News, PopMatters, and Senses of Cinema, among many other outlets.

text:
More than a dozen Ecuadorian fishermen are suing the US government after they survived a military drone attack in the Pacific ocean earlier this year that sank their boat and left two of them with serious burns from the explosions.

The 17 March attack on the La Negra Francesca Duarte II was part of the Trump administration’s Operation Southern Spear campaign, announced in November 2025 ostensibly to counter “narco-terrorists” it said operated in the Caribbean and Pacific.

The Washington office on Latin America (Wola) said as many as 250 people have been killed by the US military in subsequent attacks. The group considers the actions extrajudicial executions because the government has provided no proof that the victims were engaged in trafficking.

In the lawsuit seen by the Guardian, to be filed in US district court for the western district of Pennsylvania on Monday, the 16 fishermen insist they had no connection with the drug trade and were illegally targeted by the crew of an unidentified US military vessel about 385 nautical miles from the port of Manta as they returned from a two-week fishing trip.

Two armed drones, the filing states, exploded on their boat, setting it ablaze and destroying it completely, and two of the crew “were themselves set on fire and burned on their legs, arms and back”.

The men say they jumped overboard and into small emergency boats that they rowed towards the vessel, pursued by a surveillance drone. They were greeted by US military personnel in camouflage uniforms who, they said, restrained them with zip ties and placed plastic hoods over their heads.

In an interview in June, the boat’s captain, Hernán Flores, described the moments after the boat he commanded for about 20 years was set alight. “Some guys looked for an extinguisher, but the fire was already spreading,” he said. “So some of our crew leapt into the water.”

The lawsuit seeks unspecified financial compensation for the attack, and for their subsequent “kidnapping and torture” that they say occurred when they were taken to a detention center in El Salvador and imprisoned for several weeks.

“They go out fishing, they don’t come home for a month, they’re like in a migrant detention center in El Salvador, and as we know those centers are not so nice,” said Dan Kovalik, a Pittsburgh-based attorney who is filing the lawsuit on behalf of the men.

“So there’s a lot of trauma there. It was catastrophic for them. They are home now, but they are struggling financially, and the two guys who were hurt bad are still dealing with that.”

Kovalik said the loss of the fishing vessel meant none of the plaintiffs had been able to work or support their families, and they were angry that, until their lawsuit, there was no recourse against the US authorities for what happened to them.

“They would also like the US to stop these boat strikes. That’s another goal of all this, and I think the US public and the media have been, honestly, not outraged enough about these strikes.”

The lawsuit states that the “manifestly unlawful” attack on the fishermen came soon after Ecuadorian authorities inspected the boat for themselves and determined it was not carrying drugs, nor its crew affiliated with any cartels.

It said the attack was illegal because, as with other strikes during Operation Southern Spear, it was conducted without congressional authority.

Additionally, the lawsuit alleges, “the wanton, willful and outrageous attacks upon, and kidnapping and torture of, plaintiffs at sea constitute torts under general admiralty and maritime law.

“There is no actual armed conflict that could justify the use of military force against the boats, nor was there one on March 17 when the attack took place. The US’s campaign of bombings against defenseless vessels and individuals violates long-standing and well-accepted international law.”

A spokesperson for the department of defense said in a statement on Friday: “As a matter of policy, the department does not comment on pending or ongoing litigation.”

In June, after details of the attack on the La Negra Francesca Duarte II first emerged, the Pentagon and US Coast Guard denied participating in operations involving Ecuadorian fishing vessels.

“We have no knowledge of, nor were Department of War forces involved in, the incidents described in those reports,” a spokesperson for US Southern Command (Southcom) said in a statement.

“US forces conduct operations under established legal authorities and hold its forces to the highest standards of professionalism, safety, and compliance with US and international law.”

Kovalik said he expected the government to contest the lawsuit, filed in a Pennsylvania district he said had “experience in admiralty cases”.

But he said it would help shine a light on the policies and actions of the Trump administration at a time when the Democratic party was about to take over control of Congress and launch its own investigations.

“Some of the Democrats that we met with are very interested in doing hearings on these boat strikes,” he said.

“We hope this case will encourage the Democrats when they get sworn in in January to start some hearings. I think it will have that impact.”

The fishermen’s lawsuit will join previously filed, similar litigation against the Trump administration. In January, the families of Chad Joseph, 26, and Rishi Samaroo, 41, Trinidadian fishermen killed in a US military strike in the Caribbean three months previously, filed a first-of-its-kind suit in Massachusetts.

The American Civil Liberties Union is among advocacy groups demanding an end to what it calls “a terrifying, lawless killing campaign at sea”.
