text:
On Lawfare Live on Friday, Nov. 13, at 4 p.m. ET, Wittes spoke with Roberts, Parloff, Columbus, and Bower to cover the latest litigation over Trump administration policies, including the politicization of the Justice Department, an update on President Trump’s monuments, immigration roundups, and more.

Nick Bednar reviewed Michael Lewis’s book “Blockers,” describing how Lewis used vignettes of career civil servants to follow the second Trump administration’s campaign to push out experienced federal employees. Bednar noted that although Lewis makes a few stray administrative law errors in his analysis, he effectively communicates why the public should care about those who do the work of the government.

On Lawfare Daily from last week’s Lawfare Live, Benjamin Wittes sat down with Molly Roberts, Roger Parloff, Anna Bower, and Eric Columbus to discuss the latest litigation over Trump administration policies, including D.C. and Virginia’s suit to block construction of the triumphal arch, the Ahmed Soliman case, the politicization of the Justice Department, election litigation in California and Alaska, President Trump’s defamation suit against the Wall Street Journal, and more.

Matthew Tokson outlined how automated license plate readers (ALPRs) likely violate the Fourth Amendment in the absence of a warrant. Although up until recently courts held that ALPR systems were legal, Tokson detailed how the Supreme Court’s ruling in Chatrie v. United States—which held that a warrant is required to obtain data from Google Maps—has guided lower courts in echoing these concerns with ALPRs, which can expose extensive location data.

Julia Curlee argued that the war in Iran was a policy failure—not an intelligence failure—and that voters held the White House accountable for it, giving Democrats control of both chambers of Congress in the midterms. Curlee maintained that the Iran war followed a year in which the White House dismantled the institutions that should have warned Trump against it. She contended that the new Congress should investigate this damage and enact statutory reforms to protect intelligence analysis and personnel and keep the intelligence committees informed.

Aaron S.J. Zelinsky drew on the history of the U.S. Court for Berlin to apply lessons to the newly-revived Alien Terrorist Removal Court. Zelinsky outlined the history of the U.S. Court for Berlin, an Article II court established to exercise jurisdiction over West Berlin but which convened only once for a plane hijacking case, United States v. Tiede. Zelinsky examined what Tiede can reveal about the independence of Article III judges and argued that a court without precedent faces novel problems at every step.

Bailey Schiff argued that a future nuclear deal with Iran should close off the country’s plutonium pathway, which runs through the spent fuel at the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant. Schiff explained that Iran’s development of a plutonium weapon could be slow now but has the potential to accelerate, especially with the help of Russia, although it remains to be seen if Iran has the necessary reprocessing capability, specialized equipment, or expertise to build it. Schiff held that Washington should constrain this pathway by seeking a deal to suspend Iran's plutonium reprocessing activities.

Viola Rothschild detailed how China, following the dissolution of the U.S. Agency for International Development, sees foreign aid retrenchment as a historic opportunity to cautiously move forward and reap the rewards of U.S. withdrawal. Rothschild noted that Chinese analysts remain wary of rushing through this window of opportunity and explained turbulence in the foreign aid sector as a microcosm of shifts in international power.

On Lawfare Daily, Justin Sherman sat down with Oscar Jonsson to discuss the origins and evolution of the Russian General Staff, its role in the early Putin system amid reforms and power consolidation, the General Staff’s role—or lack thereof—in Russia’s initial invasion of Ukraine in 2014, the future of Russian military thought and planning, and more.

On Lawfare Daily, Peter Harrell sat down with Aya Ibrahim to discuss what a progressive economic and national security agenda under a Democratic Congress could look like with regard to artificial intelligence (AI) regulation, U.S.-China policy, and more.

In the latest edition of the Seriously Risky Business cybersecurity newsletter, Tom Uren analyzed supermarket freezer hacks in France, how French authorities have attributed these attacks to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and why they resembled Russia’s cyber campaigns in Europe. Uren also detailed three Chinese cyber operations and the contrasting tactics each deployed, and more.

On Lawfare Live on Nov. 9 at 3:30 p.m. ET, Kate Klonick and Michael Feinberg sat down to discuss the explosive allegations about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the role of seduction in intelligence gathering, how the public should think about the growing scandal, and more.

Jay Healey and Benjamin Pearl argued that often-burdensome cyber regulations should instead seek to create regulatory harmony, allocating resources toward safety rather than compliance. Healey and Pearl contended that unwieldy regulations generate a “harmonization tax”—the cost of addressing compliance tasks—which overwhelms companies but generates little pay off in security. The authors analyzed the benefits of using AI systems to streamline regulations.

Healey argued that cyber reporting regulations should spell out the specific policy purposes each incident report serves to promote regulatory harmony. Healey outlined a decision-support framework which sorts reporting purposes into three categories: government knowledge of incidents, government knowledge of vulnerabilities and threats, and key stakeholder knowledge of incidents. Healey concluded that this structure can reduce inconsistent reporting regulations by determining which particular issue regulation seeks to address.

Satya Thallam argued that the AI testing failures at OpenAI and Anthropic were not primarily caused by models outsmarting their keepers, but took place because the models’ testing environments were misconfigured. Thallam outlined a mandatory incident reporting regime for Congress to set up so that industry incentives are changed to invest more in security and safety testing while providing transparency.

On Lawfare Daily, Kevin Frazier sat down with Roberto Tallarita to discuss Anthropic’s recently filed s-1, the company’s experiment in corporate governance, how to maintain a commitment to safety precautions even when that is in tension with profit, and more.

authors: Ann E. Marimow and Hamed Aleaziz The New York Times
description:
The Supreme Court case is expected to be the culmination of years of litigation over the ability of the government to prohibit migrants from claiming asylum at the border.
Next year, the court will consider the administration's policy of indefinitely detaining immigrants who crossed the border illegally years ago.
In the asylum case the justices accepted Friday, a central question is whether the president can override immigration law set by Congress.
In his second term, the president adopted the prohibition on asylum claims at the border and has been fighting over the policy in court.
The immigrant rights groups brought the initial legal challenge on behalf of more than a dozen people who had been detained or removed from the United States without their asylum claims being addressed.
text:
WASHINGTON -- The Supreme Court announced Friday that it will review the legality of the Trump administration's policy of categorically denying asylum claims from people crossing the southern border, taking up another major test of the president's immigration agenda.

On President Donald Trump's first day back in office, he effectively shut down the ability of people fearing torture and persecution to apply for asylum protections at the border and then remain in the United States, declaring there was an "invasion" along the southern border. In a proclamation, he invoked what he called "the inherent right and duty of the executive branch to defend our national sovereignty."

Immigration rights groups quickly challenged the proclamation, and lower courts have found it to be illegal. But it has still largely been in force under a temporary court order. The Supreme Court case is expected to be the culmination of years of litigation over the ability of the government to prohibit migrants from claiming asylum at the border.

This Supreme Court term, which began in October and will conclude next summer, is shaping up to be dominated by Trump's aggressive immigration policies. In December, the court will review the administration's efforts to deport immigrants to third countries where they have no ties, including nations that have faced claims of human rights abuses. Next year, the court will consider the administration's policy of indefinitely detaining immigrants who crossed the border illegally years ago.

In the asylum case the justices accepted Friday, a central question is whether the president can override immigration law set by Congress. During the first Trump administration, officials struggled to come up with restrictive asylum policies at the border that would survive judicial scrutiny.

In his second term, the president adopted the prohibition on asylum claims at the border and has been fighting over the policy in court. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the justices in court filings that their intervention was "urgently warranted" in part because the policy was Trump's "main tool for stemming an unprecedented crisis of uncontrolled illegal entry."

Trump's initial proclamation was followed by guidance from the Department of Homeland Security that blocked people from applying for asylum who had crossed illegally.

As a result, the number of people crossing the southern border illegally has dropped to levels not seen in decades. Border Patrol agents made just over 6,000 arrests in June 2025, for instance, according to figures from Homeland Security. During the height of such crossings during the Biden administration, more than 200,000 people crossed in December 2023.

The immigrant rights groups brought the initial legal challenge on behalf of more than a dozen people who had been detained or removed from the United States without their asylum claims being addressed.

Many of those people had experienced political persecution in their home countries of Afghanistan, Cuba, Egypt, Peru and Turkey, according to court filings. Their lawyers said some were subjected to "traditional torture" at the hands of those governments.

In July 2025, Judge Randolph D. Moss of U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia ruled against the Trump administration's asylum policy, finding that the Constitution and federal immigration law did not give Trump the expansive authority he claimed.

A divided appeals court panel in April largely upheld Moss' decision and rejected the administration's view that it could "unilaterally and heedlessly return individuals even to countries where they will most certainly face persecution."

The 2-1 decision from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia said Trump had to follow requirements outlined in the Immigration and Nationality Act and could not categorically deny asylum claims from people crossing from Mexico into the United States.

text:
The Supreme Court has granted review in Mullin v. RAICES, a challenge to President Trump’s proclamation completely shutting down asylum at the border.

The American Civil Liberties Union, National Immigrant Justice Center, Center for Gender & Refugee Studies, Texas Civil Rights Project, ACLU of the District of Columbia, and ACLU of Texas brought the federal lawsuit on behalf of a nationwide class of people barred from seeking protection in the United States under this proclamation, as well as three immigrant legal service providers, Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services (RAICES), Las Americas Immigrant Advocacy Center, and the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project.

The federal district court in Washington, D.C. and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit both rejected the Trump administration’s unlawful proclamation barring people from seeking asylum by invoking Section 212(f) of the Immigration and Nationality Act and citing a nonexistent “invasion.”

The lower federal courts ruled in the plaintiffs’ favor because the Trump administration’s action is contrary to laws enacted by Congress to ensure that people receive an opportunity to have their asylum claims heard.

The Supreme Court granted the government’s petition to hear the case, and argument is expected in spring 2027.

The following is reaction to the Supreme Court decision to hear the case:

“The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger,” said Lee Gelernt, lead counsel and deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project. “The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger. We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court.”

“The plaintiffs in this case fled persecution and torture, including political imprisonment and threats from the Taliban. Yet, the Trump administration refused to honor its obligation to consider them for asylum,” said Keren Zwick, executive director of the National Immigrant Justice Center. “Some plaintiffs were removed to third countries and then pushed back to the very place they fled; others faced prolonged detention without access to legal due process. Even after the lower courts rejected the president’s proclamation, the administration has continued to block access to asylum at the U.S. border. This vicious attack on due process and human rights has put thousands of lives in danger. We are honored to represent these asylum seekers, and their advocates, as this important case proceeds.”

“For nearly two years, the Trump administration’s unlawful asylum shutdown has deprived people seeking safety of their rights, placing vulnerable families, children, and adults in harm’s way,” said Melissa Crow, director of litigation at the Center for Gender & Refugee Studies (CGRS). “Refugees fleeing persecution and torture have been denied access to the asylum process and deported to danger. The lower courts got it right: The president cannot unilaterally rewrite our immigration laws and defy the will of Congress to get its way. It is now up to the Supreme Court to decide whether it will uphold the rule of law or bend to the administration’s agenda.”

“No one seeking safety at our borders should be denied that opportunity. It is incredibly timely that the Supreme Court will hear our case, as the nation saw a clear mandate from midterm voters earlier this month. Our communities made their voices heard on immigration, economic justice, and the many misdirections this administration has taken,” said Rochelle Garza, president of the Texas Civil Rights Project. “Asylum seekers deserve to have their rights protected, and we will continue fighting to ensure that the dedicated organizations who serve them directly have the ability to do so.”

“The Supreme Court faces a stark choice. Respect the rule of law and uphold the right to asylum, or allow the executive to decide on its own who gets to ask for safety,” said Nicolas Palazzo, interim executive director of Las Americas Immigrant Advocacy Center. “For the people we represent in El Paso and along the border, the court’s answer will decide whether they find protection or are sent back to the danger they fled.”

“Congress has determined that the United States has not only a moral but a legal obligation to provide people seeking safety at our borders a process to access protection. This attempt to unilaterally stop all asylum processing at the border is an unprecedented and illegal overreach that puts countless people in danger,” said Laura St. John, the legal director for the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project.

RITZVILLE — The Adams County Sheriff's Office said it will appeal a decision announced Friday in a lawsuit brought against the ACSO by the Washington Attorney General's Office, which started in March 2025.

The ruling by Spokane County Superior Court Judge Marla Polin orders ACSO to change policies and practices that the judge ruled violate the Keep Washington Working Act.

According to Mike Faulk, deputy communications director for the AG's office, a lawsuit may be brought in the superior court in the county of origin or in the two nearest judicial districts.

Sheriff Dale Wagner responded in a media release, saying the county would appeal.

"I respect the judicial process, but respecting the process does not mean we must agree with every ruling. We intend to pursue the appropriate legal avenues to challenge this decision and defend what we believe is our responsibility to protect our residents," Wagner wrote.

Faulk said the ruling requires Adams County to comply with state law, specifically the Keep Washington Working Act.

"We had two years of negotiations with the county that ultimately did not resolve and we had to file this lawsuit," Faulk wrote in response to an email from the Columbia Basin Herald. "The court's decision is what's binding on the county."

The Keep Washington Working Act includes restrictions on information that local and state law enforcement officials can share with federal immigration authorities. The lawsuit alleged ACSO was sharing current booking information with federal authorities. Polin said the information was "nonpublicly available," and ordered ACSO to cease that practice.

During the relevant period, the general public couldn't see or access the list, she wrote.

"Nonpublicly available personal information is not defined in KWW, but must be interpreted in a manner that furthers the legislature's goal of eliminating coordination between local law enforcement and federal immigration authorities for civil immigration purposes," Polin wrote.

"The fact that (ACSO) made some information about those in its custody available to the public through an online jail roster, and later a mobile application, does not change the court's conclusion that the new in-custody list was 'nonpublicly available.' Those other mechanisms for publishing a jail roster, by design or defect, did not provide contemporaneous information about those in (ACSO's) custody, or did not provide as much information," she said.

The practice the ACSO used violated the Legislature's intent, she said.

The Keep Washington Working Act was passed in 2019, and Polin said ACSO sent release information to federal immigration authorities in connection with inquiries from federal agencies for cases that weren't criminal in nature.

The ASCO provided that information after the passage of KWW, between 2021 and 2023. Sheriff's deputies also allowed federal immigration agents to talk to people who were in custody, she wrote.

"(Keep Washington Working) imposes an obligation on law enforcement agencies to ensure that federal immigration authorities only conduct in-custody interviews in connection with criminal matters, absent consent or a legal obligation," Polin wrote.

She found that ACSO also failed to adopt written policies that aligned with Keep Washington Working requirements. The AG's office issued guidance to law enforcement agencies on the kind of policies they should adopt.

"Defendant decided to adopt the AGO's KWW guidance but instead continued to use and rely on policies that predated KWW's enactment," Polin wrote.

Wagner said he issued verbal orders that ACSO was to stop sharing the in-custody lists with federal authorities, and Polin ruled that was insufficient.

The county will be required to revise its policies and train staff in the revised policies, Polin ruled.

text:
Two members of the Orange County Sheriff's Department have been placed on leave during an investigation into their actions when a man visiting his son on Halloween at the county jail was taken into custody by federal agents.

The deputy and Orange County Sheriff’s Special Officer were placed on leave during an investigation into whether they violated department policy and a state law that limits how local and state law enforcement agents can assist in federal immigration enforcement, such as ICE operations. SSOs typical handle security duties at county buildings, courthouses and correctional facilities.

Family members identified the father detained by the masked federal agents in protective vests labeled "Police ICE" as 69-year-old Jesús Esparza. His daughter Adriana Esparza told Telemundo 52 earlier this month that her father, who works in construction, has no criminal record and has lived in the United States since 2000. She said he was taken into custody as he left the jail.

New video of the Halloween incident outside Men’s Central Jail was released Friday. The video was obtained by NBCLA after filing a public records request.

The video shows ICE agents parked outside the jail in an unmarked black SUV. Two sheriff's department members can be seen on the sidewalk appearing to speak with someone inside the SUV.

"The department identified a Deputy and Sheriff’s Special Officer (SSO) exiting the Intake Release Center, approaching the black SUV, and appearing to have a five second conversation with the people in the vehicle. Shortly after the Deputy and SSO left, a second vehicle arrived," the department said in a statement. "ICE agents exited both vehicles and entered the public courtyard outside the visitor’s entrance. The ICE agents contacted and arrested a man who appeared to be hiding in the public courtyard."

Both members were placed on administrative leave during the investigation involving the video, which also showed federal agents placing a man in custody inside the SUV.

In a statement Friday, the department said it received a complaint Nov. 3 OC Sheriff's "personnel may have communicated with ICE agents." The department immediately began an internal investigation, the agency said.

In its statement, the department said local law enforcement may communication with ICE to release criminal offenders form custody facilities under "very limited circumstances."

"Securing the border and enforcing immigration law are important federal responsibilities," Orange County Sheriff Don Barnes said in the statement. "The Orange County Sheriff’s Department does not enforce federal immigration law. That has not and will not change.

"I will fully cooperate with ICE to the extent the law allows to prevent serious criminal offenders from returning to the communities they have preyed upon. Personnel acting outside the law and Department policy will be held appropriately accountable. We will enforce state and local laws equally, without bias, and without concern for anyone’s citizenship. I want the community to continue to feel safe in calling for assistance, reporting crime, and visiting the jail regardless of their immigration status.”

Orange County Supervisor Vicente Sarmiento, in a Nov. 2 letter to Barnes, expressed concerns about the detention and presence of federal agents outside the jail and whether the department was in violation of the SB54, also known as the California Values Act. Effective since January 2018, the act limits the use of state and local resources for federal immigration enforcement purposes.

Barnes issued a response, denying any cooperation that violates state law.

Family members said Esparza is being held by federal authorities at the Otay Mesa Detention Center.

Telemundo 52 reached out to ICE for details about why Esparza was taken into custody.

Family members said they are concerned Esparza could be deported to Mexico after more than two decades of living in the United States.

description:
That record high is being touted by the Trump administration, which has said it aims to deport one million immigrants annually.
For more on these numbers, we turn to John Sandweg, who served as acting ICE director under President Obama.

text:
Amna Nawaz:

The Supreme Court said today it would hear the Trump administration's ban on asylum claims at the southern border. President Trump enacted the ban the first day of his second term, and a lower court judge has since ruled the policy is illegal.

This comes as the Department of Homeland Security reports immigrant deportations and arrests hit an all-time high.

William Brangham has the latest.

William Brangham:

Amna, more than 491,000 people were arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials in the last fiscal year, and more than 483,000 of those people were deported. That record high is being touted by the Trump administration, which has said it aims to deport one million immigrants annually.

For more on these numbers, we turn to John Sandweg, who served as acting ICE director under President Obama.

John, very nice to have you back on the program.

This new set of numbers is a record high for ICE deportations and arrests, breaking last year's record. What do you make of these numbers?

John Sandweg:

Yes, it's a truly remarkable number, William.

You have to remember historically a significant portion of ICE's deportations actually came from the border. So these were individuals that were not arrested by ICE agents, but rather Border Patrol agents handed over to ICE, and then ICE executes the removal.

Typically, the reason that's significant is those individuals can be deported much more quickly. And if you look back in 2012, the prior -- the original record during the Obama administration of 410,000 removals, over about 250,000 of those individuals were actually those apprehended at the border.

So what it highlights for me is just the remarkable way in which the Trump administration has really wrangled the immigration enforcement system to move at a pace like we have never seen before, expediting -- not only increasing the number of arrests, but expediting the processing of those individuals on the back end and then removing them from the country.

William Brangham:

And the administration argues it's only halfway there. It would like to notch up to a million deportations. Does our system have that capacity to do that?

John Sandweg:

You know, look, the administration's put a lot of resources in increasing the size of ICE. And what that does is certainly increase the number of individuals that could be apprehended annually. But their biggest challenge is on the back end, which is the immigration courts.

The majority of the immigrants that are in the interior of the United States -- at the border, there are ways to administratively what's called expedite a removal. If you have -- catch someone as they enter the United States, you can quickly serve them a deportation order without seeing an immigration judge.

But for the population in the interior, where most of this work is now focused, most of these individuals are required to see an immigration judge. We have not seen significant -- we have seen the Trump administration put a lot of pressure on those courts to expedite cases, but we haven't seen them put significant resources in there.

Unless and until we see a real expansion of the immigration courts so that these new handpicked judges by the Trump administration can issue those deportation orders more quickly, it's really hard to see -- even with all these new ICE resources coming online, really hard to see them getting up to a million deportations in a year.

William Brangham:

So, as you well know, ICE's actions on the interior have caused a great deal of blowback. We have seen children being arrested. We have seen U.S. citizens being arrested. Of course, several Americans were killed.

There was a great deal of pushback against the administration. We saw some of that reflected in the midterm elections. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin was asked about whether or not he had been told by the administration to dial that back recently. Here's what he had to say.

Laura Ingraham, FOX News Anchor:

And my question to you tonight is, have you been given instructions to lighten up on enforcement?

Markwayne Mullin, U.S. Homeland Security Secretary:

Not at all. Not at all.

Laura Ingraham:

Not at all?

Markwayne Mullin:

Not at all. We have changed our priorities from doing -- from doing, let's say, job site raids to doing warrant raids, meaning that we go into cities and we go after the worst of the worst.

William Brangham:

Worst of the worst, that's what you hear from the administration constantly. Are these types of raids the best way to try and capture and remove the hardened criminals in this country?

John Sandweg:

Yes, unfortunately not.

As you look at this data today, right, what you're seeing is it's really not about the worst of the worst. The problem, the challenge that the secretary faces, and the contradiction in what he says is that, in immigration enforcement, if you're trying to drive up the total number of deportations, trying to hit a high number like this administration is trying to do, it pushes ICE to focus on more on those noncriminal populations.

There are a couple of reasons for this. The first is that generally that population is easier to find. The hardened criminals are more adept at hiding, and they make it harder on the agents to track them down. It requires a lot more work just to make that one apprehension.

But the second problem is that, because of those due process issues I mentioned a moment ago and these backlogs in the immigration court, it pushes the ICE agents to focus on populations not based on whether or not you have a criminal history, but whether or not on -- or on how quickly ICE can actually deport you after they arrest you.

And so what you're seeing, a lot of what we're seeing the ICE do today, through these tactics and through some of their targeted operations, is focusing on populations that are quick, easy to deport, because either, A, let's say they were previously ordered to deport five, six years ago, but ICE gave them a stay, allowed them to stay in the country for humanitarian circumstances, or just people who didn't leave the country, but were not detained when they went through the court process.

In either of those cases, typically, those populations tend to be the more sympathetic populations, right, the populations that lived here longer, that don't have a criminal history. And so that's the juxtaposition's position. As they feel this pressure to ramp up the number of arrests, the only way to do that is not by focusing on the worst of the worst, but on the rest of the population, which is just easier to remove.

William Brangham:

All right, that is former Acting Director of ICE John Sandweg.

Always great to hear from you. Thank you.

John Sandweg:

Thank you so much.

text:
Orange County Sheriff Don Barnes has launched an investigation into his own department amid reports that a deputy and a sheriff’s special officer improperly cooperated with ICE outside a county jail, something that’s strictly limited under California law.

The probe comes after local immigration advocates last month warned of a 45-day ICE surge ramping across Southern California with Anaheim officials reporting potential activity in Garden Grove, Orange and Costa Mesa early Friday morning.

“Along with our region, Anaheim is seeing increased federal immigration enforcement activity since early October. We urge a high level of awareness for those concerned,” reads Anaheim’s immigration update page.

Surveillance video from the sheriff’s department on Halloween showed ICE agents parked on a public street outside the county jail who were met by a deputy exiting the county jail and having a brief conversation, according to a Friday news release from the sheriff’s department.

“The department identified a Deputy and Sheriff’s Special Officer (SSO) exiting the Intake Release Center, approaching the black SUV, and appearing to have a five second conversation with the people in the vehicle,” reads the release.

“Shortly after the Deputy and SSO left, a second vehicle arrived. ICE agents exited both vehicles and entered the public courtyard outside the visitor’s entrance. The ICE agents contacted and arrested a man who appeared to be hiding in the public courtyard.”

At least two employees have already been placed on administrative leave according to Barnes’ news release.

While the sheriff’s department is barred from transferring prisoners directly to immigration authorities under California law, sheriffs can notify them when prisoners with immigration holds who’ve been convicted of a serious felony are released so that federal officers can pick them up outside the jail.

Last year, the sheriff’s department notified ICE of over 300 prisoners being released, and they were taken into ICE’s custody 271 times.

While Barnes has repeatedly spoken out about concerns over the state Sanctuary Laws, claiming it leads to more immigration raids in neighborhoods to compensate for the lack of coordination between law enforcement agencies, he’s also said he will abide by those laws.

“I will fully cooperate with ICE to the extent the law allows to prevent serious criminal offenders from returning to the communities they have preyed upon. Personnel acting outside the law and Department policy will be held appropriately accountable,” Barnes wrote in a Friday statement.

“We will enforce state and local laws equally, without bias, and without concern for anyone’s citizenship,” he continued. “I want the community to continue to feel safe in calling for assistance, reporting crime, and visiting the jail regardless of their immigration status.”

The investigation also comes as police oversight commissioners in Santa Ana this week called for a probe into the arrest of two ICE observers outside of the city’s police headquarters while they were tracking ICE agents last month.

The arrest sparked scrutiny on how cooperative police in OC’s only Sanctuary City are with federal agents, with both the city’s subsequent own legal analysis and the county’s District Attorney’s office finding there was not enough evidence to charge the advocates with a crime.

“We are reviewing the circumstances surrounding the arrests, including the decision-making process, supervisory oversight, and the importance of protecting constitutional rights,” Santa Ana Police Chief Robert Rodriguez said in an email Friday.

“We have a responsibility to examine our actions and acknowledge opportunities for improvement. That is what we intend to do.”

text:
Federal

Republicans Elect Jim Jordan as House Leader, Retain John Thune in Senate

On November 10, House Republicans elected Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) to lead their conference in the next Congress, defeating current Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-Louisiana) in a 106–73 secret-ballot vote. Jordan will succeed Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana), who did not seek the position. Senate Republicans reelected Sen. John Thune (R-South Dakota) without opposition. Both will serve as minority leaders beginning in January 2027, following Democrats’ election victories in both chambers.

Jordan currently chairs the House Judiciary Committee and has also served on the House Oversight Committee. The elections selected party leaders, not committee chairs or ranking members; the reports did not identify who will succeed Jordan as the Judiciary Committee’s top Republican. Those separate committee selections will help determine which lawmakers lead immigration-related legislative work and oversight in the new Congress.

Secretary Mullin Signals Openness to Permanent Legal Status for DACA Recipients

On November 9, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said he was open to discussing legislation that would provide permanent legal status for recipients of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA). DACA currently provides eligible immigrants who arrived as children temporary protection from deportation and renewable work authorization, but not permanent residence or a direct path to citizenship. Mullin said President Trump had encouraged him to engage with Democrats who had contacted him about immigration legislation, but emphasized that the administration remained opposed to what he called “amnesty” and had not discussed changing its enforcement policies. He said any permanent status for DACA recipients would be up to Congress and offered no details on eligibility, timing or a potential pathway to citizenship.

The comments followed President Trump’s November 8 CBS interview in which he said his deportation policy “might be too tough” and may have contributed to Republican losses in the midterm elections. Trump also expressed interest in reaching an immigration agreement with the incoming Democratic congressional majorities, without outlining a specific proposal.

Reports Raise Concerns About ICE Recruit Vetting During Hiring Expansion

A November 10 investigation identified at least 19 Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) recruits hired despite records of past misconduct or criminality. The review examined records exposed in a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) data breach and identified former police officers whose histories included a fatal shooting and dismissal over concerns about on-duty behavior. The findings follow a September report detailing a whistleblower complaint alleging that some applicants received job offers before completing basic fingerprint, identity or credit checks. The official’s allegations have become part of an ongoing DHS inspector general audit of vetting practices.

ICE has also begun dismissing some employees hired during its expansion, which brought approximately 12,000 recruits into the agency. Former DHS officials said some dismissals involved performance problems or background issues they believed should have been identified before hiring. An ICE spokesperson described the personnel decisions as routine and said the agency removes employees who do not meet its standards. The agency also said applicants may begin training on temporary status while full background investigations remain pending and that its Office of Professional Responsibility evaluates applicants’ information under established vetting requirements.

Legal

Supreme Court Allows Border Wall Construction to Continue in West Texas

On November 9, the Supreme Court paused a lower court injunction blocking border barrier construction in West Texas’s Big Bend region, allowing work to resume while litigation continues. The unsigned decision said the government was “exceedingly likely to prevail” on its argument that the district court lacked authority to consider the plaintiffs’ challenge to the Department of Homeland Security’s environmental and conservation law waivers. The court declined to immediately reverse the lower court’s ruling, leaving the underlying dispute unresolved.

The lawsuit, brought by an environmental organization, a church preservation group and a local landowner, challenges the administration’s authority to waive legal requirements for the project. Plaintiffs cite potential damage to property, ecosystems and cultural sites, while the administration argues that additional barriers are necessary to prevent crossings from shifting into the region as construction proceeds elsewhere. According to the government’s court filing, plans include 30-foot steel barriers on private property and patrol roads, vehicle barriers and other infrastructure in park areas, but not border walls within Big Bend National Park or Big Bend Ranch State Park.

State and Local

ICE Agents Block Hospital Ambulance Entrance, Drawing Protests in Los Angeles

Federal immigration agents blocked the ambulance entrance at Adventist Health White Memorial Medical Center in Los Angeles’s Boyle Heights neighborhood overnight November 6–7, prompting the hospital to divert ambulances to nearby facilities for approximately two hours, according to a hospital spokesperson. Agents had brought a person in their custody to the emergency department for treatment. Hospital officials said they neither requested nor authorized the obstruction. Hospital President Daniel Fontoura said staff also denied a request for agents to remain present during a physician-patient consultation and contacted the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) when access for emergency vehicles was blocked.

Community members and local officials gathered outside the hospital to protest and seek an explanation from hospital leadership. LAPD said its officers responded to maintain public safety and did not assist with immigration enforcement. Immigration and Customs Enforcement declined to discuss the operation, citing operational security, and said it does not target hospitals. Hospital leadership said the facility does not participate in immigration enforcement and provides care regardless of immigration status.

Detention of University of Maryland Student and Mother Draws Community Support

A University of Maryland freshman and her mother were detained during a scheduled immigration check-in in Baltimore in early November, according to the student’s boyfriend, Cesar Saavedra. The student, Maria Flores Garcia, came to the United States from El Salvador as a child and graduated as valedictorian of Parkdale High School in Prince George’s County in 2026. She now studies public health at the university on a scholarship. Saavedra said both women were subsequently held in Louisiana and launched a fundraiser to help them obtain an immigration attorney.

Local leaders have called for the women’s release, and the university said it was working to provide resources where possible and appropriate. The Department of Homeland Security said Flores Garcia was placed in removal proceedings after being apprehended in December 2016 and received a final removal order in February 2021. The department said she would remain in immigration detention pending deportation.

The U.S. Senate is scheduled to be in session from Monday, November 16, through Friday, November 20. The U.S. House is scheduled to be in session from Tuesday, November 17, through Friday, November 20.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Justice Department has functioned for nearly two years as an extension of the White House, unchecked by a Republican-controlled Congress as it pursued investigations into President Donald Trump's enemies, fired waves of career employees and defended administration stances that judges across the country repeatedly deemed legally dubious.

Now, sweeping Democratic gains in Congress have shifted the balance of power in Washington, teeing up an onslaught of expected investigations into those actions and others as well as scrutiny from the majority party that the current Justice Department had until now managed to skirt.

The department has, at least publicly, appeared unbowed by the altered landscape.

Attorney General Todd Blanche says the department will cooperate with Congress but has also insisted that "we will not back down" from the Republican president's agenda. Meanwhile, a top aide told prosecutors on a call to prepare to be on "wartime" footing and a U.S. attorney publicly warned a top Democrat about planned congressional investigations.

It sets the stage for a pugilistic dynamic as Democrats promise to join already-skeptical courts in reining in the Trump administration while a Justice Department depleted by the losses of thousands of career employees and the postelection departures of senior leaders pledges to push ahead with its agenda.

A call for a 'wartime' footing

Even though Democrats hold the gavel, they're short on foolproof ways to guarantee Republican cooperation. Lawsuits can take years, subpoenas can be arduous to enforce and criminal contempt referrals for noncompliance would be sent to the Trump administration Justice Department, where they will almost certainly not be acted on.

"It's a standoff and I don't know what the answer to that is yet," said Stan Brand, a former general counsel for the House of Representatives. "I don't know if the Congress knows."

Nonetheless, Democrats are eager to highlight what they view as abuses of power, including a succession of investigations the department has launched into the president's perceived adversaries, many of which have been rejected by grand juries, dismissed by judges or have otherwise stalled without apparent progress.

WATCH: Rep. Garcia says voters gave Democrats a mandate to pursue accountability

In just the eventful weeks leading up to the election, the department unsuccessfully sought an indictment against former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson, accelerated an investigation into Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar, employed an unusual maneuver to file a fresh criminal case against former FBI Director James Comey and charged two ex-FBI officials in a complaint that was swiftly dismissed by a judge.

Political pressure from the White House is unlikely to wane given the promotion of Stephen Miller, a devoted Trump loyalist, to chief of staff.

And Justice Department leadership has suggested it won't let Democrats' threats of investigations deter its pursuit of the White House's priorities, and may become even more aggressive in pressing the president's causes.

WATCH: White House threatens Democrats over plans to investigate Trump officials

"We will not back down. This will not slow us down. This will not stop us," Blanche said in a Fox News interview Monday. "President Trump has two years remaining in this administration and you better believe that we're going to use it effectively."

In a call with U.S. attorneys across the country this week, a top Blanche aide, Aakash Singh, told prosecutors to prepare to be on a "wartime" footing, and suggested more U.S. attorneys may be pushed out after a spate of postelection departures, according to people familiar with the call who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal department discussions.

The Justice Department said the "'wartime' reference had everything to do with public safety," noting that some "newly elected state and local leaders are no longer interested in partnering with federal law enforcement."

Any additional U.S. attorney departures would be on top of a string of significant departures in the days after the election, when the Senate-confirmed leaders of the department's National Security, Civil and Civil Rights divisions all announced their resignations. The divisions will have temporary leaders but are unlikely to get Senate-confirmed ones in light of the Democratic majority.

"What that means for DOJ, potentially, is just a lot of inaction, with tough decisions not being made because typically those tough decisions are made by confirmed people at the top of the components," said Greg Brower, a former U.S. attorney in Nevada during President George W. Bush's administration who was later the FBI's chief congressional affairs official.

The department said in a statement that it has "full confidence in the leaders stepping in to guide our Divisions, and its mission is unchanged: enforce the law, combat crime, and protect the American people."

Early rhetorical clashes between lawmakers and the department

To be sure, tensions between the Justice Department and Congress of an opposing party are a staple of oversight dating back decades and across administrations.

The Republican-led House voted in 2012 to hold then-Attorney General Eric Holder in contempt of Congress. Democrats did the same in 2019 when William Barr led the Justice Department. There were even interparty clashes during the first Trump administration.

But the situation now is unlike anything the current department has experienced.

As the minority party in both the House and Senate, Democrats decried during hearings and in letters what they saw as the department's erosion of independence but had little power to demand accountability.

On the rare occasion when the department did appear fazed by congressional oversight, it was generally because of Republican resistance, including over the handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files or an ultimately abandoned fund to compensate Trump allies.

READ MORE: Read the letter the White House's top lawyer sent Rep. Garcia over threats to investigate Trump

The Democrats' planned inquiries have already invited opposition from Republicans and the White House, with Trump accusing Democrats of "extortion" and ordering the attorney general to conduct an investigation.

The White House has issued a warning on expected investigations, asserting in a letter from counsel Will Scharf that such inquiries — a routine function of Congress — may amount to "blatant criminality." Members of Congress enjoy broad legal protections for acts they take as lawmakers under a constitutional principle known as "speech and debate."

"My first-year law students would fail if they wrote a letter like that," Brand said.

Additionally, the top federal prosecutor in Houston sent a warning letter to Sen. Richard Blumenthal over the Connecticut Democrat's inquiry into funding for Trump's White House ballroom. In the letter, U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz ordered Blumenthal to preserve all records relevant to his inquiry, and accused the senator of intimidating "citizens for engaging in philanthropic practices that will benefit our nation for generations."

Blumenthal responded that he would not be intimidated.

Blanche told reporters Thursday that there were no open investigations into Democrats' rhetoric and acknowledged that it's not a crime to warn of looming investigations. But he again expressed concern over what he described as threats against the administration.

Leah Foley, the U.S. attorney for Massachusetts, said in an interview with The Associated Press that the message from Washington was for prosecutors to continue their aggressive focus on the administration's priorities of tackling fraud, violent crime, drug trafficking and cartels.

"I've been through so many administrations as a prosecutor," said Foley, who co-chairs a committee that advises the attorney general on policies and priorities. "This is a lot of noise that's coming out of the elections and posturing going on. But things are going to settle down and we've operated proficiently through divided governments before and we'll continue to do so."

text:
A judge ruled on Friday Adams County has violated state law by collaborating with federal immigration enforcement.

The state’s Keep Washington Working Act , passed in 2019, prohibits local law enforcement from asking people about their immigration status or holding them for immigration agents.

“Today’s ruling allows our state to continue building trust and confidence between law enforcement and immigrant communities as the federal administration undermines those efforts with its draconian policies,” Attorney General Nick Brown wrote in a statement announcing the outcome of the lawsuit.

A majority of people locked up by immigration enforcement have no criminal record. Amid concerns of racial profiling by law enforcement, many U.S. citizens now carry passports in their daily lives. Many immigrant communities, throughout Washington State and across the spectrum of legal status, have strained relationships with local law enforcement.

“This is not about politics, race, or immigration status,” wrote Adams County Sheriff Dale Wager in a press statement acknowledging the legal blow, “It is about public safety, accountability, and the ability of law enforcement agencies to work together to protect the communities we serve.”

The start of the lawsuit

The AG’s office initially launched the lawsuit back in 2025, after a man in the country without legal status was booked by Adams County on criminal charges that were later dropped. Instead of releasing the man, local law enforcement officials placed him on a call with federal immigration enforcement, and later took the man to the agents. The man was then arrested and taken to the Northwest ICE Processing Center. He was later released, and is pursuing legal status.

Spokane County Superior Court Judge Marla L. Polin found that those actions, and others, were in violation of the state's Keep Washington Working Act. Other violations, according to the lawsuit, included sending daily custody lists to federal immigration authorities, failing to adopt the state's guidance and failing to address yearslong complaints sent to Adams County from the AG's office.

In 2022, the AG’s office sent a letter to Adams County Sheriff Wagner and Prosecuting Attorney Randy Flyckt, raising concerns about their cooperation with federal immigration agencies.

According to the letter, county officials aided Immigration and Customs Enforcement more than 200 times between May 2019, when the Keep Washington Working Act took effect, and December 2021.

Since then, the Attorney General’s Office began meeting with Adams County to address those concerns.

“Over the course of almost two years, they did those meetings, said they were changing policy, said they were acting consistent with state law, and then, in fact, were not,” Brown said back in 2025. “[They] never once claimed that what they were being asked to do somehow violated federal law.”

Sheriff’s legal defense has ties to national group

Sheriff Wagner and others were represented by special deputy Attorney Joel Ard. Ard is with the Ard Law Group and backed by America First Legal, a law firm founded by Stephen Miller, current chief of staff of President Donald Trump. Miller is an architect behind the president’s mass deportation efforts. During enforcement actions, U.S citizens and immigrants have been killed. Thousands of unlawful detainment lawsuits have been filed, overwhelming courts.

Wagner said he plans to appeal the judge’s ruling.

“I respect the judicial process, but respecting that process does not mean we must agree with every ruling,” Wagner wrote.

“Our States continued pursuit of these policies represents, in my view, a misguided political agenda that puts ideology ahead of common sense and public safety. I believe these restrictions make Adams County and Washington state less safe.”

The lawsuit requires Adams County to fall into compliance with the Keep Washington Working Act.

title: CBP is Detaining Children Incommunicado in Windowless Cells
description:
Customs and Border Protection facilities are barren, brutal and meant only for brief processing, but CBP is holding families incommunicado for weeks.
Now, children from countries where they were persecuted or to which they cannot return are locked in CBP detention, sometimes for over a month.
Most months, over 150 children spend more than three days locked in a CBP cell, and some of those children spend over 25 days without seeing the sun.
Children are detained in large cement cells whose only window faces in, towards the guards monitoring their movements.
Because the cells are windowless, children don’t know if it is day or night.
text:
Customs and Border Protection facilities are barren, brutal and meant only for brief processing, but CBP is holding families incommunicado for weeks.

Today, Flores counsel filed a Motion for Clarification, asking the Court to confirm that children in immigration detention have a right to call a lawyer to report violations of the Flores Settlement Agreement, which has protected the rights of children detained by the U.S. government for decades.

Customs and Border Protection (CBP) operates hundreds of immigration detention facilities across the country, primarily along the border meant for people who turn themselves in or are encountered just after crossing the border. These facilities are intended only for very brief stays, just enough time for CBP to process the person and determine the next steps in their case. CBP’s own policies direct it to hold adults for no more than 72 hours.

As the administration implements sweeping restrictions on asylum, CBP has adopted a general policy against releasing recent arrivals, proudly announcing “zero Border Patrol releases” in fiscal year 2026. Now, children from countries where they were persecuted or to which they cannot return are locked in CBP detention, sometimes for over a month. Most months, over 150 children spend more than three days locked in a CBP cell, and some of those children spend over 25 days without seeing the sun.

CBP prisons are some of the most brutal prisons in the country. Children are detained in large cement cells whose only window faces in, towards the guards monitoring their movements. The cells are empty aside from a metal prison toilet, which is covered only by a chest-high partition on one side. Children must sleep on thin plastic mats on the cement floor, without a pillow, with nothing but a mylar blanket for warmth.

When one mother’s eight-year-old son had an allergic reaction to the material of the mats, she began to have him lie on top of her at night, using herself as a mattress while she lay awake, desperate to protect him. After a week detained, she explained, “We haven’t seen the sun. We haven’t been outside. The only thing my son has outside the cell is these thirty minutes [per day],” when guards permit him to sit just outside his cell inside another room in the prison and draw. “I beg him to eat but he won’t. If they ever give us anything he will eat, I take a tiny bite and give the rest to him.”

Many facilities leave blinding lights on 24 hours a day. Because the cells are windowless, children don’t know if it is day or night.

“In the morning, they bring us a burrito and that’s the way we learn that it is the morning,” explained the father of a 16-year-old girl who was detained for days in a cell alone. “My daughter is alone in her room. There is no one to speak to and there are no games, books, TV, nothing to do but sleep and think . . . she is completely alone.”

Although all interviews and telephonic judicial hearings, if the family gets a hearing at all, occur while the family remains detained, CBP officials often do not allow children to use a phone. One mother explained, “I want a lawyer [but] they didn’t let me have a phone call . . . All I want is to call my son . . . For eight days, my family has not known if we are alive.”

Further, CBP fails to provide children access to a phone if they wish to call Flores counsel and refuses to facilitate calls with class members when Flores counsel requests to schedule them. Flores counsel are responsible for helping children protect their rights under the Settlement, including their rights to safe, sanitary and humane conditions and quick processing for release from these restrictive, unlicensed facilities which are not intended for children. Without phone calls, children have no voice, and no way to advocate for themselves.

“We should not have to seek intervention of the Court to ensure that children can call their lawyers to ask for help when their rights are being violated,” said Sarah Kahn, Senior Staff Attorney at the Center for Human Rights and Constitutional Law. “Preventing a child from calling a lawyer is a clear indication that the people who run these horrific prisons and draconian systems understand what they’re doing. They know they are torturing children. They know they are denying them their rights to due process, protection and safety. And they don’t want the children to tell anyone.”

###

The Center for Human Rights and Constitutional Law (CHRCL) is a legal non-profit committed to protecting and advancing the rights of immigrants through legal action, advocacy, and education. Through impact litigation, we challenge unlawful immigration policies to drive systemic change and establish stronger legal protections for immigrants. At the local, state, and federal levels, we advocate for fair and humane policies that uphold the rights of all immigrants. For more information, please visit centerforhumanrights.org.

The National Center for Youth Law centers youth through research, community collaboration, impact litigation, and policy advocacy that fundamentally transforms our nation’s approach to education, health, immigration, foster care, and youth justice. Our vision is a world in which every child thrives and has a full and fair opportunity to achieve the future they envision for themselves. For more information, please visityouthlaw.org.

title: Supreme Court to Decide Whether Trump Can Block Asylum at Border - Law Commentary
description:
Under the policy, migrants caught crossing the border illegally can be deported without receiving an initial interview to determine whether they face persecution if returned to their home countries.
Federal immigration law generally allows people who arrive in the United States or are already present to apply for asylum, regardless of how they entered.
The Trump administration argues that the president's authority to suspend entry permits officials to reject asylum applications from migrants covered by the proclamation.
Federal officials have credited the restrictions with reducing unlawful border crossings and contend that lengthy asylum proceedings encourage additional migration.
The Supreme Court agreed to review two questions in Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services.
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court agreed Friday, November 13, 2026, to decide whether President Donald Trump can bar migrants from seeking asylum at the southern border under a proclamation declaring an invasion, taking up his administration's appeal of rulings that found the restrictions unlawful.

The case involves a policy Trump issued on January 20, 2025, hours after returning to the White House. Citing an invasion at the U.S.-Mexico border, the president suspended entry for certain migrants and directed immigration officials to deny them access to asylum and other protections while using expedited procedures to remove them from the country.

Under the policy, migrants caught crossing the border illegally can be deported without receiving an initial interview to determine whether they face persecution if returned to their home countries. The restrictions also extend to certain people arriving at official border crossings who lack required medical or criminal history information.

Federal immigration law generally allows people who arrive in the United States or are already present to apply for asylum, regardless of how they entered. The law requires immigration authorities to evaluate claims from people seeking protection based on persecution or a well-founded fear of persecution tied to their race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership in a particular social group.

The Trump administration argues that the president's authority to suspend entry permits officials to reject asylum applications from migrants covered by the proclamation. Federal officials have credited the restrictions with reducing unlawful border crossings and contend that lengthy asylum proceedings encourage additional migration.

Three immigrant-rights organizations and 13 individuals challenged the policy in February 2025, alleging that federal authorities were denying asylum seekers required screening interviews and exposing them to deportation without an opportunity to establish their eligibility for protection.

U.S. District Judge Randolph Moss ruled against the administration in July, finding that the proclamation exceeded presidential authority by replacing immigration procedures established by Congress. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit upheld the ruling in April 2026, concluding that the administration had unlawfully restricted access to asylum and created removal procedures outside the federal immigration system.

The appeals court allowed the asylum restrictions to remain in effect during further review, although protections against deportation to countries where migrants could face persecution or torture remain subject to separate legal requirements.

The Supreme Court agreed to review two questions in Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services. The justices will determine whether the proclamation and its enforcement procedures violate federal immigration law and whether federal judges can grant relief covering an entire class of migrants affected by the restrictions.

The asylum dispute joins other immigration cases on the Court's docket, including a challenge to the administration's policy of deporting migrants to countries other than their own. The justices are scheduled to hear arguments in that separate case on December 9.

text:
Three organizations that helped Eden Prairie residents during Operation Metro Surge earlier this year were among the recipients of the city’s 2026 Human Rights Awards.

Members of the Human Rights and Diversity Commission announced the winners at the Nov. 10 City Council meeting. PROP Food Shelf, Eden Prairie Schools and the Eden Prairie Community Response Network were recognized for their responses to increased immigration enforcement.

Operation Metro Surge was a federal immigration enforcement operation that began in Minnesota in December 2025, bringing thousands of federal agents to the state and disrupting daily life for students, businesses and immigrant families.

In a separate category, Eden Prairie High School student Finn Bidwell received the youth award for his Eagle Scout project.

Greg Leeper, chair of the Human Rights and Diversity Commission, presented PROP with the nonprofit award. PROP has served Eden Prairie and surrounding communities for more than 50 years, providing food assistance, housing stability, employment support and mental health services to those in need.

During Operation Metro Surge, PROP developed support systems for families, such as expanded food access through mobile distribution, curbside pickup, home delivery and proxy shopping. The organization also worked with community liaisons to reach families facing language and transportation barriers, while helping households recover from missed rent and utility payments.

Christy Nicolaisen, PROP’s executive director, said staff and volunteers were behind the organization’s accomplishments.

“You couldn’t do anything without the volunteers and the staff, and I’m just so proud to represent them,” she said.

Eden Prairie Schools was presented with the business award for its support of students and staff affected by Operation Metro Surge. The school district relied on cultural liaisons to help bridge cultural and language barriers and assist immigrant families.

District staff guided families through bureaucratic barriers, such as legal paperwork related to school enrollment and guardianship, while working with outside agencies to provide families with basic necessities.

Superintendent Josh Swanson commended district staff for jumping in to support families. He also thanked the city for its partnership with Eden Prairie Schools, which further helped families during Metro Surge.

“Our first core value is we believe each person has a true value,” Swanson said. “That’s how our staff operates every single day, and there’s a sampling of amazing people here who care for our kids and families.”

The commission honored the Eden Prairie Community Response Network with the individual award for its crisis response during Metro Surge. The organization included more than 400 Eden Prairie residents who delivered groceries, helped keep students safe at bus stops, provided translation services, donated essentials, supported local businesses and provided community education to raise awareness of the impacts of increased enforcement.

The Rev. Trish Vanni accepted the award on behalf of the network’s members, noting Minnesota’s “amplified sense of what the common good is.”

“It was the most amazing interfaith mobilization of people of goodwill who care deeply about each other, and so it’s an incredible honor to accept this award on behalf of all of those wonderful people, many of whom are still watching,” Vanni said.

Bidwell, an Eden Prairie High School student and Eagle Scout with Troop 479, received the youth award for his Eagle Scout project, which raised funds and built an outdoor storage shed for St. Andrew Lutheran Church.

The Human Rights and Diversity Commission awarded Bidwell for his commitment to contributing his time and abilities to make a positive difference in the community.

New York, November 13, 2026—The Committee to Protect Journalists calls on U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement authorities to immediately and unconditionally release Afghan journalist Shaban Ali Rafat and grant him full access to a hearing on the merits of his asylum claim. CPJ warns that deporting Rafat to Afghanistan would expose him to significant risks of persecution and retaliation by the Taliban.

Rafat has been in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody in California since January 21, 2025, when he attempted to enter the United States to seek asylum, and now faces deportation to Afghanistan, according to his attorney David Tarr.

“Rafat fled Afghanistan because the Taliban made it impossible for him to work as a journalist without risking his life. Deporting him now would deliver him directly into the hands of the very persecutors he escaped,” said CPJ Americas regional program director Jose Zamora. “His prolonged detention is a betrayal of the United States’ commitments to press freedom and human rights. U.S. authorities must release Rafat and provide him with asylum.”

Before the Taliban takeover of Afghanistan in August 2021, Rafat worked as a producer and reporter for state-owned Maaref TV and served as a senior media officer at Kabul University, where he extensively covered the 2020 terrorist attack on the university and the plight of the Hazara community — a persecuted ethnic and religious minority of which he is a member.

Afghanistan’s Hazara community has faced escalating persecution and violence since the Taliban’s return to power in August 2021. In 2026 alone, the Taliban shut down three Hazara media outlets, and detained their senior managers in an effort to suppress the community’s media outlets and journalists in Afghanistan.

CPJ’s emails to Department of Homeland Security and ICE representatives seeking an update on the status of Rafat’s asylum claim did not receive an immediate reply.

description:
Shortly after, the 2028 presidential race will begin to kick into gear.
The cost of living was a clear motivating factor for voters in the 2026 midterms.
How should the next Republican presidential candidate approach governing?
Democratic 2028 field is open.

text:
The 2026 midterm elections have (for the most part) come to a close.

In the coming months, attention will shift to the inauguration of the newly Democratic-controlled Congress. Shortly after, the 2028 presidential race will begin to kick into gear.

Below are five charts on what Americans expect from the next Congress and an early look at the trends and names to watch in the 2028 presidential race.

1. For the next Congress, the top priority is clear. The cost of living was a clear motivating factor for voters in the 2026 midterms. Across partisan lines, it remains the top issue that Americans want the next Congress to address, more so than issues like AI regulation, immigration reform, or investigating the Trump administration.

2. Hopes and fears for the next Congress. Majorities of Americans want Trump and Democratic leaders to work together – but are concerned Congress might get caught up in investigating Trump or that Trump will take action without the support of Congress. Trump will govern with a Democratic Congress for the first time in his White House tenure, meaning we may see a new power dynamic between the two branches of government. Watch this space.

3. A crucial question to answer for Republicans. How should the next Republican presidential candidate approach governing? Republicans right now are divided between following in the footsteps of Trump or taking a new direction. MAGA Republicans, unsurprisingly, are more likely to prefer the former. Trump’s successor would likely have to balance the desires of both factions.

4. Republican 2028 field has clear frontrunners. On the Republican side, frontrunners such as JD Vance, Marco Rubio, and Ron DeSantis are well known and thought of as good candidates among Republicans. That’s not to say an outsider couldn’t emerge. But they would face an uphill battle to get there.

5. Democratic 2028 field is open. Among the Democratic base, no potential presidential candidate is both widely well-known and widely thought of as a great candidate. Figures like Kamala Harris, Gavin Newsom, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have widespread name recognition among Democrats but are not widely seen as strong candidates. Conversely, figures like Pete Buttigieg, Jon Ossoff, and Mark Kelly are not as well-known, but are seen as strong candidates among those that do know them. Can someone rise to the occasion? Or will a new figure emerge from the mist?

Based on what we know about presidential approval and the main issue, if the 2028 election were held today, the political environment would likely be unfavorable for a Republican candidate. But if the past two years prove anything, it’s that two years is more than enough time for the political environment to turn upside down.

Critical questions to watch going forward: Over the next two years, who gets blamed if the cost of living doesn’t improve? Or, who gets credit if the cost of living improves? Will the war in Iran end? If so, how quickly can Republicans recover if gas prices go down? Economic issues are the country’s top concern right now. But will another issue – perhaps AI – take over as the defining issue of 2028?

GAINESVILLE, Fla. (WCJB) — A 23-year-old University of Florida College of Engineering student is being held in an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility in Georgia, and his family and fellow students are sharing his story as they seek his release.

Juan Sanchez, known to his family as “Juandi,” is a senior at UF and was one semester away from completing his degree in chemical engineering. His family told TV20 he wants to return home to Gainesville and finish his studies.

ICE arrested Sanchez on Nov. 3 as he was traveling through Atlanta for a job interview with Nestlé and was waiting for a flight to Gainesville, according to the family.

TELEMUNDO GAINESVILLE: Estudiante de la Universidad de Florida permanece detenido por ICE en Georgia

Shawn, Sanchez’s stepfather, spoke to TV20 on behalf of the family. Shawn said ICE officers approached Sanchez and asked whether his name was Juan Sanchez.

“He of course affirmed that. And they immediately put him in handcuffs and took him into custody,” Shawn said. “They didn’t explain to him what was going on.”

Sanchez entered the United States from Ecuador on a tourist visa, along with his mother and sister. The visa has expired. At the time of his arrest, Sanchez had a pending asylum petition and a valid employment authorization through 2030.

“This isn’t to attack our government,” Shawn said. “The rules are there. And Juandi was following the rules as he was given.”

Shawn said Sanchez called his mother from custody around 8 p.m.

“She was just crying,” Shawn said. “She hung up the phone and immediately her knees hit the ground, and she didn’t want to talk for whatever it was, 20 to 30 minutes.”

As of this report, Sanchez remains at the Stewart Detention Center in Lumpkin, Ga. His bond hearing is set for Friday, Nov. 20.

His family and fellow UF students in Gainesville are working to secure his release.

On Thursday, students rallied to seek justice for Sanchez. The family is hopeful and wants Sanchez back. A gofundme has been created to help the family cover the cost of attorneys and court proceedings.
