text:
Immigration was top of mind for some voters during the 2026 midterms — a priority reflected in a flurry of activity across many state legislatures throughout the 2026 sessions. It is poised to remain a key issue as lawmakers look ahead to 2027 sessions and navigate changing political landscapes.

With most states having concluded their 2026 sessions, the American Immigration Council tracked more than 190 immigrant-related state bills that passed in 40 state legislatures nationwide. Here is our analysis of legislative trends from this year and what it means for 2027.

See how all 50 states score on immigration-related policies in our new States Index interactive tool.

Immigrant support and protection

In response to unprecedented levels of federal immigration enforcement, lawmakers passed innovative measures to protect immigrant communities, further expanding their role in immigration policy and their influence on immigrants’ daily lives. Across the political spectrum, states also continued to build on proven policies that address immigrant workforce integration and well-being.

Enforcement: Across 30 states, legislatures passed 140 bills that seek to support and safeguard immigrant communities. This includes 39 bills related to immigration enforcement, such as limiting coordination with federal immigration enforcement, prohibiting 287(g) agreements, and protecting sensitive locations, such as schools and healthcare facilities.

Detention: Responding to the historic expansion of immigration detention under the second Trump administration, legislatures also focused on reducing states’ roles in civil immigration detention. These included exploring oversight mechanisms for detention facilities, prohibiting public bodies from entering or remaining in agreements to detain individuals for civil immigration violations, and prohibiting the approval of construction or operation of buildings for private immigration detention use. California passed a first-in-the-nation tax on private immigration detention companies.

Data Privacy: As the federal government expanded its use of federal, state, and local data for immigration enforcement, states passed policies to better safeguard state-held immigrant data. Several states passed bills to curtail the collection of immigration- and citizenship-related data by government entities, limit the disclosure of certain identifiable data to third parties, like data brokers, and restrict the use of automated license plate reader data in immigration enforcement.

Services and Benefits: States also prioritized immigrants’ well-being by passing policies that expand language access, including for civic engagement, and responding to federal cuts to certain noncitizens’ access to health care and food benefits, like those enacted through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Enacted policies ranged from efforts to protect individuals affected by federal benefits cuts to expanding state-funded food assistance and increasing access to health coverage for qualified noncitizens.

Workforce: Legislators on both sides of the aisle continued to prioritize access to workforce opportunities, especially in occupational and professional licensure pathways. Twelve states — including six with Republican governors and six with Democratic governors — passed 13 workforce policies related to integrating foreign-trained individuals into the workforce. Most of these policies created more opportunities for foreign-trained physicians to demonstrate that their skills meet U.S. standards and qualify for a license to practice. Other policies expanded occupational and professional licensure to qualified DACA recipients and foreign-trained dentists.

Restrictive state policies

Alternatively, several states prioritized policies that aligned with the Trump administration’s mass immigration enforcement agenda or anti-immigrant rhetoric.

Noncitizen Voting and Benefit Access: Eight states passed 11 policies restricting noncitizen voting, despite its prevalence being miniscule. Some focused on stricter citizenship verification requirements through the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) program, while others increased documentary proof of citizenship for voter registration.

Seven states also passed nine policies that require stricter immigration status checks for people seeking public benefits and assistance, often reiterating that undocumented immigrants are ineligible for certain benefits—something the federal law already restricts. Enacted policies include requirements to verify citizenship and immigration status through SAVE when determining eligibility for public assistance and for state and local entities to report individuals unlawfully present in the United States who receive public benefits to a state immigration division or federal officials.

State Support for Immigration Enforcement: Five states enacted legislation to strengthen state and local coordination with federal immigration enforcement.

In Tennessee, three new laws collectively mandated that sheriff’s departments enter into 287(g) agreements and honor immigration detainers, and that state courts cooperate with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and immigration authorities enforcing federal immigration laws, with judges risking removal for obstructing DHS operations. In Mississippi, the state Department of Public Safety and county law enforcement agencies operating detention facilities must now make “reasonable attempts” to enter 287(g) agreements. The Mississippi legislature also prohibited state and local entities from enacting policies that limit federal immigration enforcement.

Meanwhile, Kansas expanded legal protections for cooperating with federal immigration enforcement and made it easier for local law enforcement agencies to enter into 287(g) agreements.

Other enacted policies include restrictions on access to identification cards, including commercial driver’s licenses, increasing state penalties for individuals with a valid order of removal who fail or refuse to depart, and limiting certain noncitizens’ access to pretrial release.

WASHINGTON (OSV News) — The U.S. Supreme Court said Nov. 13 it would take up a case regarding President Donald Trump’s executive order banning asylum claims at the southern border.

A federal judge previously ruled that the policy, enacted by Trump on the first day of his second term, was unlawful, but it has remained in effect amid ongoing litigation.

The Trump administration asked the high court to overturn the lower court ruling.

James Percival, general counsel for the Department of Homeland Security, said in a post on X, “The single most important factor in the President’s success at the border has been this executive order, which he signed on day one.”

“After successfully preserving this authority in lower courts for two years, we look forward to presenting our arguments to the Supreme Court,” he said.

The American Civil Liberties Union, alongside other organizations, challenged the policy on behalf of those barred from making asylum claims.

‘Courts are right to reject this unprecedented power’

“The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger,” Lee Gelernt, lead counsel and deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, said in a statement. “The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger. We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court.”

Federal law grants the right to seek asylum to those who fear persecution in their countries of origin, but grants the executive branch the authority to decide whether those claims are granted. However, the Trump administration has argued it can deny asylum claims outright.

The Trump administration’s record at the Supreme Court on its hardline immigration policies is mixed. In a landmark ruling in June, it struck down Trump’s executive order limiting birthright citizenship, finding the order violated the 14th Amendment. The same month, the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to end a program temporarily shielding eligible Haitian and Syrian immigrants living in the U.S. from deportation.

Earlier this year, the Supreme Court also ruled on a separate but related policy, allowing the Trump administration to reimplement a policy of turning away asylum-seekers along the U.S.-Mexico border before they enter the country, known as “metering.”

Court taking up ‘weighty immigration authority, legality issues’

Ashley Feasley, the legal expert in residence at the Immigration Law and Policy Initiative at The Catholic University of America Columbus School of Law, told OSV News that in taking up the case, the Supreme Court “continues its run of taking up cases this session that have weighty immigration authority and legality issues.”

“The Court will be specifically looking at whether a Presidential Proclamation issued by President Trump in January 2025 can effectively prevent certain individuals from entering the country and claiming asylum and other lesser protections like withholding of removal,” Feasley said. “The outcome of this case will have large policy implications as it will likely shape the Trump Administration’s and future Administrations’ ability to operationalize access to asylum at U.S. borders.”

Catholic social teaching on immigration balances three interrelated principles: the right of persons to migrate in order to sustain their lives and those of their families; the right of a country to regulate its borders and control immigration; and a nation’s duty to regulate its borders with justice and mercy.

The high court is expected to hear the case in spring 2027, with a decision by the end of its term, typically in June.

text:
By LINDSAY WHITEHURST

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court agreed Friday to consider President Donald Trump’s ban on asylum at the southern border, a pillar of the Republican president’s far-reaching crackdown on immigration.

The Trump administration is asking the justices to overturn lower court decisions that found it was illegal to block asylum applications following an executive order that called the situation at the southern border an “invasion.” The suit is the latest in a series of immigration cases before the high court.

Federal law allows people to seek asylum if they fear persecution in their home countries, no matter how they arrived in the U.S.

At the same time, it also lets the executive branch decide whether people are granted asylum. The Trump administration argues it can categorically deny asylum to migrants covered by the order and should not have to accept applications destined to be rejected.

Federal attorneys say yearslong processing times had previously contributed to a major influx of migrants at the southern border as many were released into the country while awaiting a decision.

“Since the proclamation took effect, border encounters have fallen by 93 percent, dropping to the lowest levels since the 1960s,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote. The executive order has been the “single most important factor in the President’s success at the border,” the Homeland Security Department’s general counsel, James Percival, said in a social media post.

Attorneys from the American Civil Liberties Union and several immigration rights groups counter that border crossings were already falling before Trump took office.

They say his executive order is an unlawful attempt to “invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates” legal protections aimed at protecting people fleeing danger in their home countries.

The executive branch does decide whether to grant asylum, which allows people to live and work legally in the U.S. But those decisions are supposed to be made on an individual basis and the law doesn’t allow the administration to unilaterally stop people from even applying, immigration attorneys argue.

“The plaintiffs in this case fled persecution and torture, including political imprisonment and threats from the Taliban,” said Keren Zwick, executive director of the National Immigrant Justice Center. “Yet, the Trump administration refused to honor its obligation to consider them for asylum.”

The ban was one of a series of immigration restrictions Trump rolled out upon his return to office in 2025. It has remained in place during the litigation.

The Supreme Court is expected to hear the case in the spring and hand down a decision by the end of June.

It’s the third major immigration case the high court will hear this term. The justices will also decide whether people can be swiftly deported to countries other than their homelands and if immigrants can be detained indefinitely during deportation proceedings.

text:
November 13, 2026 3:00 pm

WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court has granted review in Mullin v. RAICES, a challenge to President Trump’s proclamation completely shutting down asylum at the border.

The American Civil Liberties Union, National Immigrant Justice Center, Center for Gender & Refugee Studies, Texas Civil Rights Project, ACLU of the District of Columbia, and ACLU of Texas brought the federal lawsuit on behalf of a nationwide class of people barred from seeking protection in the United States under this proclamation, as well as three immigrant legal service providers, Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services (RAICES), Las Americas Immigrant Advocacy Center, and the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project.

The federal district court in Washington, D.C. and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit both rejected the Trump administration’s unlawful proclamation barring people from seeking asylum by invoking Section 212(f) of the Immigration and Nationality Act and a nonexistent “invasion.”

The lower federal courts ruled in the plaintiffs’ favor because the Trump administration’s action is contrary to laws enacted by Congress to ensure that people receive an opportunity to have their asylum claims heard.

The Supreme Court granted the government’s petition to hear the case, and argument is expected in spring 2027.

The following is reaction to the Supreme Court decision to hear the case:

“The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger,” said Lee Gelernt, lead counsel and deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project. “The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger. We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court.”

“The plaintiffs in this case fled persecution and torture, including political imprisonment and threats from the Taliban. Yet, the Trump administration refused to honor its obligation to consider them for asylum,” said Keren Zwick, executive director of the National Immigrant Justice Center. “Some plaintiffs were removed to third countries and then pushed back to the very place they fled; others faced prolonged detention without access to legal due process. Even after the lower courts rejected the president’s proclamation, the administration has continued to block access to asylum at the U.S. border. This vicious attack on due process and human rights has put thousands of lives in danger. We are honored to represent these asylum seekers, and their advocates, as this important case proceeds.”

“For nearly two years, the Trump administration’s unlawful asylum shutdown has deprived people seeking safety of their rights, placing vulnerable families, children, and adults in harm’s way,” said Melissa Crow, director of litigation at the Center for Gender & Refugee Studies (CGRS). “Refugees fleeing persecution and torture have been denied access to the asylum process and deported to danger. The lower courts got it right: The president cannot unilaterally rewrite our immigration laws and defy the will of Congress to get its way. It is now up to the Supreme Court to decide whether it will uphold the rule of law or bend to the administration’s agenda.”

“No one seeking safety at our borders should be denied that opportunity. It is incredibly timely that the Supreme Court will hear our case, as the nation saw a clear mandate from midterm voters earlier this month. Our communities made their voices heard on immigration, economic justice, and the many misdirections this administration has taken,” said Rochelle Garza, president of the Texas Civil Rights Project. “Asylum seekers deserve to have their rights protected, and we will continue fighting to ensure that the dedicated organizations who serve them directly have the ability to do so.”

“The Supreme Court faces a stark choice. Respect the rule of law and uphold the right to asylum, or allow the executive to decide on its own who gets to ask for safety,” said Nicolas Palazzo, interim executive director of Las Americas Immigrant Advocacy Center. “For the people we represent in El Paso and along the border, the court’s answer will decide whether they find protection or are sent back to the danger they fled.”

“Congress has determined that the United States has not only a moral but a legal obligation to provide people seeking safety at our borders a process to access protection. This attempt to unilaterally stop all asylum processing at the border is an unprecedented and illegal overreach that puts countless people in danger,” said Laura St. John, the legal director for the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project.

“Across this country, the American people firmly reject an unchecked executive that operates with disregard for the law,” said Faisal Al-Juburi, co-chief executive officer of RAICES. “Our system of checks and balances exists for moments precisely like this — to ensure no single branch can consolidate power at will. By agreeing to hear this case, the Supreme Court faces a critical constitutional responsibility: to uphold the limits of executive power and make clear that no president is beyond congressional authority. Future generations will look back at this decision, and the court must demonstrate that the rule of law applies equitably to all.”

text:
WASHINGTON – The Supreme Court on Nov. 13 said it will review President Donald Trump’s asylum ban at the United States-Mexico border, adding yet another dispute over a Trump immigration policy to the list of cases the court is considering.

The administration says Trump's policy of not allowing immigrants to seek asylum if they cross the border illegally is the “most important and effective” piece of the president's efforts to secure the southern border, which is one of his top initiatives.

But a federal judge ruled last year that Trump lacked the “sweeping authority” he asserted.

An appeals court likewise said the president cannot enact a categorical ban on asylum requests for some applicants.

The Justice Department told the Supreme Court that presidents have inherent authority to secure the border and protect national security.

On his first day back in office, Trump issued a proclamation declaring crossings at the southern border an “invasion” and sought to prevent many immigrants arriving there from applying for asylum.

Immigrant rights groups and individual immigrants sued. They argue that Trump is eviscerating the protections Congress created for people escaping dangerous situations.

“The plaintiffs in this case fled persecution and torture, including political imprisonment and threats from the Taliban. Yet, the Trump administration refused to honor its obligation to consider them for asylum,” said Keren Zwick, executive director of the National Immigrant Justice Center.

Federal immigration law allows anyone in the country or at an official entry port to apply for asylum.

Processing an asylum request can take years, and many migrants have been allowed to remain in the United States in the meantime.

That’s created an incentive for migrants to come to the United States, the administration argues, even if they know their asylum claims will eventually be rejected.

The Justice Department says that because the decision of whether to grant asylum is up to the government, the president can also broadly decide that anyone who illegally crosses the border is not eligible for asylum.

That policy has dramatically reduced – by 93% − the number of migrants apprehended at the border, according to the government.

Immigrant rights groups challenging the policy responded that border apprehensions were already down more than 90% from their peak before the change took effect.

“If the Executive Branch nonetheless believes it needs new tools to manage the border,” lawyers for the groups told the Supreme Court, “Congress must provide them.”

Other immigration cases the court will hear this term include challenges to two more practices important to the president’s crackdown on immigration.

The court will decide whether the administration can detain millions of immigrants without giving them a chance to seek bond, and whether it can deport immigrants to countries other than their own without letting them argue that they could be persecuted or tortured there.

Decisions are expected by the end of June.

Last June, the court said the federal government may systematically turn back asylum seekers before they cross ports of entry along the U.S. border with Mexico, a previous migrant management practice that the Trump administration may want to bring back.

Adams County violated state law when its Sheriff’s Office illegally collaborated with federal immigration officials, a Spokane County Superior Court judge ruled today in a lawsuit brought by the state Attorney General’s Office (AGO).

The judge found Adams County violated the state Keep Washington Working Act in multiple ways, and concluded the law does not violate the state or U.S. constitutions. It’s the first time a state court has interpreted and applied the provisions of the Keep Washington Working Act, which was signed into law in 2019.

In addition to declaring Adams County’s conduct unlawful, the court also entered a permanent injunction that prohibits the county from continuing to engage in its unlawful conduct. It requires the county revise its policies for consistency with the AGO’s model guidance around the law and train staff on the revised policies.

“This is a victory for the rights and dignity of all Washingtonians, regardless of where they were born, and an affirmation that local law enforcement cannot be co-opted by the federal government,” Attorney General Nick Brown said. “Today’s ruling allows our state to continue building trust and confidence between law enforcement and immigrant communities as the federal administration undermines those efforts with its draconian policies.”

The AGO filed suit in March 2025, alleging the Sheriff’s Office violated the Keep Washington Working Act by illegally facilitating immigration arrests at the Adams County Jail, helping federal agents question people in custody, and routinely giving federal immigration officials the confidential personal information of hundreds of Washingtonians.

The lawsuit followed more than two years of negotiations with the county, which had been progressing until the county abruptly changed its stance following the presidential inauguration in January 2025. Prior to that about-face, Adams County told the Attorney General’s Office that it was working to follow state law — just like hundreds of Washington sheriffs’ offices, police departments, jails, and state agencies have all successfully done since Keep Washington Working was enacted in 2019.

The judge’s ruling can be read here. The court concluded Adams County violated the law by:

Sending daily new in-custody lists to federal immigration authorities;

Sharing the anticipated release time of inmates in their custody with federal immigration authorities;

Giving federal immigration authorities access to interview an individual in its custody regarding a noncriminal matter without first obtaining the individual’s written consent; and

Failing to adopt policies that are consistent with the AGO’s KWW Guidance and compliant with KWW.

More information about Keep Washington Working can be found here: Immigration and Keep Washington Working Guidance | Washington State

The state was represented in this case by Managing Assistant Attorney General Emily Nelson and Assistant Attorney General Ben Seel, who received substantial assistance from paralegals Tiffany Jennings, Rory Pela, and Panda Halford, investigator Rebecca Pawul, and supervision from Managing Assistant Attorneys General Lane Polozola and Teri Healy.

text:
By VALERIE GONZALEZ

McALLEN, Texas (AP) — Immigrant children are spending up to a month in cold, sunless rooms meant to house them for no more than three days, according to legal advocates charged with ensuring the government abides by a court agreement.

The Center for Human Rights and Constitutional Law, the National Center for Youth Law, and Children’s Rights filed a motion Friday afternoon asking a judge to clarify the children’s right to counsel as part of a longstanding court agreement between them and the federal government.

The U.S. Attorney General and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Multiple parents held in CBP stations this year in Del Rio, Texas, Laredo, Texas and San Diego, California, reported either no access to a phone call with attorneys or calls that lasted less than five minutes.

Immigrant children in federal custody are protected under the Flores Settlement, a court agreement between the federal government and legal advocates representing immigrant children. It created standards to ensure safe and sanitary conditions in federal custody. It also allows CBP to detain children in their facilities for up to 72 hours. The federal government has a pending appeal with an appellate court to terminate the agreement.

Typically, immigrant children arrested alone or with their families by Border Patrol are processed in temporary stations and then transferred to another agency where they could be placed in long-term detention centers or released with ankle monitors.

Despite a record low number of border arrests, an annual report filed with the court by CBP found that officials took more than the recommended time to process families from March through June, the last month reported. Legal advocates found many children spent weeks and up to a month at these temporary facilities not designed for long-term stays.

Immigrant parents described being held with their children in cold rooms with cement floors and windows that only faced indoors. Lights are kept on all day and night, and many reported losing their sense of time.

“In the morning they bring us a burrito and that’s the way we learn that it is the morning,” one parent held with her teenage daughter in Laredo, Texas, in November said in her declaration. Others said they tried to steal glimpses of wristwatches as agents walked by.

Thin mats and Mylar blankets are provided at night, but one parent said the mats gave her child a rash. She came up with a solution: “At night I lie on my back and I tell him not to touch the mat but to lie on top of me, to sleep on my chest. His rash has gone down since we began sleeping this way, with me as his bed, protecting him.”

Families with young children reported being held in detention pods with no books, toys or television. One mother who was allowed to stay with her four-year-old daughter by her side said they were able to step outside the pod for an hour a day. “That is not enough for a child, to be locked in a cell 23 hours a day,” she said.

Parents were also concerned for their children’s well-being. The mother of the four-year-old said her child lost weight in the two weeks of her detention and developed a stutter that only worsened after witnessing a man, handcuffed and chained at the legs and waist, walking out of the facility to be deported.

“She started crying, asking if they would chain her and take us from here the same way. Her stutter increased after that. Every time she thinks of it, she starts to cry again,” the mother said.

In a brief list of orders from their private conference earlier in the day, the justices announced that it will review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that struck down the policy as an overreach by the government. The court also added a second case involving the standard for securities-fraud cases to its oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term.

The asylum case is the latest addition to the court’s burgeoning immigration docket, which already includes a challenge to the Trump administration’s practice of deporting immigrants to countries that are not identified in their removal orders (a policy known as “third-party removals”) and its policy of detaining immigrants who are apprehended within the United States without the opportunity for a hearing.

Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services has its roots in a Jan. 20, 2025, proclamation by President Donald Trump declaring that “an invasion is ongoing at the southern border” and suspending (that is, temporarily blocking) the entry of noncitizens “engaged in the invasion.” Trump also indicated that such noncitizens could no longer seek protections, such as asylum, that would allow them to remain in the country.

The Department of Homeland Security issued guidance that (among other things) barred any noncitizens from applying for asylum. The guidance also indicated that anyone who entered the country despite Trump’s suspension of entry would be quickly removed without some of the procedural protections provided by law.

The challengers in the case are a group of 13 individuals who say that they have been persecuted or tortured in their home countries, as well as three immigration-related nonprofits. They sought to file a class-action lawsuit in federal court in Washington, arguing that both the proclamation and the guidance violate federal immigration law.

U.S. District Judge Randolph Moss recognized a class of challengers, made up of immigrants who are or would be subject to Trump’s proclamation. He concluded that the DHS guidance was unlawful and threw it out, and he barred DHS officials from implementing those actions under the proclamation.

A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit initially paused part of Moss’ order, but a different panel later largely upheld it on the merits. Judge J. Michelle Childs, joined by Judge Cornelia Pillard, wrote that the “text, structure, and history” of federal immigration law “make clear that in supplying power to suspend entry by Presidential proclamation, Congress did not intend to grant the Executive the expansive removal authority it asserts. The Proclamation and Guidance are thus unlawful to the extent that they circumvent … removal procedures and cast aside federal laws affording individuals the right to apply and be considered for asylum or withholding of removal protections,” a more limited form of protection from deportation.

Judge Justin Walker dissented in part. Although he contended that Trump has the discretion to deny all asylum applications and therefore can dispense with the application process altogether on the ground that he would deny the applications, he agreed with the majority that the government “cannot remove aliens to countries where they will be persecuted, and the Proclamation and Guidance cannot strip them of mandatory procedures that protect against that removal.”

The D.C. Circuit agreed to keep its ruling on hold while the government appeals, allowing the government to maintain the asylum restrictions.

Contending that the U.S.-Mexico border “had become overwhelmed by an ungovernable influx of millions of aliens, creating chaotic conditions that criminal and terrorist organizations exploited to threaten our national security,” the Trump administration came to the Supreme Court in August, asking the justices to weigh in. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the justices that “suspending the illegal entry of aliens and precluding their access to asylum” is “[t]he most important and effective pieces of the President’s response.”

Trump’s proclamation, Sauer continued, “rests on a commonsense understanding of the President’s inherent and delegated powers to exclude aliens.” Therefore, he said, Trump “acted well within his authority in preemptively indicating that asylum applications filed by aliens who violate the proclamation’s entry suspension would be denied—and in effectuating that discretionary policy choice by directing that the government need not accept futile asylum applications from those aliens.”

Sauer also told the court that the lower courts did not have the power to apply their order to a whole class of challengers. Federal immigration law, he argued, expressly bars lower courts from issuing orders that require federal officials to enforce or implement specified provisions of federal immigration law –including those “allowing aliens to assert an asylum claim … and obtain a hearing before being subject to expedited removal.”

And in any event, Sauer continued, the class of challengers also violates the rules governing class actions because it “sweeps in aliens who are currently overseas and have no imminent plans to enter the United States (much less enter illegally).” Those noncitizens, he wrote, have not been injured and therefore cannot be part of the class; they “will become future class members here only if they choose to illegally enter the county.”

The challengers urged the justices to deny review, telling them that the D.C. Circuit’s ruling “correctly held that the President may not invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.” They also pushed back against the administration’s suggestion that the proclamation and guidance were intended to address an “unprecedented crisis,” countering that “the facts say otherwise. By January 2025, before the Proclamation took effect, border apprehensions had returned to historically routine levels, down over 90 percent from their peak. If the Executive Branch nonetheless believes it needs new tools to manage the border, Congress must provide them.”

The statute on which Trump relies for the proclamation, the challengers continued, “does not speak to the removal of noncitizens who are already here. Nor does it authorize the Executive Branch to abrogate Congress’s protections against removing noncitizens to persecution or torture.” Instead, they wrote, federal immigration law “provides that noncitizens ‘may apply’ for asylum, ‘irrespective of … status’” or where and how they entered the United States. In conflict with “statutory command,” the challengers contended, “the Proclamation and Guidance dictate that statutorily eligible noncitizens may not apply for or receive asylum.”

The challengers also rejected the administration’s suggestion that the lower courts could not have broadly barred the Trump administration from implementing the proclamation and guidance. The law stripping the lower courts of the power “to enjoin or restrain the operation of” some federal immigration laws does not apply here, they said, because Trump’s proclamation relies on other laws that are not implicated by that bar.

The court agreed to consider the legality of Trump’s proclamation and the guidance, as well as Moss’ power to enter an order providing broad relief, but it turned down the government’s request to weigh in on whether the class violates the rules governing class actions.

The court also agreed to hear Robinhood Markets v. Sodha on Friday, involving whether a California-based financial-services company violated federal securities laws when it failed to disclose some interim financial data as part of its initial public offering in July 2021, although that data was not scheduled to be reported until August of that year. In a lawsuit brought by investors, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit ruled against the company, prompting it to come to the Supreme Court in February.

The company asked the justices to decide two questions, involving the effect of the company’s failure to disclose interim financial data that investors may consider significant to their decisions on compliance with federal securities laws and regulations.

The investors asked the justices to stay out of the case, telling them that “[t]here is nothing radical … about the decision below,” much less anything worthy of the Supreme Court’s intervention. Although the company “disagree[s] with the outcome,” the investors said, it “do[es] not propose that this Court adopt legal rules in place of the existing standards.”

In a brief filed last month at the court’s request, the Trump administration agreed with Robinhood that the court should weigh in on the first question presented by the company’s petition for review. Sauer told the justices that the 9th Circuit’s ruling “threatens significant untoward consequences.”

The court on Friday agreed to decide one of the questions posed by Robinhood Markets’ petition: “[w]hether an issuer can be found liable under the misleading-omissions prong” of the law at the center of the dispute “based on a determination that the issuer failed to disclose interim financial information that is material within the meaning of” that provision, “without an additional inquiry to determine whether the omission rendered any affirmative statement misleading.”

The justices will likely hear oral arguments in these cases sometime next spring.

text:
The Supreme Court agreed Friday to decide if President Donald Trump may categorically ban migrants arriving at the southern border from applying for asylum, setting up arguments on another divisive policy the White House sees as critical to its anti-immigration agenda.

The appeal will almost certainly be heard early next year and decided before July.

It adds another case to a Supreme Court term that is already heavy on Trump’s hardline immigration policies, including one on the administration’s removal of migrants to countries they have no connection with and the push to direct certain migrants to mandatory detention.

Trump signed the proclamation on his first day back in office, suspending entry for migrants “engaged in the invasion across the southern border.” The document specifically restricted migrants from invoking asylum protections included in federal law “until I issue a finding that the invasion at the southern border has ceased.”

The president has argued that people crossing the border illegally claim asylum as a way to stall their deportation because it can take years to adjudicate an asylum claim, and an applicant can be released into the US while that process plays out.

But the Immigration and Nationality Act, a law enacted by Congress, specifically allows migrants to claim asylum, even as it leaves the decision about whether to grant safe harbor up to administration officials. Thirteen individuals and three immigrant rights groups challenged the Trump policy last year.

A federal appeals court in April upheld a district court decision that found the administration’s effort violated the INA. But the court stayed its decision, allowing the Trump administration to continue the policy while it appealed.

“Barring foreign individuals who are physically present in the United States from applying for asylum and, if they make the statutory showing that they are eligible, from being considered to receive it cannot be squared with the statute,” wrote US Circuit Judge Michelle Childs, who was named to the court by former President Joe Biden.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer, the administration’s top appellate lawyer, described the asylum measures as a “cornerstone” policy that has been its “most effective” change in “resolving a border crisis.”

The appeal also quoted Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as saying that “one of the ‘key magnets’ for that flood of aliens was ‘asylum.’”

text:
By LINDSAY WHITEHURST

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court agreed Friday to consider President Donald Trump’s ban on asylum at the southern border, a pillar of the Republican president’s far-reaching crackdown on immigration.

The Trump administration is asking the justices to overturn lower court decisions that found it was illegal to block asylum applications following an executive order that called the situation at the southern border an “invasion.” The suit is the latest in a series of immigration cases before the high court.

Federal law allows people to seek asylum if they fear persecution in their home countries, no matter how they arrived in the U.S.

At the same time, it also lets the executive branch decide whether people are granted asylum. The Trump administration argues it can categorically deny asylum to migrants covered by the order and should not have to accept applications destined to be rejected.

Federal attorneys say yearslong processing times had previously contributed to a major influx of migrants at the southern border as many were released into the country while awaiting a decision.

“Since the proclamation took effect, border encounters have fallen by 93 percent, dropping to the lowest levels since the 1960s,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote. The executive order has been the “single most important factor in the President’s success at the border,” the Homeland Security Department’s general counsel, James Percival, said in a social media post.

Attorneys from the American Civil Liberties Union and several immigration rights groups counter that border crossings were already falling before Trump took office.

They say his executive order is an unlawful attempt to “invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates” legal protections aimed at protecting people fleeing danger in their home countries.

The executive branch does decide whether to grant asylum, which allows people to live and work legally in the U.S. But those decisions are supposed to be made on an individual basis and the law doesn’t allow the administration to unilaterally stop people from even applying, immigration attorneys argue.

“The plaintiffs in this case fled persecution and torture, including political imprisonment and threats from the Taliban,” said Keren Zwick, executive director of the National Immigrant Justice Center. “Yet, the Trump administration refused to honor its obligation to consider them for asylum.”

The ban was one of a series of immigration restrictions Trump rolled out upon his return to office in 2025. It has remained in place during the litigation.

The Supreme Court is expected to hear the case in the spring and hand down a decision by the end of June.

It’s the third major immigration case the high court will hear this term. The justices will also decide whether people can be swiftly deported to countries other than their homelands and if immigrants can be detained indefinitely during deportation proceedings.

text:
Lauren Boebert, the firebrand conservative Republican Colorado representative whose three terms in Congress have been marred by multiple controversies, was defeated in her re-election bid.

The gun rights advocate, born-again Christian and one-time QAnon fan lost to Democrat Eileen Laubacher by a less than 1% margin, according to the Associated Press.

“I’m honored by the trust the people of Colorado’s fourth district have placed in me. This campaign was never about party labels. It was about putting people first,” Laubacher said in a statement. “To those who voted for me, thank you, I will strive to make you proud. To those who didn’t, I’ll fight just as hard for you and hope to earn your support.”

This district, which spans the eastern plains of Colorado, is one of the state’s most conservative seats and has long been a Republican stronghold. Laubacher is a retired two-star navy rear admiral, who was deployed to Afghanistan and later worked on the national security council under the Biden administration.

Laubacher just became a registered Democrat in 2025, saying in a debate with Boebert the Republican party had become “nearly unrecognizable”. She focused her campaign on decades of military and national security service.

In a statement congratulating Laubacher, Suzan DelBene, chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, declared: “Lauren Boebert’s sideshow is over.”

Both Laubacher and Boebert moved to Colorado’s fourth congressional district in recent years. Boebert accused Laubacher of moving there and changing parties in order to run for Congress. Likewise, Boebert has been questioned for her move to the district in 2024 after barely eking out a win in the third district’s previous election.

Boebert said the move was because of “dark money” flowing from Hollywood to “steal” district three’s congressional seat: “It’s coming from Hollywood … when you have Barbra Streisand coming in and donating to the Democrat, when you have Ryan Reynolds coming in and donating to the Democrat … It shows you that Hollywood is trying to buy their way into Congress.”

Boebert’s tenure in Congress has been racked with controversy. She decried the 2020 presidential election as being rigged, demanded to carry a handgun on the House floor and was accused of helping incite the January 6 insurrection by tweeting “Today is 1776” the morning of the riots, among other actions. Boebert later condemned the attack on the Capitol.

She went viral in 2023 when she was filmed groping her date, vaping and being escorted out of a Beetlejuice musical in Denver in 2023. Initially, Boebert joked that she would “plead guilty to laughing and singing too loud”, but the incident later led to her publicly apologizing and divorcing her husband (who was not her date).

And just weeks before the election, she was hit by an ethics complaint over allegations she had sexual relationships with three staffers and had paid one to stay silent, allegations she has denied and called “politically motivated”.

Despite the dust-ups and being a Maga loyalist, Boebert did occasionally stand up to Trump. She was one of the most vocal members of Congress calling for the release of the Epstein files, even after the White House tried to persuade her to remove her name from a discharge petition for the documents.

This earned the ire of Trump, who has called Boebert a “carpetbagger” and “dumb”. The president’s first veto of his second term was for a bill sponsored by Boebert that would have funded a drinking water project in district four. The bill had passed the House and Senate unanimously.

“Nothing says ‘America First’ like denying clean drinking water to 50,000 people in south-east Colorado many of whom enthusiastically voted for him all three elections,” Boebert said in a statement at the time.

“But hey, if this administration wants to make its legacy blocking projects that deliver water to rural Americans; that’s on them.”

text:
Senior Tory and Reform politicians have clashed over immigration policy in the Oxfordshire village of Piddington after the government approved plans to convert a defence site into accommodation for asylum seekers.

Zia Yusuf and Chris Philp raised their voices and spoke over each other in front of TV cameras and local people for more than three minutes. Yusuf urged his fellow home affairs spokesperson to apologise for his record as a minister. Philp said they should instead “stand in solidarity with residents” and Yusuf should “read the room”.

The clash came hours after villagers said they would launch a legal challenge to plans to house more than 1,200 detained asylum seekers near them.

It emerged on Thursday that Angela Rayner, the housing and communities secretary, had approved full planning permission, a decision welcomed by the Home Office, which wants to end the use of asylum hotels.

In their clash, Yusuf said: “Chris, would you like to apologise for the things you did in government to bring hundreds of thousands of people into the country illegally?”

Philp, who served as an immigration minister, said: “That is disingenuous, Zia, as usual … I hope today we can stand in solidarity with the residents. Listen to the people clapping and read the room.”

As the two men’s voices grew louder, Philp said: “You are in a hole, stop digging.”

Downing Street has defended the plans to convert a military base near a tiny Oxfordshire village into asylum-seeker accommodation, insisting the safety of the public would always be its “top priority”.

Tim McNally, the parish council chair, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme there would be “many actions” by villagers, and that ministers should “absolutely” be braced for a legal challenge, which would need to be lodged within six weeks.

Ministers have faced opposition over the plans from villagers, who even made a symbolic attempt to declare the village independent from the rest of the country after a referendum of its 350 residents. Asked how the village would respond, McNally said: “There’s going to be many actions, you will see. We will disclose that as we move forward.”

Campaigners could also apply the new Hillsborough law, which is being considered by parliament. Once passed, the law would create a legally enforceable duty of candour that compels public officials and authorities to act transparently when investigations and inquiries take place.

“Today is a day of reflection, and we’ll work out where we plan to go from this point. But I will say, the Hillsborough law is there for a reason, and we’re going to apply it,” McNally said.

A Home Office spokesperson said a final decision to proceed had yet to be taken. “The government is working on a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country, with over £1bn saved in costs since the election,” they added.

“This includes closing all asylum hotels and moving to alternative accommodation, including former military sites. These are designed to be self-contained, with 24/7 security and CCTV, to minimise the impact on the local community.”

text:
At a school-turned-shelter in Panama City, where scores of asylum seekers who were expelled from the United States had taken refuge, PHR’s medical director conducted a forensic medical evaluation of a woman from Afghanistan who had worked for a women’s rights organization. After the Taliban takeover in 2021, her organization’s offices were ransacked and directors imprisoned. Despite going into hiding, a group of men found her and beat and raped her, warning they would return to imprison and kill her. She fled Afghanistan and made her way to the U.S.-Mexico border with the goal of requesting asylum and joining her family members in California. Instead, upon arriving at the border, she was detained in a U.S. detention center before being forced onto a military plane to Panama, where she was then detained in abhorrent conditions and held incommunicado for several weeks.

This is just one of many harrowing stories told to PHR’s team of expert clinicians who deployed to Panama last year to support a lawsuit brought by the Global Strategic Litigation Council against the Panamanian government for the detention and treatment of 112 migrants expelled from the United States without due process.

PHR’s team conducted evaluations of 29 people seeking asylum from countries such as Cameroon, China, Eritrea, Iran, and Russia. We captured physical and psychological evidence of the persecution, torture, and ill-treatment they had faced in their countries of origin that substantiated their claims of “credible fear of return,” as well as chilling accounts of their treatment by U.S. and Panamanian officials.

PHR’s findings from these evaluations provided critical evidence that was submitted as part of the Global Strategic Litigation Council’s lawsuit. After the lawsuit was filed, the Panamanian government extended the period that these migrants were able to remain in the country and allowed them to seek asylum. PHR also mobilized the powerful evidence we documented in Panama to fuel legal action against the Trump administration, including at the U.S. Court of Appeals and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

The fight against the U.S.’s inhumane immigration policies did not stop there. We used our expertise documenting the harms experienced by children in immigration detention to defend the Flores Settlement Agreement – the foundational framework that has governed the treatment and release of immigrant children in U.S. custody for three decades – against the Trump administration’s attempts to dismantle it. PHR and partners submitted an amicus brief in a case at the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit arguing that the lifesaving protections in the Flores Settlement Agreement remain medically necessary and legally indispensable for protecting immigrant children.

Meanwhile, as protests grew in response to U.S. immigration raids across the country in 2025, U.S. federal law enforcement repeatedly misused crowd-control weapons – such as rubber bullets and flash-bang grenades – against peaceful protestors, journalists, and medics, causing serious injury and violating the right to peaceful assembly.

PHR met this moment by leveraging our expertise from nearly four decades of research on the health harms of crowd-control weapons to provide expert submissions in three lawsuits challenging the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) use of force during protests in Los Angeles, California; Chicago, Illinois; and Portland, Oregon. In each case, the district court granted a preliminary injunction or temporary restraining order halting DHS’s use of crowd-control weapons against non-violent protestors, often citing declarations by PHR experts in their decision.

PHR’s Forensic Evidence in Service of Justice Around the World

Kenya: While many of the strategic litigation initiatives above have swiftly catalyzed change, securing justice for human rights violations often takes years, if not decades. In 2025, we reached a landmark milestone in a case that PHR, three Kenyan NGOs, and eight sexual violence survivors brought at the High Court in Nairobi in 2013 to hold the government of Kenya accountable for sexual violence committed in the wake of the country’s 2007 violent presidential election.

In a historic move, the government of Kenya paid 16 million Kenyan shillings (approximately $124,000) in compensation to four of the eight survivors, marking the first time in Kenya’s history that survivors of conflict-related sexual violence received financial remedy for the harm they endured. This long-awaited payment came nearly five years after the High Court awarded the compensation in its groundbreaking judgment in 2020 and 12 years after the case was initiated. For these four survivors – who believed they would never receive their court-ordered compensation – as well as for sexual violence survivors across the country, this victory serves as an affirmation that justice, even if long delayed, is indeed possible.

Myanmar: PHR’s forensic medical evidence is informing a landmark genocide case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice. After Myanmar’s security forces launched widespread and systematic violence targeting the Rohingya people in northern Rakhine State, PHR launched a series of investigations into the crimes committed – including mass killings, torture, mutilations, and sexual violence – that drove more than 900,000 Rohingyas into makeshift refugee camps in Bangladesh.

During oral arguments, The Gambia’s legal team cited PHR’s findings extensively, including our evidence on crimes against children, sexual violence, and long-term disability resulting from injuries sustained during the clearance operations. This historic moment is the culmination of years of sustained collaboration with The Gambia’s legal team. The reliance on PHR’s forensic medical evidence in a case at the highest level of international law – which will help define state accountability for genocide – underscores the vital role that our forensic expertise plays in advancing justice and reaffirms that persistence pays off.

Peru: In 2025, Peru’s National Court of Justice convicted three police officers for the 2008 aggravated torture and rape of an LGBTQI+ Peruvian, Azul Rojas Marín, sentencing each to 17 years in prison and ordering compensation for Ms. Rojas. This marked the first time in Peru that state agents were convicted for torture due to prejudice against an LGBTQI+ person. PHR experts supported the case by conducting a forensic medical evaluation of Ms. Rojas. Along with submitting a medical affidavit on the findings to the court, our experts were cross-examined in the trial. The lead prosecutor credited the forensic medical evaluation as indispensable to the case’s outcome.

When PHR’s founders first brought forensic medical evidence to bear on human rights atrocities, the idea that medicine could be a tool for international accountability was still novel. Four decades later, forensic medical expertise and evidence are a cornerstone of justice processes and PHR regularly receives requests for support from justice mechanisms. In a major development last year, PHR formalized a partnership with the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights to support their investigations around the world.

To meet the growing demand for case support from partner organizations and justice mechanisms, PHR recently formed a new Medical Expert Taskforce (MET). The MET brings together more than 25 expert clinicians from PHR’s wider pro bono global network who we will mobilize to provide cross-specialty forensic expertise to support justice and accountability efforts around the world. With this dedicated taskforce, PHR is better equipped than ever to deploy forensic expertise in service of justice and accountability wherever it is needed.

text:
COLUMBIA — The American Civil Liberties Union of South Carolina is suing to stop a federal immigration enforcement policy that allows migrants to be re-detained even if they haven’t been deemed a flight risk or a danger to the community.

The lawsuit was filed Nov. 12 by the ACLU chapters in Georgia, North Carolina and South Carolina against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and Immigrations, Customs and Enforcement, or ICE, on behalf of four plaintiffs:

Livinton Sosa Martinez , a 41-year-old Nicaraguan man who resides in Greensboro, N.C.

Raquel Mariona Ebora, a 39-year-old Honduran woman who resides in Dunn, N.C.

Alvaro Ibañez Cardenas , a 35-year-old Venezuelan man who resides in Athens, Ga.; and

Ambrosio Trujillo Zavaleta, a 46-year-old Mexican man who resides in Savannah.

All four have families and have built a life in the U.S., the lawsuit states. They have been “re-detained” and subsequently released after being determined again not to be a flight risk or danger to the community.

The case was filed in the Northern District of Georgia Atlanta Division. ICE’s Atlanta Field Office covers Georgia, North Carolina and South Carolina.

Neither the Department of Homeland Security nor the ICE field office in Atlanta responded to a request from The Post and Courier seeking comment.

Each of the plaintiffs have complied with the conditions set on them by the U.S. government, the ACLU said, including showing up for court hearings and attending immigration check-in appointments. They are normally allowed to live in the U.S. if they’re not considered a flight risk or a community danger.

The lawsuit comes amid an the immigration crack down carried out the by the Trump administration. The policy against re-detention changed in May 2025, according to the lawsuit. People have been detained again without any “material changes” to a person’s status. The administration has pushed for people to “self-deport.”

“DHS is now systematically stripping people of longstanding protections and arbitrarily re-detaining them in harsh conditions. Our clients are challenging unlawful re-detentions so immigrants have a fair chance to build lives in the communities they call home,” said Corina Scott, a staff attorney for the ACLU of North Carolina.

During the first 18 months of President Donald Trump’s second term, his administration removed about 980,000 people, according to data released in October by the Migration Policy Institute. According to an analysis by MPI, more than two-thirds of those removals were of migrants initially intercepted at the border.

However, fewer people have been removed from the U.S. since Trump returned to office than compared to other administrations, according to a Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse report released Nov. 11.

Homeland Security removed 39,893 people from the U.S. in the first full month of Trump’s second term, according to information in the Department of Homeland Security’s Enforcement Integrated Database (EID), which is managed by ICE. In July, that number dropped to 26,908 people.

According to the latest available data, from August 2025 through July 2026, federal authorities removed 316,601 people from the U.S. That is 29 percent less than the 446,180 people removed during former President Joe Biden's last full year in office.

According to the lawsuit, ICE almost never carried out arrests of detained noncitizens without a criminal conviction or final deportation order. Starting in May 2025, however, re-detain arrests increased in the Atlanta ICE Field Office, which covers South Carolina.

“South Carolinians shouldn’t have to live in fear that they or their neighbors, coworkers or family members will be baselessly torn from their community and thrown back into detention,” said Sarah Schreiber, staff attorney at the ACLU of South Carolina.

text:
U.S. Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., speaks outside the U.S. Capitol during a press conference with business leaders to push for work protections for immigrants on Wednesday, November 11, 2026. (Photo by Ariana Figueroa/States Newsroom)

This story by Ariana Figueroa appeared on Colorado Newsline on November 11, 2026.

Democrats and business leaders publicly lobbied the Trump administration Wednesday to prioritize work permits and other protections for long-term immigrants during the lame-duck session of Congress and beyond.

Citing the midterm elections, when Democrats flipped the U.S House and Senate, and President Donald Trump’s recent admission that his immigration crackdown hurt Republicans at the ballot box, Democratic lawmakers argued that voters were clear about wanting immigration reform before the start of the next Congress.

Congress has a lengthy to-do-list for the lame-duck session, possibly including government funding, the annual defense policy bill, the farm bill, a measure to regulate the college sports landscape and permitting reform to ease regulation on large construction projects.

“We owe it to these families to try anything, and I’m willing to try anything,” Arizona Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego said.

He was joined by American Business Immigration Coalition Action, which lobbies for work permits and legal pathways for long-term immigrants, and the South Texas Builders Association, a local trade group that represents the construction industry that has a workforce that is 30% immigrant nationwide, and Democratic U.S. House members from Texas.

Asked how receptive the White House would be to work permits for immigrants, which the administration has vigorously worked to limit, Gallego didn’t directly answer.

Trump’s mixed signals

The administration has revoked millions of immigrants’ work permits in the last two years. Many were workers in hospitality, healthcare and the construction industries.

But shortly after the midterm elections, the president said he was open to making a deal on work permits in certain industries.

At the same time, though, he elevated Stephen Miller, an official who has crafted some of the president’s harshest immigration policies, to White House chief of staff.

“I think right now the best thing the White House could do is to actually try to send some type of signal, besides talk, that they’re serious about this, and the way to do that is to have some reforms already at (Immigration and Customs Enforcement),” Gallego said.

“Whether it’s shutting down the detention centers, giving (a) certain level of protections, whether to veterans so they don’t get deported, to maybe parents of U.S. students so they don’t get deported, something to show that it’s not just talk, and this isn’t going to be a policy that’s led by Stephen Miller,” he added.

The vice chair of South Texas Builders Association, Benny Melendez, had a pointed message for Miller.

“If you want to continue harassing our communities, prepare yourself not only to lose your job, but … these same communities you are now harassing will make sure you lose the White House” in 2028, he said.

Next Congress

If lawmakers are unable to get any major reforms through the crowded end-of-year session, Democrats are looking ahead to when they control both chambers next year.

House Republicans on Tuesday elected Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan, a staunch Trump supporter who has not supported immigration reform, to lead them in the minority.

Texas Democratic Rep. Henry Cuellar, the incoming chair on the subcommittee that handles government funding for the Department of Homeland Security, said he’s not worried about Jordan because Democrats will have a majority in January.

Cuellar, whom Trump pardoned after he and his wife were indicted on charges of bribery, money laundering and conspiracy, said he’s going to use his subcommittee gavel to add guardrails on ICE and clear the backlog at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, which processes legal immigrants.

Gallego said he thinks the Senate will be able to get to 60 votes on some type of immigration reform legislation in the 120th Congress, when Democrats will have at least 54 and up to 56 seats depending on races that are still too close to call.

Whether that overhaul is in one bill or a series of increments is up for debate, Gallego said.

“If we can pass a big, beautiful conference immigration reform bill, the Trump immigration reform bill, and if that gets them on our side or not, then let’s do that,” Gallego said. “But if that doesn’t work, then I do think incremental passes to start protecting different communities I think is also an option. We should not avoid that either.”

text:
WASHINGTON - The U.S. Supreme Court agreed on Friday to consider the legality of President Donald Trump's restrictions on access to asylum at the U.S.-Mexico border, a hardline immigration policy his administration has credited with helping reduce border crossings.

The justices took up Trump's appeal of a lower court's ruling that found he exceeded his authority by denying migrants caught entering the country illegally the chance to apply for asylum.

The court is expected to hear arguments in the case in the coming months and rule by the end of June.

Trump, who has described the influx of migrants as an invasion, announced the new curbs just hours into his second presidential term on January 20, 2025. His policy sweeps more broadly than similar curbs put in place by his predecessor, Democratic former President Joe Biden, who limited asylum eligibility at the southern border in a bid to reduce illegal crossings.

Trump's asylum policy is one of a number of measures his administration ​has taken as part of his crackdown on immigration pursued since returning to office last year. Top officials have also sought to persuade other nations to join in a global campaign to roll back asylum protections in an effort to reshape the post-World War Two framework around humanitarian migration.

Under Trump's policy, migrants caught crossing the southern border illegally are barred from pursuing asylum claims. The prohibition also applies to migrants who arrive at official border crossings and lack certain medical or criminal history information, a requirement that advocates say is often impossible to meet for people fleeing violence.

Trump's proclamation announcing the asylum restrictions — and the fast-track deportation procedures they are meant to enable — said the policy would remain in effect until the Republican president determines that the "invasion at the southern border" has ended.

'Credible fear' interviews

Immigrant rights groups filed a class-action lawsuit challenging the policy on behalf of would-be asylum seekers who say they were denied a "credible fear" interview by U.S. immigration officials before facing deportation. Such interviews are meant to determine whether migrants seeking asylum would face persecution in their home country based on race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group or political opinion.

A Washington, DC-based federal judge ruled in favor of the immigrant rights groups in July 2025. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit in April upheld the judge's ruling but largely agreed to block the decision from taking effect to let the administration appeal to the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, has been largely deferential to Trump in his second presidential term in challenges to his immigration policies.

In June, the court handed Trump a victory by backing the federal government's authority to turn away asylum seekers when officials deem US-Mexico border crossings too overburdened to handle additional claims.

In September, the court let the administration resume deporting ​migrants to countries other than their own without offering them the chance to show the harms they may face, bolstering a tool his administration has used for rapid ‌expulsions as part of his immigration crackdown. The justices are due to hear arguments over the legality of that policy on December 9.

text:
Two Russian climbers charged with scaling the Empire State Building face possible prison time and deportation after their attorney accused Manhattan prosecutors of withdrawing a proposed misdemeanor plea agreement the night before their November 12, 2026, court appearance.

Ivan Kuznetsov, 32, and Angelina Nikolau, 33, appeared in Manhattan Criminal Court, where attorney Noam Biale said the agreement would have allowed them to resolve the case on lesser charges and reduce the risk of losing their ability to remain in the United States. The Manhattan District Attorney's Office disputed his account, saying prosecutors had never made a formal plea offer.

Biale warned that deportation to Russia could expose Kuznetsov to military conscription for the war in Ukraine and Nikolau to imprisonment over her artistic expression.

The couple, who live in the United States on talent visas, continue to face felony burglary and reckless endangerment charges stemming from their July 1 climb. Certain criminal convictions can make foreign nationals subject to deportation, depending on the offense and federal immigration law. Even a misdemeanor conviction can carry immigration consequences.

Just two weeks earlier, Biale had indicated that negotiations with prosecutors were approaching a resolution. At an October 27 hearing, a judge also lifted the couple's requirement to report for monthly supervision check-ins. Their latest appearance ended with the felony charges still pending and another hearing scheduled for January.

The couple's July 1 climb of the Empire State Building's broadcast antenna led to felony charges after prosecutors accused them of unlawfully entering restricted areas, damaging a security-door lock and endangering responding officers.

Authorities said police had to wait approximately 30 minutes for the building's broadcast antenna to be powered down before climbing roughly 1,250 feet to intercept them. Prosecutors cited the emergency response in support of the reckless endangerment allegations.

Kuznetsov and Nikolau, featured in the 2024 Netflix documentary Skywalkers: A Love Story, climbed the antenna without safety equipment, unfurled a banner promoting love and peace, and staged an apparent marriage proposal above Manhattan.

In an interview aired November 11, Kuznetsov said the couple was prepared to accept responsibility for the climb and expressed regret for the officers who responded.

title: U.S. Supreme Court takes up Trump's asylum ban | National | thecentersquare.com
description: (The Center Square) — The U.S. Supreme Court on Friday agreed to hear a case challenging President Trump's order banning asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border.
text:
The Supreme Court Building in Washington, D.C. Photo: Andrew MacDonald / Unsplash

(The Center Square) — The U.S. Supreme Court on Friday agreed to hear a case challenging President Trump's order banning asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border.

Justices on the high court agreed to hear Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, a case centered around the Trump administration's 2025 policy banning migrants from claiming asylum at the southern border.

The order was implemented on Jan. 20, 2025, Trump's first day in office during his second term. Under the order, anyone who crosses the border without necessary paperwork can be removed without the ability to claim asylum.

Solicitor General John Sauer argued the president had inherent authority to restrict asylum for immigrants. He also said Congress gave authority for the president to have discretionary authority over asylum claims.

"That proclamation rests on a commonsense understanding of the President’s inherent and delegated powers to exclude aliens," Sauer wrote in a petition to the high court. "Moreover, the [Immigration and Nationality Act] makes clear that asylum is a purely discretionary benefit."

However, lawyers for the Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services argued that the Trump administration created an additional discretionary authority that was not authorized by Congress to employ.

"The government cannot evade Congress’s limits on eligibility bars by creating a categorical ban on asylum and labeling it an exercise of 'discretion,'" the lawyers wrote. "When a group of noncitizens can never receive asylum, no ordinary speaker of English would say they are 'eligible.'"

The case will be added to the high court's docket amid a slew of immigration and asylum issues on the docket. On Nov. 30, the court will hear Wassily v. Blanche, a case challenging whether immigrants who received asylum can obtain lawful permanent resident status after the asylum status was terminated.

“The Attorney General may terminate asylum for a host of reasons – several of which rest entirely outside an asylee’s control,” lawyers for two immigrants involved in the case wrote in a petition to the high court. “Many of these former asylees and derivative spouses and children may have established strong ties to the United States over a long period of time.”

Justices on the high court will likely hear Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services in early 2027. A decision is expected in the case by June 2027.
