text:
The Supreme Court agreed Friday to consider President Donald Trump’s ban on asylum at the southern border, a pillar of the Republican president’s far-reaching crackdown on immigration.

The Trump administration wants to overturn lower court decisions that found the executive order banning asylum applications is illegal.

Democrats are preparing an onslaught of probes into the Trump administration. Investigations into the federal government’s purchase of an immigration detention facility in Minnesota, whether Robert F. Kennedy Jr. lied to Congress about his 2019 trip to Samoa and several others have been announced.

Democratic lawmakers are in Denver for their What’s Next conference, hosted by a new group called Majority Democrats, to revel in their gains and consider their legislative priorities.

Here's the Latest:

Democrats have surpassed seats gained in the 2018 midterms

Democrats have now won 256 House races, a gain of 41 seats. Ten races that will finalize the balance of power have not been called. The party has now surpassed the 40 seats it gained in the 2018 midterm elections during President Donald Trump’s first White House stint and could exceed the 43 seats it picked up in 1974 under the shadow of Watergate and President Richard Nixon’s resignation. In the Senate, Democrats have gained eight additional seats with one race still outstanding. This is the most Democratic pick ups in the Senate since President Ronald Reagan’s second midterm in 1986. The party’s post-World War II record of 15 Senate pick-ups in 1958 will remain out of reach this year.

Some Democrats take dim view of Talarico’s pitch to work with Trump

Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas said Democrats should be willing to work with Trump to make his last two years in office “the most productive of any presidency in American history.”

The idea got a cold reception from four current and future Democratic governors, spoke from the same stage where Talarico made his pitch a day earlier at Majority Democrats’ “What’s Next” conference in Denver.

Democrats should pass bills they think will help Americans live better lives and dare him to veto them, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger said.

“Frankly, he likes attention,” Spanberger said. “Eventually he’ll want to do a signing ceremony, and eventually he might sign a couple of them.”

Democrats should invite Trump’s support, but not seek to compromise with him, said Gov.-elect Phil Weiser of Colorado.

“Never bend the knee,” Weiser said. “Never try to give up on what we believe in, thinking we’re going to get something for it, because we won’t.”

Rep. Lauren Boebert loses bid for reelection

The controversial congresswoman was ousted by Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral who challenged the three-term Republican from Colorado.

Boebert had survived a close call in the 2022 election when she represented a more centrist district in the western half of the state. She moved to a new, even more conservative district on the other side of the state to ensure her combative brand of politics didn’t cost her. But with Republicans struggling across the country, she couldn’t hold on.

Rubio to assail use of international law to stymie American power in speech before conservative legal group

Secretary of State Marco Rubio is poised to assail the use of international law and standards to deprive nations like the U.S. of their sovereignty in a speech defending America’s right to act in its own interests.

Rubio plans to criticize “global bureaucrats and activist judges” who use the rules-based international order to promote universal values, according to excerpts of the speech that he will deliver later Friday to the conservative Federalist Society.

Rubio will in particular attack the International Criminal Court for attempting to bring the United States, which is not a party to the tribunal, under its jurisdiction. Rubio has vowed to dismantle the court unless it takes dramatic action to abandon investigations and attempted prosecutions into U.S. citizens of the citizens of U.S.-allied nations that are also not members.

Beyond the ICC, Rubio is set to denounce an interpretation of international law by a “global elite” to try to constrain American power and raise questions about “whether Americans have a moral right to exist as a distinct nation and people.”

Supreme Court to decide on legality of Trump executive order suspending asylum

The Supreme Court agreed Friday to consider President Donald Trump’s ban on asylum at the southern border, a pillar of the Republican president’s far-reaching crackdown on immigration.

The Trump administration wants to overturn lower court decisions that found the executive order banning asylum applications is illegal.

Federal law gives people the right to seek asylum if they fear persecution in their home countries, no matter how they arrived in the U.S.

At the same time, it also allows the executive branch to decide whether people are granted asylum. The Trump administration argues it can categorically deny asylum to migrants covered by the order and should not have to accept applications destined to be rejected.

Federal attorneys say long yearslong processing times had previously contributed to a major influx of migrants at the southern border as many were released into the country while awaiting a decision.

But immigration attorneys at the American Civil Liberties Union and National Immigrant Justice Center counter that border crossings were already falling before Trump took office.

They say his executive order is an attempt to unilaterally “eviscerate” legal protections aimed at protecting people fleeing danger in their home countries.

Incoming Nevada governor wants the state to join popular vote compact

Democrat Aaron Ford told Reno-based KOLO-TV that he changed his position on Nevada joining the national popular vote movement after doing more research and finding that the Electoral College has “racist underpinnings.”

The state’s first Black governor also noted that it has allowed some candidates to become president despite losing the popular vote nationally – most recently Republicans Donald Trump in 2016 and George W. Bush in 2000.

Nevada was one of six states where Democrats won full control of the legislature and governor’s office in the midterm elections. Those states represent a total of 71 Electoral College votes.

The 18 states that are currently part of the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact represent 222 of the 270 Electoral College votes needed to win the presidency. Under the plan, the states would allocate their electoral votes to the winner of the popular vote.

It is certain to face legal challenges that would likely land before the U.S. Supreme Court.

Congress requests Nvidia and Commerce Department officials testify

The chair of the House Foreign Relations Committee wants Nvidia’s general counsel and a senior Commerce Department official to appear before Congress.

Rep. Brian Mast’s letter this week to Jeff Kessler, undersecretary of commerce for industry and security, seeks a Dec. 2 hearing on computer chip smuggling and “reported interference by private companies into export control policies and enforcement investigations.”

Mast also wants Nvidia chief counsel Tim Teter to appear the same day for a closed-door interview about similar reports. Mast’s letter warns failing to cooperate would lead to a subpoena.

The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security in 2024 began investigating Megaspeed International, whose CEO has been accused of spying for China and had an affair with then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

The bureau later handed off the investigation to the Justice Department. A person familiar with the bureau’s investigation denied any intervention from Nvidia. The person wasn’t authorized to discuss the matter publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.

Protesters shout down Hakeem Jeffries at Democratic conference in Denver

As Jeffries began to speak, a handful of activists stood up and began yelling at him, demanding action on a Green New Deal and an arms embargo against Israel.

The audience booed them and chanted “Hakeem!” as the activists slowly left the hall, yelling “You don’t even care about us!”

Jeffries is speaking at the “What’s Next” conference in Denver, where Democrats are discussing how to hold onto the power voters gave them last week.

As Jeffries and moderator Jessica Tarlov continued their conversation, Jeffries was repeatedly interrupted.

A woman in the audience shouted “Nobody trusts you!”

A few minutes later, as Jeffries laid out his vision of how to get to universal healthcare. One man stood up and yelled, “The American people demand impeachment!” He continued to shout profanities at Jeffries, and as he was led out, another man stood up and began yelling at the Democratic leader.

“I’m from Brooklyn, this is light work,” Jeffries said.

Investigation into Congressional medical office found lapsed inspections, poor oversight

The Pentagon watchdog says multiple Navy personnel assigned to the office that provides medical care to Congress and the Supreme Court requested “health and safety transfers” and a formal complaint was filed, reinforcing “the need to strengthen oversight.”

The inspector general’s report also says investigators weren’t able to confirm the Office of the Attending Physician’s pharmacy had undergone regular inspections. It says a lack of Pentagon oversight of the office’s clinical quality management and pharmacy operations increases risks to patients and Navy medical personnel.

The report follows the sudden departure of Dr. Brian Monahan, a Navy rear admiral and the office’s attending physician. The Navy is investigating but didn’t announce the departure.

The watchdog says Monahan, who held the post for 18 years, recused himself from the investigation.

“The recusal of the senior-most official in the OAP also significantly limited our ability to identify potential issues, deficiencies, and areas for improvement,” the report said.

Democrats target RFK Jr. while courting MAHA supporters

When Democrats take over Congress in January, one of their many oversight targets will be Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Some high-ranking lawmakers have suggested impeaching him for his overhaul of longstanding vaccine guidance and cuts to medical research. But those efforts could conflict with another growing priority for many lawmakers on the left: nurturing common ground to secure support from Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again followers.

It could prove a difficult balance, since many MAHA activists still view Kennedy as their closest ally.

“It’s an unenviable position for Democrats to be in,” said Matt Motta, a professor at Boston University School of Public Health.

Democrat senator opens probe of $495 million immigration detention center

Sen. Maggie Hassan, who expects to chair the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, said the $495 million paid to buy an immigration detention facility in Minnesota was about six times more than the price offered to the state, which it declined to pay.

Hassan called on Secretary Markwayne Mullin to preserve all documents related to the purchase as the committee probes whether spending by the Department of Homeland Security was subject to “improper influence, corruption, or other violations of federal law.”

She sent a similar letter to CoreCivic, the private company that sold the facility. A company statement said the price reflected what it would cost to build the facility at today’s construction prices, minus depreciation, and was determined following an independent appraisal.

Who is Chris Van Hollen, Chuck Schumer’s challenger for majority leader?

The Democratic senator is a two term incumbent who previously represented Maryland in the House and in the legislature.

An attorney and legislator, Van Hollen was born in Karachi, Pakistan, amid his parents’ diplomatic service there, and captured attention when he pushed back against the administration’s immigration agenda.

He traveled some 2,000 miles to El Salvador to meet with the wrongly deported Kilmar Abrego Garcia, helping to establish hope and momentum for Abrego Garcia’s family in Maryland as well as the overall anti-Trump resistance.

Democratic political group launches new push to shape AI agenda before 2028

Tomorrow Together is investing $1.1 million to shape how to talk with voters about artificial intelligence, deepening its investment on an issue party leaders believe creates a stark contrast with Trump’s opposition to regulating the powerful technology.

It’s one of several Democratic groups that tried to counter the industry’s huge campaign war chest during the midterms. It pushed for new limits on AI and data centers and spent $6.5 million on candidates calling for more regulation amid fresh warnings that the technology poses existential risks to humans.

“Getting this right is going to be critical to winning people’s votes,” said Maddie Kriger, the group’s chief program officer. “It’s also not out of the realm of possibility we will see more and worse AI incidents in the next year, and we want to be prepared to move to help people and take action if that does happen.”

ICE agents came to meatpacking country. Then voters went to the polls

Immigration raids in late September sparked outrage after federal agents caused fear and disruption in the Dodge City, Kansas, area, a hub for the U.S. meatpacking industry. Voters turned out to rebuke the crackdown, helping to elect a Democratic U.S. senator from Kansas for the first time in nearly a century.

Trump has sent mixed messages on immigration enforcement since Democrats won back control of Congress, suggesting his approach to deportations was too harsh for voters while also promoting hard-liner Stephen Miller as his chief of staff. Both parties will be recalibrating their approach ahead of the next presidential campaign.

In this traditionally Republican corner of Kansas, the raids ignited a maelstrom of rage and turned many who had been apathetic into determined voters.

▶ Read more

Bessent airs frustrations with Commerce delays over Nvidia chips export enforcements

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he’s frustrated with the Commerce Department’s delay in controlling the export of advanced Nvidia chips to China.

Bessent said on CNBC Friday that the Treasury, State and Defense departments as well as the U.S. Trade Representative were in favor of adding Nvidia partner Megaspeed to an export control list for months, but that the Commerce Department was in charge of the matter.

“I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s,” Bessent said.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after acknowledging an affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence reportedly suspects to be a Chinese spy.

The GOP-led Senate Banking Committee sent letters Thursday seeking testimony from Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Jensen Huang about the department’s role and the national security implications of Nvidia chip sales to China.

What Schumer’s supporters are saying

Ohio Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown said Senate Majority Leader is a difficult job, experience is necessary and Schumer has proven himself with legislative successes when they held the Senate under President Joe Biden.

“Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?” posted Maine Sen. Angus King. “Chuck Schumer is one of the principal architects of the most successful election in modern history, and I see no reason to change the leadership that helped make that success possible.”

Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto, D-Nev., posted Thursday evening that Schumer was key in “securing a historic majority. I will be supporting him as our Democratic leader.”

What Van Hollen’s supporters are saying

While most Democratic senators have either said they are supporting Schumer or are undecided, Van Hollen has at least two backers: Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who won a competitive election in his state last week, and progressive standard-bearer Bernie Sanders.

El-Sayed posted on X Thursday night that their majority will need “bold leadership.”

“I called on Sen. @ChrisVanHollen to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience,” El-Sayed wrote. “We need both right now. Which is why I’m proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority.”

Sen. Sanders posted Thursday night that the American people “want a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families. That is why I am supporting Senator Chris Van Hollen to lead Senate Democrats.”

Van Hollen’s run exposes a rift in the party

Divisions over Schumer have simmered over the last two years, since he sided with Republicans on a spending vote in 2025.

Even as Schumer has redeemed himself within his caucus since then — leading them through a government shutdown last year and orchestrating huge wins in the election — many in the Democratic base are agitating for generational change.

Van Hollen, 67, is not that much younger than Schumer, 75, but he’s positioned himself as a new face and said he’s considering a run for president.

Schumer is preparing a plan for the Democrats first 100 days in power

Schumer has been working with Democratic senators one-on-one to form an agenda for 2027 that includes healthcare and tariff legislation and efforts to stop the Iran war.

In a statement after Van Hollen’s announcement, Schumer said he welcomes any discussion about the future of the caucus.

“I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader,” Schumer said. “I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.”

Van Hollen to challenge Schumer for Senate Democratic leader

“The American people called for change,” Van Hollen said as he announced his challenge of Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer.

“It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership,” Van Hollen said. “This is not about any one person — it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”

The question of whether to reelect Schumer has already divided the caucus and many senators have declined to say publicly how they will vote. In private deliberations about what message to take from the election, many are torn — Schumer recruited many of the party’s winning candidates and raised money for them, but progressive groups are pushing for his removal.

Some Republicans gingerly push back on Trump rhetoric

Few echoed Trump’s argument in a social media post this week that there were problems with the election. In conceding her closely fought Senate contest in Mississippi, Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith said she would “respect the decision” of voters.

And several Republicans, including Sens. Joni Ernst of Iowa, Tim Scott of South Carolina and John Cornyn of Texas and Rep. Mike Lawler of New York, posted pictures of incoming Democrats in a nod toward postelection unity.

Rep. James Comer of Kentucky meanwhile pushed back against White House warnings that oversight could amount to “blatant criminality.”

“Regardless of who is in the White House, there’s always going to be a strong desire for the Oversight Committee to be a check and balance on the executive branch,” said Comer, who oversaw extensive investigations of Democratic President Joe Biden as House Oversight chairman.

Hegseth vote was a test of Republican independence from Trump

It’s perhaps their biggest question going forward. Trump’s policies on trade and the war in Iran contributed to voter discontent with the GOP, and now that he’s in the last two years of his second term, the election defeats challenge the durability of his Make America Great Again movement.

But House Republicans showed no rush to distance themselves from the president as even his critics helped block an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Only Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie, who led the push alongside Democrats, broke ranks.

“What I found out tonight is they still haven’t broken from the spell of Donald Trump,” Massie said after the vote. “He still controls this conference.”

Senate Republicans showed less desire for combat

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., unsuccessfully sought to delay his party’s leadership elections in the Senate, arguing for a different approach.

“You cut rural healthcare spending, when you abandon pro-lifers, when you abandon the poor, when you abandon the needy, when you abandon working people, you’re gonna get your butt kicked,” Hawley said. “And you’re gonna deserve it.”

Hawley and a small group of conservatives huddled for hours in the Old Senate Chamber arguing for a consideration of alternatives to John Thune of South Dakota. But no one came forward.

“It’s a bad job,” Hawley acknowledged before Republicans ultimately backed Thune without so much as a voice vote.

“We’re going to let our leader be the leader,” said Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, who will lead party efforts to regain seats in 2028.

House Republicans opted for a bare-knuckled leader

Republicans are weighing how to proceed, balancing calls for moderation against an impulse for hard-line positions that might reenergize the party’s base. Each chamber took different tracks, previewing divisions that may lie ahead.

In the House, the Republicans who will remain in Washington next year largely represent staunchly conservative districts where Trump remains popular. Their decision to elect Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan as their next leader reflected a fighting stance.

Jordan is a co-founder of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, currently chairs the Judiciary Committee and has previously chaired the Oversight Committee. From those positions, he’s waged heated fights against Democrats and become a top Trump ally.

“The way that Jim fights says a lot about where this conference is,” said Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla.

GOP lawmaker’s lament: ‘We have failed’

There was widespread frustration that Republicans who were awarded full control of the White House and Congress just two years earlier had lost touch with voters.

“We collectively failed,” said Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., who is trailing her Democratic challenger in a district Republicans carried by more than 18 percentage points in 2024. “The American people let us know we have failed in this governing experience for this Congress.”

The anger is sharp in part because of the rosy predictions from top Republicans ahead of the election. House Speaker Mike Johnson had insisted the polls were wrong and Republicans would retain their majority. Back on Capitol Hill this week, Johnson blamed voters, saying they made the “wrong choice.”

Rep. Virginia Foxx, R-N.C., who is also trailing a Democratic rival, said people kept telling her she couldn’t lose. But she knew otherwise.

“I couldn’t get anybody to listen to me,” she said. “People just didn’t think it could happen, but we knew it could.”

text:
By Lindsay Whitehurst / Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court agreed Friday to consider President Donald Trump’s ban on asylum at the southern border, a pillar of the Republican president’s far-reaching crackdown on immigration.

The Trump administration wants to overturn lower court decisions that found the executive order banning asylum applications is illegal.

Federal law gives people the right to seek asylum if they fear persecution in their home countries, no matter how they arrived in the United States.

RELATED: Supreme Court grants review of Trump administration’s mandatory detention policy for immigrants

At the same time, it also allows the executive branch to decide whether people are granted asylum. The Trump administration argues it can categorically deny asylum to migrants covered by the order and should not have to accept applications destined to be rejected.

Federal attorneys say long yearslong processing times had previously contributed to a major influx of migrants at the southern border as many were released into the country while awaiting a decision.

But immigration attorneys at the American Civil Liberties Union and National Immigrant Justice Center counter that border crossings were already falling before Trump took office.

They say his executive order is an attempt to unilaterally “eviscerate” legal protections aimed at protecting people fleeing danger in their home countries.

SEE ALSO: Supreme Court lets quick deportations to third countries resume for now while it weighs Trump policy

The executive branch does decide whether to grant asylum, which allows people to live and work legally in the U.S. But those decisions are supposed to be made on an individual basis and the law doesn’t allow the president to unilaterally stop people from even applying, those attorneys argue.

The asylum ban was one of a series of immigration restrictions Trump rolled out upon his return to office in 2025. It has remained in place during the litigation.

Key aspects of the H-2A agricultural guestworker program are subject to federal court battles that will shape its regulations and how they’re enforced, according to a legal expert.

For instance, the U.S. Supreme Court is expected to decide whether farmers are entitled to a federal jury trial over civil penalties for alleged H-2A violations, said Leon Sequeira, an attorney and former U.S. Assistant Secretary of Labor.

The eventual ruling could be “earth-shattering,” as it has the potential to “upend” the U.S. Department of Labor’s current practice of imposing fines through an in-house administrative process, which is totally controlled by the agency’s own employees, Sequeira said.

“This is a huge, huge case for the H-2A program. It probably will be the most impactful case in the history of the program, at least on the enforcement side,” he said during the Worker and Farmer Labor Association’s Nov. 12 conference in Salem, Ore.

A New Jersey vegetable farm, Sun Valley Orchards, was assessed $550,000 by the DOL and was repeatedly dealt setbacks in trying to challenge the fines, but ultimately prevailed before the Third U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals last year.

The Third Circuit ruled that the enforcement of H-2A contracts involves “private rights” that must be subject to a jury trial in federal court.

The DOL has challenged that ruling before the nation’s highest court, arguing that H-2A pertains to immigration, and thus relates to “public rights” that can be adjudicated through the in-house administrative process.

“Whichever way it goes will have a monumental impact,” Sequeira said.

Currently, farmers can still challenge the penalties imposed by DOL in federal court once the in-house administrative process is concluded, but few are willing to spend that much time and money on litigation with an uncertain outcome, he later told Capital Press.

If such civil penalties were decided directly by a jury trial in federal court, the legal battle wouldn’t be as drawn-out and the DOL might be more selective about the cases it choses to litigate — or more reasonable about negotiating a resolution, Sequeira said.

Additionally, federal courts must currently adopt a deferential standard of review when they encounter the DOL’s determinations, which means the agency’s decisions are upheld as long as they’re reasonable, he said.

If such cases went directly to federal court, they would be reviewed “de novo,” or with fresh eyes, without deferring to the agency, Sequeira said.

The Supreme Court’s eventual ruling is expected to have implications for the federal government’s enforcement of other regulatory violations as well, beyond the H-2A program, he said.

“This issue about jury trials and prosecution by agencies, this is not limited to DOL. This is going on across the government,” he said. “What does every federal agency or nearly every agency do? They go after people and assess fines, and try to collect through in house agency courts.”

The DOL’s “adverse effect wage rates,” or AEWR, which determine how much H-2A workers are paid, are also in the midst of a fight in federal court, Sequeira said.

Last year, the agency enacted new AEWR rules that were challenged by the United Farm Workers organization, he said. The lawsuit argued that DOL should not reduce H-2A wages based on free housing provided by employers and challenged other aspects of how the rates are calculated.

In August, the federal court overseeing the case decided that DOL committed procedural violations in implementing the AEWR rules and order the agency to reconsider or better explain them by the end of the year, Sequeira said.

It’s unclear whether the DOL will be able to issue new regulations by Dec. 30 as ordered by the judge, or if the agency will challenge the legality of that deadline, he said. “That is a potential avenue for appeal if they decided to appeal, so that’s still at least theoretically possible.”

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court agreed Friday to consider President Donald Trump’s ban on asylum at the southern border, a pillar of the Republican president’s far-reaching crackdown on immigration.

The Trump administration is asking the justices to overturn lower court decisions that found it was illegal to block asylum applications following an executive order that called the situation at the southern border an “invasion.” The suit is the latest in a series of immigration cases before the high court.

Federal law allows people to seek asylum if they fear persecution in their home countries, no matter how they arrived in the U.S.

At the same time, it also lets the executive branch decide whether people are granted asylum. The Trump administration argues it can categorically deny asylum to migrants covered by the order and should not have to accept applications destined to be rejected.

Federal attorneys say yearslong processing times had previously contributed to a major influx of migrants at the southern border as many were released into the country while awaiting a decision.

“Since the proclamation took effect, border encounters have fallen by 93 percent, dropping to the lowest levels since the 1960s,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote. The executive order has been the “single most important factor in the President’s success at the border," the Homeland Security Department's general counsel, James Percival, said in a social media post.

Attorneys from the American Civil Liberties Union and several immigration rights groups counter that border crossings were already falling before Trump took office.

They say his executive order is an unlawful attempt to "invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates” legal protections aimed at protecting people fleeing danger in their home countries.

text:
Washington — The Supreme Court on Friday said it will take up a legal fight over President Trump's directive suspending access to the asylum system and other legal protections for migrants illegally crossing the southern border.

The case is the latest involving Mr. Trump's second-term immigration agenda that the Supreme Court will decide in the coming months. The justices are also considering the legality of removing migrants to third countries and indefinitely detaining immigrants in the U.S. illegally without access to a bond hearing.

A decision in the cases is expected by the end of June or early July.

Mr. Trump has made cracking down on immigration a cornerstone of his second term, which has seen enhanced enforcement operations in major U.S. cities and mass deportations of people in the U.S. illegally. Unlawful crossings at the U.S.-Mexico border have reached historic lows and immigration detentions have set new highs under the president's second administration.

As part of his efforts to curb illegal immigration into the U.S., Mr. Trump issued a proclamation on his first day back in the White House claiming that there is an "invasion" at the southern border. The president suspended the entry of migrants crossing the southern border between ports of entry and barred them from seeking asylum and other legal protections that would allow them to remain in the U.S.

The Department of Homeland Security then issued guidance implementing the president's directive. Immigration authorities have since relied on the policy to summarily remove migrants entering the country illegally without allowing them to apply for asylum.

In February 2025, three nonprofit groups and 13 people filed a class-action lawsuit challenging Mr. Trump's proclamation and the administration's guidance. Several months later, a federal judge in Washington set aside the Trump administration's asylum restrictions and found them unlawful.

The judge, Randolph Moss, found that neither the Constitution nor federal immigration law gave the Trump administration the authority to replace the rules and procedures enacted by Congress. The judge also said that immigration law does not give the president the unilateral authority to limit the rights of noncitizens in the U.S. to apply for asylum or other protections.

As part of his decision, Moss certified a class of all people covered by the president's proclamation and blocked the Trump administration from enforcing the directive against them.

The Trump administration appealed, and in April, a divided three-judge panel upheld the district court's decision and ruled that the proclamation and guidance exceeded the president's authority. The two judges in the majority also found that the president does not have the power to suspend migrants' right to apply for asylum or deport migrants under his administration's new summary removal proceedings.

The Trump administration has continued to enforce its policy suspending access to asylum while legal proceedings have continued, and the D.C. Circuit halted its ruling against DHS pending Supreme Court review.

text:
A man is suing the federal government after immigration enforcement agents allegedly seriously injured him during an arrest in January in St. Paul.

The lawsuit alleges that agents used excessive force in the arrest of Orbin Henriquez Serrano, a 28-year-old man from Honduras. The incident left him in need of knee surgery. It also alleges agents engaged in racial profiling in stopping him in the first place, and arrested him without a warrant.

Henriquez Serrano had stopped at a Speedway gas station on Snelling Avenue before work, just days after federal agents had killed Renee Good. Nearly 20 agents, led by then-Border Patrol Commander Greg Bovino, stopped him and asked about his immigration status.

The lawsuit alleges that agents did not have a warrant, but “profiled Mr. Henriquez Serrano based solely on his Hispanic appearance.”

A state court record search shows no charges for any crimes for Henriquez Serrano.

Henriquez Serrano told agents he would not talk to them without a lawyer and got back into his car, according to the lawsuit. Agents surrounded his car, and without warning, one broke the driver’s side window with a hammer.

Several bystanders took video of the incident, which was shared widely on social media. The lawsuit notes that some agents pushed observers, and alleges that Bovino “failed to maintain proper supervision” and instead “snarled at protesters.”

Agents then pulled Henriquez Serrano out of the passenger door of his car and forced him to the ground. He was unconscious by the time agents dragged him to their vehicle.

“The agents either failed to notice that Ms. Henriquez Serrano was no longer conscious or they didn’t care,” the lawsuit says. “Instead, they kept yelling at his defenseless and motionless body.”

Agents drove Henriquez Serrano to the federal Whipple building. The lawsuit alleges that this broke rules governing arrests, which require agents to give aid if someone is unconscious before moving them.

Shortly after the arrest, Henriquez Serrano was shackled and taken to Camp East Montana in Texas. After a week there, he was shackled again and put on a plane to Honduras, where he’s remained since.

While there, the lawsuit says, he’s been dealing with anxiety and trouble sleeping. He also sustained a knee injury during the arrest. According to the lawsuit, agents reinjured his ACL, which he had surgery on in 2022. He’ll need surgery again to repair the damage.

In April, Henriquez Serrano filed complaints with the Department of Homeland Security, Immigration and Customs Enforcement and U.S. Customs and Border Protection; no agency made a decision on those complaints. He was required to wait six months after filing those complaints to file a lawsuit.

The Department of Homeland Security has not responded to a request for comment.

The lawsuit asks for over $1 million to be paid to Henriquez Serrano.

This story is part of our live coverage. Go to live updates.

text:
WASHINGTON — Taking up another key aspect of President Donald Trump’s hard-line immigration agenda, the Supreme Court on Friday agreed to decide whether the administration has the authority to ban asylum claims at the southern border.

Although a federal judge ruled that the policy Trump enacted on the first day of his second term was unlawful, it has remained in effect while litigation continues.

The Supreme Court’s ruling, due before the end of June, will be the final word on the Trump administration’s sweeping assertion of presidential power over people trying to make asylum claims at the border, notwithstanding federal law enacted by Congress that lays out a procedure to do so.

The asylum dispute is the third significant case on Trump’s immigration policies that the court is considering, while the justices could take up other Trump-related cases in the coming months.

The ban stems from a proclamation the president issued Jan. 20, 2025, that declared an “invasion” on the southern border.

Under one of its provisions, anyone who crosses the border without required paperwork can immediately be removed without the ability to claim asylum.

Immigration hawks have long complained that people who enter the country illegally apply for asylum in order to stay in the country while their cases are processed, even if they do not have valid claims.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in court papers that the president has sweeping authority to bar entry to the U.S., both under specific federal immigration laws and the powers delegated to him in the Constitution.

The policy “rests on a commonsense understanding of the President’s inherent and delegated powers to exclude aliens,” Sauer wrote.

He pointed to a provision of immigration law that says the president can restrict entry of anyone when he deems it would be “detrimental to the interests of the United States.”

The policy was challenged by 13 unnamed plaintiffs, as well as three immigration groups: the Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, the Las Americas Immigrant Advocacy Center and the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project.

Their lawyers at the American Civil Liberties Union argue that the ban flouts the asylum rules implemented by Congress in the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA). Under that process, immigrants can argue that they have “credible fear” of torture or persecution if they are returned to their home country.

The president “may not invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute,” they wrote in court papers.

In July 2025, Washington-based U.S. District Judge Randolph Moss ruled against the administration, saying that nothing in the Constitution or immigration law “grants the president ... authority to replace the comprehensive rules and procedures set forth in the INA.”

In April this year, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit upheld Moss’ ruling, leading the administration to seek Supreme Court review.

In one of the two other immigration cases on the Supreme Court docket, the justices will consider the administration’s ongoing efforts to deport immigrants to “third countries” they have no previous connection to if they cannot be returned to their home nations.

The other case concerns the administration’s attempt to detain indefinitely thousands of people in deportation proceedings, a break from previous administrations, which released those immigrants while their cases were adjudicated.

The asylum case follows a related ruling in favor of the president’s authority over the border in June.

The Supreme Court has had a steady stream of Trump-related immigration cases dating back to his first term, when it upheld his travel ban on people from mostly Muslim-majority countries entering the United States.

text:
13th November 2026

IPRT welcomes the publication of the CPT’s new Standards on Immigration Detention.

The Committee has issued a number of guiding principles, including that immigration detention must not be punitive. A fundamental aspect of this principle is that prisons are designed for people who have been convicted or suspected of a criminal offence and are not suitable for administrative detention. In this context, the Committee has observed people in immigration detention in prisons at a disadvantage regarding access to legal assistance, contact with the outside world and out-of-cell time. This is particularly important for those who are applying for international protection, who require access to a solicitor and expert legal guidance in the application process.

While states have a right to establish their own immigration policies, the state also has a duty to uphold its obligations under the European Convention on Human Rights, including the absolute prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 3. This means that any place of detention, including immigration detention, must respect the basic dignity and humanity of the people who are placed there.

As a member of the NGO Coalition on the EU Migration Pact in Ireland, IPRT has consistently raised concerns regarding the use of prisons as detention facilities for immigration and asylum purposes. With the commencement of the new International Protection Act earlier this year, IPRT remains concerned about the use of immigration detention under the new system and the placement of people in administrative detention in prisons. For the period from January to September this year, data from the Irish Prison Service (IPS) indicates that the average number of people per month being held in prisons for immigration purposes was 39, which is more than triple the average for the same period in 2024.

In our recent PIPS 2025 report, we note that not only is holding people in prison for immigration purposes contrary to Ireland’s human rights obligations, but it places increased strain on a prison system that is already operating at unsafe capacity levels. As it stands, it is unclear what the future of immigration detention in Ireland will look like. IPRT urges the government to implement the CPT standards and adhere to its human rights obligations.

text:
This article originally appeared in the National Post.

By David Thomas, November 13, 2026

The immigration plan released as part of Budget 2026 raises serious questions about whether the Liberal government is truly committed to reducing immigration.

The Immigration Levels Plan for 2027-2029 sets out the annual targets that Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) is instructed to pursue.

The targets for the next three years remain at 380,000 new permanent resident admissions, which is the same target set last year for 2026. However, the plan indicates that this target is actually just a midway point in projected admissions, which could potentially reach 422,000 each year for the next three years. If so, this level is not considerably lower than the 483,640 individuals who became permanent residents in 2024 or the former targets for 2025 and 2026, which had been set at 500,000 annually in the 2023 plan.

But are these numbers telling the whole story?

In last year’s plan, the government also included a so-called “one-time” initiative to grant permanent residence to up to 148,000 people already living in Canada (mostly protected persons and temporary workers) during 2026 and 2027. It seems that plan will not, in fact, be a one-off. Last week’s budget included another “time-limited” additional allotment of 200,000 permanent residence spots for people already in Canada by the end of 2027.

In that case, isn’t the real number 580,000 permanent residence admissions for next year?

Prime Minister Mark Carney has acknowledged that immigration levels under Justin Trudeau’s government were “far too high” and outpaced Canada’s capacity to accommodate population growth with housing, infrastructure, health care and other essential services. Carney promised to lower and stabilize permanent resident admissions. However, in a recent interview with the New York Times, Carney hinted that he was contemplating a “controlled increase” in immigration levels.

Beyond his government’s messaging around stable immigration intake, it’s worth looking at the broader picture. It may provide a clearer indication of what Carney has in mind.

One major consideration is Canada’s temporary resident population. As of July 2026, Statistics Canada reported approximately 1.5 million people holding work permits, another 399,133 holding study permits and an additional 220,770 holding both. These remain substantial numbers, even after the reductions in international student and temporary worker levels in prior years.

There is also the asylum system. Statistics Canada measures this using the broader category of asylum claimants, protected persons and related groups. The number stood at approximately 530,090 in the July report. There are also large groups that are not counted in the statistics, such as temporary status holders waiting for extensions (now estimated to take 310 days to process) and the estimated 500,000 to 600,000 people who remain in Canada without any valid status. These figures need to be understood separately from ordinary work and study permits, but they are another important part of Canada’s overall immigration picture.

There’s also a fundamental change coming to how the Canadian government determines citizenship. The Carney government has enacted amendments to the Citizenship Act, originally proposed by the Trudeau government, allowing citizenship by descent to extend beyond the first generation of Canadians born abroad.

Under the new legislation, people born abroad before Dec. 15, 2025, may qualify through multiple generations of Canadian ancestry, even if they have never lived in Canada themselves. In 2024, the parliamentary budget officer estimated that approximately 115,000 people could be affected by these changes over five years. The actual number of people who may ultimately establish their entitlement remains uncertain.

All of this raises a broader question: Is the government actually reducing immigration, or is it simply measuring it in a way that understates the overall scale of population growth and the number of people obtaining permanent status?

Canadians were told that our country would “return to sustainable immigration levels through continued decreases to temporary resident arrivals and stabilized permanent resident admissions.” But when permanent resident admissions, temporary residents, asylum claimants and expanded citizenship by descent are considered together, the picture is considerably more complicated.

It appears that substantial population growth remains part of Canada’s foreseeable future. The question is whether the government has a credible plan to ensure that housing, infrastructure, healthcare and public services can keep pace — and whether Canadians have had a meaningful say in how quickly their country should grow.

David Thomas is a lawyer and mediator in British Columbia. He worked for 25 years as an immigration lawyer before serving as chairperson of the Canadian Human Rights Tribunal. He is now a senior fellow at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute.

text:
Earlier this month, voters made their voices heard, and they plainly had a lot to say. While there are lots of important takeaways from this year’s midterm elections, there were a few that stood out as we at CAC think about the work we’ve been doing over the last two years—and will continue to be doing in the years to come.

First, voters want a check on the Trump administration and a return to the rule of law. That’s something that we’ve been working for in cases up and down the federal courts. For example, CAC filed an amicus brief supporting D.C. District Court Judge Boasberg’s authority to investigate the administration’s defiance of his court’s order to halt and turn around the planes illegally transporting Venezuelan immigration detainees to a notorious Salvadoran prison where they would be subjected to physical abuse and deprived of food, water, and medical care. Our brief explains that federal courts have the inherent authority to investigate and sanction bad-faith conduct, including fraud on the court.

And we filed an amicus brief in support of Maurene Comey’s challenge to the Trump administration’s attempt to terminate her. Comey, an award-winning prosecutor, was allegedly fired because members of President Donald Trump’s inner circle wanted to punish her father, James Comey. Last month, the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York delivered a win for the rule of law when it reinstated Maurene Comey. Echoing CAC’s amicus brief, the court held that civil service statutes constrained the administration’s ability to fire Assistant U.S. Attorneys.

Second, voters are deeply concerned about corruption. We are too, and that’s why when Florida officials gave President Trump a piece of state-owned property worth hundreds of millions of dollars, we went to court to challenge this violation of the Constitution’s Domestic Emoluments Clause. The Domestic Emoluments Clause provides that when the President is in office, he or she “shall not receive within that Period any other Emolument”—meaning any benefit, profit, or gift—“from the United States, or any of them.” The Founders were deeply concerned that government corruption could undermine the new republic, leading Presidents to put their personal interests above those of the nation. Our lawsuit, on behalf of a Miami nonprofit, Miami residents, and a Miami Dade College student, asks the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida to void this unconstitutional transaction and hold President Trump accountable to the Constitution.

Third, voters are deeply concerned about the impact of data centers on our communities. In Southaven, Mississippi, Elon Musk’s xAI, which runs the “Grok” chatbot, installed and is illegally operating 60 unpermitted gas turbines. To satisfy the bot’s massive power demands, these turbines are pumping air pollution into a nearby residential community, creating noise and smog while driving up health risks. The NAACP and its local affiliate sued xAI on behalf of community members for violating the Clean Air Act. The plaintiffs invoked the Clean Air Act’s citizen-suit provision, which allows injured persons to initiate a lawsuit against polluters. Instead of stepping in to enforce the law, the Trump administration is trying to intervene to get the lawsuit dismissed, arguing that this important mechanism for holding polluters accountable is unconstitutional. CAC filed an amicus brief explaining why the Clear Air Act’s citizen-suit provision is constitutional.

While the voters made their voices heard earlier this month, there’s going to be a lot of work to do to achieve the change that they’re seeking. We’re energized to be doing that work and are ready for this next chapter.

text:
We’re here to cover the moments that matter. Help us keep showing up.

DECORAH — Community members gathered at Water Street Plaza on Thursday, Nov. 5, to protest the detention of a Decorah-area resident by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), calling for his release and demanding that local officials stop cooperating with federal immigration authorities.

The protest followed the detention of Jaime Ulises Melgara Rivera, who was arrested by the Winneshiek County Sheriff's Office on Nov. 2 following a traffic stop and subsequently transferred into ICE custody, according to organizers with Decorah Community for Immigrant Rights (DCIR).

Joshua Ratel-Khan, a DCIR member, said Rivera had been booked into the Winneshiek County Jail before ICE took custody of him the morning of Nov. 5.

According to the Winneshiek County Sheriff's Office arrest report, Rivera, 34, of Mabel, Minnesota, was arrested at 3:08 p.m. Nov. 2 following a traffic stop at the intersection of Mechanic Street and West Water Street in Decorah. He was booked into the Winneshiek County Jail on charges of no valid driver's license, failure to yield upon left turn and failure to provide proof of insurance.

Organizers criticized the decision to transfer Rivera to federal immigration authorities.

“It's disgusting that someone who just had a mere traffic violation was arrested and put over into ICE's hands as a result,” Ratel-Khan said.

An online announcement promoting the protest identified the initial traffic stop as involving a failure to yield. It also said Rivera was taken to the county jail because he did not have a driver's license or car insurance. The announcement said local authorities detained him until ICE arrived.

Ratel-Khan said Rivera was taken into ICE custody the morning of Nov. 5 and believed he was being held at the Linn County Jail in Iowa. He said he contacted the Winneshiek County Jail seeking information about Rivera's whereabouts but received little information beyond confirmation that ICE had picked him up.

DecorahNews.com had not independently confirmed Rivera's location or the transfer to ICE as of publication.

The lack of information about Rivera's situation was a central concern among protesters, who argued that local cooperation with federal immigration authorities can leave families and community members uncertain about the whereabouts and circumstances of detained individuals.

“When I called the Winneshiek County Jail today, they didn't even know what had happened to him,” Ratel-Khan said. “They just said that he had been picked up by ICE. They don't know anything more than that.”

Ratel-Khan questioned the accountability surrounding the transfer, saying residents should not be handed over to a federal agency without their community knowing what happens to them.

The protest's demands extended beyond Rivera's individual case. Demonstrators called for his release and urged the city of Decorah, the Winneshiek County Sheriff's Office and other local government entities to end their cooperation with ICE.

During remarks at the gathering, speaker Gabriel Eide called on the Decorah City Council, the city's Human Rights Commission, the sheriff's office and the Winneshiek County Board of Supervisors to take action. He urged attendees to make their opposition known and become involved in efforts to prevent similar incidents.

“We do not want our community to be a part of what is happening,” Eide said, encouraging residents to make their voices heard and sign up for opportunities to become involved in the organizing effort. “Nobody should be taken from our community.”

Community members remember Rivera

Beyond calls for policy changes, the gathering included emotional reflections from people who know Rivera personally.

Speaker Mariann Fant, who said she had attended an English club with Rivera, described him as “outgoing, friendly and eager to connect with others.”

Fant remembered their conversations as a lively exchange, saying Rivera would ask about other people's days, share stories about his own and always have something to say in return.

She said Rivera's personality made him difficult to overlook when he entered a room.

“And it doesn't really matter what you say, because he's got a response to that,” Fant said, describing his ability to carry on conversations in his second language as admirable.

The possibility that Rivera might not return to the English club was particularly upsetting to Fant.

“I hope, I hope that we can get him back to English Club,” she said.

The remarks underscored the personal impact of the detention on people who viewed Rivera not simply as someone caught up in an immigration enforcement action, but as a friend and familiar presence in their community.

Ratel-Khan questioned the consequences of an arrest that, according to organizers, began with a traffic violation and asked attendees to consider how many people had committed similar traffic infractions without facing consequences beyond a warning or citation.

For Rivera, however, the situation had resulted in detention by federal immigration authorities and uncertainty about his future, Ratel-Khan noted.

He also urged attendees to consider the possibility of a friend or loved one being taken into federal custody without their family knowing where they were being held.

Push for local policy changes

The protest also brought renewed attention to DCIR's effort to establish a separation ordinance in Decorah.

The proposed ordinance seeks to limit cooperation between local law enforcement and ICE, including practices that could facilitate the transfer of people from local custody into federal immigration detention.

Ratel-Khan said the organization believes local resources and law enforcement practices should not be used to facilitate immigration enforcement.

He said the group has been advocating for a separation ordinance because local cooperation can create a pathway for federal immigration authorities to take custody of people who initially encounter local law enforcement for other reasons.

“There's no reason our tax dollars, our city resources, should ever be used to put someone like Jaime into ICE custody,” Ratel-Khan said during the rally.

In July, the Decorah Human Rights Commission advanced a proposed separation ordinance to the City Council following a 3-2 vote. The proposal came after immigrant-rights advocates spent months organizing in support of restrictions on local cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

The Decorah City Council subsequently rejected the ordinance in a 7-0 vote on July 20.

Council members cited concerns about potential conflicts with Iowa law and the possibility of financial consequences for the city. Under Iowa law, local governments found by a court to have intentionally violated requirements concerning cooperation with federal immigration authorities can face the loss of state funding.

The proposed ordinance had included restrictions on unnecessary sharing of information about individuals in police custody, direct transfers of people from local custody to ICE and other forms of assistance to federal immigration enforcement.

Ratel-Khan has previously argued that local jails and police departments play an important role in federal immigration enforcement.

In July, he told Radio Iowa that local jails were a primary way ICE takes people into custody in Iowa.

Despite the City Council's rejection of the ordinance, DCIR members have continued advocating for changes to local policies.

At Thursday's gathering, speakers emphasized that residents still have opportunities to influence local decisions through public meetings, community organizing and direct communication with elected officials.

Calls for accountability and continued organizing

Ratel-Khan said the detention illustrates why local residents should pay attention to how their government interacts with federal immigration authorities.

He said Rivera's detention might not have become widely known if a community member had not happened to check the Winneshiek County inmate website and noticed his presence in the jail.

Ratel-Khan said similar situations have occurred previously in the county. He pointed to public records discussed during the lawsuit initiated by Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird involving Sheriff Dan Marx as evidence that other detainees had experienced similar circumstances.

He argued that immigration-related detentions can happen without widespread public awareness, leaving families and friends searching for information.

For Ratel-Khan, the issue ultimately comes down to what kind of community Decorah wants to be.

“I think that we have the choice about what kind of community Decorah will be,” he said.

He said he wants to live in a community where residents look out for one another and local officials take concrete steps to prevent people from being transferred into immigration custody through local cooperation.

The gathering concluded with continued calls for Rivera's release, greater public awareness and participation in efforts to change local policies.

text:
Laflota/Depositphotos

A Supreme Court decision changes Texas plans

A Texas border project can move forward after the U.S. Supreme Court lifted a construction ban on November 9, 2026. The decision affects Big Bend, where roads, barriers, and surveillance technology have faced challenges over environmental protections.

The ruling permits the Trump administration to resume work while the underlying lawsuit continues. However, the justices have not issued a final judgment on the project.

Depositphotos

The justices voted eight to one

The Supreme Court granted the federal government's emergency request in an unsigned 8-1 decision, setting aside an injunction that stopped construction. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only justice who publicly opposed granting the request.

The majority concluded that federal law strongly favors prompt border construction and limits judicial review of certain decisions made by Homeland Security. Jackson offered no explanation for her disagreement.

Shutterstock

A 517-mile stretch is involved

The project covers the Big Bend Border Patrol sector, stretching approximately 517 miles along the U.S.-Mexico boundary in West Texas. It includes remote desert landscapes, communities along the Rio Grande, and several areas managed for public recreation and conservation.

Federal plans involve different types of border infrastructure across the sector, rather than a continuous steel wall through every mile. Specific designs vary by location.

BalkansCat/Depositphotos

The project is not just a border wall

In May 2026, Customs and Border Protection said a major construction contract would not fund 30-foot steel walls inside Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park, or Black Gap Wildlife Management Area.

Instead, the agency outlined plans for cameras, sensors, low-profile vehicle barriers, and patrol roads, although some construction details remain subject to change.

Other parts of the sector have different construction plans, including taller physical barriers. This distinction matters when describing the project.

Shutterstock

Big Bend's landscape creates challenges

Big Bend National Park covers more than 801,000 acres, stretching from the Chisos Mountains to the Rio Grande. The park's long international boundary places its landscape directly alongside areas where federal officials want better patrol access.

Its desert terrain also affects construction choices, since roads must navigate mountains, canyons, and remote stretches.

Fun fact: The park shares 118 miles of border with Mexico.

Depositphotos

The Rio Grande shapes construction plans

The Rio Grande shapes both the international boundary and the visitor experience in Big Bend National Park. Federal planners must consider river access while deciding where patrol routes and vehicle barriers could operate.

Park officials also manage scenic canyons that attract hikers, photographers, and river visitors throughout the year.

Fun fact: Santa Elena Canyon stretches roughly 20 miles along the river.

Depositphotos

Three plaintiffs started the legal challenge

The legal fight began in April, when Friends of the Ruidosa Church, the Center for Biological Diversity, and river guide Danny William Miller Jr. sued federal officials. Their complaint questioned whether Homeland Security could bypass numerous laws to accelerate construction across the region.

The plaintiffs argued that these waivers threatened environmental and historical protections. They also challenged the legal authority behind the government's decision.

Depositphotos

A federal judge stopped the work

On October 2, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone ordered a temporary halt to construction and ground-disturbing activities throughout the Big Bend sector. Her written explanation followed on October 14, outlining concerns about the government's use of broad legal waivers.

The injunction required federal officials to comply with otherwise applicable laws while the case continued. That order prompted the administration's emergency Supreme Court request.

Depositphotos

A 1996 law became the deciding factor

A federal immigration law enacted in 1996 sits at the center of the Supreme Court dispute. Its Section 102 permits the Homeland Security secretary to waive certain legal requirements to speed border barrier and road construction.

The same provision restricts lawsuits over those waivers to constitutional claims. The justices found that the challengers' major questions argument remained a statutory dispute, not a constitutional claim.

Depositphotos

Federal officials cited rising delay costs

Federal officials argued that delaying construction would cost the government approximately $500,000 each day. They also maintained that building barriers and installing detection equipment would improve agents' ability to monitor remote stretches and respond to crossings.

The Supreme Court considered the government's interests alongside the concerns raised by opponents. Its order favored allowing work to proceed during further litigation rather than continuing the construction freeze.

Depositphotos

Billions are committed to border projects

Congress approved approximately $46.55 billion for border infrastructure nationwide in 2025. Separately, five federal construction contracts associated with the Big Bend sector total roughly $7.5 billion, covering planned barriers, patrol roads, and surveillance systems. These contract values do not mean the projects have been completed.

A roughly $1.7 billion contract awarded in May 2026 includes approximately 17 miles of vehicle barriers and an additional 205 miles of supporting infrastructure, potentially including patrol roads and surveillance technology.

The specifications vary by location, and the contract represents planned work rather than completed construction.

MichaelVi/Depositphotos

Border crossing figures fuel disagreement

Customs and Border Protection recorded 3,096 apprehensions in Big Bend during fiscal 2025, about 1.3% of the 237,538 recorded along the southwestern border. Opponents cite the low share when questioning extensive construction.

Federal officials argue that gaps in surveillance can still create operational challenges across remote terrain. The disagreement concerns which areas need physical barriers and where technology or patrol access could serve instead.

How does fingerprint verification help U.S. border officials identify travelers with outstanding legal issues? Take a closer look at U.S. Customs and Border Protection says fingerprint verification led to traveler's arrest.

Depositphotos

Local tourism adds another concern

Local business owners have raised concerns about how construction might affect tourism, river recreation, and access to public lands. National Park Service research estimated that visitors spent $56.8 million in nearby communities during 2024, supporting hundreds of jobs.

That spending helps explain the economic concerns surrounding the project. Federal officials say they are coordinating with park staff to preserve visitor access wherever possible.

text:
An 18-year-old accused of seriously injuring a pedestrian while allegedly doing car stunts in New Haven over the summer was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents on Tuesday.

Jaime Enrique Diaz-Perez was taken into custody on State Street during a “targeted enforcement operation,” according to a spokesperson with the Department of Homeland Security.

The spokesperson noted that Diaz-Perez was arrested by the New Haven Police Department in August and charged with felony assault, evading responsibility and interfering with police. According to the DHS, ICE lodged a detainer against him on Sept. 3, but the state Department of Correction released him into the community.

Andrius Banevicius, a spokesperson for the DOC, denied that the department released Diaz-Perez. According to Banevicius, he went to court on Sept. 3 and posted bond before he was “released directly from court.”

When he was apprehended by ICE, Diaz-Perez allegedly refused to get out of the vehicle he was in and kicked ICE officers, a DHS spokesperson said. He was taken into custody after a passenger in the vehicle allegedly tried to interfere with the detainment, according to the DHS.

New Haven police released video of the incident, which was caught on the city’s cameras. Police said they were not notified about the operation beforehand.

The video shows an agent activate their emergency lights while driving behind the SUV Diaz-Perez was riding in, which pulled over and was then surrounded by two unmarked cruisers and a pickup truck. Multiple agents then approached the SUV. Their vests appear to say “police” on them.

The video appears to show Diaz-Perez being dragged out of the rear of the SUV and handcuffed on the ground. A front seat passenger got out of the vehicle but was quickly ushered back inside by an agent, the video shows.

After being handcuffed, Diaz-Perez was brought to his feet and placed in the backseat of an unmarked cruiser.

“Diaz-Perez will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings,” a DHS spokesperson said.

According to New Haven police, Diaz-Perez was arrested on Aug. 30 when officers responded to East Shore Park on the report that a pedestrian was struck by a vehicle and seriously injured shortly before 3:40 a.m. Police said they found that a group of people were doing donuts and other “reckless” car stunts in a parking lot when one of them, who was identified as Diaz-Perez, struck someone on foot who was filming the stunts.

The victim was “violently struck” and thrown several feet into the air, according to police. Police said the 30-year-old suffered life-threatening injuries and was later released from a hospital.

Diaz-Perez is believed to have taken off after the crash, police said. He was arrested the same day and later posted $200,000 bond, according to court records. The case remains pending in New Haven Superior Court.

“Mr. Diaz-Perez is accused of committing very serious crimes that nearly cost someone their life and he must be held accountable for his actions,” Mayor Justin Elicker said Thursday. “At the same time, when someone is accused of a crime, they are entitled to due process and their day in court.

“The Trump Administration and ICE continue to show complete disregard for our judicial process, and the reports of ICE’s aggressive tactics yesterday are deeply concerning,” Elicker said. “As we have said time and time again, no one wants violent criminals in our community — and we hold people accountable regardless of their documentation status. However, it’s also important that all parties follow the law — and that includes ICE officers and our federal government.”

According to the DHS, Diaz-Perez is originally from Guatemala and was previously arrested by Border Patrol in January 2022 after he allegedly entered the country illegally near Hidalgo, Texas. The DHS said alleges that he was later released under the Biden administration.

“To be clear: work authorization does not confer legal status in the U.S.,” the spokesperson said.

The DHS also issued a reminder that “obstructing law enforcement is a federal crime and assaulting law enforcement is a felony.”

“ICE law enforcement officers are trained to use the minimum amount of force necessary to resolve dangerous situations to prioritize the safety of the public and our officers,” the DHS spokesperson said. “Officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics and regularly receive ongoing use of force training, and they are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct.

“Violence against ICE officers, or any law enforcement personnel, will not be tolerated,” the spokesperson said. “Our officers carry out their congressionally mandated duties in service to public safety and the rule of law. Any bystander or individual who assaults, obstructs, or violently attacks officers will be subject to arrest and prosecution permitted by law.”

text:
The Canadian government is back in court over its policy of returning asylum seekers to the United States amid warnings that President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown is putting vulnerable migrants at risk.

Refugee organizations say people fleeing persecution face detention by ICE, separation from their families and possible deportation to countries where their lives could be in danger.

Amnesty International Canada, the Canadian Council for Refugees (CCR), the Canadian Council of Churches and former refugee claimants are challenging the policy, arguing that it discriminates against vulnerable groups, including women and LGBTQ asylum seekers.

Read More on News

Protesters gathered in Toronto and Montreal this week to support the legal challenge and demand that Canada scrap its Safe Third Country Agreement (STCA) with the United States. Demonstrators in Montreal carried signs reading "Canada must protect, not send back" and "Humanity has no borders."

The dispute comes as Trump's administration expands immigration detention and deportation operations, raising fresh questions about whether the United States can still be considered a safe destination for people seeking protection.

The Federal Court is hearing the latest stage of a longstanding constitutional challenge, while a separate lawsuit filed in June has raised further questions about Canada's treatment of asylum seekers.

Why Is Canada Sending Asylum Seekers Back to the US?

The dispute centers on the STCA, which has operated between Canada and the United States since December 29, 2004.

Under the agreement, asylum seekers are generally expected to request protection in whichever of the two countries they enter first.

That means someone who travels through the United States before reaching Canada can be turned away at the Canadian border, even if they would prefer to seek asylum in Canada.

There are exceptions, including for certain people with family members in Canada, unaccompanied minors and some holders of immigration documents.

In March 2023, the agreement was expanded under former President Joe Biden and former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau to cover people seeking asylum within 14 days of crossing between official border checkpoints, closing a route previously used by some asylum seekers.

Canada argues that the arrangement helps manage asylum claims between the two countries and prevents people from making duplicate applications.

What Are Groups Saying?

Ketty Nivyabandi, secretary general of Amnesty International Canada's English-speaking section, said: "The United States is not a safe place for migrants and refugees, particularly those who are racialized women, children, or LGBTQI+ people. The practice of sending some of the most vulnerable people in society back to the U.S.—right into the hands of ICE—is unjust and un-Canadian."

CCR President Asma Faizi said: "The evidence we present in this case, and the horrors of ICE that Canadians can see unfolding on their news screens, make it clear that the U.S. asylum system is broken and dangerous—particularly for racialized women, children, and LGBTQIA+ refugees.

"Since the Canadian government is not acting on what is plain for all to see, we are asking the court to strike down the designation of the U.S. as a safe country for refugees."

Janet Anstead, general secretary of the Canadian Council of Churches, said: "The treatment of individuals, especially the most vulnerable, under the U.S. asylum system is antithetical to our core Christian values. We are grateful to stand in solidarity with Amnesty International Canada and the Canadian Council for Refugees as we insist that Canada stay true to its ideals as enshrined in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms."

The Constitutional Challenge

The first case asks whether Canada's policy of returning certain asylum seekers to the United States violates equality protections under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

The challenge dates back to 2017 and has already reached Canada's highest court.

In 2020, a Federal Court judge ruled that the STCA violated constitutional protections relating to liberty and personal security. That decision was subsequently overturned by the Federal Court of Appeal.

In June 2023, the Supreme Court of Canada unanimously rejected the challenge under Section 7 of the Charter, finding that the legal framework contained safeguards intended to prevent people from being returned to danger.

However, the judges left a separate question unresolved: whether the agreement discriminates against particular groups of asylum seekers.

That issue, involving equality protections under Section 15 of the Charter, was sent back to the Federal Court.

The November 2026 hearings are the latest stage of that longstanding constitutional challenge.

The Separate Safeguards Challenge

A second constitutional challenge was launched in June 2026 by Amnesty International Canada, the Canadian Council for Refugees and families who sought asylum in Canada.

That lawsuit accuses Canadian authorities of failing to provide safeguards recognized by the Supreme Court in 2023 to prevent vulnerable asylum seekers from being returned to danger.

Unlike the November proceedings, which focus on alleged discrimination, the second case concerns whether Canada's handling of individual asylum claims violates constitutional protections relating to liberty and personal security.

What Is Canada's Government Saying?

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada said it could not comment on ongoing court proceedings but defended the agreement as a way to keep the border orderly.

"It helps avoid sudden spikes in asylum claims that could overwhelm border crossings, housing, and processing systems," Canada's immigration department said.

"This means Canada can keep the border orderly while continuing to offer protection to people who need it."

What Happens Next

A further hearing in the longstanding constitutional challenge is scheduled for December 16.

The Federal Court must consider whether Canada's designation of the United States as a safe country for refugees violates constitutional protections against discrimination.
