text:
A man who was deported to Honduras after being arrested during Operation Metro Surge at a St. Paul gas station is suing the U.S. government.

The lawsuit states Orbin Mauricio Henriquez Serrano, 28, is seeking $1,015,000 after he was racially profiled, injured by being thrown to the ground and denied medical care while in federal custody.

READ MORE: Video shows federal agents making detainment at St. Paul gas station

Metro Surge arrest lawsuit

Big picture view:

Henriquez Serrano was driving to work on the morning of Jan. 11 when he stopped at a Speedway gas station in St. Paul, the lawsuit states. It was there that he encountered Gregory Bovino and several ICE agents who "profiled, assaulted, and beat Mr. Henriquez Serrano to unconsciousness in front of horrified witnesses," the lawsuit states.

Serrano is alleging that agents singled him out because he appeared Hispanic, demanded his name and immigration status, and surrounded his car after he declined to speak without an attorney. The lawsuit states agents had neither a warrant nor grounds for arrest.

Dig deeper:

Videos taken by several witnesses at the scene show that agents smashed the window of Serrano's Jeep, pulled him out of the vehicle, threw him to the ground and twisted a previously operated-on knee, causing him to lose consciousness.

Greg Bovino, a public figure of the federal government's immigration enforcement at the time, was inadequately supervising the agents and was "snarling at protesters," the lawsuit states.

Agents then picked up his motionless body and carried him into an SUV before he was taken to the Whipple Federal Building, the lawsuit states. The next morning, he was moved to Camp East Montana in El Paso, Texas, where he says he was only given Tylenol days after being injured during the arrest.

Serrano says he was then deported after a week in Texas without an opportunity to speak to a lawyer or appear before a judge while seeking asylum.

The lawsuit adds that Serrano still suffers from lasting knee damage, nightmares, anxiety and trouble sleeping.

The lawsuit is also claiming agents that Serrano suffered from assault; battery; false arrest and imprisonment; negligence and negligent supervision; and interference with personal property stemming from the broken car window.

What's next:

Serrano is seeking $1,015,000 in damages and a judicial declaration that the U.S. Government violated the law.

title: Texas Democrats demand immediate immigration reform deal following midterm election victories
authors: Kyle McClenagan, David Martin Davies, Texas Public Radio, Eleanor Fitzgerald, San Antonio Report, Andrea Drusch, Diego Medel
description:
They argued that the election results, particularly the support Democrats received from Latino voters, sent a message about the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement policies.
“Whoever wants to get our support in ’28 has to prioritize immigration reform, period,” Pulido said.
Asked whether immigration enforcement had become too aggressive, Trump acknowledged that some Americans believe his administration has gone too far.

text:
Sign up for TPR Today, Texas Public Radio’s newsletter that brings our top stories to your inbox each morning.

Just days after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the November midterm elections, Texas lawmakers representing heavily Latino districts are calling on President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans to negotiate a bipartisan immigration reform agreement before the new Congress takes office in January.

At a news conference outside the U.S. Capitol, Democratic lawmakers joined immigration advocates and business leaders in demanding immediate protections for undocumented immigrants who have lived and worked in the United States for years.

They argued that the election results, particularly the support Democrats received from Latino voters, sent a message about the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement policies.

“The United States of America rebuked Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign,” said San Antonio Democratic Congressman Joaquin Castro.

The lawmakers say they want to use the remaining weeks of the current congressional session to pursue a compromise rather than wait for the incoming Democratic majorities.

Newly elected South Texas Democratic Congressman Bobby Pulido warned that Democrats cannot take Latino voters for granted.

“Whoever wants to get our support in ’28 has to prioritize immigration reform, period,” Pulido said.

For Pulido, the issue is personal. He said immigration enforcement has created fear throughout the Rio Grande Valley, where many households include both U.S. citizens and immigrants without legal status.

“In the Rio Grande Valley, there’s tons of mixed-status families. Good people. They’re people that we love, that we know and we’ve known forever,” Pulido said. “And right now they’re afraid to go out to the grocery store.”

Houston Democratic Congresswoman Sylvia Garcia said families are being separated every day and that delaying negotiations until January would prolong their uncertainty.

“I think we can get it done and get it done now. Why wait? El tiempo es ahora,” Garcia said, using the Spanish phrase meaning “the time is now.”

Laredo Democratic Congressman Henry Cuellar said for years Republicans have insisted on solving border enforcement as a pre-condition for considering immigration legislation that would provide legal protections or a pathway to citizenship for some undocumented immigrants.

Cuellar said the country can maintain strong border security while protecting immigrants’ rights.

“We can always have strong border security. We will have strong border security. But at the same time, we can be respectful to the immigrants and the rights and the dignity that they deserve,” Cuellar said.

Cuellar said he has already discussed immigration enforcement with members of the Trump administration and is willing to work with Republicans on policies that prioritize deporting immigrants convicted of serious crimes.

“If they want to focus on criminals, we’re with you 100%,” he said.

Democrats also point to recent comments from Trump during an interview on CBS’s “60 Minutes” as a possible indication that the president is willing to reconsider the scope of his immigration crackdown.

Asked whether immigration enforcement had become too aggressive, Trump acknowledged that some Americans believe his administration has gone too far.

“I think it might be too tough, yeah,” Trump said.

Asked about the possibility of reaching an agreement with Democrats, the president appeared open to negotiations.

“Well, the deal would be we would work something out,” Trump said. “I think that’s something that’s actually doable.”

However, Trump has not publicly committed to a specific immigration reform proposal, and substantial disagreements remain over deportations, border security and legal status for undocumented immigrants.

James Hollifield, a political science professor at Southern Methodist University who studies immigration politics, said the Republican Party remains closely aligned with Trump’s immigration agenda.

“It’s still a very hardcore Trump group, MAGA group, and I don’t think that they will be in a mood to reach across the aisle and pass a bipartisan immigration reform,” Hollifield said.

He also questioned whether Trump would ultimately sign legislation that significantly changed his administration’s policies.

“If there were a bill to emerge, it would probably get a veto from him,” Hollifield said.

Hollifield said Republicans paid a political price for the administration’s immigration policies in the midterm elections, but he believes the party’s remaining congressional members are unlikely to support a major change in direction.

“I do think it costs the Republicans, but I don’t think the Republican Party, especially those who are left in Congress, are yet ready to turn a page on this,” he said.

Hollifield predicted that the country could face another two years of legislative gridlock over immigration, even with Democrats controlling Congress.

Immigration reform advocates and business leaders say they are unwilling to accept another prolonged stalemate.

Mario Guerrero, CEO of the South Texas Builders Association, said Democrats must deliver results after winning the support of voters frustrated with the administration’s immigration policies.

“Don’t play with us, and don’t waste this opportunity like Biden and Obama did,” Guerrero said.

Guerrero said he voted for Trump three times before switching his support to Democrats in this year’s election.

His political shift illustrates the challenge facing both parties as they compete for Latino voters. Given how powerful this swing bloc has been in the last two elections, it’s clear their demand for action will have consequences in the next election.

Sign up for TPR Today, Texas Public Radio’s newsletter that brings our top stories to your inbox each morning.

Just days after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the November midterm elections, Texas lawmakers representing heavily Latino districts are calling on President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans to negotiate a bipartisan immigration reform agreement before the new Congress takes office in January.

At a news conference outside the U.S. Capitol, Democratic lawmakers joined immigration advocates and business leaders in demanding immediate protections for undocumented immigrants who have lived and worked in the United States for years.

They argued that the election results, particularly the support Democrats received from Latino voters, sent a message about the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement policies.

“The United States of America rebuked Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign,” said San Antonio Democratic Congressman Joaquin Castro.

The lawmakers say they want to use the remaining weeks of the current congressional session to pursue a compromise rather than wait for the incoming Democratic majorities.

Newly elected South Texas Democratic Congressman Bobby Pulido warned that Democrats cannot take Latino voters for granted.

“Whoever wants to get our support in ’28 has to prioritize immigration reform, period,” Pulido said.

For Pulido, the issue is personal. He said immigration enforcement has created fear throughout the Rio Grande Valley, where many households include both U.S. citizens and immigrants without legal status.

“In the Rio Grande Valley, there’s tons of mixed-status families. Good people. They’re people that we love, that we know and we’ve known forever,” Pulido said. “And right now they’re afraid to go out to the grocery store.”

Houston Democratic Congresswoman Sylvia Garcia said families are being separated every day and that delaying negotiations until January would prolong their uncertainty.

“I think we can get it done and get it done now. Why wait? El tiempo es ahora,” Garcia said, using the Spanish phrase meaning “the time is now.”

Laredo Democratic Congressman Henry Cuellar said for years Republicans have insisted on solving border enforcement as a pre-condition for considering immigration legislation that would provide legal protections or a pathway to citizenship for some undocumented immigrants.

Cuellar said the country can maintain strong border security while protecting immigrants’ rights.

“We can always have strong border security. We will have strong border security. But at the same time, we can be respectful to the immigrants and the rights and the dignity that they deserve,” Cuellar said.

Cuellar said he has already discussed immigration enforcement with members of the Trump administration and is willing to work with Republicans on policies that prioritize deporting immigrants convicted of serious crimes.

“If they want to focus on criminals, we’re with you 100%,” he said.

Democrats also point to recent comments from Trump during an interview on CBS’s “60 Minutes” as a possible indication that the president is willing to reconsider the scope of his immigration crackdown.

Asked whether immigration enforcement had become too aggressive, Trump acknowledged that some Americans believe his administration has gone too far.

“I think it might be too tough, yeah,” Trump said.

Asked about the possibility of reaching an agreement with Democrats, the president appeared open to negotiations.

“Well, the deal would be we would work something out,” Trump said. “I think that’s something that’s actually doable.”

However, Trump has not publicly committed to a specific immigration reform proposal, and substantial disagreements remain over deportations, border security and legal status for undocumented immigrants.

James Hollifield, a political science professor at Southern Methodist University who studies immigration politics, said the Republican Party remains closely aligned with Trump’s immigration agenda.

“It’s still a very hardcore Trump group, MAGA group, and I don’t think that they will be in a mood to reach across the aisle and pass a bipartisan immigration reform,” Hollifield said.

He also questioned whether Trump would ultimately sign legislation that significantly changed his administration’s policies.

“If there were a bill to emerge, it would probably get a veto from him,” Hollifield said.

Hollifield said Republicans paid a political price for the administration’s immigration policies in the midterm elections, but he believes the party’s remaining congressional members are unlikely to support a major change in direction.

“I do think it costs the Republicans, but I don’t think the Republican Party, especially those who are left in Congress, are yet ready to turn a page on this,” he said.

Hollifield predicted that the country could face another two years of legislative gridlock over immigration, even with Democrats controlling Congress.

Immigration reform advocates and business leaders say they are unwilling to accept another prolonged stalemate.

Mario Guerrero, CEO of the South Texas Builders Association, said Democrats must deliver results after winning the support of voters frustrated with the administration’s immigration policies.

“Don’t play with us, and don’t waste this opportunity like Biden and Obama did,” Guerrero said.

Guerrero said he voted for Trump three times before switching his support to Democrats in this year’s election.

His political shift illustrates the challenge facing both parties as they compete for Latino voters. Given how powerful this swing bloc has been in the last two elections, it’s clear their demand for action will have consequences in the next election.

text:
Federal immigration officers arrested a woman in a targeted operation outside of Trinity Food Mart in downtown Durham on Nov. 5.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson identified the woman as Cristina Martinez-Gonzalez of Mexico. Officials told WUNC News she was the sole target of an immigration enforcement operation at the intersection of W. Trinity Avenue and Foster Street.

Martinez-Gonzalez is accused of unlawfully crossing the southern border in 2000, and again in 2018, officials said.

DHS said Martinez-Gonzalez is charged with felony illegal re-entry. She is not wanted for any other charges and DHS did not disclose any criminal convictions on her record.

DHS did not provide further details on where she is currently being detained.

Word of her arrest first spread after a witness recorded videos and photos at the scene and posted them to Facebook. Volunteers with the immigrant rights group Siembra NC also confirmed the presence of an unmarked vehicle left behind by an officer.

Advocates and witnesses characterized Martinez-Gonzalez's arrest as unusual for its proximity to downtown Durham, and the incident spread fears that there was an larger immigration operation underway in Durham. DHS confirmed that only Martinez-Gonzalez was targeted.

Siembra Defense Manager Andreina Malki said Martinez-Gonzalez was running errands and making purchases in the area at the time of the arrest.

"When she was near her car, that's when agents approached her and detained her," said Malki, who has since been in touch with the detainee's family. "We got in touch with the family very soon after she was detained. She was able to make a quick phone call and then the agents took her phone. The family knew she had been detained, but they didn't know where she was being taken."

The agents appeared to have been using an unmarked sedan and a van.

The family has sought legal support for Martinez-Gonzalez's case and declined to provide further details through Siembra NC.

"People get really afraid that there's a broader indiscriminate operation and it causes as a lot of fear," Malki said.

The arrest disrupted operations at the nearby Central Park School for Children across the street, the INDY Week reported.

School officials did not immediately respond to WUNC News' request for comment.

ICE reports record arrests, detentions

In a statement, ICE said the agency arrested and deported more people during a recent 12-month period than at any time in its 23-year history, according to the Associated Press.

ICE said it deported 483,200 people in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30.

This is up 9% from its previous high of 442,640 in the same period a year earlier and up 78% from 271,480 in 2024.

More than 65,000 people are in detention, a record number during an unprecedented nationwide immigration sweep by the Trump Administration.

title: The faces, stories and human costs of Trump's immigration policies - CALÓ News
description: This article was produced by Capital & Main. It is published here with permission.
text:
The question of who would hold the detention center accounta…

On Monday, Nov. 16, students across Los Angeles and the San …



Federal agents attempt to detain an individual, who was later released, as he exited immigration court at the Jacob K. Javits Federal Building on June 30, 2025 in New York City. Photo by Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images.

This article was produced by Capital & Main . It is published here with permission.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers put a man on the ground in Hillcrest, New York, in late October, put their knees into his back and shot him with a Taser, according to the Human Impact Project .

The incident is one of more than 300 reports tracked by the project in which immigration officials injured someone to the point that they needed medical treatment.

Run by nonprofit Human Security Initiative, Human Impact Project scrapes court records, media reports, self-reported social media posts and GoFundMe accounts for information about the impacts of the Trump administration’s immigration policies. Though the project uses AI for the initial data gathering, human rights researchers fact-check those findings before adding them to the project website, according to organization founder Julia Neusner.

“The idea was to try to understand the scope of enforcement impacts across all these different sources with a focus on individual people,” Neusner said. “Other folks are tracking numbers. We wanted to track the stories and the impact on people.”

ICE did not respond to a request for comment from Capital & Main.

The project recently surpassed 5,000 published reports, and Neusner and her team began analyzing trends in the data. The results serve as a reminder of the immigration-related news stories that have come out in the past two years — arrests of U.S. citizens , detention of pregnant people in inhumane conditions, deportations to third countries of people who won protection in the U.S. and arrests at courts .

Even though the headlines may be familiar, Neusner said, the volume of stories and the extent of the abuses they describe still shock her.

That includes an Instagram post of a family detained in Key Largo, Florida. The woman, a U.S. citizen who is also pregnant, and her husband were on their way to vote in the recent midterm election when agents detained them and separated them from their young child, according to the database. They remained in custody for about a week.

Neusner said the project also reveals stories that the public — and even journalists — may have missed.

“There’s so many everyday abuses, people being beat up in arrests, horrendous conditions in detention,” Neusner said. “The sheer volume of these stories was quite shocking, and the things happening that don’t make it to mainstream press.”

She said the report of an incident involving ICE officers detaining a father who went to visit his son at a jail in Santa Ana, California, recently caught her attention. The father, a 69-year-old construction worker from Mexico, was the primary caregiver for another one of his sons who is only 13.

She also pointed to several stories where ICE officers mistook someone they detained for someone else or identified them by the wrong name.

That includes a Florida woman originally from Guatemala who is arguing in court that ICE detained her under a name she has never used .

The database also includes the story of a Coachella Valley, California, farmworker whom immigration officials mistakenly detained in December and who — 10 months later — is still in ICE custody.

In both cases, judges have denied their petitions for release from custody, according to the database.

Neusner said people can use the database to learn more about stories happening in their area. It features a map showing where the different incidents took place.

The greater Los Angeles area has the most of any geographic location, with more than 500 stories logged there.

An entry from Nov. 1 there pulls information from an online fundraiser asking for help to pay legal fees for a detained grandfather. Another from Oct. 30 details how ICE officers dragged a Venezuelan man outside his North Hollywood apartment and shot him with a Taser. Witnesses said the officers attempted to hogtie him. One of the officers shoved a nearby dog walker into some bushes and pointed a gun inches from the person’s face.

In another online fundraiser from Oct. 30 cited by the project, a family asks for help after ICE detained the father , a truck driver with a pending application for a U visa, a type of visa given to crime victims. The mother has cancer and has started working as a delivery driver to take care of their children on her own, the database says.

An Instagram post from Oct. 27 documents ICE arresting a food truck vendor operating Emin’s Kebab in the Echo Park neighborhood of Los Angeles.

Neusner and her team supplement the information found online with their own research on the ground. They recently went to Tapachula and Villahermosa in southern Mexico to speak with people from other countries sent there by U.S. immigration officials.

Neusner said she sees several ways that people could use the database. She said when her cousin’s wife had a green card appointment approaching, the family searched to see whether ICE officers were detaining people at the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services office in their area. Neusner said she was able to determine that those arrests had happened in other areas, including in San Diego , but not where her family member would soon have the interview.

That information helped allay the family’s worry leading up to the appointment, and the family member now has a green card, Neusner said.

She also hopes the database will connect people, including journalists, to what’s happening near them. Lawyers can look at pages compiled for specific detention centers to pull information about reported conditions to include in habeas corpus petitions to try to get their clients out of custody, she said. The database has catalogued the complaints in more than 1,200 habeas petitions, she said.

In the future, she also hopes the database will serve as a historical record for potential reparations. She said the database archives all of the source documents it uses.

“If there is some sort of future accountability process, these stories will be preserved,” Neusner said.

text:
ATLANTA — Today, four individuals filed a class action lawsuit challenging the unlawful re-detention of immigrant community members following the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) abrupt and unexplained reversal of longstanding federal immigration policy.

The policy reversal is part of the federal government’s broader campaign to expand immigration detention and accelerate mass deportations. As a result, thousands of noncitizens previously released from immigration custody now face the threat of arbitrary re-arrest and indefinite detention despite complying with release conditions and ICE’s prior determination that they posed no danger or flight risk. Since May 2025, hundreds, if not thousands, of people have been re-detained in the ICE Atlanta Field Office’s area of responsibility alone: North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia.

The American Civil Liberties Unions of North Carolina (ACLU-NC), South Carolina (ACLU-SC), and Georgia (ACLU-GA), and Foley Hoag LLP filed the lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia on behalf of four plaintiffs, all of whom have pending applications for immigration relief:

Livinton Sosa Martinez, a 41-year-old Nicaraguan man who resides in Greensboro, North Carolina;

Raquel Mariona Ebora, a 39-year-old Honduran woman who resides in Dunn, North Carolina;

Alvaro Ibañez-Cardenas, a 35-year-old Venezuelan man who resides in Athens, Georgia; and

Ambrosio Trujillo Zavaleta, a 46-year-old Mexican man who resides in Savannah, Georgia.

Sosa, Mariona, Ibañez, and Trujillo seek to represent a class harmed by DHS’s “Re-Detention Policy.” Please see a summary of each plaintiff’s experience and their quotes below/here. They are asking the court to declare the policy unlawful, block its continued use, and restore the longstanding “Changed Circumstances Policy.” Plaintiffs also request that the court temporarily halt the re-detention policy while the case proceeds.

For more than four decades, the ICE Atlanta Field Office followed DHS’s Changed Circumstances Policy, which barred immigration officers from re-detaining individuals previously released from immigration custody absent an individualized determination that their circumstances had materially changed. Under this policy, ICE did not seek to detain noncitizens who were previously released to await the outcome of their immigration proceedings and were complying with conditions of their release, like attending immigration check-ins and court hearings.

But around May 2025, DHS abruptly abandoned that longstanding policy and adopted the Re-Detention Policy, authorizing officers to re-arrest and re-detain individuals without determining whether any material change had occurred.

Plaintiffs filed suit against DHS, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Acting ICE Director David Venturella, and Acting Atlanta Field Office Director Kristen Sullivan, challenging DHS’s policy change under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). The APA allows courts to strike down government policies when agencies make changes without a reasoned explanation, fail to consider the impact on people who relied on longstanding policies, or adopt policies that violate the constitution and other laws. Here, the Fourth Amendment protects people from being re-detained on the same immigration charges without an individualized determination that their circumstances have materially changed.

Many people built their lives, maintained employment and paid taxes, pursued educational opportunities, and cared for their families in reliance on DHS’s longstanding Changed Circumstances Policy. Since its reversal, individuals have been re-arrested without warning at routine ICE check-ins, resulting in separated families, disrupted businesses, and people being cut off from essential medical care. ICE detains individuals in facilities far from their homes, which has made it more difficult for detained people to communicate with attorneys, gather evidence, and pursue their immigration claims.

A federal district court has already found DHS’s re-detention policy unlawful and temporarily halted its use in the ICE San Francisco Field Office’s area of responsibility, concluding that the agency radically departed from longstanding practice without providing the legally required justification.

“Our clients have complied with the rules the government placed on them. They have shown up for court hearings, attended immigration check-in appointments, and adhered to the conditions of their release, all while building their lives around the understanding that doing so would allow them to remain free as their immigration cases proceeded,” said Corina Scott, Staff Attorney at the ACLU of North Carolina. “DHS is now systematically stripping people of longstanding protections and arbitrarily re-detaining them in harsh conditions. This new policy, which is yet another example of ICE’s violence in our communities, makes one thing abundantly clear: our government’s abuse of power is the real threat, not our immigrant neighbors.”

“Many of our immigrant neighbors, friends, colleagues, and family have built their lives on the promise that if they followed DHS’s conditions, they would not be re-detained. Last year, the rug was pulled out from under them by an administration more concerned with meeting arrest quotas and treating them as numbers, rather than individuals with families, livelihoods, and futures,” said Raneem Ashrawi, Staff Attorney at the ACLU of Georgia. “Mr. Trujillo, Mr. Ibañez, and the thousands of other class members, have unique stories and circumstances that ICE officers have now been instructed to disregard, with no reasoned process or consideration. This lawsuit is an important step in our ongoing efforts to ensure the rights of all Georgians are upheld, and we look forward to continuing to work alongside our partners in the Carolinas to do so.”

“South Carolinians shouldn’t have to live in fear that they or their neighbors, coworkers, or family members will be baselessly torn from their community and thrown back into detention,” said Sarah Schreiber, Staff Attorney at the ACLU of South Carolina. “We are proud to stand with our fellow ACLU affiliates to defend our clients and the rule of law against these egregious and unjustifiable abuses.”

DHS is using the threat of arbitrary immigration detention as a tool of intimidation — undermining due process, tearing families apart, and punishing people for complying with the conditions of their release. This lawsuit seeks to hold the federal government accountable, restore longstanding protections against unlawful re-detention, and prevent immigration officers from taking away people’s freedom without an individualized justification.

text:
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration said Thursday that it deported a record number of illegal immigrants in the past year — with nearly a half-million people living in the US without legal permission forced to return to their homelands.

About 60% of those removed since President Trump returned to office were charged with or convicted of a crime within the US — and were not merely accused of unlawfully residing in the country, according to a Trump administration official.

The Thursday announcement did not provide detailed criminal statistics on the 483,200 removals in fiscal 2026, which ended Sept. 30, though a handful of dangerous perps were highlighted in a Department of Homeland Security press release.

The number outpaced the 442,640 deportations in the prior year, which included most of Trump’s first year back in power.

Both years dwarfed the annual tallies under former President Joe Biden — with the latest number roughly equal to three years of enforcement under the prior administration.

“FY26’s total is also more than eight times the number of deportations in Biden’s first fiscal year, as FY21 saw just over 59,000 deportations,” DHS said.

“FY26’s arrest total includes nearly 475,000 administrative arrests, which is by far the highest total in ICE’s history.”

The release came one day after Syracuse University’s well-regarded immigration data hub reported that “contrary to news reporting and public perception, the number of individuals removed from the United States actually declined after President Trump assumed office in January 2025.”

The university’s Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse (TRAC) data, which runs through August, cited information gathered through Freedom of Information Act litigation.

The discrepancy may be because, according to TRAC, the DHS figures count people who voluntarily self-deported — something that can be stipulated to curtail court proceedings, and which the Trump administration also incentivized with free plane tickets and $3,000.

“When ICE speaks about removals, in the fine print they usually include removals plus returns,” TRAC reported. “Removals bar an individual from legally returning to the United States for a period of years. For returns, reentry is not legally barred.”

DHS did not provide further clarification when asked for comment.

title: ICE Deportations And Arrests Reach Record Highs | iHeart
description:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) deported a record 483,200 people in fiscal year 2026, surpassing the previous record of 442,640 set in 2025.
According to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), ICE also made over 491,000 immigration arrests, with nearly 475,000 being administrative arrests for civil violations rather than criminal charges.
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin praised ICE's efforts, stating, "Fiscal Year 2026 saw the highest number of ICE deportations and arrests for any year in ICE’s history."
The figures mark a significant expansion of immigration enforcement under President Donald Trump, who acknowledged in a "60 Minutes" interview that the crackdown may have been "too tough" in some cases.

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) deported a record 483,200 people in fiscal year 2026, surpassing the previous record of 442,640 set in 2025. According to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), ICE also made over 491,000 immigration arrests, with nearly 475,000 being administrative arrests for civil violations rather than criminal charges.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin praised ICE's efforts, stating, "Fiscal Year 2026 saw the highest number of ICE deportations and arrests for any year in ICE’s history." The figures mark a significant expansion of immigration enforcement under President Donald Trump, who acknowledged in a "60 Minutes" interview that the crackdown may have been "too tough" in some cases.

The deportation total for 2026 was about 18% higher than the 409,849 removals recorded in 2012 and nearly 78% higher than the 271,484 deportations in 2024. Despite the record numbers, a CBS News analysis found that more than half of ICE arrests in July 2026 involved immigrants with neither criminal convictions nor pending charges.

The Trump administration has defended the campaign as a public safety mission, highlighting deportations involving individuals accused or convicted of serious crimes. However, the Migration Policy Institute reported that only about 20% of deportations between January 2025 and July 2026 involved someone with a criminal conviction.

The record figures come as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress in January, with some voicing support for more scrutiny of the administration's immigration operations. President Trump expressed interest in working with congressional Democrats to create and pass immigration legislation, acknowledging the political toll of the crackdown.

text:
Earlier this month, a little more than three years after his son Kylan died of a fentanyl overdose at CoreCivic’s Trousdale Turner Correctional Facility, Tim Leeper was informed that his family’s lawsuit against the prison and its leadership had been dismissed.

In an order filed Nov. 3, U.S. District Court Judge Waverly Crenshaw wrote that the evidence of danger, disorder and misconduct at the prison was strong but could not be tied directly to Leeper’s death. Still, he emphasized the troubling picture painted by that evidence.

“The record in this case reflects a serious drug problem at TTCC, and the Court does not minimize it,” he wrote. “Drugs in prisons, including facilities that CoreCivic operates, have generated repeated litigation in this Circuit and repeated harm to inmates. The Court is disturbed by the danger that problem poses to inmates.”

Trousdale is Tennessee’s largest prison, and reports of drugs, violence and death have been near-constant since it opened. The Banner reported in 2024 that nearly two dozen Trousdale employees, including officers and staff, had been criminally charged for, among other things, smuggling drugs and cell phones.

Kylan Leeper died there on Oct. 6, 2023, just five months after arriving at the prison. But as life-altering as it was for his family, it was hardly a surprising event at the prison. Citing testimony from former Trousdale staff, including the former warden, Crenshaw wrote that it was not uncommon for Trousdale to see 10 or 15 overdoses per day in the summer and fall of 2023 and that a number of them were fatal. The judge’s opinion documents the steps taken by CoreCivic to try to address the crisis, including “body scanners, a canine unit, mail and package scanning, drone detection, perimeter patrols, shakedowns, urinalysis, and video surveillance.” But it also states that the prison was clearly understaffed and suggests that people in positions of power there likely contributed to the problem.

The Leeper family’s original complaint described Jermaris Porter, then an assistant warden at Trousdale, as a central figure in a blatant drug ring at the prison. Porter has since left Trousdale and briefly worked at an Alabama prison before leaving that job under unclear circumstances. Crenshaw wrote in his opinion that the Leepers’ case against Porter was the strongest, but still not sufficient.

“In sum, the Estate’s evidence shows that Porter broke the rules. He escorted unsearched inmates between units, met with gang-affiliated inmates behind closed doors, skirted security screening, and may have even delivered drugs himself,” Crenshaw wrote. “But the Estate has not come forward with evidence connecting that conduct, or any drug trafficking that Porter allegedly engaged in or enabled, to the risk that Leeper faced in Foxtrot Bravo in the time leading up to his death.”

For Tim Leeper, who made speaking out about conditions in Tennessee prisons and advocating for the people inside them the cause of his life, the lawsuit’s dismissal was a gut punch.

“To me that says, there’s nothing you could ever do, there’s no case, no evidence that you could bring … it means they are too big to fail,” he told the Banner. “If somebody like me, who has the means to hire a lawyer and spend over $50,000 on private investigators to get the information that I got, and it’s still not enough? There’s no hope for holding the prison system accountable.”

Yet almost as soon as he finished describing that defeat, he made it clear that he is not defeated.

“It’s not that we’re demoralized, and we haven’t given up hope,” he said. “But it makes you realize what kind of Goliath you’re fighting.”

Although the family could appeal Crenshaw’s decision, Leeper said he doesn’t think they will. But his advocacy won’t slow down, he said.

“I’m willing to do this for the rest of my life; I’ve got businesses that I’ve basically walked away from to do this,” he said. “This is my work and my mission in life.”

Through his organization, Kylan’s Light, and the various Facebook groups where the loved ones of people incarcerated in Tennessee prisons come together, he stays in touch with an ever-growing community of people willing to join him.

He said he will continue lobbying state lawmakers for prison-related policy changes, as he’s been doing since his son’s death. But he also said reform isn’t likely until people outside the state’s prison change their view of the people inside them.

“Until we begin to see these people as human beings and not just ‘inmates’ or ‘prisoners’ or ‘offenders,’ the message won’t change,” he said. “And that’s my job is to change the way that we see people. As a believer, I feel like God sees people as souls and if he sees them as a soul and I’m a believer I should probably see them the same way.”

text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (LEX NEWS) — A high-stakes international custody battle involving a Kentucky foster toddler known as "Baby T" is drawing legal scrutiny and raising questions about cross-border jurisdictional limits.

Caleb Yeske, who cared for the girl as a foster father for more than a year after she entered his care at one month old, has raised alarms over the child's safety following her return to her biological mother in Guatemala.

The case centers on a series of legal actions that began after the child's biological mother in Louisville—who had faced an attempted murder charge involving the child and later pleaded guilty to second-degree wanton endangerment—was taken into U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody and deported to Guatemala.

He says despite concerns raised by Kentucky foster care officials, a Jefferson County family court judge ordered the child reunited with her mother.

"If the goal of foster care and the expectation is that the child's safety and well-being comes first, how, how was any of this with the child's best interest in mind?," Yeske told LEX NEWS in an interview.

Yeske later traveled to Guatemala to check on the toddler, stating that local child protection authorities eventually removed her from his care on Oct. 30 amid concerns over her health, living conditions, and nutrition.

"That's the very difficult part of this is that when they did take the child, we knew that we were concerned about her health. She was covered in, essentially, flea bites all over her body," said Yeske.

Advocates and attorneys are now pressing for transparency, pointing to complex legal questions regarding how state family courts and child welfare systems handle cases where children are relocated across international borders outside the jurisdiction of U.S. courts.

Despite the international gap and heartache, Yeske says he hopes to one day reunite with Baby T.

"The biological mother had never even met the child since she gave birth to her, and so she had no idea who this baby was or how to care for her, and we continue to, the main reason that we're concerned right now is for the child's safety and well-being."

text:
It’s just after noon on a recent Friday in Chelsea, and Martín Gurfinkiel has been up since 5 a.m. Operating on four hours of sleep, his eyes are bloodshot and his mind is churning about the packed day ahead. Normally he’d be earning money with food deliveries, but now he’s focused on reaching the family’s immigration attorney — and soon he’ll pick up his stepchildren from school.

“Tomorrow is Emiliana's birthday, so I brought a cake to school, and I just need to do everything: clean the house, cook, work, deal with the lawyers,” he said. “I'm just exhausted of all of this.”

This has been Gurfinkiel’s daily routine since his wife, Melanie Tinoco, was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in early October, leaving him in charge of her two kids, 7-year-old Emiliano and 12-year-old Emiliana. After putting them to bed, he’ll try going to sleep at midnight — though with all the thoughts racing through his head, that usually takes a while.

“It may not seem like it, but I’m ruined emotionally,” he said.

Gurfinkiel is among scores of people across Massachusetts in mixed status families, scrambling to fill the shoes of a parent swept up by federal immigration police. Nearly 9 in 10 people arrested by ICE are men, so mothers are often left caring for kids. But amid a massive ramp-up in enforcement under President Trump’s latest term, more fathers, grandparents, siblings — and stepparents like Gurfinkiel — are assuming the role of primary caretaker.

Gurfinkiel said he and Tinoco moved to the Boston area last spring, shortly after marrying in Miami. He’s 33, from Argentina, she’s 29, from Ecuador, and her two kids are from a previous relationship.

"I’m like the mom and the dad now. I'm the only one they can trust and ask things of."

Martín Gurfinkiel

He said he never imagined himself taking on the role of both parents.

“I don’t know how to be a father,” he sighed. “It’s all new to me. But that’s part of life.”

Realizing the hour, Gurfinkiel rose from the sofa in their small, two-bedroom, $2,600-a-month apartment. He drove through Chelsea traffic to pick up Emiliana from middle school, then headed to Emiliano’s elementary school.

The boy's teacher, Erica Pisano, handed him off to his stepdad in the schoolyard.

“Bye, sweetie,” she said. “Have a wonderful weekend.”

Pisano, a second grade teacher in Chelsea, said Emiliano seems to be doing OK. But she worries about the effect ICE arrests can have on students.

“I honestly have no idea how some of these kids process,” she said. How they “come to school, are learning new ideas and functioning and not thinking about what's happening to their family.”

Arrested at Target

The story of Tinoco’s detainment is another example of how a brush with local police can land immigrants in ICE custody.

Tinoco has a work permit and an asylum claim. She entered the U.S. through the Mexico border and was arrested by Customs and Border Patrol in 2024.

Gurfinkiel, a legal permanent resident, said he and Tinoco were at a Target store in the Fenway on Oct. 1, fulfilling an order for an Uber Eats delivery. He said she walked into the lobby to grab a carriage, carrying items they planned to buy. Two security workers approached and commanded her to follow them into a back room.

Gurfinkiel said he tried to explain it was a misunderstanding.

“They told me, ‘No, no, right now it's too late for pay,’ " he recalled. “And I say, ‘But we never left the building.’ I tried to explain again, and they told me, ‘No, you can leave, but she needs to stay.’ "

Boston police arrested Tinoco and charged her with shoplifting. When officers released her that night, Gurfinkiel said, four plainclothes agents were waiting outside the police station and put her in handcuffs.

“You're in shock,” he said. “You don't know what's going on, or if she's getting kidnapped or what. So I came home. I was scared. I told the kids that she was grabbed by ICE.”

They couldn't believe it at first, he said. Then they started to cry.

“I told them the truth,” Gurfinkiel added. That “they need to trust me, that we need to pray and try to be strong for mom, because if we … show weakness, it's going to be even more hard for her.”

Nearly six weeks later, Tinoco remains in ICE custody at a facility that houses women in Dover, New Hampshire.

According to an administrative ICE warrant submitted in court, Tinoco was arrested because of “ongoing removal proceedings” against her. A rap sheet on the court docket shows her only previous charge was for “alien inadmissibility” in 2024. Prosecutors refer to her as a “criminal alien.”

Families in limbo

A Brookings Institution study last May estimated 145,000 U.S. citizen children saw a parent booked into detention since the start of the second Trump administration. That figure included nearly 3,000 in Massachusetts.

If you add non-citizen children, the number is even higher.

“The families that are left behind are really struggling,” said Jillian Phillips, a social worker in Worcester, who is supporting 30 families affected by ICE detentions. “ It completely shifts the whole dynamic.”

Of the 30 detainees, she said the vast majority are parents. All but two are men.

Phillips said in many immigrant families with small children, the men are the breadwinners and the women are the caretakers, often because childcare is too expensive. She said it can be particularly hard for men to adapt.

“Most men don’t carry the childcare burden, especially in most immigrant communities,” Phillips said. “So it is a true culture shock.”

Incarceration of any kind can also come with heavy costs for the children left at home. But immigration detention adds an element of uncertainty.

“What might happen to that parent that they love?” said Dr. Altaf Saadi, associate professor of neurology at Harvard Medical School. “Could that person be harmed in detention? Could they be deported and face permanent separation?”

Saadi has studied the wellbeing of children with parents in ICE custody. According to her research, nearly 70% of kids saw declines in grades, and 16% dropped out of school. The majority experienced a deterioration in mental or physical health.

“That can look like decreased sleep, changes in appetite, weight loss, losing their hair, waking up in the middle of the night because of nightmares,” Saadi said.

Family separation isn’t unique to the Trump administration — the families surveyed in Saadi’s work were detained under President Joe Biden. But the scale of immigration enforcement has increased dramatically under Trump, with ICE arrests more than tripling in Massachusetts. And the Department of Homeland Security has lowered its threshold for detaining parents.

Saadi said one of the most vital things a child loses is emotional support. And it's up to caretakers like Martín Gurfinkiel to try to fill the void.

One thing Gurfinkiel is happy to do while Tinoco is in detention is spoil the kids. He gave Emiliana a guinea pig so she’d have some company; Emiliano gets extra time to play video games. They're both allowed to use their phones more.

If there's any silver lining in all of this, Gurfinkiel said, it's that he's become closer to his stepkids.

"I’m like the mom and the dad now. I'm the only one they can trust and ask things of,” he said. “I have a connection to them that I didn't have before."

‘It’s hell to not be able to see them’

Melanie Tinoco is asking a federal judge to order her release while her immigration case plays out.

But Massachusetts federal prosecutors said in a court filing that under the 2025 Laken Riley Act, her detention is mandatory, as it requires ICE to detain people without legal status who are charged with certain low-level crimes, including shoplifting.

In a recent call from ICE lockup in New Hampshire, Tinoco told Gurfinkiel the worst part of all this is being without her children.

“It’s hell to not be able to see them,” she said in Spanish.

“I never saw this situation coming," Tinoco added, "but he has shown me that he is the man I want for the rest of my life."

Gurfinkiel believes Tinoco will be released. But if not, even little Emiliano knows the backup plan.

“If she is deported, Martín, my sister and I are going to Ecuador,” Emiliano said in Spanish.

His stepdad nodded.

“Why would I live in the United States if I'm trying to make a life for myself, and someone is ruining the lives of people and families who want to work and get ahead?” he said.

By Tim Sullivan / Associated Press

MINNEAPOLIS — Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested and deported more people during the last fiscal year than at any time in its 23-year history, the Department of Homeland Security said Wednesday, as President Donald Trump followed through on promises of mass deportations that helped win back the White House but also fueled the political blowback that led to Democrats’ overwhelming victory in last week’s midterm elections.

ICE said it deported 483,200 people in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30, the highest number since 2014, when 405,090 people were deported under former President Barack Obama, when some activists labeled him the “deporter in chief.”

The 2026 numbers were up 9% from its previous high of 442,640 in the same period a year earlier and up 78% from 271,480 in 2024, the last year of Joe Biden’s presidency.

ICE had not released such counts since Donald Trump returned to the White House, including for 2025.

SEE ALSO: ‘Why are you taking her?’ ICE arrests surge in El Paso region as families feel the impact

“Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, ICE has been unleashed to target and remove illegal aliens so that we can save American lives,” said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

Yet much remained unsaid in the DHS press release, including how many deportees had criminal histories and a detailed breakdown of the statistics. In addition, deportation numbers can be notoriously fuzzy, with totals counted in different ways in different years.

“It is accurate that ICE is making record numbers of arrests,” said Marc R. Rosenblum, a visiting fellow at the Migration Policy Institute and a former top official overseeing statistics at the Department of Homeland Security. “They have record resources. They’ve doubled their staffing. They’re getting a lot of support from other law enforcement agencies.”

SEE ALSO: She should be celebrating Senior Night. Instead, this El Paso teen is in Dilley ICE detention.

But the sparse data in Wednesday’s announcement means “we can’t really see what’s going on in any kind of detailed way.”

Trump had campaigned on ridding America of criminal migrants, saying he’d be targeting the “worst of the worst.”

But that is rarely the case. In July, for instance, only roughly one-quarter of deportees had criminal convictions, according to the Deportation Data Project. More than half weren’t even facing charges.

FROM THE ARCHIVES: Fact Check: Did President Obama remove more noncitizens from the U.S. than any other president in U.S history?

The numbers released Wednesday also fell well short of the White House goal of 1 million deportations annually, a promise it made when it received billions in additional funding from Congress, supercharging the government’s immigration bureaucracy.

Trump returned to power last year promising to end illegal crossings at the southern border. His administration has pushed through restrictions on both legal and illegal immigration and speeded up deportations. Immigration crackdown operations are often purposefully high-profile, in part to frighten migrants into leaving of their own accord.

SEE ALSO: He fled Afghanistan fearing the Taliban. Now a judge has temporarily halted his deportation

But the crackdown hasn’t always gone as planned.

The biggest shift came earlier this year in Minneapolis, when more than 2,000 federal officers were deployed to the city and thousands of protesters turned out to confront masked and often heavily armed agents spilling from convoys of unmarked vehicles.

Two U.S. citizens — Renee Good and Alex Pretti, both 37 — were killed in confrontations with agents, and the administration quickly backed away from high-profile operations.

While arrests dropped after the killings, they quickly returned to record numbers, albeit in quieter immigration sweeps.

ELECTION RESULTS: El Paso reelects 3 state representatives as Democrats gain ground across Texas

By last week’s elections the White House’s immigration message had splintered, with even some deeply Republican rural areas voting Democratic after people saw longtime migrant neighbors, many of them key workers on farms, ranches and meat processing facilities, taken in arrests.

The highest recorded number of deportations on record came during President Dwight D. Eisenhower’s crackdown on illegal immigrants from Mexico. The often-chaotic policy saw deportation numbers spike dramatically in the early 1950s, cresting at 1.1 million in 1954.

text:
Stephen Miller’s appointment to the coveted White House chief of staff role is already raising doubt among Democrats that there will be any hope of bipartisanship when they take control of Congress next year. But at least one Republican in a competitive district sees an opportunity for compromise.

Rep. Nick LaLota, a Republican from New York who narrowly won his reelection bid, told The Washington Sun that Miller, known for his hard-line immigration policies, could help persuade reluctant House members to support a deal. LaLota pointed to the president’s comments in a recent “60 Minutes” interview on CBS as evidence the president is serious about pursuing an immigration deal.

LaLota believes Miller’s street cred with the MAGA base could help build a bridge to those on the far right if the president decided to cut a deal. “I think there is a negotiation to be had, not just with Democrats, of bringing Republicans online,” LaLota told The Sun. “Stephen Miller could have a large hand on bringing those sorts of Republicans on board with some sort of compromise effort.”

The conflicting reactions to Miller highlight the challenges awaiting a divided government in January, as lawmakers weigh whether they can find common ground with a White House that has elevated one of the most controversial figures in the administration.

Trending

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next speaker of the House, has repeatedly offered a stark assessment.

“I’ve been very clear about Stephen Miller. His appointment was dangerous and reckless and irresponsible, in my view,” said Jeffries, who recently labeled Miller “a stone-cold racist.”

Given their mutual hostility, it’s unclear who could serve as a mediator between Democrats and the president’s right-hand man and other top White House aides.

Rep. Nanette Barragán, who’s been on the front lines with Democrats trying to shape immigration policy, was skeptical that Miller would be willing to engage, but she stopped short of closing the door on future negotiations.

“I don’t think it shows a branch on immigration to put Stephen Miller in that position because he can’t be trusted, but I’m willing to oversee my skepticism on that if they deliver,” the California Democrat told The Sun.

Democrats say their concerns are based on Miller’s long-standing history pushing far-right immigration rhetoric and proposals. Miller’s position on immigration dates back to his time as a policy staffer with then Alabama Sen. Jeff Sessions. Now, he’s known as the architect of the Trump administration’s immigration policy, which has dramatically slowed illegal crossings at the southern border but also enforced mass arrests and deportations that are unpopular with voters.

For LaLota, Miller’s influence with the president and congressional hardliners could prove useful in trying to strike a deal.

He said that Congress has an opportunity to codify some of Trump’s border-security initiatives for administrations to come while taking a “different approach” to deportations by prioritizing people convicted of violent crimes and those he described as illegally relying on public benefits.

Ultimately, LaLota contends, Miller reports to the president.

“The decision-making starts at the president, and then he surrounds himself with staff members who can execute on his decision-making,” LaLota said.

Rep. Glenn Grothman (R-Wisconsin) defended the administration’s actions and dismissed any criticism from Republicans who think the political backlash over the administration’s immigration policies helped contribute to Democrats’ huge gains during the midterm elections.

“When you’re trying to remove even 1 or 2 million, that’s a difficult task,” Grothman said.

Democrats, for the most part, doubt Miller would be interested in establishing the relationships it takes to pass bipartisanship legislation.

Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, who is expected to chair the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said he was surprised that Miller was tapped for the big promotion and questioned whether his rhetoric makes him a viable candidate to serve as a negotiator.

“The devil is always in the details,” Meeks said. “But what we can only go by is what our eyes have seen and our ears have heard.”

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez questioned whether Miller would remain in the post, a sentiment Jeffries has also expressed after multiple turnovers in the administration.

“I don’t know how long Stephen Miller is going to be in that job,” she said, but she described his influence as a potentially dangerous development. Ocasio-Cortez told reporters: “I don’t see how Stephen Miller can sustain the amount of input and decision-making. I think it’s actually a very dangerous point that we’re at in our country because he is so unstable, and for him to be the primary adviser to the president, I think actually puts our entire nation in a very risky and volatile place. And my hope is that the president can find someone who serves him better.”

The White House pushed back on criticism of Miller, noting he’s been endorsed by members of Republican leadership and the House Freedom Caucus, including its chair, Rep. Andy Harris of Maryland, who characterized Miller as a valuable asset.

In a statement to The Sun about the possibility of an immigration deal, Harris said: “No amnesty. No compromises. Full stop.”

The White House maintained that Miller had already shepherded bipartisan proposals. “Unlike the hardcore, partisan Democrats who refused to work with the President and blocked many of his popular policies, Stephen Miller has a track record of spearheading bipartisan efforts: public safety reform, making our cities such as Washington, D.C. and Memphis safe again, drug pricing transparency, and unleashing a nuclear energy renaissance,” Taylor Rogers, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement to The Sun.

In terms of any possible middle ground on immigration, Rogers added: “President Trump’s strong immigration policy remains unchanged, and the Democrats should work with the Administration to keep our southern border secure, remove dangerous illegal criminals from our communities, and stop the illicit trafficking of lethal drugs.”

Miller’s appointment comes as Democrats prepare to take the reins of both chambers in January and Republicans grapple with the fallout from the midterms and what’s doable in the short time they have left in the majority.

Rep. Warren Davidson (R-Ohio) suggested Miller’s appointment could have consequences for the White House’s relationship with the legislative branch, although he expects little immediate impact during the lame-duck session.

title: Conservative Jewish groups hail Stephen Miller's appointment to White House chief of staff
description:
Liberal Jewish groups expressed alarm, saying his hard-line politics endangered the community.
The chief of staff holds one of the most powerful White House positions, acting as a gatekeeper to the president and helping to shape his daily agenda.
Liberal Jewish voices warned that Trump’s promotion of Miller to the role of White House chief of staff could make Jewish communities more vulnerable.
The groups on the right that welcomed Miller’s appointment have generally been pleased by the steps Trump has taken to counter antisemitism on the left.
The White House press office, which fields media communications for the chief of staff, did not respond to requests for comment.
text:
JTA – Right-leaning pro-Israel groups hailed US President Donald Trump’s appointment of Stephen Miller as the next White House chief of staff, welcoming the Jewish aide’s appointment as a safeguard against antisemitism in an era marked by an increase in attacks on Jews and Israel. Liberal Jewish groups expressed alarm, saying his hard-line politics endangered the community.

In a letter congratulating Miller, groups including the Combat Antisemitism Movement, the Louis D Brandeis Center for Human Rights Under Law, and the Zionist Organization of America expressed an interest in working with Miller to “hold institutions accountable when they fail to protect Jewish Americans from discrimination and harassment”.

The writers, who also included the American Association of Jewish Lawyers and Jurists, the Coalition for Jewish Values, and the Israeli-American Civic Action Network, described Miller’s appointment as “a meaningful reflection of the longstanding contributions of Jewish Americans to public service”.

Just days after the Republican Party incurred massive losses in the midterm elections, Trump announced that he was replacing former chief of staff Susie Wiles with Miller, who had previously served as her deputy. In a Truth Social post, he described Miller as one of his “most trusted advisers”.

The chief of staff holds one of the most powerful White House positions, acting as a gatekeeper to the president and helping to shape his daily agenda.

Liberal Jewish voices warned that Trump’s promotion of Miller to the role of White House chief of staff could make Jewish communities more vulnerable.

“We expect this appointment to only reinforce some of the most dangerous ways the administration has normalised antisemitism and broader extremism,” Amy Spitalnick, chief executive of the Jewish Council for Public Affairs, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, noting Miller’s embrace of anti-immigrant rhetoric popular on the far right.

Spitalnick said there is a throughline between the hard-line immigration policies Miller has shaped as a longtime confidant to Trump and the flourishing of antisemitism in recent years.

“At the core of the anti-immigrant agenda Miller has spearheaded are deeply antisemitic conspiracy theories about ‘replacement’ and ‘invasion’ that have already fuelled a cycle of deadly violence targeting Jews and others,” she said.

The duelling sentiments from across the Jewish political spectrum were a signal of how divided the community has become during the second Trump term over the best means of combatting antisemitism: Through aggressive policing of elite institutions, which Trump favours, or through opposition to what liberal groups say is the president’s systematic corrosion of civil rights protections.

The groups on the right that welcomed Miller’s appointment have generally been pleased by the steps Trump has taken to counter antisemitism on the left. In January 2025, Trump issued an executive order requiring new measures for combatting antisemitism. The Justice Department then launched a multi-agency Task Force to Combat Anti-Semitism. This past May, the department announced the formation of an Advisory Committee on Anti-Semitism, while emphasising a “commitment to protecting Americans from unlawful discrimination and antisemitic threats”. Much of the focus has been on allegations of antisemitic harassment on university campuses.

While it’s unclear what Miller will do on these specific issues, his supporters see his key role as likely to strengthen such efforts.

Miller has longstanding links to Trump, including on a personal level. Miller’s wedding officiant at the Trump DC hotel was Rabbi Aryeh Lightstone, who was involved with the administration’s Abraham Accords to establish peaceful relations between Israel and several Arab neighbours.

But Miller’s critics have pointed out that he, along with Trump and other top Republicans, has embraced troubling conspiracy theories that can be linked to Jews. Namely, that Democrats want to flood America with immigrants who are likely to vote against Republicans. At Trump’s October 2024 campaign rally at Madison Square Garden, Miller declared, “America is for Americans and Americans only.”

A more extreme version of the conspiracy theory, which blames Jews for organising an “invasion” of people of colour to replace whites, fuelled a number of deadly attacks over the past decade, including the massacre at the Tree of Life synagogue in Pittsburgh in 2018.

The White House press office, which fields media communications for the chief of staff, did not respond to requests for comment.

Spitalnick also slammed the current administration for failing to “protect the civil rights of Jewish – and all – people” by rolling back programmes aimed at countering hate, including at the Office for Civil Rights in the Department of Education and extremism prevention programmes at the Department of Homeland Security.

Spitalnick also referred to a 2019 letter sent by Jewish Democratic members of Congress urging Trump to dismiss Miller, who was his senior adviser at the time. The lawmakers argued that his “support for white nationalist and virulently anti-immigrant tropes is wholly unacceptable and disqualifying for a government employee”.

Regarding the current appointment, Spitalnick warned that Miller’s role could “make Jewish and so many other vulnerable communities less safe, instead of advancing the civil rights and pro-democracy policies we know are inherent to our security”.

“As the president and vice-president are now seemingly pinning the US election results on Israel, we should be concerned about further scapegoating of the Jewish and Israeli American communities,” she added.

The liberal pro-Israel lobby J Street, meanwhile, posted a Haaretz analysis that likened Miller to Itamar Ben-Gvir, a far-right minister in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition known for his extreme nationalistic rhetoric.

“Stephen Miller and Itamar Ben-Gvir both owe their prominence and access to power to their enablers – Trump and Netanyahu – and both traffic in racism and nativism to attempt to build power and incite fear,” the J Street post stated.

Robert Reich, US secretary of labour in the Clinton administration, wrote in a Facebook post that Miller’s appointment was “not a positive development for anyone interested in mending our government or healing our nation”. Reich, who is Jewish and also served in the Ford and Carter administrations, expressed concern that Miller would have outsized influence on the president’s decisions.

“Miller is bigoted, xenophobic, and vicious – the architect and chief advocate of Trump’s loathsome immigration policy,” Reich stated, accusing him of conducting a “brutal Kristallnacht against undocumented immigrants”. Kristallnacht refers to the wave of deadly anti-Jewish violence in parts of Nazi-occupied Europe in 1938.

Katie Miller, who is also Jewish and married to Stephen Miller, defended her husband this weekend, after Michigan Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed called him a “broken man” on ABC’s This Week with George Stephanopoulos.

“Stephen has contributed far more to America at 41 than Abdul El-Sayed will in a lifetime,” she wrote on X, alongside a photo of Miller running around with their children.

text:
A Cuban father of a US-born child was detained by immigration officers in Kentucky for nearly six months; a November 10 federal ruling found his detention unlawful and ordered his immediate release

| | TIMESOFINDIA.COM | Nov 13, 2026, 13:48 IST

A Cuban man detained by US immigration authorities for nearly six months must be released immediately, a federal court in Kentucky ruled on Tuesday. The court found that officials had failed to follow the required legal process before keeping him in custody, violating his constitutional right to due process.

Tired of too many ads?go ad free now

The ruling available on Justia, concerns Damichel Jesus Viamontes Castellano, who was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers on May 19. He had earlier been taken into custody by US Border Patrol agents in Texas in 2022 but was allowed to remain outside detention while his immigration case proceeded.

Castellano has since been held at the Oldham County Detention Center in La Grange, Kentucky. His immigration case took another turn on July 28, when an immigration judge directed that he be removed to Cuba. However, he challenged that decision, and his appeal is still being considered by the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA).

The pending appeal was important to the court's decision because the removal order had not yet become administratively final. The judge also noted that both sides agreed that Castellano's detention fell under Section 1226(a) of the Immigration and Nationality Act. This provision allows immigration authorities to hold a person while deciding whether they should be removed from the country.

Castellano has family and business connections in Kentucky. He is the father of a child born in Louisville in 2024 who is a US citizen. His mother is also a lawful permanent resident and has an approved family petition filed on his behalf. He runs an active Kentucky business, as its sole organiser and registered agent.

According to the court, officials had not properly assessed whether he needed to remain in custody or informed him of the procedure available to challenge that decision.

Tired of too many ads?go ad free now

How ICE brought Castellano back into custody

Castellano first came to the attention of US immigration authorities in 2022, when Border Patrol agents arrested him in Texas. He was issued a notice to appear in immigration proceedings and subsequently released on his own recognisance.

ICE revisited his case in May. Officers found that he had earlier received the immigration notice and had faced charges of DUI and reckless driving in February 2025. These charges prompted the agency to plan a targeted operation to take him into custody.

ICE arrested him on May 19 and withdrew the release granted to him in 2022. Officials issued several immigration documents, including a warrant of arrest, but did not give him Form I-286, the notice used to communicate an initial custody decision.

That missing document became central to the court proceedings. It allows a detained person to understand the government's decision and seek a review by an immigration judge, including a hearing to request release on bond.

The court found no record showing that ICE had considered Castellano's individual circumstances before deciding to detain him. Under the applicable rules, officers must examine whether a person is likely to attend future immigration hearings and whether their release would create a safety risk.

The judge also found that the government had not established that Castellano received the required information about his detention or how he could challenge it.

Why court rejected government's argument

The government maintained that Castellano should have approached the immigration court himself to seek a fresh decision on his custody. Its lawyers argued that he could have filed a request for a bond hearing rather than approaching the federal court directly.

Castellano argued that immigration officials had failed to complete the initial steps required by their own rules and could not shift the responsibility to him after leaving those steps unfinished.

The federal judge accepted this argument. The court found that the authorities had not carried out the initial custody review or provided the necessary notice. It therefore declined to make Castellano complete another administrative process before considering his challenge.

The judge also considered the time he had already spent in custody. By the time he approached the court, he had remained detained for more than 120 days without an independent judicial examination of the decision to keep him there.

The ruling further addressed the responsibility of proving whether detention was necessary. The government wanted the detained person to demonstrate that they were neither a danger to the community nor likely to flee.

The court disagreed with this approach. It held that the government must establish through clear and convincing evidence that a person presents a danger or flight risk during a bond hearing under Section 1226(a).

In explaining its position, the judge pointed to the difficulties faced by people in immigration detention. They may struggle to collect documents and evidence, understand complicated immigration procedures or obtain legal assistance. The court said these difficulties made it important for the government to justify continued detention.

It also considered Castellano's earlier release. ICE had allowed him to remain outside custody after his 2022 arrest but later decided to detain him again. The court found that the government had not shown why keeping him confined without the required review was justified.

ICE directed to release him immediately

The judge concluded that the failure to assess Castellano's case individually and inform him of his right to challenge detention had deprived him of due process under the Fifth Amendment to the US Constitution.

The court also considered the impact of detention on personal freedom and the government's reasons for holding him. It found that immigration authorities had not established a sufficient basis for continuing his confinement without following the prescribed safeguards.

It consequently granted his petition for a writ of habeas corpus, along with his request to expedite the proceedings.

The ruling also places conditions on any attempt to detain him again. Unless circumstances have materially changed, officials must first provide him with a bond hearing under Section 1226(a).
