text:
Donald Trump’s response to the November 3 Democratic sweep—which stripped Republicans of control of Congress, in part due to voters’ rejection of the extremism of his immigration policy—was to select Stephen Miller, the architect of his administration’s most anti-immigrant measures, including the separation of children from their parents, as his new chief of staff on Friday.

Already on Saturday, agents from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) escalated their abuse of power when, for two hours, they blocked the entrance to the emergency room at Adventist Health White Memorial Medical Center in Boyle Heights, Los Angeles, where they had transported a detainee who required medical attention.

Because of the blockade, ambulances that arrived during that time had to be diverted to other hospitals. Boyle Heights is a historic, predominantly Latino neighborhood. Would they have blocked the entrance to an emergency room in an economically privileged neighborhood?

And on Sunday, in an interview with CBS’s “60 Minutes,” Trump admitted that his policy of detentions and deportations has been “too tough” and that voters rejected the arrest and removal of people with established lives and jobs.

He even spoke of the possibility of negotiating a deal with the Democrats to regularize the status of those immigrants who have been settled in the United States for 10 years or more. But on Monday, Trump backtracked, stating that “there will be no amnesty… my public policy has not changed.”

Miller’s appointment does not point toward compromise or moderation, despite the disastrous political results for the Republicans.

The fact is, Miller doesn’t care if the Republican Party implodes as long as he can continue his anti-immigrant crusade, which began during his teenage years in Santa Monica, California.

His affinity for white supremacist ideas is nothing new. In college, he worked with white nationalist Richard Spencer. In the Senate, while working for another anti-immigrant figure—former Attorney General and former Republican Senator from Alabama, Jeff Sessions—Miller promoted white nationalist ideas to guide public policy proposals.

That same sympathy for white supremacists—which he shares with the president—is what has guided this administration’s policies, from the cancellation of DACA, the Muslim ban, and the separation of families, to its obsession with reducing or even eliminating legal immigration to the United States.

And now he has a powerful platform as Trump’s chief of staff. If he did so much damage as deputy chief of staff, what will happen now?

One major difference is that, starting January 3, 2027, there will be a Democratic Congress with overwhelming majorities that will not be a rubber stamp for the White House.

With that in mind, a coalition of organizations sent a letter to Democratic congressional leadership urging them to hold accountable, on the very first day of their term, those responsible for an immigration policy that has caused humanitarian and economic harm—and even deaths.

“Congress must act immediately to rein in ICE, starting with day-one subpoenas for the architects, willing accomplices, and perpetrators of Donald Trump’s mass deportation agenda. Stephen Miller, White House ‘border czar’ Tom Homan, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, and Acting Director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement David Venturella are the first in line who must be held accountable for the human and economic disaster they have created,” states the letter signed by, among others, UnidosUS, Voto Latino, CHIRLA, We are CASA, Latino Victory Project, Hispanic Federation, and America’s Voice.

The groups demand that Miller be the first witness to testify under oath; that subpoenas be issued on the first day for Homan, Mullin, and Venturella; and that new ICE spending and contracts be frozen.

A Democratic-controlled Congress provides more checks and balances. It can exercise greater oversight of ICE’s operations, demand accountability, and exert more control over ICE’s massive budgets, since the House of Representatives has authority over the public funds agencies use.

Of course, the misnamed “Big Beautiful Bill” of 2026 guarantees ICE’s multibillion-dollar budget for the remainder of Trump’s presidency, and new legislative attempts to reduce those funds will likely face presidential vetoes.

The power to conduct investigations and subpoena officials to testify under oath carries significant weight, but with Trump and Miller in the White House, what lies ahead for the new Democratic Congress and the immigrant community is an intense clash of powers.

The total number of deportations breaks all records in ICE’s 23-year history, including the previous record of 442,640 deportations made in 2025.

The report comes days after US President Donald Trump acknowledged his administration’s immigration crackdown may have been “too tough”.

“Fiscal Year 2026 saw the highest number of ICE deportations and arrests for any year in ICE’s history. September 2026 was the best September in ICE’s history in terms of arrests,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement.

ICE said it made more than 48,000 arrests in September, ending a two-month run of record highs that reached 50,925 in August.

Vague figures?

“There is no question the administration has increased enforcement more than any prior president. There’s also evidence that the illegal immigrant population has declined significantly because of increased out-migration due to a fear of enforcement,” Steven Camarota, director of research for the Washington, DC-based Center for Immigration Studies (CIS), told Al Jazeera.

However, he highlighted ambiguity in the figures DHS released.

“Of course the data is always incomplete and it’s difficult to measure. On the specific numbers released today, the big issue that I have not been able to determine is what percentage of these individuals are interior enforcement and what percentage are removals from the interior of the United States and what percentage are those turned around at the border or at airport.

“Increased removals, sometimes called deportation, certainly can encourage more people to go home, and clearly that is a central goal of this administration,” Camarota concluded.

‘Too tough’

Trump has acknowledged that his administration’s immigration policies “might be too tough”.

“A lot of people would say it is great but a lot of people would think it is too tough,” Trump said in a recent interview with CBS’s 60 Minutes.

Trump, however, defended his performance. “For getting people out, I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out; I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation or breaking of the law that was they came into the country illegally.”

Trump’s immigration crackdown has become a political vulnerability, with his approval rating on the issue falling to 38 percent from 50 percent at the start of his presidency, based on Reuters/Ipsos polling.

‘We will rip ICE apart’

The Democrats appear to be gearing up to halt Trump’s immigration crackdown when they take control of Congress next year. They plan to target ICE tactics ⁠and expand paths to legal status, despite limits on ⁠how much they can achieve.

“We will investigate the administration weaponising DHS against Americans (and) its out of control immigration policies,” Bennie Thompson, a Mississippi Democrat and the soon-to-be chair of the House Homeland Security Committee, told the Reuters news agency in a statement.

At a news conference in the US Capitol with House members and newly elected representatives from southwestern border states, Henry Cuellar, a centrist Texas Democrat, ‌said he had already had conversations with Trump officials about focusing deportation efforts on criminals.

“We’re not going to be extreme,” Cuellar said, nodding to conservative voters across the US who cast their votes for Democrats.

But a number of Democratic voices sounded firmer.

“We will rip ICE apart,” Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan said while celebrating her triumph in Minnesota, where federal immigration agents shot dead two people during an enforcement surge in January.

Two US citizens, Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good, were killed in Minneapolis, in incidents that were caught on bystander video.

Their shooting deaths have gone viral, prompting international outrage. Other footage shows masked agents deploying chemical agents and beating civilians who were documenting their activities or protesting – activities protected under the US Constitution.

title: It's Time to Reform Our Immigration Courts - Progressive.org
description:
Earlier this fall, sitting in the back of an immigration courtroom in Hyattsville, Maryland, I watched an immigration judge convince an elderly man that he didn’t need an attorney.
While immigration judges sit on a bench and wear robes, they are not members of the independent judiciary.
While much of the national outrage has understandably been focused on ICE itself, we should also commit to a top-to-bottom reform of the immigration court system.
That starts with establishing an independent judiciary for immigration proceedings, protecting immigration judges from political hiring and firing, and ensuring that everyone appearing before an immigration judge is afforded an attorney.
These types of basic reforms would afford Americans the minimum level of due process currently lacking in immigration courts across the country.
text:
Earlier this fall, sitting in the back of an immigration courtroom in Hyattsville, Maryland, I watched an immigration judge convince an elderly man that he didn’t need an attorney.

The man was facing the threat of deportation to a country where he said he’d experienced attempts on his life in the past. His voice was quiet, but he repeatedly and clearly asked for time to find an attorney, which the judge had previously said was his right.

But now, no matter how many times the man asked, the judge told him not to bother with an attorney for his next hearing. Eventually, the man gave up and agreed, likely to his detriment.

Over the last year, in my role as a immigration court observer through a program with the American Bar Association and the Acacia Center for Justice, I have witnessed many such affronts to judicial fairness and due process. The Trump Administration has ordered immigration judges to cut the time migrants have to find an attorney to just ten days, as part of a broad effort to speed up deportations.

While immigration judges sit on a bench and wear robes, they are not members of the independent judiciary. They are not confirmed by the Senate or elected at the local level. Nor are their jobs protected from political interference.

Immigration judges reside within the executive branch, are appointed by the Attorney General, and can be fired if the administration does not like their rulings. And in fact, during the most recent fiscal year, 38 percent of all immigration judges in the United States were fired or resigned, setting the stage for President Donald Trump to pack the benches with his own picks. In response, the national approval rate for asylum cases has fallen from more than 50 percent to less than 6 percent since the term of former President Joe Biden.

Even worse, I’ve watched “detained respondents”—immigrants held in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) camps across the country—give up their cases altogether and self-deport before ever getting an evidentiary hearing, just to get out of the camps. So far in Trump’s second term, these facilities have detained more than 610,000 people, or nearly 2 percent of the U.S. population.

Immigration offenses are civil cases, meaning that people are being held in detention although they have not been accused of any crime. I’ve seen detainees break down while telling the judge they don’t understand why they’ve been locked up for months with no hearing, no attorney, and no bail.

As an observer, I’m only allowed to see initial hearings for adults. But behind closed doors, children as young as three years old are being forced to represent themselves. This practice has occurred under presidents of both political parties, but the Trump Administration cut funding for migrant children’s attorneys, leading to as many as 25,000 children losing their lawyers.

Add in the U.S. Supreme Court’s September 2025 ruling allowing immigration enforcement to stop and detain individuals on the basis of their race, and it is clear the system is not designed to ensure justice. It’s designed to cleanse the United States of a population that Trump has said is “poisoning the blood of our country.”

That should terrify us all, and it should spur immediate action.

While much of the national outrage has understandably been focused on ICE itself, we should also commit to a top-to-bottom reform of the immigration court system.

That starts with establishing an independent judiciary for immigration proceedings, protecting immigration judges from political hiring and firing, and ensuring that everyone appearing before an immigration judge is afforded an attorney. Congress should also define reasons for migrants to be detained before their hearings, eliminating the broad leeway that has allowed ICE to lock up hundreds of thousands of people.

And of course, the Supreme Court should immediately overturn Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s career-defining decision to legalize racial profiling in immigration enforcement—a decision he has already sheepishly tried to walk back in footnotes to subsequent decisions.

These types of basic reforms would afford Americans the minimum level of due process currently lacking in immigration courts across the country. Because what is happening today is not justice, it’s a travesty.

text:
A group of protesters gathered outside San Diego's federal building Thursday to share outrage over the detention last week of an 8-year-old Haitian boy following an immigration check-in.

The boy, a third grader at Fay Elementary School in City Heights, was taken into federal custody last Wednesday. Video recorded by volunteer observer Karen Pohl at the federal building shows three armed federal agents walking the boy away from ICE’s field office and into an elevator.

"It just shocked the crap out of me, basically, because I never thought they'd take a kid that young alone," Pohl said.

Pohl was among hundreds of people — parents, teachers, activists, elected officials and others — who united outside the Edward J. Schwartz federal building, which houses ICE's office and immigration court. Weekly protests against the Trump Administration's immigration policies have been held outside the federal building for more than a year, but the boy's detention drew a larger-than-usual crowd.

San Diego City Councilmember Sean Elo-Rivera encouraged the crowd to "say it loud enough that they hear it in this building and in D.C.," leading chants of, "Bring him home, bring him home."

San Diego Unified School District leaders said last week the boy previously had Temporary Protected Status, which was revoked earlier this year. District officials said he was living with his uncle after his father was deported more than a year ago. The child recently received a letter to meet with ICE and his uncle took him to the check-in because he "did not want to break the law," the district said.

ICE said during that check-in, the uncle could not establish legal guardianship under requirements of the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act. ICE said the agency then determined the boy was an unaccompanied minor and placed him in the care of the Office of Refugee Resettlement "to ensure the child's safety."

The uncle's attorney told NBC 7 the uncle did have a notarized letter from the boy's father but ICE said they needed a court order, and they took the 8-year-old into custody.

"I told the child, you’re going to be OK, just to calm him down, you know? Because he’s 8 years old," Robert Ferretti recalled. "And then the officer said, 'Yeah, in those places, they have ice cream and video games, and it's set up for kids so they feel comfortable.'"

"Allegations that ICE took a third grader into custody to be placed in detention are FALSE, and any suggestion otherwise is a depraved attempt to smear our ICE law enforcement officers and undermine the work of President Trump and Secretary Mullin to protect children," a DHS spokesperson said in a statement, when asked about the case.

"The government says it was protecting him? Protecting him from what?" San Diego Education Association President Monique Barrett said at the protest Thursday, surrounding by teachers at Fay Elementary. "I know what trauma does. It shapes how children sleep, learn and trust and those wounds can last a lifetime."

"A child's humanity outranks every badge," she added.

DHS said the child was initially brought to the U.S. by a man "claiming" to be his father, who was previously deported to Mexico by Customs and Border Protection. It’s not clear where the boy’s mother is. The child remains in the custody of the Office of Refugee Resettlement, but it's also not clear exactly where.

The incident garnered the attention of the San Diego Unified School District and later San Diego's elected representatives who wrote letters to DHS and the U.S. Health and Human Services Agency demanding answers.

Cody Petterson, a board trustee with the SDUSD, said the district does not know where the child is being held, but they believe it may be Los Angeles. Either way, Petterson added, he's "certainly not with family or with a designated caregiver.”

The Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to end TPS for Haitians earlier this year.

TPS is a humanitarian designation created by Congress in 1990 to prevent deportations to countries suffering from natural disasters, civil strife and other instability. It was first granted to Haitians in 2010 by the Obama administration after a catastrophic 7.0 earthquake, which caused more than 200,000 deaths and the collapse of hundreds of thousands of buildings. TPS has been extended several time since as the island nation fell into deeper crisis.

This summer's Supreme Court ruling is not the first time Haiti has come up in the Trump administration, with the president using an expletive to describe Haiti and African countries during a 2018 closed-door meeting. In 2024, Trump repeated a baseless claim during a presidential debate that Haitian immigrants were eating pets.

Since 2018, thousands have been killed and more than 600,000 Haitians have been displaced - many to the United States. More than 350,000 Haitians live in the U.S., including thousands locally.

text:
By Emma Alejandro

Staff Writer

U.S. Federal Judge Valeria Caproni of the Southern District of New York issued a temporary restraining order barring already scheduled deportation flights of 150-200 Afghan nationals through Nov. 7, according to NBC News.

As noted by Afghanistan International, the Trump administration had initially arranged to fly dozens of Afghan immigrants out of Alexandria, Louisiana. The plan involved deporting asylum-seeking immigrants transiting through Pakistan and back overland into Afghanistan.

However, on Nov. 3, 65 members of Congress signed a letter authored by Rep. Scott Peters raising concerns that sending Afghan nationals back would result in knowingly subjecting vulnerable people to perilous conditions. They expressed the deportation would expose them to “persecution, torture, or even death,” according to The Independent.

From the Office of Rep. Scott Peters, Rep. Peters commented in endorsement of the congressional block, "Our nation made a promise to stand by the Afghans who risked their lives and their family safety for us and for our safety, and sending them to the Taliban breaks that promise."

The congressional letter was directed to homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, according to The Independent.

Within the letter, warnings from advocacy groups were cited, including AfghanEvac, the American Civil Liberties Union, Human Rights First, Refugees International, and the Public Affairs Alliance of Iranian Americans. They stressed that Afghanistan is currently listed as a Level 4 “Do Not Travel” country by the State Department.

Another point of contention, according to the Scott Peters press release, is that many of the detained Afghanistan immigrants and their family members assisted U.S. troops, thereby putting a target on their back in the case they were to return. After the Taliban returned in 2021, families who helped U.S. forces in any way in toppling the regime after 2001 have since been subject to revenge killings as retribution, as reported by The Human Rights Watch.

The New York Times also argued that out of the scheduled 150 Afghan nationals, there was at least one woman and one homosexual man. As homosexuality is considered illegal and punishable by persecution, and women have faced severe restrictions in daily activity under the Taliban regime, both have more than reasonable means to fear for their lives if sent back.

In light of these threats, according to The New York Times, the homosexual detainee was ordered to be immediately released by the court on Nov. 3. Another man whose wife worked with the U.S. military for 14 days was postponed in his removal operations on Nov. 2.

The Trump administration contended with the court that Immigration Customs Enforcement schedules flights weeks in advance and the court has limited intervention authority. Nevertheless, ICE and Judge Caproni reported individually in follow-ups that no Afghan nationals that were previously scheduled would be deported from the U.S. up to Nov. 7.

According to NBC News, lawyers representing some of the 150 detainees presented that the role of the Pakistani government facilitating transportation of Afghan nationals had no place in deportation operations between the U.S. and Afghanistan. Third world countries have been used as a deterrent in order to explore mass-deportation efforts under the Trump administration’s positioning.

Yet, in its defence before the court, the Trump administration maintained that the transfer of Afghans to Pakistan could not be classified as a third-country deportation, as Pakistan was designated merely as a transit route rather than a destination, according to Afghanistan International.

According to the Office of Rep. Scott Peters, President of AfghanEvac Shawn VanDiver remarked, "A week ago, there was a plane. Today, the government told a federal judge there isn't one. That didn't happen by accident. Veterans, advocates, 66 members of Congress, and thousands of Americans got this flight stopped, and the court made sure it stays stopped this week. This is a reprieve, not a resolution."

The New York Times significantly noted that the congressional block expired on Nov. 7, meaning the court order did not halt deportations altogether, but for a brief period of time. AfghanEvac and other legal representatives also emphasized this is not a permanent cancellation of removal proceedings for the detained Afghans, according to the Office of Scott Peters.

These targeted efforts against asylum-seeking immigrants are consistent with a rise in anti-immigrant sentiment under the Trump administration. According to The Middle East Institute, the Department of Homeland Security ended Temporary Protected Status for more than 9,000 Afghans from 2025.

There are hundreds of Afghan detainees being held in facilities in Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention in Louisiana, leaving their fates undecided, as reported by The Independent. However, according to The Hill, with Republicans set to lose control of the House following the midterm elections, more advocates within a new congressional majority will continue to debate the U.S.’ role toward Afghanistan asylum-seeking immigrants.

text:
The Trump administration is preparing to kick nearly 80,000 people, about half of them children, off federal housing assistance over their family’s immigration status, threatening to drive thousands into homelessness.

On Thursday, the Department of Housing and Urban Development published a final rule that’s on track to effectively bar families of mixed immigration status from receiving most federal housing assistance, which allow people to receive housing vouchers to reside in privately owned rental homes or in government-owned or -assisted public housing units.

As it stands, undocumented immigrants and temporary non-residents in the United States already are barred from personally receiving most forms of federal housing assistance. But if some members of the family are eligible, the eligible members can receive prorated assistance to help cover their housing, and the non-eligible family member can live with them.

The new rule, which goes into effect in mid-December, would disqualify an entire family if one member is ineligible after a temporary grace period, forcing them to choose between separation and eviction.

Families are “going to be faced with the impossible choice of deciding whether they want to split up so that some people can stay housed, or to stay together and risk homelessness and eviction,” said Marie Claire Tran-Leung, Evictions Initiative Project director at the National Housing Law Project.

Children will bear a disproportionate burden, Tran-Leung said. Of the nearly 80,000 people who could be affected, according to estimates from Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, nearly 37,000 are children.

Many families have one parent who doesn’t qualify, one parent who’s a citizen or otherwise eligible immigrant — i.e. a permanent resident — and kids who hold U.S. citizenship. According to Tran-Leung, the typical mixed-status family in HUD housing is a family of four that fits that profile.

This rule is “going to tear families apart and take adults away from their children,” said Deborah Thrope, chief program officer at the National Housing Law Project.

Beyond potentially leaving tens of thousands of families and children homeless or separated, the change could cost the already beleaguered federal housing agency hundreds of millions of dollars, housing experts told The Intercept. This would likely worsen conditions across the board for the roughly 9 million people in federal housing, who would now be subject to onerous documentation requirements.

“The impacts are not just limited to mixed-status families,” said Renee Williams, senior advisor for public policy at the National Low Income Housing Coalition.

Currently, both U.S. citizens and non-citizens are required to submit a declaration under penalty of perjury attesting that their citizenship or immigration status makes them eligible for housing assistance. Non-citizens under age 62 must submit a document that proves their immigration status. And additional documentation can be requested by local housing agencies or landlords.

The rule change would upend the current system. U.S. citizens would have to go through the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements program, also known as SAVE, to verify their eligibility status.

“It’s a system that hasn’t been used to verify citizenship before but now is because of the work that DHS and DOGE did together on a very expedited timeline at the beginning of the Trump administration,” said Tran-Leung. “This causes a lot of concern for us about the very significant risks of residents who are citizens being caught up in verification issues and potentially losing their housing.”

If SAVE cannot verify someone’s eligibility, the new rule requires the person to provide documentation proving their status. The rule would give families 30 days to obtain evidence of immigration status, in addition to the initial 30-day grace period where families can receive pro-rated assistance before having to go through verification.

Tran-Leung and other experts worry that the new documentation requirements could make it harder for low-income tenants — particularly older immigrants over the age of 62, who were previously exempted from verification requirements — to access the program.

Older people, low-income people, and people who’ve experienced homelessness are far more likely to lack access to proof of citizenship such as a passport, valid photo ID, or birth certificate. That means an untold number of the millions of eligible people in federal housing programs could lose assistance just for lack of documentation.

“For folks who may not have easy documentation accessible, who may not have access to a birth certificate, who may not have access to a passport, we’re really worried,” said Williams.

The changes would also burden housing agencies financially by requiring their staff to review documents that were previously not required by federal law.

It is unclear just how expensive these additional administrative costs will be for HUD. But an analysis from HUD itself found that because mixed-status families receive assistance prorated, it would cost the federal government $300 million in additional funds to serve the same number of families as it does now.

For example, a family of four with one ineligible member currently receives 75% of a full household subsidy. A family of four that is not mixed status receives 100% of the subsidy, making it more expensive for the agency to house the non-mixed-status family even though the two families have the same number of people.

“At the same time, HUD is requesting fewer funds from Congress to end homelessness,” said Kayla Blackwell, senior housing policy analyst at the National Low Income Housing Coalition. President Donald Trump recently proposed cutting $3.8 billion from the agency’s affordable housing, homelessness, and community development programs.

HUD Secretary Scott Turner has justified the rule by claiming that mixed-status families are “pushing aside hardworking U.S. citizens” for housing. But experts said the changes will make the system worse for everyone.

“This is scapegoating immigrant families, and HUD is doing less,” said Blackwell.

For the families who either are forced out of the program or leave willingly due to fears around their status, the road ahead is difficult. The majority of mixed-status families live in California, Texas, and New York, where the cost of living can be incredibly high.

“It’s going to be really difficult, I think, for families to be able to stay in their communities and not be displaced if they lose their access to HUD assistance,” said Blackwell.

text:
A lot of things happened. Here are some of the things. This is TPM’s Morning Memo.

The Retribution: Somalia Edition

All of the discussion of the Trump White House’s resistance to oversight from the new Democratic Congress seems almost quaint in the context of the Trump DOJ raiding the home of a sitting Democratic member of Congress days before the election.

In a new development on that front, the NYT reports that the Trump administration took the unusual step of indicting one of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s former bodyguards in April for a felony related to his green card application in an attempt to flip him against her:

Mr. Mohamed’s lawyer, Bruce Rivers, said that prosecutors spent months trying to turn the bodyguard into an informant to bolster their case against Ms. Omar. In a move he described as shocking, Mr. Rivers said that prosecutors repeatedly told him and Mr. Mohamed that the investigation into Ms. Omar was “100 percent being run by 1600 Pennsylvania Ave.,” the address of the White House.

“I’ve never seen anything like this in my almost 28 years practicing law in federal court,” said Mr. Rivers, a veteran criminal defense lawyer in Minneapolis.

The case was by the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Minnesota, but as the NYT notes: “The government lawyers assigned to the case were early-career federal prosecutors who were promoted to leadership roles in the U.S. attorney’s office in Minneapolis after several veteran attorneys left the office early this year in protest over its handling of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in Minnesota.”

As the NYT puts it, the Trump DOJ “failed” to flip the bodyguard, but he was offered immunity and was brought before a D.C. grand jury investigating the Minnesota Democrat, where he reportedly testified to having no substantive knowledge of Omar’s immigration and marriage history.

That was on Sept. 3.

The next day the Trump DOJ moved to dismiss the indictment, with the explanation from prosecutors that the bodyguard was in removal proceedings: “Accordingly, there is no longer a federal interest in continuing prosecution in light of his anticipated removal from the United States.” Take that as you will.

Oversight Agonistes

Before the election, Greg Sargent and Brian Beutler spoke to a number of House and Senate Democrats and senior aides about whether they were prepared for the extreme resistance to congressional oversight that the Trump White House was expected to demonstrate. Their conclusion:

Every Democrat we spoke with agreed that the Trump administration is world-historically corrupt, and most expected his lawbreaking to persist or even escalate. Some do seem willing to contemplate suspension of the regular order of things, if that’s what it takes to slow or stop the lawlessness. Others, though, seem more resigned to running a playbook for normal times, one that’s plainly unsuited to the coming moment.

The Trump White House resistance is already manifesting in absurd claims that congressional oversight is itself criminal.

For Your Radar …

Rep. Jared Huffman (D-CA), the ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, is demanding that the Interior Department preserve documents related to President Trump’s pet construction projects around D.C., CNN reports:

Multiple credible whistleblowers have approached Huffman’s committee in recent weeks to voice concern that the Interior Department is getting rid of records in anticipation of forthcoming scrutiny, the sources told CNN. The agency oversees much of the national parkland Trump wants to use for his projects.

The Interior Department called the whistleblower claims “100% false.”

Josh Marshall: Understanding the Scandal/Accountability Conveyor Belt

Still Basking in the Election Aftermath

A sampling of election news:

House: Not a single Democratic incumbent in the House lost in the general election, the WaPo notes.

Ohio-10: Rep. Mike Turner (R-OH), who was swept out of office by the blue wave after nearly a quarter of a century in the House, blames his loss on that controversial ad by GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy: “That final ad from Vivek really was kind of a lightning strike at the end, and it had an impact up and down the ticket in all the races … Absolutely that was the margin at the end.”

North Carolina: Democrats are one uncalled state Senate election away from having a trifecta in North Carolina. But in that very close race, state Sen. Danny Britt (R) still leads Catina Hamm (D) by 228 votes even though the race has tightened since election night. The race remains within the margin for a recount.

Quote of the Day

After all three levels of the federal courts blocked its lawsuit seeking to use the Big Lie of rampant noncitizen voting to interfere in the California election, the Trump DOJ moved to dismiss the case with a pissy filing complaining about all that losing.

U.S. District Judge David O. Carter granted the dismissal, but not without taking a parting shot at the administration:

This lawsuit attempted to disrupt an ongoing election and create confusion and uncertainty for voters and election workers alike. The right to vote is sacred. So, too, is trust in our democracy. text:
Warehouses in two small Georgia cities that Immigration and Customs Enforcement planned to transform into detention facilities are now up for sale.

The warehouses in Social Circle and Oakwood are part of a portfolio of properties put up for bidding by commercial real estate company Cushman & Wakefield. The other properties include warehouses in Salt Lake City, Detroit, El Paso, and Central Pennsylvania.

Bidding on the warehouses is set to end on Thursday. The deadline comes a little more than a month after the Department of Homeland Security officials sent letters to the cities saying that they were considering putting their properties up for sale.

DHS bought a 540,408-square-foot warehouse in Oakwood for $68.2 million in 2025, a deed shows. Oakwood officials first learned in February that the federal agency was considering converting the warehouses into an ICE detention facility. A similar warehouse on Hightower Trail in Social Circle was also purchased in February.

In documents obtained by CBS News Atlanta, the two sites were part of a plan by the federal agency to create new large-scale "hubs" across the country that would hold thousands of detainees by the end of 2026.

Social Circle's facility was expected to house between 7,500 to 10,000 detainees. Oakwood was to be designated a "processing site," where detainees would stay for some time between three and seven days. The facility was expected to house an average daily population of 1,000 to 1,500 detainees.

Officials in both cities pushed back against the plan, citing concerns over the lack of communication and fears that the large-scale projects would severely impact infrastructure like water and sewage systems. Social Circle Social Circle officials cut off water to site of planned Georgia ICE detention "mega-center" in March, saying that it wouldn't be removed until ICE showed how it would prevent the facility from exceeding its limited water and sewer capacity.

In April, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin put a pause on the $38-billion plan to scrutinize all contracts signed under former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.

title: How Democrats Can Start the Next Era of Immigration Reform Now - TIME
description:
Yet in an interview with Ross Douthat on 60 Minutes recorded before Miller’s appointment, Trump suggested he was open to an immigration deal with Democrats.
Now, with a fronteriza elected governor of Texas and Democratic leadership across all four southern border states, border communities have an opportunity to shape the policies that directly affect their lives.
Border states should begin preparing now rather than waiting for another crisis.
A functioning immigration system should bring in the workers communities need while providing a way for undocumented immigrants already doing those jobs to obtain legal status.
His bill creates new visas for careworkers while allowing eligible undocumented workers already in the U.S. to obtain legal status.
text:
The 2026 midterm election results rebuked President Donald Trump’s failures on the economy and, in several competitive races, his immigration agenda. Latino voters who backed him in 2024 swung back to Democrats, helping deliver the politically unthinkable. Texas elected its first Democratic senator since 1988 and its first Latina governor, while Democrats won governorships in all four southern border states and every southern border congressional district. Over the last two years, Trump quieted the border but the backlash against his mass deportation campaign overshadowed that achievement, suggesting voters want a secure border without seeing the same aggressive enforcement tactics in their communities.

The party has been given a chance to persuade voters that it can offer a better alternative to Republicans on immigration. If Democrats blow it, they may not get another one in 2028.

Trump is certainly not going to make it easy. He responded to his midterm losses by elevating Stephen Miller, the architect of mass deportations, to White House chief of staff. Yet in an interview with Ross Douthat on 60 Minutes recorded before Miller’s appointment, Trump suggested he was open to an immigration deal with Democrats. He walked those comments back a day later, saying there won’t be amnesty for undocumented immigrants and that his policy hasn’t changed.

On the defensive front, Congress is limited in what it can do to rein in mass deportations. The multi-year funding Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) received in the last two years, more than $113 billion, cannot be taken away without new legislation and, absent a veto-proof majority, Trump’s signature. That being said, if they can collect a veto-proof majority, Congress should try to limit how that funding is used by passing new legislation. With the money and infrastructure already in place, oversight of ICE and the Border Patrol will be essential to exposing abuses, holding the administration accountable, and slowing them down.

But reining in ICE doesn’t eliminate the need for an affirmative vision. Democrats have to get organized and do both. Any Democratic plan needs to address the border. And the key to doing so lies in the hands of locally elected Democrats. Rather than waiting for the next Democratic president to do better on the issue, the four newly elected Democratic governors along the southern border have an opportunity to rebuild trust now.

For decades, Washington has made border policy with too little input from the Americans forced to live with its consequences. I grew up in one of these communities in southern New Mexico. Lawmakers have ignored Border Patrol’s violent tactics and racial profiling against Latino border residents, failed to provide resources to help communities manage migration emergencies, and neglected Americans who live in colonias, underserved settlements that lack the basic necessities most Americans take for granted, from clean drinking water to functioning sewage systems.

Now, with a fronteriza elected governor of Texas and Democratic leadership across all four southern border states, border communities have an opportunity to shape the policies that directly affect their lives. The four governors should develop a border security compact that sets shared priorities for state-level border operations, economic development, asylum reform, and preparations for future migration emergencies, and then use that compact to press Congress and the administration for action.

This is one area where there may be welcome collaboration from the Trump Administration. Working with federal officials and Mexico, the governors can make clear that Democrats will not tolerate chaos at the border while advancing a new system in which seeking humanitarian protection no longer requires relying on human smugglers to cross illegally into the United States.

The governors must also prepare for the possibility of another migration surge after Trump leaves office, regardless of who succeeds him, Democrat or Republican. Four years of restrictive immigration policies and cruel enforcement could create pent-up demand for migration, and misinformation about whether the border will reopen will abound. Border states should begin preparing now rather than waiting for another crisis.

As Democrats move to constrain ICE and rebuild trust on the border, they must also respond to the voters who placed their “I Voted” stickers on the memorials of Renee Nicole Good, Alex Pretti, and Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. Those tributes were reminders that millions of American citizens live alongside neighbors, coworkers, and loved ones who remain vulnerable to deportation because Congress has failed to give them a path to legal status.

Democrats should start strong in January and pass the American Dream and Promise Act, a House bill that creates a pathway to permanent residence and citizenship not only for Dreamers, but also for the hundreds of thousands of Temporary Protected Status holders who have lived and worked in the United States for years. That should be the floor of their ambitions on legalization, not the ceiling.

Doing so may require reaching across the aisle, either to build a veto-proof majority or to collaborate with Trump. Democrats should argue that legalizing undocumented immigrants who have had no chance to access legal status because of a civil immigration violation can be a solution to problems Americans experience every day, from the shortage of workers building new homes to the rising cost of child care. A functioning immigration system should bring in the workers communities need while providing a way for undocumented immigrants already doing those jobs to obtain legal status. These new legal pathways should reflect the needs of the economy, including visas for care workers and construction workers.

Representative Gabe Vasquez of New Mexico has already demonstrated what this approach can look like. Months before winning reelection in a competitive border district, he introduced the Careworker Visa Act at a time when many Democrats were reluctant to discuss immigration. His bill creates new visas for careworkers while allowing eligible undocumented workers already in the U.S. to obtain legal status. This, I believe, is the future of immigration reform.

Rather than simply investigating the deportation of veterans and military families, Democrats should advance legislation giving legal status to the families of service members and challenge Republicans to oppose it. They should do the same for construction workers needed to build new housing. And they should introduce a bill allowing states to request more visas for industries facing labor shortages and shrinking populations, building on legislation introduced by Senators John Curtis and Mark Kelly. Advance existing bills that help keep rural hospitals open by bringing in the doctors and nurses their communities need. Put each proposal before Congress, ask Republicans to sign on, and give Trump the opportunity to sign it. If he refuses, show Americans what they lose by his inaction.

text:
WASHINGTON - President Donald Trump threatened on Thursday to double tariffs on Mexico if it does not stop more than a thousand migrants walking north toward the United States after last week's US election, warning that they would not be allowed to enter.

"Here we go again!" the Republican president wrote on social media. "They will not be accepted! MEXICO MUST STOP THEM, NOW, and if they do not do so, the Tariffs on Mexico will be IMMEDIATELY DOUBLED. MEXICO, THE GOVERNOR OF TEXAS, THE VERY LIBERAL NEW GOVERNOR OF TEXAS, OUR GREAT BORDER PATROL, & ICE, HAVE BEEN SO INFORMED. There will be no leniency!"

An estimated 1,500 people, mostly from Central America, set off on Tuesday from the southern city of Tapachula near the Guatemalan border. The migrants are hoping that the election victory by Democrats that gives the party control of Congress starting in January could open pathways for them to live and work in the United States.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum recognized that a group of people were walking northward toward the United States, but said that no migrant caravans have arrived at the US border since Trump returned to power last year.

People in the migrant caravan have been informed of how difficult it is to enter the US, and Mexico is looking to return them to their countries of origin, Sheinbaum told a regular press conference.

"There will be no acts of repression," Sheinbaum added.

Some local media have reported that authorities in the southern state of Chiapas have turned back migrants as they sought to join the group this week.

Mexico's migration institute and the Chiapas state government did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

"We will utilize all assets to make sure our borders are secure," US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote on social media following Trump's tariff threat. "This illegal migrant caravan will NOT be allowed to enter our country. Full stop."

The United States and Mexico are negotiating a trade agreement after Trump chose in July to not extend the US-Mexico-Canada trade pact.

The Trump administration's tough immigration policies mostly stopped the flow of migrants to the US southern border, leaving many Mexican migrant shelters empty.

Trump was elected to a second term as president in 2024 in part over concern among US voters about the border. Since then, Trump has highlighted some migrant caravans but also said in recent months the issue has become less politically potent for him and his fellow Republicans.

"I am sure the new governor is going to want to have security at the Texas border," Trump told reporters after the November 3 midterm election, referencing the newly elected Texas governor, Democrat Gina Hinojosa.

Trump also has acknowledged political backlash from his administration's deportation program through US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

On Sunday, Trump told the CBS program "60 Minutes" that the deportation force had been "too tough" and that he was open to making an immigration deal with Democrats after they take control of Congress.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security on Thursday confirmed that a once-empty prison in Appleton, Minnesota, is now open and being used for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations.

According to DHS, the facility opened on Monday to "strengthen America's ability to enforce its immigration laws and carry out the American people's mandate for mass deportations."

The 1,600-bed Prairie Correctional Facility had been empty since 2010, according to Tennessee-based CoreCivic, which owns the prison.

"The site gives ICE immediate capacity to detain and remove those who have no legal right to remain, protecting American communities and restoring the integrity of our borders without waiting years for new construction," DHS said in a statement. "Every day, DHS is conducting law enforcement activities across the country to keep Americans safe. It should not come as news that ICE will be making arrests in states across the U.S. and ensuring we have resources to carry out President Trump's mission."

In August, CoreCivic announced a five-year contract with ICE and later completed a sale of the facility to the federal government for nearly $500 million.

The sale prompted Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison to call on Congress to investigate what he called a "corrupt $420 million prison overpayment," saying the state declined to purchase the prison previously for $75 million.

At the time of the August announcement, the activist group Indivisible Twin Cities said it was "outraged and horrified" by the contract and called the facility a "concentration camp."

"After the siege on our state by out-of-control federal agents who flagrantly ignored the law, it is an insult to our communities to open a for-profit concentration camp in our state. We oppose any concentration camp in Minnesota, or anywhere else," the group said.

When ICE and Border Patrol agents flooded into the state late last year, many detainees were held at the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building in Minneapolis before being moved to facilities in other states. Minnesota officials, immigration lawyers and others alleged the conditions within the building were deplorable, citing leg restraints for detainees, a shortage of beds and bathroom facilities and barriers to accessing legal aid.

The massive federal immigration operation in Minnesota, called Operation Metro Surge, sparked protests and lawsuits. During the operation, immigration agents in January shot and killed two Minnesotans, Alex Pretti and Renee Good. An ICE officer also faces charges for lying to the FBI in the Minneapolis nonfatal shooting of a Venezuelan man, which also occurred in January.

Appleton is in western Minnesota, about 30 miles from the South Dakota border.

title: What It's Really Like to Live With an ICE-Issued Ankle Monitor - Talking Points Memo
description:
When Linda and I spoke in October, her GPS ankle monitor was giving her constant electrical shocks.
She was able to connect with Envision Freedom Fund, a bond fund, which posted bond for her, and she was released.
But immediately after Linda left the jail she was brought to another room, she said, where she was also forced to put on the ankle monitor.
Now it’s extremely common for immigrants to be released from detention, only to be forced to wear an ankle monitor.
But before he was allowed to go, he was brought back to 26 Federal Plaza, where agents put an ankle monitor on him.
text:
When Linda and I spoke in October, her GPS ankle monitor was giving her constant electrical shocks. “It’s crazy, my leg is numb,” she said. When she tried to message Immigration and Customs Enforcement about the problem, she received no answer. She planned to go to her local ICE office later that day to get it fixed — the fourth time, she said, that she had to seek such help with a malfunctioning monitor since she had started wearing one four months earlier.

In July, Linda — a pseudonym because she still has an open immigration case — flew from New York to Hawaii for work. When the 35-year-old arrived at her gate for her flight back home, ICE officers were waiting and detained her. She came to the U.S. eight years ago on a visa and overstayed, but she has no criminal record. She’s had nightmares of flying somewhere and realizing she didn’t have the necessary documents to get back home. Now her worst nightmare was coming true.

She was held in a Hawaii jail for a month. She already struggles with mental health issues; she worried she would harm herself while detained. Eventually, she was able to get a bond hearing, where she was told she had to pay $10,000 to be released, far higher than what she could cover on her own. She was able to connect with Envision Freedom Fund, a bond fund, which posted bond for her, and she was released. In theory, bond is meant to ensure someone returns to immigration court and doesn’t flee since that’s the only way to get the money back. But immediately after Linda left the jail she was brought to another room, she said, where she was also forced to put on the ankle monitor.

GPS monitoring of immigrants isn’t new; its use doubled under President Joe Biden’s watch. But before the second Donald Trump administration, it was more often used in the place of detention. “It was uncommon for someone to be released on bond and put on some kind of physical technological surveillance because it was seen as redundant,” said Elizabeth Nguyen, program director at the Community Justice Exchange, a network of bail and bond funds. If someone was able to pay bond and get released from immigration detention, they were usually able to continue living their lives as normal. “It was just not something that we were seeing before,” said Rosa Santana, co-executive director of Envision Freedom Fund.

Now it’s extremely common for immigrants to be released from detention, only to be forced to wear an ankle monitor. Even getting released has become far more difficult as the Trump administration has fought against people’s ability to get a bond hearing and, in the rarer and rarer instances where people are granted bond, the amounts they have to pay have dramatically increased. Those lucky few who are granted bond face the new hurdle of GPS monitoring. The increase in the tactic appears to have occurred after the Trump administration issued a memo in June 2025 instructing ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations employees to, for all immigrants not being detained, “escalate their supervision level to GPS ankle monitors whenever possible.” After Trump revoked Temporary Protected Status for Haitians, many were called into ICE offices and made to wear ankle monitors.

The effects were deadly for at least one immigrant. On August 31, Pierre Damas Bel, a 20-year-old Haitian immigrant, died by suicide after being made to wear an ankle monitor, walking into oncoming highway traffic in Springfield, Ohio. His family have said that the mental toll of the monitor led to his death. Co-captain of a soccer team, he had pleaded with ICE to let him take it off because he couldn’t play in it; in his Reserve Officers’ Training Corp class, everyone was handed a uniform except for him. His classmates bullied him over it. “I’m walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg, carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation that I never imagined I would experience,” he wrote in an Instagram post before his death.

According to a report by Envision, nearly 54,000 immigrants were wearing these monitors by July 2026, more than three times as many as at the start of 2025. Santana estimated that 98 percent of the people the fund pays bond for have come out wearing an ankle monitor or are made to put one on in the days after their release. “It’s almost everybody,” she said.

Miguel had never in his life been incarcerated before last year; after he entered the United States at the southern border, he was “viviendo normal,” living normally, in New York City and never had any legal problems. But then he went to a regular ICE check in at 26 Federal Plaza in lower Manhattan and was detained, spending two months in jail, most of it at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn. “Fue bastante tortuosa,” he said: it was quite tortuous. He was elated when he was released on bond.

But before he was allowed to go, he was brought back to 26 Federal Plaza, where agents put an ankle monitor on him. He accepted it, he said, because his other choices were going back to jail or being deported. He ended up wearing the monitor for ten months, and it changed everything, he said. He didn’t want anyone at his job installing windows to know, so he bought baggy pants and boots to fit over it and walked differently so his coworkers wouldn’t see it. When he was suspended at high heights, he had to be extra careful not to let it bang loudly against the ladder or the building. The charge on his device only lasted four hours, and when it ran out it made a loud noise, so he had to find a way to discretely charge it during the workday.

It also changed his personal life. “Es bastante pesado,” he noted: it’s very heavy, so he had to adjust the way he slept, lying on his side and dangling his foot over the bed so it wouldn’t hit the rest of his body and wake him up. Even today, months after the monitor was taken off, he still feels it, akin to a phantom limb. But worse than the physical discomfort was the mental toll. “Sentía mucha rabia, mucha impotencia,” he said: I felt a lot of rage, a lot of impotence. He saw it every morning when he woke up, and it reminded him of the story of the elephants and the post: although the giant, strong creatures are only tied with a thin rope, they can’t get free.

This phenomenon is not just happening in New York. The majority of people whose bond is paid through members of the Community Justice Exchange have ended up on GPS surveillance, either through an ankle monitor, watch, or phone app. “We’re seeing it everywhere,” Nguyen said. Her organization has also seen cases of people who were detained but won their cases for asylum and were released, only to be put on GPS monitors.

Julia Zalenski, co-founder of the bail and bond fund Prairielands Freedom Fund in Iowa, has seen an increase in GPS monitoring for people who have been released from immigration detention. “It’s very common right now for us to post bond for someone, then have them immediately receive a notice to appear to be put on ATD [Alternatives to Detention] monitoring,” she said by email. “In some places it’s certainly more common than not, and a few locations seem to try and put everyone who is released from detention on ATD.”

This monitoring is a huge burden on people. The batteries have to be charged for at least two hours a day; if not, they start beeping and result in immediate calls from ICE. They cut and irritate people’s skin. It’s hard to wear work boots with the monitors, making it difficult for some people to do their jobs. Many can’t exercise with one on. “It’s also the stigma,” Santana noted. Some people have family members who don’t want them to stay with them if they’re wearing a monitor out of fear of being in ICE’s spotlight.

People forced to wear ankle monitors also have to not only check in at ICE offices regularly but, as a new addition, have ICE officers visit their homes to make sure they haven’t left and are abiding by requirements. There’s “the additional harm of, then ICE knows exactly where you are at any point in time,” Nguyen said. “Folks unfortunately are just trapped and totally ensnared in the detention and deportation machine.”

“It is just a continuation of being locked up,” Santana said. “It’s hard for people to disconnect, ‘Okay I am really free,’ when you are being monitored 24 hours a day, seven days a week.”

Through tears, in October Linda described avoiding her beloved local library, where she used to go weekly, because it has metal detectors at the doors that would be set off by her monitor. “It’s so shameful because people don’t understand,” she said. “People look at me and judge me, and I’m avoiding that.” She likes to run, but she had given that up because it had become impossible. She hadn’t been going on any dates. She loves concerts, but she had to check ahead of time to see if the venue had a metal detector; when she recently went to a ballet at Lincoln Center, she had to walk through one and kept wondering what the security staff were thinking. “The things that I used to do for leisure, it’s just like I can’t,” she said. “It stops me from doing the stuff that I used to like.” She was grateful for the onset of colder weather, making it easier for her to wear pants that covered the monitor.

There were physical repercussions, too. The monitor was heavy, and she noticed that she’d been walking differently to compensate for it. She struggled to sleep with it and worried it would start beeping due to a low charge during the night. She was constantly getting blisters from it — living in New York, she walks a lot.

Keeping the battery charged was also an extra burden. There was no indicator telling her how fully charged it was, and if it got drained a loud voice repeated “low battery” until she could swap it out and charge it again. If it got fully drained, she could expect a call from ICE or even a knock on her door. It was too uncomfortable to charge it while she slept, so she charged it in the mornings before work, hoping it would last through the whole day.

It wasn’t the only way she was being monitored, either. Every eight weeks she had to check in at an ICE office. ICE officers also came to her home every eight weeks, forcing her to stay in her apartment from 6am to 6pm, waiting for them to show up.

“I’m not a criminal,” she said. “If I was, at least it’s like, okay, I did something and I’m paying the price for it.” But she noted that she decided to stay in the U.S. because it was her lifelong dream to live in New York, she wanted to get a chance at a better life, and she works, pays her taxes. “I’m not doing any harm to anybody.”

But she knew that wasn’t the point. The point was to wear her down. “They do it so eventually someone will give up,” she said.

In early November, she finally got some relief: she requested that, because she had worn the monitor for 90 days and it kept shocking her, it be removed, and her request was granted. She was switched to being monitored by an app on her phone, along with regular ICE check-ins. She finally contemplated being able to go to the library, to a concert, on a run, on a date. But more important than that is “the peace of mind of not having to charge it, not stressing about [it] making noises in public, no more anxiety,” she said. “That’s such a relief.”

text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested and deported more people during the last fiscal year than at any time in its 23-year history, Homeland Security said Thursday, as President Donald Trump followed through on promises of mass deportations that helped him win back the White House in 2024 but also fueled the political blowback that led to Democrats’ overwhelming victory in last week’s midterm elections.

The numbers released Thursday by the department reflect the massive funding that has gone into supercharging immigration enforcement under the Trump administration, with more money for deportation officers, detention facilities and deportation flights.

But Democratic members of Congress, buoyed by their sweeping victories in both the House and Senate, are promising vigorous oversight of the agency core to the president’s mass deportation mission.

ICE said it deported 483,200 people in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30. In 2014, 405,090 people were deported under then-President Barack Obama, when some activists labeled him the “deporter in chief.”

The 2026 number was up 9% from its previous high of 442,640 in the same period a year earlier and up 78% from 271,480 in 2024, the last year of Joe Biden’s presidency.

“Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, ICE has been unleashed to target and remove illegal aliens so that we can save American lives,” said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

Details of ICE arrests remain fuzzy

Yet much remained unsaid in the DHS press release, including how many deportees had criminal histories and a detailed breakdown of the statistics. In addition, deportation numbers can be notoriously fuzzy, with totals counted in different ways in different years. And the Trump administration largely stopped publishing regular data on immigration enforcement once it took office, instead releasing information intermittently in press releases or on social media without the detailed data reports that it used to deliver.

“It is accurate that ICE is making record numbers of arrests,” said Marc R. Rosenblum, a visiting fellow at the Migration Policy Institute and a former top official overseeing statistics at the Department of Homeland Security. “They have record resources. They’ve doubled their staffing. They’re getting a lot of support from other law enforcement agencies.”

But the sparse data in Thursday’s announcement means “we can’t really see what’s going on in any kind of detailed way.”

Homeland Security’s statistics office used to publish data monthly about immigration arrests and deportations, while ICE’s website used to have a dashboard detailing information about ICE detentions, arrests and deportations. But that stopped at the beginning of the second Trump administration, raising questions about how many people the department was actually arresting and removing from the country.

The conservative Oversight Project, which would like to see the administration carry out more deportations, has filed a lawsuit seeking to get deportation data from the government.

Scott Mechowski is a visiting fellow for deportation studies at the Oversight Project and used to be ICE’s deputy field office director for enforcement and removal operations in New York. He said without more detailed information from the department about how they’re counting deportations and what they’re including, he’s skeptical of the figures released Thursday.

“Show me the data,” said Mechowski. “Even if the numbers are what they said they were, even then, it’s going to fall short of the president’s campaign promise.”

The Oversight Project has released a report detailing how the administration can reached the promised million deportations a year, including by ramping up arrests and enforcement at worksites.

Many voters found Trump’s deportation efforts excessive

Trump had campaigned on ridding America of criminal migrants, saying he’d be targeting the “worst of the worst.”

But that is rarely the case. In July, for instance, only roughly one-quarter of deportees had criminal convictions, according to the Deportation Data Project. More than half weren’t even facing charges.

The numbers released Thursday also fell well short of the White House goal of 1 million deportations annually, a promise it made when it received billions in additional funding from Congress, supercharging the government’s immigration bureaucracy.

Trump returned to power last year promising to end illegal crossings at the southern border. His administration has pushed through restrictions on both legal and illegal immigration and speeded up deportations. Immigration crackdown operations are often purposefully high-profile, in part to frighten migrants into leaving of their own accord.

But the crackdown hasn’t always gone as planned.

The biggest shift came earlier this year in Minneapolis, when more than 2,000 federal officers were deployed to the city and thousands of protesters turned out to confront masked and often heavily armed agents spilling from convoys of unmarked vehicles.

Two U.S. citizens — Renee Good and Alex Pretti, both 37 — were killed in confrontations with officers, and the administration quickly backed away from high-profile operations.

While arrests dropped after the killings, they quickly returned to record numbers, albeit in quieter immigration sweeps.

By last week’s elections the White House’s immigration message had splintered, with even some deeply Republican rural areas voting Democratic after people saw longtime migrant neighbors, many of them key workers on farms, ranches and meat processing facilities, taken in arrests.

The highest recorded number of deportations on record came during President Dwight D. Eisenhower’s crackdown on illegal immigrants from Mexico. The often-chaotic policy saw deportation numbers spike dramatically in the early 1950s, cresting at 1.1 million in 1954.

__

Associated Press writer Rebecca Santana in Washington contributed to this report.

text:
On 10 November 2026, Tanyakorn Thippayapokin, Advocacy and Engagement Coordinator at Asylum Access Thailand (AAT), delivered a statement at the Civil Society Press Conference on the Outcomes of Thailand’s Fourth Universal Periodic Review (UPR IV), held at SCC Creative Space in Bangkok. Her statement focused on refugee protection and transnational repression (TNR), highlighting the international recommendations received by Thailand, the remaining protection gaps, and the concrete actions the Thai government must take moving forward.

The Situation of Refugees and Transnational Repression in Thailand

Thailand currently hosts approximately 5,500 urban refugees and asylum seekers, most of whom continue to lack clear legal status. At the same time, refugees, activists and human rights defenders from Cambodia, Viet Nam, Laos, Myanmar and China continue to face surveillance, harassment, intimidation and the risk of being returned to unsafe situations. The forced return of 40 Uyghur men to China in February 2025 is a stark example of these concerns.

Furthermore, Freedom House has identified Thailand as the country with the highest number of recorded incidents of transnational repression globally. This reflects the reality that Thailand is not only a place of refuge for people fleeing persecution, but can also become a place where people continue to face threats and insecurity even after crossing borders in search of safety.

The demands of civil society organisations and networks therefore go beyond humanitarian assistance. They call for legal protection, respect for the principle of non-refoulement, and concrete measures to ensure that Thailand does not become an operational base for transnational repression.

International Recommendations from UPR IV

The fourth UPR cycle marked an important development, as transnational repression was raised directly in recommendations to Thailand for the first time. A total of 19 recommendations addressed non-refoulement and deportation, while four recommendations specifically addressed TNR, made by the Netherlands, New Zealand, Belgium and Canada.

Spain, Sweden, Togo and Australia recommended that Thailand accede to the 1951 Refugee Convention. France called for the adoption of formal legislation recognising refugee status. Germany, the Republic of Korea and the United Kingdom recommended reviewing deportation criteria and procedures, with Germany and the Republic of Korea specifically referring to the Prime Minister’s Regulation on Deportation B.E. 2569. Other recommendations called for an end to child immigration detention and expanded work rights for refugees.

On TNR, Canada called on Thailand to develop and implement specific legislation to prevent and address transnational repression, consistent with the Prevention and Suppression of Torture and Enforced Disappearance Act and the principle of non-refoulement. The Netherlands linked TNR to Section 13 of the same Act and the National Screening Mechanism (NSM). Norway and the United Kingdom emphasised the importance of individual risk assessments, access to legal assistance, and judicial review or effective appeal mechanisms before any return takes place.

These recommendations demonstrate that the concerns raised by civil society and refugee communities are not isolated or limited to a particular group. They are human rights issues that have attracted international attention.

Remaining Gaps and the Thai Government’s Response

Despite these developments, significant gaps remain. Although recommendations called for a review of deportation regulations, none directly called for the suspension of the implementation of the 2026 deportation regulation. Issues concerning the use of Interpol Red Notices, certain forms of cross-border cooperation, digital surveillance and investigations into disappearances linked to TNR also received insufficient attention. Furthermore, there were no clear recommendations on allowing asylum seekers to access the NSM without first being detained, addressing the issue of double bail requirements, or establishing a maximum period for immigration detention.

In its response, Thailand’s Ministry of Interior referred to the legal right to appeal a deportation order within seven days. However, it remains unclear whether effective judicial review is available before removal takes place. Work rights remain limited to displaced persons from Myanmar residing in nine temporary shelters and do not extend to urban refugees. Regarding children, the government referred to separating children from detention as a measure of last resort, but did not directly address the issue of child immigration detention. Similarly, clear government positions on accession to the Refugee Convention and addressing TNR are still needed.

What Thailand must demonstrate after UPR IV is therefore not simply an acknowledgement of the recommendations, but a commitment to translating them into concrete action.

First, the Cabinet and Ministry of Interior should suspend the implementation of the 2026 deportation regulation pending a review and consultation process. This must be accompanied by protection measures for individuals covered by the NSM or UNHCR protection, as well as guarantees of judicial review before any removal takes place.

Second, the government should ensure independent investigations into disappearances and potentially unlawful returns that may constitute human rights violations. It should also urgently establish an effective mechanism to respond to transnational repression, with the capacity to prevent abuses, protect those affected and ensure accountability.

Third, Thailand should move forward with developing comprehensive refugee legislation and a roadmap towards accession to the 1951 Refugee Convention. It must end child immigration detention and provide individuals recognised as protected persons under the NSM with access to lawful employment.

Equally important, refugees and affected communities must not remain merely subjects of reports or recommendations. They must be meaningfully involved in designing laws, shaping policies and monitoring government implementation. Refugee protection is not simply about providing shelter to people fleeing persecution. It is about guaranteeing that no one is returned to danger and that no one is made unsafe simply for seeking safety in Thailand.

The UPR review may be over, but the responsibility to protect human rights continues. The time has come to turn international recommendations into meaningful changes in people’s lives.

Read the Joint Press Release calling on the Thai government to take concrete action on human rights following Thailand’s Fourth Universal Periodic Review (UPR IV). The joint press release was issued by 10 civil society organisations and networks: Manushya Foundation, Amnesty International Thailand, Asylum Access Thailand, Tamtang Foundation, Isan Democracy Movement, the PATANI Working Group for Monitoring on International Mechanisms, Indigenous Women’s Network in Thailand (IWNT), MovED (People’s Movement to End Discrimination), Young Pride Foundation, and the Thai CSOs Coalition for the UPR and UN Mechanisms.

text:
FRESNO, Calif. (KFSN) -- On Thursday, the Fresno City Council voted to approve a resolution restricting Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents from staging or using city spaces for their operations.

"ICE has been using our downtown garages and our parking lots at the tower theater as staging areas for their enforcement on a daily basis, said Fresno City Councilmember Miguel Arias.

The restricted areas would include city-owned parks, parking lots or buildings unless federal agents have a valid judicial warrant or court order.

Immigrant advocates rallied outside council chambers. Inside, dozens of impassioned residents gave emotional testimony.

"I myself as a female that is a brown woman I face fear. I am on the lookout for all those license plates out there and I shouldn't even have to do that," resident Eileen Hernandez said.

"If we had not seen in recent years and up until now the abuse of power by the federal government that has intimidated and created a climate of terror among immigrant families," said Jesus Martinez with the Central Valley Immigration Integration Collaborative.

Councilmember Nick Richardson, the sole no-vote, told Action News he believes the resolution is incomplete.

"If you don't have a real plan to follow through with anything, it's just words on a page," Richardson says.

During the city council meeting, Mayor Jerry Dyer revealed he had a call with the Department of Homeland Security and White House officials earlier this week.

He criticized the ICE priorities and called their tactics 'archaic' while expressing concern about future enforcement of the policy, asking what consequences could be for ICE.

"I just hope that there's not an expectation that we are going to have armed police officers going out and confronting armed ICE agents because I can't see any good from that," said Dyer.

Councilmember Annalisa Perea acknowledged there isn't a plan at this point but argued that moving forward is urgent, explaining that with this vote, the city manager and city attorney will be tasked with implementation.

Advocates say similar policies have been enacted successfully in other cities.

"Just a couple of days ago, we saw in Alameda County that they issued a cease and desist letter to ICE," Sukaina Hussain with the California Immigrant Policy Center said. "In cities of Fremont and Santa Rosa, they have also passed similar resolutions. What we've seen there is local law enforcement cars that are on traffic patrols are used to go usher folks out of those spaces."

No deadline has been set for when a plan will be produced or how it could be implemented.
