text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in Washington state are preying on vulnerable farm workers and snatching them off the street like “serial killers,” a top union leader told Newsweek.

The last few months have seen a surge of ICE activity in the state, with an Freedom of Information Act request revealing that ICE officers have arrested 2,500 people between March and August of this year.

The highest proportion of incidents have taken place in Yakima County, which has seen 445 arrests over the past three months, many of which are reported to be dairy farm workers currently dealing with a outbreak of avian flu that has killed at least one person and potentially infected many more.

Read More on News

Newsweek has contacted ICE and the Yakima County Health Board for comment.

“Yakima is ground zero for ICE right now. They have more deportations than Seattle,” Elizabeth Strater, national vice president of the United Farm Workers (UFW) union, told Newsweek. "There are roving patrols of ICE agents, in unmarked cars, masked and armed, and they are picking farm workers off one at a time. One car at a time, going after people on their way to work on agricultural roads.

“They’re not doing the big showy raids. They’re just picking people off like serial killers. The only way the family finds out what’s happened is that they find the car abandoned on the side of the road. And it’s in vast numbers.”

Aside from the moral argument, the ongoing targeting of dairy workers in the area may also be contributing to a public health crisis in Yakima, as the threat of deportation has prevented workers infected with avian flu from seeking medical treatment.

“If a worker is at risk or if he's gotten infected, they don't go to the doctor,” a UFW spokeswoman” told KING-TV in Seattle. “They don't want to miss work, especially with what's going on nationally with the administration and the ICE raids.”

Nearly all the raids in Yakima take place at either traffic stops, or at check-ins with other enforcement agencies. These detainments are referred to as “at large” or street arrests by ICE. David Morales, a volunteer with the Yakima Immigrant Response Network, said nearly all of the detainees they have worked with over the past six months have been in the country for at least five years, with many residing in the U.S. for decades.

“These are really deeply embedded families, and they have many loved ones who are students and full participants that have been employed for decades,” Morales told the Yakima Herald-Republic. “It's a completely different feel when that's happening, because you're completely splitting families apart and just ripping the fabric out of a community.”

'The Cats are Dying'—Fears for Animals as Bird Flu Surges

The backdrop to the raids is the continued spread of avian flu in Yakima County, which has infected at least 33 herds and caused one confirmed death. The Yakima health board reported just three confirmed cases in a recent press release, but the UFW claims there are many more.

“They’re being told there’s a cattle virus,” said Strater, adding that it was "terrifyingly" easy for UFW members to find symptomatic workers. “They are not being told that they are at risk themselves. It wasn’t until a person died that word of mouth started spreading.”

Strater said she believes the majority of infections are being transmitted by aerosolized milk from infected cows coming into contact with the victim’s eyes.

“Between cattle, it’s udder to udder through the milking equipment, but for workers I think the highest number of infections is milk to eye, because it’s difficult to protect the eyes," Strater said. "For the people who are very, very sick, it’s possible they’re inhaling aerosolized milk, and that may be why they’re getting sicker than the people with eye symptoms.”

The vast majority of dairy workers in Yakima are non-English speaking immigrant workers. Although the Health District has set up a hotline offering advice to workers developing symptoms after being exposed to infected dairy, it is in English only and of little use to the Spanish-speaking workers.

“The workers don’t know what to do with the cattle at all,” said Strater. “They say, ‘We don’t know what the cattle need. We don’t know if we’re supposed to be discarding the milk. We don’t know how to discard it.’ The cats are getting into it, and the cats are dying. Even different supervisors on different shifts are giving them different information.

“There might be something on the Yakima County Health Department website, but that’s not where workers are getting their information, and they don’t have the information they need.”

Worsening Health Crisis

The economic conditions imposed upon the workers, plus the nature of their work, have combined to worsen the ongoing health crisis.

“[The workers] can’t miss work because the cattle have to be cared for,” Strater added. “It’s not like a crop where some of the fruit might go off but it’ll still be there in a couple of days. The cattle have to be cared for every single day, and sick cattle need more care. Whether the milk is infected or not, they need to be milked or they’ll die.”

In order to stop the spread of the disease, workers need a “robust, bilingual, culturally competent, multi-agency response,” because they are a “firewall” for the rest of the general public.

“There should be flu clinics that prioritize every dairy worker and their immediate family members," Strater said. "There should be surveillance testing of these workers, the human workers, not the livestock. And when they have to miss work for testing, treatment or quarantine, they need to be compensated. They need to be paid, because they cannot afford not to be, on a very literal level.

“These are very economically vulnerable people. They’re poor. That’s why they do that work. And the workers are desperate for information on how to care for the cattle, and for themselves.”

DHS later issued a notice directing top officials to preserve their records, but said at the time that it could not confirm all responsive records had been preserved.
The records — part of a rolling production from DHS in American Oversight’s ongoing litigation seeking text messages and other communications from Noem and other senior DHS officials — come as Lewandowski faces mounting congressional scrutiny.
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, American Oversight released records it obtained through a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) that include Signal chats and text messages from devices belonging to then-Secretary Kristi Noem and Deputy Secretary Troy Edgar. The messages, reported on by Politico, show the department’s top leadership — including Corey Lewandowski, Noem’s closest adviser — trading candid updates on the administration’s deportations of people to third countries, including a flight that sent eight men to war-torn South Sudan. Most of them had no ties to the country. The policy’s legality is now before the Supreme Court, which will hear arguments in December.

The records show then-acting Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Director Todd Lyons giving updates to the group on July 5, 2025: “Mission completed in South Sudan. landed at 2340 EST. They departed with no issues.” Lewandowski replied, “Praise Jesus.” The flight ended a weeks-long legal fight over a group of men the administration had held at a U.S. military base in Djibouti. The eight men came from Cuba, Laos, Mexico, Myanmar, South Sudan, and Vietnam.

Ten days later, on July 15, 2025, Tricia McLaughlin, DHS’s top spokesperson at the time, asked the group, “Was there a third country removal flight today? And if so, can we get rap sheets of these guys?” After Lyons said he would look into it, Lewandowski wrote, “I love deportations.” Lyons replied, “And they are only going to get better sir!” Lyons later told McLaughlin he had “just sent you the crim breakdown.”

“These messages reveal a disturbing culture of cruelty at the highest levels of the department and, even more troubling, are exactly the kind of messages the department once claimed it was no longer preserving. The public should not have to rely on federal lawsuits to learn what senior government officials are saying and doing behind closed doors,” said Chioma Chukwu, Executive Director of American Oversight. “As some of the officials involved still hold positions of power at DHS, and legal challenges to third party removals are still being litigated, Congress has a duty to investigate — to demand answers, obtain every record of how these decisions were made, and put those officials under oath. When the people running the deportation machine celebrate human suffering behind closed doors, the public deserves to see every word. Proper oversight is nonnegotiable.”

The records also show how closely the department’s leadership tracked the litigation and the press coverage surrounding the Djibouti detentions. On July 3, 2025, an official identified as “James” — likely DHS General Counsel James Percival — told the group, “Supreme Court finally ruled on Djibouti. Full stay.” Lewandowski responded, “So long overdue,” and McLaughlin wrote that she was “Giving to NYT and Will Cain show and putting out a release.” In a June 2025 text to Noem’s device, McLaughlin wrote that DHS had “been pushing the deplorable conditions that ICE agents are facing thanks to this district court judge out of Boston.” And in May 2025, as the first flight bound for South Sudan drew scrutiny, she texted Noem’s device that DHS had “not been commenting, but this flight is driving a lot of our coverage.” After McLaughlin sent a South Sudan press conference roundup, Noem’s device replied: “Great job.”

Nearly all the messages obtained were created after April 9, 2025 — the date after which, DHS told American Oversight in July 2025, “text message data” was “no longer maintained.” The statement came in response to a request for texts from Noem and other top officials. A month later, DHS said it “no longer has the capability to conduct a search of text messages.” After American Oversight sued over the department’s apparent failure to preserve top officials’ texts, DHS told the court that its earlier statements were “erroneous” — while disclosing that it had disabled its text-archiving system in April 2025 and was relying on officials to manually preserve their own messages. DHS later issued a notice directing top officials to preserve their records, but said at the time that it could not confirm all responsive records had been preserved.

The records — part of a rolling production from DHS in American Oversight’s ongoing litigation seeking text messages and other communications from Noem and other senior DHS officials — come as Lewandowski faces mounting congressional scrutiny.

She was issued a final order of removal in August 2013, according to a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson.

text:
Nearly two months after ICE agents whisked a beloved California nurse and professor from her home in Lodi, her university has ramped up calls for her release.

“She needs to come home,” said Eileen Fry-Bowers, dean for the University of San Francisco’s nursing school,in reference to Ann Lawani, who was arrested by immigration agents in September and has since been shuffled between detention centers in California, Texas, and Louisiana, in a series of opaque transfers.

Lawani, 39, came to the US in 2007. She established herself as a nursing professional, obtaining a master’s and doctoral degree in the field, before stepping into academia.

She steers two programs at the University of San Francisco, one a master’s entry program geared toward students with non-nursing backgrounds and another a bachelor’s program for students seeking to work in public health safety-net institutions.

“She basically has her hands on almost 300 students that she engages with on a regular basis,” Fry-Bowers said.

Lawani’s detention has sparked outcry from local lawmakers, who have advocated on her behalf to ICE authorities, as well as her students and colleagues, who say her absence is deeply felt on campus.

One of those students, Casey Murray, a nursing science graduate student, described Lawani as a warm educator who could recall the first and last names of pupils she had not seen since orientation.

“We have 37 days left until we graduate,” Murray said. “She has supported us to the fullest extent up until the point that she was kidnapped. We want her at our graduation, and we want her home with her family.”

Federal immigration officials say Lawani entered the US on a visitor’s visa in 2007, which she overstayed. She was issued a final order of removal in August 2013, according to a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson.

Natalia Santanna, Lawani’s lawyer, confirmed the removal order, but noted that DHS’s account was “incomplete”.

“Dr Lawani applied for asylum within one year of being in the United States. And, in the same 2013 order, the immigration judge found that Ann would more likely than not face persecution in Nigeria and granted withholding of removal,” Santanna said. “That is not a temporary stay. It is a continuing bar to removal to Nigeria. Dr Lawani has lived in the United States pursuant to that grant of withholding of removal since 2013.”

Santanna said they have filed a habeas petition to challenge the legality of her detainment, which remains pending in California’s eastern district court.

Meanwhile, Lawani’s students and colleagues are continuing to mobilize around her.

Lawani sent Fry-Bowers a text about being in ICE’s custody, shortly after her arrest. Fry-Bowers, who was on vacation, heard from another dean that Lawani had been absent from a meeting, which she described as out of character.

After the school heard from Lawani’s family, they jumped into action, aiding with legal representation and registering their alarm with the area’s congressional delegation.

In late October, Josh Harder, a congressman, who represents Lawani’s district, expressed his concerns about her case to DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin, among them the lack of notice before her arrest and her various whereabouts not being reflected in an online detainee database.

“Given her longstanding compliance, lack of criminal history, and substantial community ties, there is no apparent public safety justification for keeping her detained thousands of miles from home while her case proceeds,” Harder wrote then in a letter.

Fry-Bowers praised Lawani, citing her work with patients in hospice and palliative care.

“She cares for the most vulnerable, helps them maintain their dignity and comfort as they prepare for death,” she said. “She is a consummate professional. The highest praise I could ever give a nursing colleague is that I would want them taking care of my family member or myself, and she would be at the top of the list.”

title: Gov. Kotek wants Oregon to ban immigration detention centers. Others have tried and failed.
description:

State law for decades has prohibited local or state governments from participating in immigration enforcement without a court order.
“Only the federal government has the power to decide whether, how and why to hold aliens for violating immigration law.
They also confirmed they have no current plans to build immigration detention centers in the city or Oregon.
“If even a face mask ban got blocked in courts, something even more fundamental to federal or state law enforcement as detention centers would be even less likely to pass muster.”
text:
This story originally appeared in the Oregon Capital Chronicle and is used with permission.

Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek is calling upon state lawmakers to pass legislation outlawing the construction of new immigration detention centers in the upcoming legislative session next year, but previous court cases from other states suggest that such a law may not be enforceable.

The governor made her comments at a Friday press conference where she was asked what more she and state leaders could do to support Oregonians amid the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration crackdown, during which federal agents have shot people, conducted warrantless arrests and smashed car windows. Research from immigrant rights advocates has shown that counties with such centers are more likely to see immigration-related arrests.

“I would like to see a bill that we can have here in Oregon to never allow detention facilities in the state of Oregon,” Kotek told reporters. “We don’t have one now. I don’t think we should have them. We need to stop that.”

Kotek’s office declined to comment further Tuesday about the kind of legislation or specifics she would like to see. An unnamed spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that the agency has no new facilities to announce “at this time” and said that the U.S. Constitution’s supremacy clause “makes it clear that sanctuary politicians do not control federal law enforcement.”

Oregon is already one of a few states in the nation which doesn’t have an overnight, large-scale immigration detention facility for the federal government. The state is home to processing facilities in cities such as Portland where detainees are temporarily held and released or transported to long-term holding detention in Tacoma, Washington. State law for decades has prohibited local or state governments from participating in immigration enforcement without a court order.

A 2021 state law already bans the creation of private immigration detention centers in the state, and future legislation could attempt to expand that ban by attempting to change how state-run public services such as utilities or permits are granted for such projects. But in both New Jersey and California, federal courts in recent years have struck down similar laws.

The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals in 2022 ruled a California law banning private immigration detention centers in the state was unconstitutional, finding it violated the U.S. Constitution’s supremacy clause, which prevents states from impeding federal operations. The 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals in 2025 struck down a New Jersey law banning private prison companies from creating contracts with federal immigration authorities to operate the centers in the state.

“Only the federal government has the power to decide whether, how and why to hold aliens for violating immigration law. It alone has the power to make these contracts in the first place,” the New Jersey decision reads. “So this ban is in substance a direct regulation; it destroys the federal government’s marketplace.”

Call for action follows Newport settlement

Concern over a potential immigration detention facility in Oregon comes after the Trump administration admitted in federal court that it was interested in using the U.S. Coast Guard site at Newport’s municipal airport for a temporary processing or holding facility for immigration detention.

Critics saw the move as an attempt to violate the due process rights of immigrants by quickly processing them for deportation by an airport where detainees would be held far longer than necessary. A June 2025 memorandum from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement empowered temporary holding facilities to hold immigrants for up to 72 hours, six times the previous 12-hour maximum under federal regulations. A federal judge in California has sinceblocked the policy.

After Oregon sued the federal government to stop the center last year, federal officials agreed in a settlement announced in October that they would provide at least 30 days of notice before beginning any environmental permitting for such a facility in the city. They also confirmed they have no current plans to build immigration detention centers in the city or Oregon.

But that agreement did not hinge on Oregon state law, with the state’s suit using federal environmental and administrative regulations requiring further notice and study of the potential site. The period for guaranteed advance notice is limited to Newport and temporary, with an expiration in August next year.

State Rep. David Gomberg, D-Otis, told the Capital Chronicle that the settlement “leaves the door wide open” for future detention centers in Oregon or Newport after the agreement expires or the federal government decides to renew its plans. He said he is still in early conversations with lawmakers about “a tool to close that door.”

“It’s early — we had an election last week. We’re gonna have another session in two months,” he said. “We’ve got a little bit of time to sort this out.”

Tung Yin, a professor of law at Portland’s Lewis & Clark Law School, responded to Kotek’s call for action with skepticism. He pointed out that multiple federal courts have blocked state laws to prevent federal immigration agents from wearing masks following legal challenges from the Trump administration.

Oregon’s law — which focuses on allowing people to sue federal, local or state law enforcement agencies to change their facial covering policies — has yet to be tested. The federal government also sued the city of Portland in mid-October over a city ordinance that aims to prevent the use of masks and require identification from law enforcement.

“While it’s understandable that Governor Kotek would want to pursue such a bill as a statement of Oregon’s commitment to sanctuary status, I don’t see any way in which this could survive a challenge by the federal government,” Yin wrote in an email. “If even a face mask ban got blocked in courts, something even more fundamental to federal or state law enforcement as detention centers would be even less likely to pass muster.”

title: ICE says it's deporting more immigrants than ever. Many are actually leaving voluntarily.
authors: Tosin Akintola, Liz Wolfe, Ronald Bailey, J.D. Tuccille, Eric Boehm, Peter Suderman
description:
ICE claimed that its numbers in FY 2026 alone "dwarfed deportation and arrest numbers from the entirety of the Biden Administration."
Indeed, internal ICE data—obtained through the Freedom of Information Act by the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse (TRAC), a nonpartisan data research organization—show that in FY 2026, ICE recorded the highest number of deportations since FY 2009.
In FY 2026, immigration judges issued 11 times as many orders for voluntary departures as in FY 2024.
Exit polls from NBC News and CNN show that Trump's immigration enforcement tactics were unpopular with midterm voters.
Outside of partisan bluster, Democrats have shown little evidence they can act as a bulwark against the Trump administration's immigration enforcement agenda.
text:
On Thursday, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced that in FY 2026, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) "broke the record for the highest number of deportations and arrests in any fiscal year," with "more than 491,000 immigration arrests and more than 483,000 deportations."

ICE claimed that its numbers in FY 2026 alone "dwarfed deportation and arrest numbers from the entirety of the Biden Administration." Indeed, internal ICE data—obtained through the Freedom of Information Act by the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse (TRAC), a nonpartisan data research organization—show that in FY 2026, ICE recorded the highest number of deportations since FY 2009. That year, under President Barack Obama, ICE deported 489,251 people.

In a statement, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin credited President Donald Trump's "leadership" for unleashing the agency to "target and remove illegal aliens." However, the agency's data show that it has carried out fewer removal operations under the Trump administration than in previous years. ICE can conduct fewer operations while keeping its deportation numbers high because immigrants are increasingly choosing to self-deport or turn back at the border.

In July and August, voluntary departures and voluntary returns—deportation processes that allow illegal immigrants to depart the U.S. of their own volition with no removal order or "related immigration consequences"—made up 37 percent of total deportations, compared with the first three months of the Trump administration, when they accounted for "less than 5 percent." In FY 2026, immigration judges issued 11 times as many orders for voluntary departures as in FY 2024.

ICE's deportation totals—which include methods such as voluntary departures, withdrawals of applications for admission, and voluntary returns that allow reentry into the country—are typically grouped under deportations. The all-inclusive figure might play well to the president's supporters, but it obscures the atmosphere of fear and illiberalism powering the Trump administration's deportation numbers.

ICE set a goal to hire 10,000 new officers and agents within a year. To meet its goal, the agency has lowered hiring standards, sending prospective officers out to enforce Trump's immigration agenda with little training, often before their background checks are even complete. On Tuesday, The Washington Post reported that a review of a "small fraction" of the 12,000 recent hires by DHS found "at least 19 officers who had faced past allegations of misconduct or criminal charges, or had other employment red flags," including at least six cases in which officers were "fired or decertified, or resigned under threat of dismissal."

On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that David Brouillette—the rookie ICE officer who fatally shot a Colombian immigrant in Maine in July—had a "record of deep-seated anti-immigrant hostility, especially against Colombians." Despite the documented claims against Brouillette, he was "fast-tracked through a preliminary vetting process" and "allowed to skip ICE's full training course in Georgia." The Times reported that "at the time of the shooting in Maine," ICE hadn't reviewed Brouillette's background report, so it had no indication whether he had red flags that would make him undesirable as a law enforcement officer.

Being shot or beaten by unaccountable federal officers is one thing. Immigrants must also account for the possibility that they could be deported to a third country or secretly transferred out of state without notice to their loved ones or legal counsel.

In a choice between state-sanctioned violence and a peaceful return on their own terms, it's hardly surprising that immigrants would choose to depart the U.S. voluntarily rather than risk becoming another victim of the Trump administration's policies.

Exit polls from NBC News and CNN show that Trump's immigration enforcement tactics were unpopular with midterm voters. Yet the president seems ready to double down on his policies. After floating the possibility of working out an amnesty deal with the incoming Democratic-led Congress, Trump told reporters Wednesday that there'd be "no amnesty," and that he hadn't "told Stephen Miller," the mastermind behind his immigration agenda and the new White House chief of staff, to "make any changes to the administration's efforts to deport millions."

Outside of partisan bluster, Democrats have shown little evidence they can act as a bulwark against the Trump administration's immigration enforcement agenda. Trump could veto any bill passed by a Democratic-led Congress, and two years of a Republican majority have left ICE fully funded with over $152 billion in taxpayer money unspent between it and Customs and Border Protection.

Still, the incoming Congress could exercise its authority over appropriations and rescind the funds bankrolling ICE's campaign of intimidation.

text:
A government watchdog sued the Trump administration Thursday, seeking to uncover records of a secretive federal initiative to identify alleged noncitizen voters — an effort that a whistleblower warned could wrongly target eligible voters.

The challenge comes after the Trump administration vowed to scrutinize voting records from the midterms and after a whistleblower raised alarms about an immigration agency’s hunt for alleged illegal voters.

The lawsuit, filed by American Oversight against the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), seeks records detailing the government’s so-called “Unlawful Voter Initiative,” including the data sources, investigative quotas and training materials behind the program.

On Election Day, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that his department would scour voting records after the election.

“We’ll be gathering the voting logs, and we’ll be going through those and making sure that no illegals voted,” Mullin told reporters.

But questions remain about how the administration identifies suspected noncitizen voters, what information federal officials rely on and what safeguards exist to prevent eligible Americans from being wrongly targeted.

“The election may be over, but the Trump administration’s efforts to cast suspicion on American voters is far from finished,” American Oversight Executive Director Chioma Chukwu said in a statement. “As Americans showed up to the polls, Secretary Mullin announced plans to comb through voting records in pursuit of a noncitizen voting problem the evidence shows doesn’t exist.”

The watchdog’s lawsuit stems from an extraordinary whistleblower disclosure made public in September by Sens. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) and Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.).

The whistleblower alleged that USCIS had diverted officers from its Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate to search through voter data for supposed unlawful voters, instructing employees to misrepresent themselves to gain access to state voter records.

Officers were allegedly required to review at least five people per hour and 40 per day, giving them roughly 12 minutes to investigate each person. The whistleblower warned that those quotas left officers insufficient time to thoroughly examine individual cases, increasing the likelihood of errors.

Officers also allegedly did not know the source of the voter data they were reviewing.

An internal training video cited in Thursday’s lawsuit underscored the risks.

“There will be U.S. citizens in this [data] . . . unfortunately, we’re relying on the data we have available . . . the way that the systems work, it’s not perfect,” officers were told, according to a transcript of the training cited in the complaint.

Three days after the whistleblower disclosure became public, American Oversight submitted six Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests seeking records about the initiative.

Among the materials the group is seeking are communications from top administration officials, including Mullin, Deputy Homeland Security Secretary Troy Edgar, DHS Senior Counselor Heather Honey and USCIS Director Joseph Edlow.

The watchdog also wants records detailing the initiative’s investigative quotas, training materials and communications between senior immigration officials and election offices in 19 states and Washington, D.C.

Crucially, the lawsuit seeks records identifying the sources of the voter data supplied to immigration officers and the software or systems used to analyze that information.

American Oversight is not seeking the sensitive voter data itself.

Nearly two months after the watchdog submitted its requests, neither agency has produced any records, according to the complaint.

DHS acknowledged one request on Oct. 17, a month after it was submitted, but denied the group’s request for expedited processing and has not communicated with American Oversight since.

USCIS has not responded to any of the five requests submitted to it.

American Oversight is asking a federal judge to order both agencies to expedite the requests and produce all responsive, nonexempt records within 20 days of a court order.

The initiative is part of a broader Trump administration effort to use federal immigration and citizenship data to scrutinize voter rolls and investigate alleged noncitizen voting, despite a lack of evidence that such voting is widespread.

American Oversight has also sued the administration over its expansion of the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) system, which has been increasingly used to check the citizenship status of people on state voter rolls.

Chukwu warned that the administration’s continued focus on alleged noncitizen voting, coupled with the whistleblower’s allegations, risks wrongly targeting eligible voters and casting doubt on legitimate election results.

“The public deserves to see the rules, the data, and the quotas behind this operation and know what safeguards are in place to protect eligible voters,” Chukwu said. “We’re going to court to demand those answers.”

text:
Sign up for TPR Today, Texas Public Radio's newsletter that brings our top stories to your inbox each morning.

Just days after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the November midterm elections, Texas lawmakers representing heavily Latino districts are calling on President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans to negotiate a bipartisan immigration reform agreement before the new Congress takes office in January.

At a news conference outside the U.S. Capitol, Democratic lawmakers joined immigration advocates and business leaders in demanding immediate protections for undocumented immigrants who have lived and worked in the United States for years.

They argued that the election results, particularly the support Democrats received from Latino voters, sent a message about the Trump administration's aggressive immigration enforcement policies.

"The United States of America rebuked Donald Trump's mass deportation campaign," said San Antonio Democratic Congressman Joaquin Castro.

The lawmakers say they want to use the remaining weeks of the current congressional session to pursue a compromise rather than wait for the incoming Democratic majorities.

Newly elected South Texas Democratic Congressman Bobby Pulido warned that Democrats cannot take Latino voters for granted.

"Whoever wants to get our support in '28 has to prioritize immigration reform, period," Pulido said.

For Pulido, the issue is personal. He said immigration enforcement has created fear throughout the Rio Grande Valley, where many households include both U.S. citizens and immigrants without legal status.

"In the Rio Grande Valley, there's tons of mixed-status families. Good people. They're people that we love, that we know and we've known forever," Pulido said. "And right now they're afraid to go out to the grocery store."

Houston Democratic Congresswoman Sylvia Garcia said families are being separated every day and that delaying negotiations until January would prolong their uncertainty.

"I think we can get it done and get it done now. Why wait? El tiempo es ahora," Garcia said, using the Spanish phrase meaning "the time is now."

Laredo Democratic Congressman Henry Cuellar said for years Republicans have insisted on solving border enforcement as a pre-condition for considering immigration legislation that would provide legal protections or a pathway to citizenship for some undocumented immigrants.

Cuellar said the country can maintain strong border security while protecting immigrants' rights.

"We can always have strong border security. We will have strong border security. But at the same time, we can be respectful to the immigrants and the rights and the dignity that they deserve," Cuellar said.

Cuellar said he has already discussed immigration enforcement with members of the Trump administration and is willing to work with Republicans on policies that prioritize deporting immigrants convicted of serious crimes.

"If they want to focus on criminals, we're with you 100%," he said.

Democrats also point to recent comments from Trump during an interview on CBS's "60 Minutes" as a possible indication that the president is willing to reconsider the scope of his immigration crackdown.

Asked whether immigration enforcement had become too aggressive, Trump acknowledged that some Americans believe his administration has gone too far.

"I think it might be too tough, yeah," Trump said.

Asked about the possibility of reaching an agreement with Democrats, the president appeared open to negotiations.

"Well, the deal would be we would work something out," Trump said. "I think that's something that's actually doable."

However, Trump has not publicly committed to a specific immigration reform proposal, and substantial disagreements remain over deportations, border security and legal status for undocumented immigrants.

James Hollifield, a political science professor at Southern Methodist University who studies immigration politics, said the Republican Party remains closely aligned with Trump's immigration agenda.

"It's still a very hardcore Trump group, MAGA group, and I don't think that they will be in a mood to reach across the aisle and pass a bipartisan immigration reform," Hollifield said.

He also questioned whether Trump would ultimately sign legislation that significantly changed his administration's policies.

"If there were a bill to emerge, it would probably get a veto from him," Hollifield said.

Hollifield said Republicans paid a political price for the administration's immigration policies in the midterm elections, but he believes the party's remaining congressional members are unlikely to support a major change in direction.

"I do think it costs the Republicans, but I don't think the Republican Party, especially those who are left in Congress, are yet ready to turn a page on this," he said.

Hollifield predicted that the country could face another two years of legislative gridlock over immigration, even with Democrats controlling Congress.

Immigration reform advocates and business leaders say they are unwilling to accept another prolonged stalemate.

Mario Guerrero, CEO of the South Texas Builders Association, said Democrats must deliver results after winning the support of voters frustrated with the administration's immigration policies.

"Don't play with us, and don't waste this opportunity like Biden and Obama did," Guerrero said.

Guerrero said he voted for Trump three times before switching his support to Democrats in this year's election.

His political shift illustrates the challenge facing both parties as they compete for Latino voters. Given how powerful this swing bloc has been in the last two elections, it’s clear their demand for action will have consequences in the next election.

Images from inside the car taken by the fiancée of Emmanuel Lobo show an officer, who described himself as “ERO,” an acronym for ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations, asking Lobo for identification.

He then commanded Lobo to turn off the car, which he apparently did not do.

Lobo, in turn, said he wanted to call his lawyer and stated, "I cannot let you guys take me.”

Moments later, the officer reached in, unbuckled Lobo, and pulled him out of the car as his fiancée, Celeste Gomez, pleaded for the officer to stop.

Another image, from someone taking video some distance away, appeared to show Lobo on the street with two officers on top of him.

Nina Brown, who said she hired Lobo for music studio work, let out a deep breath when asked to describe the difficulty of watching the video.

text:
CHICAGO (WLS) -- Human rights law experts are reacting to the ABC7 I-Team's investigation into a Chicago father who was detained, deported and died after he was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) this summer.

How and when Ayaz Ahmed, 61, died is still a mystery.

Some experts have said the local case could be part of a larger pattern of potential human rights violations by the second Trump administration's immigration crackdown.

ABC7 Chicago is now streaming 24/7. Click here to watch

"The case of Mr. Ahmed is deeply troubling and concerning on many levels," said Anjli Parrin, director of the global Human Rights Clinic at the University of Chicago Law School and a member of the United Nations Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances.

"There are a slew of human rights violations potentially at play," Parrin said.

Ahmed was a father of five who lived in Chicago for nearly three decades until he was arrested by federal immigration agents this past June on an expired visa..

"All he wanted to do was be the breadwinner of the family," said Ahmed's son, Jawwad Mehmood.

Watch the I-Team's full investigation into the death of Ayaz Ahmed below or click here.

Prior to his deportation, Ahmed was detained at the Clay County Justice Center in Indiana for fifty days.

Ahmed had several chronic medical conditions, needing medication and a breathing pump daily, according to a letter from his doctor, and emails his attorney sent ICE and Clay County staff at the time.

But his children say that he didn't receive those medications, evidenced by what he told them over the phone.

Saleha Sahar, Ahmed's daughter, told the I-Team, "My dad called me and he was like, 'I can't breathe... I need my nasal spray. I need my asthma pump. I'm struggling to sleep. This is very hard.'"

Sahar even tried mailing the medication and items to Clay County, but it's unknown whether her father ever received them.

Officials with the Clay County Sheriff's Office told the I-Team Ahmed was held in "medical isolation" during his detention, but they wouldn't elaborate on his care citing health privacy laws.

With his health deteriorating, his children contacted ICE, lawmakers including Congresswoman Jan Schakowsky, and the Pakistan embassy; all in an effort to speed up his removal. Those efforts succeeded in late July.

But as the I-Team revealed for the first time earlier this week, flight data shows Ahmed was shackled on a 38-hour flight that took off on July 29, and stopped in three countries before it landed in Pakistan.

After deboarding, witnesses said Ahmed collapsed on the tarmac.

A postmortem report prepared by the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) in Islamabad notes Ahmed was "brought dead" to the hospital 14 hours after the ICE flight landed.

His family said they didn't learn about his death until more than a week later.

Parrin said the family's right to know what happened to their loved ones and their location is a foundational international human rights law that the U.S. and other countries have agreed to follow.

"Families have the right to know the fate and whereabouts of their loved ones," Parrin explained. "We are seeing allegations of enforced disappearances in the context of migration in the U.S. Mr Ahmed's case is not the only such allegation, and for me these are very serious and troubling violations."

In response to questions over Ahmed's detention and deportation, a spokesperson for ICE previously told the I-Team, "Any claims of neglect or mistreatment are categorically FALSE... [ Ahmed ] received all his scheduled medications during the flight. ICE has no insight into the circumstances of Mr. Ahmed's death after his arrival in Pakistan."

"There are serious questions of the healthcare that was provided here," Parrin told the I-Team.

Parrin explained that countries, like the U.S., are not only required to investigate whether they caused a death, but also prove they didn't play a role in a person's demise.

"In this case, United States authorities had custody of Mr. Ahmed until within hours of when he actually died," Parrin said. "One could argue that the conditions of his detention, the conditions of his transfer, his underlying health conditions would have, or may have played a very serious role in his death."

"This should have never happened to any human being," said Cesare P.R. Romano, an international law professor at Loyola Law School.

"It's really sad that a country like the United States, which is a country that should uphold the rule of law domestically and internationally... It's sad that it's engaged in acts that clearly contravene its international human rights obligations," Romano said, adding that the U.S. was behind the creation of many international human rights laws in place today.

For example, Romano said the U.S. has ratified the International Covenant of Civil and Political Rights, which contains the right to life.

"Here, in this case, the U.S. definitely failed its obligations under Article 6 of that treaty," Romano said.

On Thursday, ICE announced it has arrested and deported more people in the last fiscal year than any time in its 23-year history: More than 483,000 people.

A spokesperson for the agency noted that figure is much higher than the agency's previous record in 2014 when President Barack Obama's administration deported more than 405,000, earning him the label "deporter in chief."

Those statistics are the first to be released by ICE since President Donald Trump returned to the White House.

Ahmed's children say the Trump Administration's immigration policies have left a scar on their lives that may never heal.

"Not a day goes by I don't miss my father, not a day goes by," Mehmood said. "My father was my protector."

text:
Federal immigration agents arrested a man in Robbinsdale early Wednesday morning without a warrant, according to a petition for his release filed in federal court.

In a video from a neighbor that was shared widely on social media, two agents — including one in a face mask — are seen handcuffing the man as he sits in his front yard. Family members joined the man, Jose Ruelas Viorato, on the front steps.

“He’s in the process of getting papers,” a young woman says through tears. “Why are you taking him?”

“We understand, and we’re about to look him up,” one agent answers.

At one point, as agents handcuff Ruelas Viorato, he places a hand on one of the agent’s legs. The agent punches him in the face.

According to a habeas corpus petition, Ruelas Viorato has lived in Minnesota for nearly 30 years. He and his partner run a cleaning business, and he volunteers at a Minneapolis animal shelter twice a week.

The petition, filed by attorney Carrie Huxford Peltier, states Ruelas Viorato also has a legal path to citizenship. His father, a legal permanent resident, filed paperwork for him in 1999 when Ruelas Viorato was 17 years old. He also has immediate family who are U.S. citizens who could petition for his legal permanent residence.

The petition also states agents did not have a warrant for his arrest and that Immigration and Customs Enforcement has never attempted to deport him. A court records search shows he’s received several parking and traffic tickets over the last decade but has never been charged with any other crimes.

“The agents did not know who Mr. Ruelas Viorato was,” Peltier wrote in the petition. “Their vehicles pulled up behind him as he parked in front of his house; armed men jumped out and ran at him.”

Ruelas Viorato then ran toward his front door, according to the petition, and agents chased him.

“When they asked why he had run, he told them the truth: because men with guns were chasing him,” the petition reads.

Peltier argues he should be released immediately, as agents did not have a warrant to arrest him.

Robbinsdale City Council member Alejandro Cáceres-Aranda got a call from the family’s neighbor shortly after the arrest. He said he and the family believe agents followed Ruelas Viorato home from a nearby Hy-Vee, where he’d gone to get groceries.

“I don't know if they ran his plates, maybe … saw that he was Latino, and they started following him just based on racial profiling, which is what I and the family think is what happened,” Cáceres-Aranda said.

The family lives in his ward, and he spent the day helping them find an attorney and figure out where Ruelas Viorato was.

Cáceres-Aranda said the family went to the federal Whipple building, where they had trouble getting answers since the building was closed for Veterans Day.

“So we're trying to get a hold of Whipple, trying to call them, [the call] goes straight to voicemail because of the holiday,” Cáceres-Aranda said.

Ruelas Viorato was eventually able to call his family from Whipple. Shortly after, he was moved to the Sherburne County jail, where he remains in custody.

Cáceres-Aranda said it reminded him of the height of Operation Metro Surge last winter. In recent weeks, he’s heard reports of ICE vehicles spotted out on the streets but said he hasn’t heard about an arrest in the community in the last couple of months. The incident sparked a new round of fear, he said.

“This was so weird to me,” Cáceres-Aranda said. “Even neighbors are scared. I mean, we see what happened with Renee Good and Alex Pretti … lives have been lost because of this, and people definitely have that in the back of their mind.”

But he said he appreciated the family’s neighbors and friends for stepping in to video and offer help right away.

“A lot of neighbors were just coming in and out of the house — close family and friends — and they kept their door open,” Cáceres-Aranda said.

The family has started a fundraiser to cover legal fees, while they await a federal judge’s ruling on the petition for his release.

text:
The sister of David Brouillette, the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who fatally shot a Colombian man in Maine earlier this year, is shedding light on her brother’s past disparaging comments about immigrants. She told MS NOW’s Peter Alexander that she believes emails she exchanged with Brouillette are “highly relevant to investigating his actions.”

On July 13, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero was shot and killed in Biddeford, Maine, while agents said they were conducting an immigration enforcement operation. The Department of Homeland Security said officers were trying to stop a vehicle after it left the residence when an agent, later identified as Brouillette, fired because he feared for public safety. According to the lawyer for Durán Guerrero’s family, the 25-year-old was not the target of the operation and was authorized to work in the U.S. legally.

This week, Brouillette’s sister, Elizabeth Emen, shared emails she said she exchanged with her brother five years before the shooting. In the emails he criticized her relationship with her Colombian partner, the father of two children.

In an email shared with The New York Times, Brouillette said that Emen’s partner, who was in the U.S. legally, should “take his non citizen ass back to his country and enjoy his third world luxuries.” Emen told the paper that the exchange, which the Times said was confirmed by a friend who discussed the email with her at the time and a family representative, was a snapshot of his views about people born outside the country.

Brouillette declined to speak to the Times. In a statement, the DHS said that “any claims of substandard training or vetting are FALSE” and told the Times officers are “trained to use the minimum amount of force necessary to resolve dangerous situations.”

Emen told Alexander on Wednesday that when she heard news of the fatal shooting, “it felt like a nightmare.” She said she experienced “a combination of not being surprised” but also “shock and horror because of the history of his beliefs and his messages in the email.”

“When I heard about my brother’s actions on July 13, I was devastated and immediately recalled his messages in the email,” she said. “When he sent me those messages in January of 2021, that was clarity enough to me that he wasn’t safe to continue a relationship with.”

Shortly after the shooting, other people from Brouillette’s past, including two ex-wives, spoke out about a pattern of alleged violent behavior and struggles with mental health.

More articles

Emen said she was aware of her brother’s history but was “learning even more about the extent of the challenges and the violent behavior he had.”

Emen, a licensed therapist, wondered how someone with this pattern of past behavior could obtain a job like ICE officer. “I’m confused how somebody could offer him a federal enforcement role, and provide him with a weapon and the authority to use it,” she said. “It doesn’t make any sense to me given his history, and I would like some answers about that.”

She told Alexander that DHS never contacted her to ask about her brother’s past. “I wish I had been contacted,” she said. “I would have shared how our relationship ended and what I knew.”

When Alexander asked what she would say to her brother if he were listening to the interview, Emen said she still hoped he would take responsibility for what happened. “I am somebody who has hope that people can step up and become self-aware and take responsibility for their actions,” she said. “And so I’m hoping that through this process and the investigation that some form of that is available to him.”

“And if not,” she continued, “I hope that the powers that be in the systems that exist fully investigate and hold him responsible for his actions that day.”

text:
WASHINGTON — Democrats and business leaders publicly lobbied the Trump administration Wednesday to prioritize work permits and other protections for long-term immigrants during the lame-duck session of Congress and beyond.

Citing the midterm elections, when Democrats flipped the U.S House and Senate, and President Donald Trump’s recent admission that his immigration crackdown hurt Republicans at the ballot box, Democratic lawmakers argued that voters were clear about wanting immigration reform before the start of the next Congress.

Congress has a lengthy to-do-list for the lame-duck session, possibly including government funding, the annual defense policy bill, the farm bill, a measure to regulate the college sports landscape and permitting reform to ease regulation on large construction projects.

“We owe it to these families to try anything, and I’m willing to try anything,” Arizona Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego said.

He was joined by American Business Immigration Coalition Action, which lobbies for work permits and legal pathways for long-term immigrants, and the South Texas Builders Association, a local trade group that represents the construction industry that has a workforce that is 30% immigrant nationwide, and Democratic U.S. House members from Texas.

Asked how receptive the White House would be to work permits for immigrants, which the administration has vigorously worked to limit, Gallego didn’t directly answer.

Trump’s mixed signals

The administration has revoked millions of immigrants’ work permits in the last two years. Many were workers in hospitality, healthcare and the construction industries.

But shortly after the midterm elections, the president said he was open to making a deal on work permits in certain industries.

At the same time, though, he elevated Stephen Miller, an official who has crafted some of the president’s harshest immigration policies, to White House chief of staff.

“I think right now the best thing the White House could do is to actually try to send some type of signal, besides talk, that they’re serious about this, and the way to do that is to have some reforms already at (Immigration and Customs Enforcement),” Gallego said.

“Whether it’s shutting down the detention centers, giving (a) certain level of protections, whether to veterans so they don’t get deported, to maybe parents of U.S. students so they don’t get deported, something to show that it’s not just talk, and this isn’t going to be a policy that’s led by Stephen Miller,” he added.

The vice chair of South Texas Builders Association, Benny Melendez, had a pointed message for Miller.

“If you want to continue harassing our communities, prepare yourself not only to lose your job, but … these same communities you are now harassing will make sure you lose the White House” in 2028, he said.

Next Congress

If lawmakers are unable to get any major reforms through the crowded end-of-year session, Democrats are looking ahead to when they control both chambers next year.

House Republicans on Tuesday elected Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan, a staunch Trump supporter who has not supported immigration reform, to lead them in the minority.

Texas Democratic Rep. Henry Cuellar, the incoming chair on the subcommittee that handles government funding for the Department of Homeland Security, said he’s not worried about Jordan because Democrats will have a majority in January.

Cuellar, whom Trump pardoned after he and his wife were indicted on charges of bribery, money laundering and conspiracy, said he’s going to use his subcommittee gavel to add guardrails on ICE and clear the backlog at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, which processes legal immigrants.

Gallego said he thinks the Senate will be able to get to 60 votes on some type of immigration reform legislation in the 120th Congress, when Democrats will have at least 54 and up to 56 seats depending on races that are still too close to call.

Whether that overhaul is in one bill or a series of increments is up for debate, Gallego said.

“If we can pass a big, beautiful conference immigration reform bill, the Trump immigration reform bill, and if that gets them on our side or not, then let’s do that,” Gallego said. “But if that doesn’t work, then I do think incremental passes to start protecting different communities I think is also an option. We should not avoid that either.”

WASHINGTON – On November 9, Rony Alexander Gomez-Alberto, an illegal alien from Honduras, attempted to storm the cockpit of a United Airlines plane traveling from Newark, New Jersey to New Orleans, Louisiana, claiming to have a bomb. After the plane landed, he was taken into custody and charged with felony bomb threat, terroristic threats, and disorderly conduct. On November 10, ICE lodged a detainer with local authorities requesting they do not release this public safety threat without notifying ICE.

Image

Rony Alexander Gomez-Alberto

After having previously been deported twice, he illegally entered the country a third time and claimed asylum. A judge granted him asylum after he claimed to be transgender, allowing him to stay in the country.

Image

Gomez-Alberto's asylum application

“This criminal illegal alien attempted to storm the cockpit, hijack a plane, and claimed he had a bomb. Thanks to law enforcement, he is now behind bars. This twice-deported criminal illegal alien was allowed into our country because of a weak asylum system that allowed him to game the system,” said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “Under President Trump’s leadership, ICE has arrested 2,312 known or suspected terrorists and is strengthening our asylum system to put the safety of the American citizens first and crack down on fraudsters who try to game the system.”

From January 20, 2025, to November 10, 2026, ICE has arrested 2,312 known or suspected terrorists (KSTs), and has deported 2,157 KSTs.

Under the Trump Administration, DHS and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) have taken swift action to secure the asylum system and crack down on asylum fraud, so that dangerous illegal aliens like this cannot enter our country.

In May, DHS released a directive instructing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to take additional steps to crack down on fraudulent asylum claims. This includes developing anti-fraud policies that will further enforce 8 U.S.C. § 1324c(d), a law that establishes penalties for violations of document fraud. As a result of this directive, ICE attorneys have greater authority to enforce this law, including enforcement actions against immigration attorneys who file false asylum claims in an immigration court. In addition to 8 U.S.C. § 1324c(d), asylum fraud can also be prosecuted as a felony under both 18 U.S.C. § 1546 and 18 U.S.C. § 1001.

Recent cases of asylum fraud include:

On October 29, 2026, five Cuban aliens and one U.S. citizen were sentenced in Florida for their roles in an international conspiracy involving alien smuggling, asylum fraud, and money laundering schemes that brought thousands of aliens illegally into the United States. The U.S. Attorney General made the initial announcement last year of charges against 12 individuals in a superseding indictment for their roles in the conspiracy. According to court documents, the defendants operated a prolific alien smuggling operation that facilitated the unlawful entry of Cuban nationals into the United States by preparing visa applications, laundering millions of dollars in payment, and exploiting the immigration process. What began as a small operation grew into a commercial enterprise. As part of the enterprise, the defendants operated a sham immigration business, Asesoria Y Servicios Migratorios LLC, which promised asylum filings, work permits, and lawful permanent residency applications. The company churned out boilerplate asylum claims without clients’ knowledge or consent and even blocked them from accessing their own USCIS online accounts. Several other individuals have been convicted and sentenced because of this successful investigation.

Biqi “Ashley” Huang, 25, and Wentian Du, 35, were indicted in September 2026. Huang faces one count of making a false statement in a naturalization proceeding and one count of fraudulent acquisition of a firearm. Du faces one count of being an alien in possession of a firearm. According to court documents, Huang entered the U.S. on a student visa in 2023 and received lawful permanent resident status after misrepresenting the status of her marriage during a 2025 Green Card interview. Du entered the U.S. in 2022 on a B1/B2 nonimmigrant visa and applied for asylum about a year later. In June, Huang moved to New York and met Du. She then applied to join the U.S. Air Force, telling a recruiter that she wanted to enlist to obtain citizenship as soon as possible, divorce her current spouse, and marry Du.

Nazira Haji Zada, 47, an Afghan national previously residing in Fort Worth, Texas, was removed from the United States in September 2026 after conceding that she is an alien terrorist, in the first-ever case before the United States Alien Terrorist Removal Court (ATRC). Zada supported a plot to commit an ISIS-inspired mass shooting on Election Day in 2024 for which her son, Abdullah Haji Zada, and son-in-law, Nasir Ahmad Tawhedi, were previously arrested and convicted. Zada is now permanently inadmissible to the U.S.

Yuniel Lima-Santos, 31, of Tampa, Florida, pleaded guilty in August 2026 to alien smuggling, asylum fraud, and money laundering. Lima-Santos conspired with others to operate an alien smuggling organization that encouraged thousands of Cuban aliens to enter the United States using fraudulent Electronic System for Travel Authorization (ESTA) applications and visa waivers. The defendants advertised their smuggling services and bogus visa services across multiple social media platforms to solicit Cuban nationals and other aliens to attempt to illegally enter the U.S. and fraudulently obtain lawful status. Lima-Santos furthered the conspiracy by helping move aliens from their countries of origin, including Cuba, into the U.S. This included purchasing international and domestic flights to transport aliens into and throughout the United States.

Jose Gregorio Sosa Cardona, a suburban Chicago businessman, was sentenced in May 2026 to nine years in prison for immigration fraud, possessing child pornography, and committing tax fraud. Sosa Cardona operated Delta Global Solutions, Inc., which assisted individuals applying for asylum, immigrant visas, lawful permanent residence cards, and other immigration benefits. From 2020 to 2024, Sosa Cardona conspired with two employees of his firm and others to knowingly provide false and fraudulent information to USCIS for his foreign national clients who were seeking benefits. Sosa Cardona was accused of fabricating foreign law enforcement reports and foreign political party membership letters to falsely corroborate his clients’ asylum claims.

USCIS screening and vetting also helps identify individuals who may pose public-safety or national-security concerns.

For example, Edwin Antonio Hernandez, 27, of El Salvador, was arrested in January 2026 by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement during a USCIS appointment. Through the screening and vetting of his asylum and employment authorization applications, USCIS identified information concerning his criminal history and immigration status. Hernandez had previously entered the United States unlawfully and was ordered removed by an immigration judge in 2017. While in custody, Hernandez admitted to being an MS-13 member and confessed to murdering five people in El Salvador through shooting, torturing, stabbing, and dismemberment.

text:
A surefire way to get noticed as a new member of Congress is to ask tough questions.

With the new Democratic majorities in the House and Senate, freshman lawmakers will have plenty of opportunities to press Trump officials as Congress investigates the administration.

Leading a major investigation has long been a way for members of Congress to build their profile. Now, any lawmaker can go viral online after a sharp exchange with a witness — as Rep. Pramila Jayapal did when pressing then-Attorney General Pam Bondi to apologize to Epstein survivors.

Lawmakers with legal backgrounds, such as California Sen. Adam Schiff, who led the first impeachment of Trump, may have an advantage. But members like New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have shown that a law degree isn’t necessary to ask sharp questions.

The incoming freshman class includes several former prosecutors and trial lawyers who are likely to make waves. Here’s a closer look at seven of them.

Zach Dembo

Democrat, Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District

Zach Dembo won a hotly contested congressional race, defeating Republican Ralph Alvarado to flip the Kentucky seat previously held by Rep. Andy Barr, who ran for the U.S. Senate.

A graduate of Stanford University and the University of Michigan Law School, Dembo worked for Teach for America in the Mississippi Delta, served in the U.S. Navy for more than four years in the Judge Advocate General’s Corps and worked for Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear. He later served as a federal prosecutor, resigning in May 2025 because he was concerned about the “corruption and politicization” of the Justice Department.

Dembo is aware that his legal and military background positions him to investigate potential corruption within the Trump administration, specifically on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the war in Iran. He told the Lexington Herald-Leader that his professional experience made him “uniquely prepared” to serve on the House Armed Services and Veterans Affairs committees, as well as the House Judiciary and Oversight committees.

Abdul El-Sayed

Democrat, Senate, Michigan

Abdul El-Sayed brings an unusual academic background to the Senate: He earned a master’s degree at Oxford as a Rhodes scholar and a medical degree from Columbia University. His training as a doctor and researcher could help him ask sharp, focused questions on health issues in committee hearings.

El-Sayed has already said that he will support investigating the Trump administration. In an interview with CNN, he noted that the Democratic majority will have “subpoena power to be able to investigate all of the ways that this administration has used their power for their gain and enrichment, and against ours.”

During the campaign, El-Sayed showed he could explain complicated issues in clear, moral terms. That skill could serve him well when questioning witnesses who try to evade a question.

Sherrod Brown

Democrat, Senate, Ohio

As a former three-term senator returning to Congress after a two-year absence, Sherrod Brown will hit the ground running.

Brown’s experience leading the Senate Banking Committee could prove useful in investigating the Trump family’s cryptocurrency ventures and potential conflicts of interest.

He has a long record of oversight involving financial institutions, consumer protection, corporate conduct and executive branch policy that should come in handy when trying to unpack complicated financial scandals.

Scott Colom

Democrat, Senate, Mississippi

Scott Colom brings years of legal experience to the Senate. He earned a law degree from the University of Wisconsin in 2009 and became district attorney for a Mississippi judicial district in 2015. Then-President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal judgeship in 2022, but Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith helped block the nomination.

More articles

Colom’s campaign rested on many of the key issues facing the Trump administration, including banning stock trading and secret crypto profits, strengthening ethics enforcement and cracking down on corruption and public fraud. This would make him a strong fit for the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.

Troy Jackson

Democrat, Senate, Maine

Troy Jackson, who defeated five-term Sen. Susan Collins, is no outsider to politics. He was first elected to the Maine House of Representatives in 2002 as an independent, later becoming a Democrat, and went on to serve more than a decade in the Maine Senate, including six years as its president.

That experience could come in handy in the day-to-day work of organizing hearings, coordinating meetings and debating priorities, but he’s most likely to stand out in Congress for his sharp stances on issues ranging from Israel to immigration.

Unlike the lawyers on this list, his speaking style is direct and distinctly rural Maine. He speaks with a northern Maine drawl and leans on his background as a logger and union activist to talk about working-class concerns. His plainspoken, sometimes gruff style could help him cut through the polished answers witnesses often use to dodge questions.

Christina Hines

Democrat, Michigan’s 10th Congressional District

Christina Hines won a closely contested House seat after Republican Rep. John James decided to run for governor rather than seek re-election. Her campaign drew little national attention, but her legal experience could help her stand out in committee hearings. She earned a law degree from Wayne State University, taught law and worked as a prosecutor in Washtenaw and Wayne counties, handling sexual assault and child abuse cases.

On the campaign trail, Hines connected with voters by highlighting the ways in which the federal government enables sexual abuse. If Congress decides to investigate the Trump administration’s handling of the Epstein files, for example, Hines’ experience could be valuable in asking questions on a difficult topic and working directly with survivors.

Roy Cooper

Democrat, Senate, North Carolina

Republican Sen. Thom Tillis retired after tangling with President Donald Trump. The president is not likely to be any happier with his replacement.

Roy Cooper ran on an anti-corruption platform, winning handily in a state Trump won three times. His speaking style is generally soft-spoken and measured, but as a longtime prosecutor, he knows how to ask a tough follow-up question.

The former two-term governor, who has a law degree from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, was first elected to the state House of Representatives in 1986, then served four terms as state attorney general. In that role, he handled several high-profile cases, including the Duke lacrosse controversy, and arguing cases before the Supreme Court.

text:
Monroe County commissioners voted unanimously at their regular Thursday (Nov. 12) meeting to approve a legal-services agreement with Bloomington attorney Larry Allen.

The work that Allen will do is in connection with a lawsuit that asks the Monroe County circuit court to clarify whether Stinesville’s police department can sign an agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) without approval from the town’s elected board.

Early Thursday afternoon, commissioners issued a news release about the lawsuit, which was filed on Tuesday.

The agreement was added to Thursday’s agenda at the start of the meeting, on a 3–0 vote. The commissioners later voted 3–0 to approve the contract, with a maximum payment to Allen $2,500, to be made from the county’s general fund.

County attorney Jeff Cockerill said during Thursday’s meeting that Allen would perform most of the work without charge. His compensation would be $250 an hour, for limited work involving court hearings.

Allen is a former Bloomington city attorney who previously served as deputy mayor under John Hamilton as well as an assistant city attorney before that. Before joining Bloomington’s legal department in 2018, he worked in the Indiana attorney general’s office, handling appeals. He left city government at the end of 2024 for private practice and returned temporarily this year to provide legal services to Bloomington’s city council.

The lawsuit itself was already on file when the commissioners approved Allen’s contract. Filed in Monroe County circuit court at 2:45 p.m. Tuesday (Nov. 10), the complaint names the town of Stinesville, police chief Shane Pittman and Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita as defendants. Allen is listed as one of the county’s attorneys, along with Daniel Canon and Jonathan Little.

The filing came hours before the Stinesville Town Board voted 2–1 Tuesday evening to ratify its police department’s agreement with ICE. Board members Scott McGlocklin and Richard Carter supported ratification, with Kimberly Cunningham opposed.

Commissioner Jody Madeira made a point of the sequence during Thursday’s meeting. “Of note, the lawsuit was filed before the town council vote,” she said.

The agreement, signed by Pittman while he was deputy police chief, allows trained Stinesville officers to exercise certain federal immigration-enforcement powers. The county commissioners adopted a resolution on Sept. 17 asking the town board to review the agreement publicly and take a recorded vote on whether to continue it.

After that, Rokita issued a letter with an opinion that concluded that police chiefs and town marshals can enter such agreements without approval from elected governing bodies. His Oct. 6 letter also warned that government actions discouraging participation could violate state law and expose the county to civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation.

Madeira said at Thursday’s meeting that the commissioners respect Stinesville’s decision to ratify the agreement. But she said the vote does not settle all the legal questions raised by Rokita’s opinion.

The lawsuit asks the court to determine whether the agreement was legally authorized when signed and what effect Stinesville’s subsequent ratification has on its validity and applicable filing requirements.

It also seeks an order prohibiting Stinesville from carrying out the agreement until lawful authorization and statutory compliance are established. The commissioners are also asking for an order preventing Rokita from taking enforcement action against them based solely on their Sept. 17 resolution or the filing and pursuit of the lawsuit.

The commissioners said they are not asking the court to overturn Stinesville’s vote. However, the complaint does ask the judge to declare the agreement void or unenforceable unless lawfully authorized.

At Thursday’s meeting, Madeira also addressed a Nov. 5 letter from U.S. Sen. Jim Banks, who urged both the town board and county commissioners to ratify the agreement and release federal funding associated with it.

Madeira said the county commissioners have no authority to ratify Stinesville’s agreement and do not control the federal money, which goes directly to the town. “Monroe County hasn’t touched a dollar of it,” she said. She also disputed any suggestion that the commissioners had with their resolution, passed on Sept. 17, threatened to withhold county funding from Stinesville.

Their resolution, Madeira said, was aimed at ensuring that elected town officials made a public decision. “This was your decision, not ours, and not an attorney general’s, and not a U.S. senator’s,” Madeira said, addressing Stinesville’s officials.

Before the vote on Allen’s contract, commissioner Julie Thomas brought the discussion back to the matter that was actually on the agenda: “The item is the attorney representation agreement,” she said.

No members of the public spoke on the item. The agreement was approved 3–0. All three county commissioners, including Lee Jones, attended the meeting in person.

title: Denied Entry at the Border: Your Rights When a Country Refuses You Entry - Diplomacy and Law
description:
The distinction between a routine immigration refusal and a formal removal order is particularly significant.
In the United States, Customs and Border Protection (CBP) exercises substantial border-search powers under federal law.
An individual's location before formal immigration admission does not, by itself, exclude the receiving state's human rights responsibilities.
The distinction between a substantive prohibition and a procedural entitlement is essential when determining whether an admission refusal is legally permissible.
