text:
Footage of an ICE arrest in Robbinsdale shows a woman crying while she records agents taking her father away.

ICE arrest in Robbinsdale

What we know:

Videos from multiple angles show two ICE agents arresting a man who is clinging to a post attached to the front porch of a home.

The man's daughter can be heard saying, "He's in the process of getting papers! Why are you taking him?"

An agent punched the man in the face before the man was dragged to the backseat of a vehicle and pushed inside by the agents.

Dig deeper:

FOX 9 has confirmed that the man taken by ICE is Jose Ruelas Viorato, 45 years old, and that he was born in Mexico.

He is currently listed as in custody at Sherburne County jail, which is known to hold ICE detainees.

Court records show he has no violent history, but does have multiple traffic violations and petty misdemeanor for trespassing on private property at a campground.

Lawyer says arrest was unlawful

Habeas Corpus petition:

An attorney for Viorato, Carrie Huxford Peltier, is claiming the arrest itself was unlawful and that agents lacked a warrant to detain him.

The Habeas Corpus petition states that Viorato was returning home after buying groceries when armed agents emerged from multiple vehicles and ran toward him. Viorato then ran about 20 feet toward his front door before agents tackled him, handcuffed him and put him in a vehicle.

According to the petition, agents did not know who Viorato was until they checked his driver's license.

Viorato's attorney is arguing that the agents had no arrest warrant and lacked sufficient grounds to believe he was not in the country legally.

The Habeas filing also says Viorato entered the country "without inspection" back in 1997 and operates a cleaning business with his domestic partner.

The attorney also states a family immigration petition filed by Viorato's father in 1999 preserves his eligibility to seek permanent residence without leaving the United States, adding "The government has known of his presence and his family relationship to a lawful permanent resident since 1999 and chose not to detain him."

Court records cited in the petition say Viorato does not have an active removal order.

The petition also claims the arrest violated federal immigration law, Fourth Amendment protections against unreasonable Seizures, Fifth Amendment due process protections and the Administrative Procedure Act.

Immigration enforcement in Minnesota

What they're saying:

Immigration attorneys told FOX 9 they still see frequent ICE arrests across the state, even after the end of Operation Metro Surge.

Immigration attorney Paschal Nwokocha isn’t involved in Viorato’s case but said he’s noticed an increase in ICE enforcement recently.

"People with no criminal record. People who do not have immigration matters pending," Nwokocha said. "Following the draw-down, there was a little lull. But in the last month or so we have seen an uptick."

Other attorneys told FOX 9 they see less of an increase and more of a shift in Department of Homeland Security strategy.

Attorneys have said their clients are more frequently getting called into ICE offices, and their clients are getting detained at routine check-ins.

ICE response

Official statement:

A spokesperson for ICE shared the following statement:

"On November 11, ICE arrested Jose Ruelas Viorato, an illegal alien from Mexico, while conducting a targeted enforcement operation in Golden Valley, Minnesota.

"He entered the U.S. at an unknown time and place. Border Patrol arrested him in March 1998 as a minor and he was turned over to the Mexican consulate. He will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.

"During the arrest, Ruelas attempted to flee from his vehicle on foot. He ran into the front yard of a nearby residence and threw a bird feeder at the arresting officer. He then proceeded to wrap his arms around a porch beam and refused verbal commands to comply, before physically assaulting officers as he continued to resist arrest . The officer relied on his training to safely control the situation and arrest him without further incident.

"ICE law enforcement officers are trained to use the minimum amount of force necessary to resolve dangerous situations to prioritize the safety of the public and our officers. Officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics and regularly receive ongoing use of force training.

"Violence against ICE officers, or any law enforcement personnel, will not be tolerated. Our officers carry out their Congressionally mandated duties in service to public safety and the rule of law. Any bystander or individual who assaults, obstructs, or violently attacks officers will be subject to arrest and prosecution permitted by law.

"Being in detention is a choice. We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App. The United States is offering illegal aliens $3,000 and a free flight to self-deport now. We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return."

City Council member responds

The other side:

Robbinsdale City Council Member Alejandro Caceres Aranda shared the following post:

"This morning, ICE took one of our neighbors. A father, husband, and member of our Robbinsdale community with no criminal record. I have been with the family for most of the day as we try to figure everything out. If there is any community support the family may need as the situation develops, I will be sharing ways to get involved per family request. Thank you to our neighbors for bringing this to my attention."

Robbinsdale police say they weren't involved

Local perspective:

A news release from the Robbinsdale police department said they received a 911 call at 7:13 a.m. from a home in the 3600 block of 31st Avenue North from someone who said ICE was taking her dad.

A responding officer then arrived in the area and said there was no law enforcement of any kind, according to the news release. Police also called the number that dialed 911, but nobody answered.

That officer then spoke to the woman who called 911, who said "she knew there was nothing" police could do and that she "didn't know why she called," before going back inside the home, according to Robbinsdale police.

The news release states the officer then cleared the scene "less than two minutes after his arrival.

Robbinsdale police emphasized that its officers are trained on the City of Robbinsdale's Separation Agreement and that they did not have contact with any law enforcement agency when responding to the call.

name: Human Rights
title: Delia Ramirez Wants Democrats to Meet the Moment - Mother Jones
authors: Isabela Dias, Laura C. Morel, Michael Mechanic, Sophie Hurwitz, Inae Oh, Ari Berman, Schuyler Mitchell, Alex Nguyen, Garnet Henderson, Jamilah King
description:
The term “immigration reform” is thrown around on both sides of the aisle, but any prospect of an immigration overhaul that resembles an actual reform seems far-fetched.
That public opinion is demanding that we do something related to immigration, and that we pass immigration reform.
How you can double the amount of federal revenue we get in taxes if we pass immigration reform.
How you can actually lift this country’s workforce by passing immigration reform.
How you can help children who are living in trauma in this moment recover by passing immigration reform.
text:
Appearing on CBS’ 60 Minutes on Sunday, President Donald Trump acknowledged that his immigration crackdown had been “too tough” and could have hurt Republicans in a midterm election that gave Democrats control of both chambers of Congress. The president said he’d “love to do something on immigration.” When asked what a deal with the Democratic majority could look like, he revealed the self-interest behind his softer rhetoric.

“When you go into a hotel and you have a woman that’s worked there as a maid, as a cleaner, as a this, as a that, as a waitress…and all of a sudden they’re being taken out of the country, it’s tough,” he said. “But there’s a group of people that I would say on the sort of pretty far right that would like everybody taken out.” One of those people, of course, is the very man Trump promoted on Friday to serve as his chief of staff: Stephen Miller.

“It feels like gaslighting,” Democratic Rep. Delia Ramirez of Illinois told Mother Jones during a video call on Tuesday. “It’s mind-boggling to me that a president will say, ‘I just lost an election,’ that perhaps his immigration policies have gone too far, he mentions some of the people that he has benefited from—like the hotel workers in his own hotels—and that maybe he should do something about it, and is interested in working with Democrats on immigration reform—while, concurrently, he has a man who’s been the architect of mass deportations and terror standing right behind him as his new chief of staff. Which one is it? Because the dissonance could not be greater than what we’re seeing.”

Ramirez is vying to lead the House Homeland Security subcommittee on Oversight, Investigations, and Accountability. After winning reelection on November 3, she joined the chorus of Democrats pledging to investigate the Department of Homeland Security and immigration enforcement overreach. “Noem, Markwayne, Miller, Homan, Bovino, what’s up?” the congresswoman wrote on X. “Clear your schedule.”

I spoke with Ramirez on Tuesday about what the new Congress should prioritize on immigration, what accountability for DHS could look like, how Democrats can regain voters’ trust to deliver on that issue, and why immigration reform and affordability are interconnected.

This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

The appointment of Stephen Miller to be Trump’s chief of staff doesn’t exactly signal that the administration is interested in changing course on its immigration policies, does it?

Not when you have a man who has actively worked to terrorize immigrant communities and has celebrated white supremacy so publicly. It’s very difficult for us to see the president being able to lead in that way, because so many people have felt that Stephen Miller has been president in the shadows, and now he’s just got a promotion. I recognize that the president is not mentally stable and he may change his mind 20 times before we pass an immigration reform bill. We should not be legislating based on whatever the president will or will not veto.

I would call his bluff. I would have Democrats pass the most comprehensive immigration reform bill that we possibly can, bringing out of the shadows the most people possible, and then send it to him, and have him decide what he wants to do with it. What I don’t want to do is negotiate ourselves down to something that we know is mediocre and is not going to meet the moment. This is a moment where I believe that every poll will show you that the American people want to see comprehensive immigration reform, and it could be the thing we do literally 40 years later, after the last thing we in fact passed in 1986.

Voters delivered an undeniable rebuke of the Trump administration, including its immigration policies, resulting in a blue wave. Democrats, however, have been on the back foot on immigration, treating it as a liability, and voters have grown distrustful that Democrats can do better on that issue than the Trump administration. How should the party approach immigration—and message around it—going forward?

What we saw during the midterm elections was a rebuke on Donald Trump, Republicans, and their horrifying policies of corruption, hate, deportation, intimidation, retaliation, and they’ve given us a mandate for bold change and justice. They said to Democrats, this is a rebuke against Republicans, and an opportunity for you to show me what you will do with this great mandate we have given you.

Democrats must meet the moment, and meeting the moment means demanding justice for the horrors that people have lived, for the health care that they have lost, and the necessities that they can’t afford.

That includes immigration reform and the ability for Democrats to stop apologizing for immigration and for immigrants, and start affirming that immigrants are a critical part of this nation, that immigrants stabilize our economies, and that we unapologetically fully stand with the immigrant community and the establishment of permanent protections for them—permanent pathways to citizenship, protections for those seeking asylum in this country—so that we stop obsessing over the border and actually protect people and their ability to enter this country, get the visas necessary, and reunite people who have been separated from their families for so long.

We can, in fact, do that, and the American people want us to prove that we will. That means that we don’t sabotage ourselves. That means that we don’t sell ourselves short. And in the words of [Massachusetts Democratic Rep.] Ayanna Pressley, that we show what a majority can do—because mediocre policy changes will get us a 2024 repeat very quickly after.

It sounds like you’re advocating for the party to embrace an affirmatively pro-immigrant agenda.

That’s exactly right. It’s why I introduced a month ago the people’s vision for immigration reform. I wasn’t going to wait until after the elections. I wanted a roadmap that Democrats can point to as the solution and the way that they show the people that voted for the very first time and gave them this majority that they got it this time: That we will not make excuses, and we will have a positive, affirmative agenda as it pertains to immigration in this country. One that creates citizenship for the millions of people living in the shadows, establishes legal pathways, and creates and protects the ability for people to seek asylum in this country.

Last year, Chicago was one of the epicenters of ICE’s crackdown with Operation Midway Blitz. You’ve been one of the most vocal US lawmakers calling for accountability for DHS. What does accountability look like in your mind?

Let me start by saying that there is no affordability without accountability. Point blank. If you want to actually talk about why people are living and experiencing the challenges they are right now, whether it’s that they can’t afford to buy groceries, they can’t afford to drive to work or pick up their kids, or they can’t afford the rent or buy their home, or why they’re living in the shadows and their businesses are shutting down, there has to be accountability to the actors that have made that happen. And it also means accountability to those that have terrorized them.

Yes, we should be passing Medicare for all. Yes, we need to pass a bill that increases wages in this country. Yes, we should abolish super PACs and tax the rich. But we also have to understand that, as we fight for an affordable country, we have to hold every fascist in this administration accountable.

That includes [former DHS Secretary] Kristi Noem, who right now has a really good job doing nothing and getting paid a lot of money as a senior advisor in the State Department. It also means Markwayne Mullin, Pete Hegseth, Stephen Miller, Donald Trump, Tom Homan, Gregory Bovino. I could be here all day talking about all the actors that need to be held accountable, and it’s why, for me, it’s important for people to understand that resignations are not enough. They’re not going to save them from investigations, from impeachment, and accountability.

As we now hold gavels, we have the power to issue subpoenas, hold officials in contempt, and request that the courts step in when they don’t show up to our hearings.

It’s why I personally am pursuing the Homeland Security Oversight Subcommittee gavel. Because I believe that from there, where I’ve been doing oversight work the last four years since I’ve been in Congress, we’re going to be able to lead investigations into a number of things, including the use of federal funding to reward campaign donors, the medical neglect that we have seen in detention centers, the calls by Stephen Miller to ignore habeas corpus and the violation of due process, the empowerment of agents to act without accountability.

Also, and we don’t say this enough, how FEMA, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Coast Guard, and TSA have been literally defunded and gutted to support the mass deportation campaign, and how illegal it is to take money from critical missions to move it into the obsession of Donald Trump and Stephen Miller [with] ICE and deportation. There’s plenty of work to be done. We have to be willing to use our power.

What do you think Democrats should prioritize going into the 120th Congress, and, specifically, what should the House subcommittee you’re seeking to lead focus on while there’s momentum?

I introduced a bill to dismantle DHS, and I intend to dismantle DHS from the inside. Every investigation we do—whether it’s about detention, who is profiting at the expense of children who are literally in cages, or the expansion of these 287(g) agreements where local police [work] with federal agents to hunt down people—is critical to provide the evidence necessary to be able to bring the most justice.

These investigations are not just about those that need to be behind bars, but ultimately that we create systemic changes. What people have said to us over and over is that yes, we want affordability and accountability, and in that accountability, what we want is for you to prove to us that you will do everything in your power so we’re never here again.

People will say, well, DHS is not the only agency that has been problematic. Absolutely not. But there’s no other agency that has consolidated the amount of power that DHS has with the amount of money that DHS has in order to terrorize the American people and literally rob us from our civil rights, while at the same time saying that they’re doing it under the guise of protecting us from terrorism. There is no democracy if DHS continues to operate the way it does.

For me, investigations must lead into reimagining something new, where we protect cybersecurity infrastructure, where we protect FEMA, where we protect TSA, where we protect the customs functions at the border, and where we abolish ICE and CBP and reinvest funds towards healthcare, community safety, and first responders.

Since Trump’s return to the White House, Congress has given the administration nearly a quarter of a trillion dollars for immigration enforcement. What can a Democratic majority in Congress do about ICE spending, and to rein in the agency and slow down Trump’s mass deportation campaign?

The ultimate goal is to dismantle this agency, and in the interim, while we build a case to dismantle it, we need to be clawing back every dollar that was given to them, whether through the “big ugly bill” or the reconciliation process we had a few months ago.

What we need to be doing, and what I’ll be working with the Progressive Caucus, the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, and the other caucuses [to do], is to begin defunding ICE and CBP by clawing back the money that was robbed from the American people and put into these campaigns of deportation and kidnapping and terror that have brought so much money and profit to those that are either buying stocks in detention or running these detention centers.

I think we have a real opportunity to do so in the CR, the continuing resolution—to create an amendment that claws back that money. If we’re not able to get that done in the CR process before the year’s over, that [should] be a top priority of the new speaker in the first 100 days. Defund, claw back, redirect the money to CISA, to FEMA, to TSA, to USCIS, and to the office that is supposed to ensure accountability within DHS. What I’m saying is, Congress, do your job. We control the money and we control where the money goes.

The term “immigration reform” is thrown around on both sides of the aisle, but any prospect of an immigration overhaul that resembles an actual reform seems far-fetched. Is the appetite there, particularly among newly elected members of Congress?

Affordability necessitates immigration reform in this country. You cannot talk about economic stability in this country, protecting Social Security, protecting all the critical safety net programs, without understanding the intricacies of a broken immigration system and of the needs of the people. This is a moment where people in this Congress have been told by the American people what they want to see. That public opinion is demanding that we do something related to immigration, and that we pass immigration reform. We, Democrats, have less than a year to prove to the American people what we do with the vote that they gave us, and if the vote they gave us was worth it.

It means that we fundamentally change the way we talk about immigration and immigrants in this country, and we start talking about all the good things related to immigration: [That] you can’t extend Social Security by 25 years or 30 years in this country if you don’t pass immigration reform. How you can double the amount of federal revenue we get in taxes if we pass immigration reform. How you can actually lift this country’s workforce by passing immigration reform. How you can create more labor union jobs in this country by passing immigration reform. How you can help children who are living in trauma in this moment recover by passing immigration reform.

Democrats have to unapologetically, without a doubt, stand up for immigrants the way we stand up for abortion rights, the way we stand up for LGBT rights, and the way that we fight and say we stand up for our democracy. We can do that in this country and be successful, and the American people are waiting for that courage that we talk about to translate into action that they can feel. I’m hopeful. I have to be.

name: Litigation
title: Trump Administration Targets F-1 Students, Creating Turmoil for Them, US Universities, and ...
description:
Of the approximately 5,000 F-1 students whose SEVIS records ICE terminated, more than 3,000 had their F-1 visas revoked first.
Many of the lawsuits resulted in courts ordering ICE to reverse the SEVIS terminations and reinstate the F-1 students’ SEVIS records retroactively.
What F-1 students give to the United States The Trump administration has failed to consider the importance of F-1 students to American colleges and universities, employers, and the economy.
In addition to their tuition, F-1 students provide U.S.-born students with different perspectives while they acquire first-hand knowledge of what the United States has to offer.
By creating uncertainty and making F-1 students unwelcome, the administration is harming the American public it claims to be protecting.
text:
The Trump administration is targeting international students in F-1 status through a series of policies and regulations (proposed and final) that restrict their ability to live, study, and gain practical experience in the United States. According to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), approximately 1.6 million international students and their dependents are in the United States in F status. A survey found that enrollment by international students would decline if the government imposed a fixed admission period—one of the regulatory changes this administration issued. A decrease in international students means less revenue for U.S. colleges and universities as they usually pay a higher tuition amount. If schools have less revenue, then this harms U.S. citizen students. A decrease also threatens the entire country. One economic analysis found that even with a conservative estimate of only a 10% reduction in F-1 student enrollment, the negative effects on the US economy would range from $72 to $145 billion within a 10-year period.

Termination of F-1 student records

The first major attack on international students under the Trump administration came in early 2025. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) instigated student visa revocations by sharing with the Department of State (DOS) “hits” of approximately 6,400 F-1 students in the National Criminal Information Center database who had interactions with law enforcement. After DOS reported to ICE that an F-1 visa was revoked, ICE terminated the students’ records in the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS). ICE also terminated some SEVIS records for other reasons. Of the approximately 5,000 F-1 students whose SEVIS records ICE terminated, more than 3,000 had their F-1 visas revoked first.

Without an active SEVIS record, those students experienced disruptions such as being unable to register for classes or continue previously authorized work. Students were notified by their schools after Designated School Officials (DSOs), the administrators authorized by the government to oversee F-1 students, discovered the terminations in SEVIS. Immigration attorneys filed at least 65 lawsuits challenging the SEVIS terminations. Many students established that they had not engaged in activity for which SEVIS termination would be a consequence of a visa revocation. By coordinating their efforts, attorneys challenged inconsistencies and inaccuracies in declarations submitted by ICE officials. For example, ICE officials claimed that SEVIS termination was not a termination of F-1 status. Yet courts took notice that U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) and DOS had equated a SEVIS termination for failure to maintain status with the status termination.

Many of the lawsuits resulted in courts ordering ICE to reverse the SEVIS terminations and reinstate the F-1 students’ SEVIS records retroactively. In some cases, ICE reinstated the SEVIS records retroactively before receiving a court order. ICE also said that affected F-1 students would receive letters confirming the retroactive reinstatement. However, ICE also admitted that the system did not display to users such as DSOs that the reinstatements were retroactive. Attorneys have reported to the American Immigration Lawyers Association that F-1 students applying to USCIS for immigration benefits, such as work authorization for post-graduate practical training or a change to a different temporary status are receiving inquiries from the agency questioning whether they maintained their F-1 status. Individuals whose F-1 visas were revoked face challenges, including consular officer denials of applications for new visas (in the F-1 or other categories), and judicial review generally is not an option for a visa denial.

Elimination of duration of status

Through a final rule, the administration sought to impose a maximum four-year period of stay in F-1 status effective September 15, 2026. For nearly 50 years, F-1 students received “duration of status,” meaning the length of time needed to complete their degree program and any approved post-graduate training.

For now, duration of status remains in effect due to a federal district court order postponing the effective date while a lawsuit challenging the rule proceeds. If the new rule had taken effect, F-1 status would have been limited to a student’s program end date or the expiration date of their work authorization card (EAD), whichever was later, but no longer than four years. This would be a problem for F-1 students in advanced degree programs that require more than four years to complete. And many bachelor’s degree candidates do not finish their programs within four years. To stay longer, students would have to file, for a minimum $420 fee, for an extension of stay with USCIS, although there were certain transition exceptions. A USCIS officer, with no expertise in academia, would be deciding whether an F-1 student could stay and complete their degree. Post-graduate training could be severely restricted, if not eliminated, because students would have to wait for USCIS to process their extensions first (after the transition exceptions ended) and the post-graduate training is time limited.

The government appealed the court’s ruling to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit. However, the district court is proceeding on the merits and likely will issue a decision before the First Circuit resolves the appeal of the temporary postponement.

Proposed fees for Optional Practical Training

The administration also is attacking Optional Practical Training (OPT) through new required payments. OPT allows some F-1s to secure temporary employment directly related to the student’s major area of study. A proposed rule would require U.S. colleges and universities to pay $70,000 before recommending an F-1 student for initial OPT and $30,000 for any additional OPT (such as the up to 24-month extension for students in certain STEM fields). While the government labels these amounts as “fees,” a final rule likely will be challenged as unlawful taxes that DHS lacks authority to assess. The agency claims the purpose of the proposed rule is to combat “fraud and abuse” in the OPT program but gives only a few examples of bad actors among employers, not the schools. The agency does not adequately consider other alternatives or give serious consideration to the burden on schools to fund the costs or administer such payments. Comments were due by November 9, 2026.

Disrupting curricular practical training

The administration also has attacked Curricular Practical Training (CPT). CPT involves learning through practical experience such as an internship. For 2024, (the most recent data available), ICE reported that 130,566 foreign students obtained work authorization for CPT. For decades, immigration authorities interpreted a regulation that permits F-1 students to engage in CPT as meaning the training either is taken for academic credit toward the F-1’s degree or, if no credit, is mandatory to complete the F-1’s degree. However, in August 2026, ICE issued two “broadcast messages,” to DSOs who are responsible for approving CPT for F-1s, which purport to severely restrict the ability of students to utilize CPT. In the first message, which ICE claimed was a reminder to schools and DSOs, ICE interpreted the CPT as authorized only if it would be “impossible” for an F-1 student to complete their degree without it and “the work associated with CPT is required for all students pursuing that degree.” The reminder seemed like a threat as ICE said authorization inconsistent with this interpretation “may subject” a school to withdrawal of its certification to enroll F-1 students and a DSO to criminal penalties for providing false information as to the training. In the second message, ICE provided “Questions and Answers” which corresponded to its new interpretation.

The Association of American Universities and three other organizations with members affected by ICE’s action, filed a lawsuit in the federal district court in Massachusetts. They also filed a motion to stop ICE from implementing or enforcing the new interpretation while the lawsuit proceeds. One of many harms asserted is the loss of unique educational experiences that F-1s in the final year of their degree program will suffer as schools cancel CPT out of fear of losing their certification. The court heard the motion on November 6.

What F-1 students give to the United States

The Trump administration has failed to consider the importance of F-1 students to American colleges and universities, employers, and the economy. In addition to their tuition, F-1 students provide U.S.-born students with different perspectives while they acquire first-hand knowledge of what the United States has to offer. Post-graduate training, particularly in STEM fields, is an important path for F-1 students to remain in the U.S. workforce, usually through a change of status to an H-1B specialty occupation status. The Trump administration wrongly considers students and workers to be fungible. Real-world experience shows that in many industries, foreign students educated in the United States enable U.S. employers to grow their businesses and hire more U.S. workers. Foreign students educated in the United States also start businesses which provide more opportunities for U.S. workers. By creating uncertainty and making F-1 students unwelcome, the administration is harming the American public it claims to be protecting.

text:
Earlier this year, I stood outside of the Lake Worth City Hall as residents demanded that the City Council exit its 287(g) agreement. These contracts allow local government and law enforcement entities to partner with the federal government for immigration enforcement, effectively turning local police departments into appendages for United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

As I remained there, under the blistering Florida summer heat, I listened to a young woman named Jessica. At just 18 years old, she was separated from her parents when ICE apprehended and deported them to Guatemala. Fighting back tears, she shared that she hadn’t seen her parents in more than a year, missing important life milestones together like her high school graduation.

A few weeks later, I was helping journalist Adrian Carrasquillo from the Bulwark with a story about ongoing ICE raids in Doral, the city with the largest number of Venezuelan migrants in the country. As we spoke to people at Pepito’s Plaza, a Venezuelan restaurant, one of the workers told us how sales had sharply declined due to the ongoing immigration arrests, something that we both picked up on as we found the place empty for lunch. Suddenly bursting into tears, the Venezuelan worker told us that ICE had recently detained her husband in Doral. He was being held for months at the Folkston ICE Processing Center in Georgia.

For two years now, immigrants in Florida have been subjected to some of the most intense and aggressive immigration enforcement in the nation. In South Florida, we have seen ICE in unmarked cars randomly stopping people and asking their immigration status, harassing people with legal status in clear-cut cases of racial profiling. In Lake Worth, one of these stops was caught on video, showing masked ICE agents detaining a U.S. citizen and flat-out telling him the reason was that he looked like an immigrant.

Just a month before the midterm election, masked ICE agents conducted an immigration arrest in broad daylight outside of a school in Little Havana as the children ended their school days and headed home. Photos show one of the agents questioning a child as he holds his lunchbox, with his father being handcuffed and put in an unmarked vehicle.

These are just a few of the many immigration enforcement incidents that have shocked and disgusted people in South Florida. Then there was the immigrant detention camp Alligator Alcatraz, which was funded by diverting more than $1 billion from Florida’s emergency fund. Instead of spending that money as emergency funds should be spent — for example, combating the wildfires that plagued areas of the state during the drought conditions experienced earlier this year — the money was used to detain immigrants in an alligator-themed concentration camp.

A report from Amnesty International found that immigrants were tortured by being locked for hours within something called “the box,” a small cage just large enough for one person to fit inside. The stories of human rights abuses, transmitted through phone calls from detainees made to their loved ones, shocked not just the conscience of good people in South Florida, but made international headlines.

While the blue wave resulting in an extinction-level event for the national GOP did not manifest in Florida, Republicans in Florida have been put on notice. At least 16 State House seats and one State Senate seat flipped from Republican to Democrat. The GOP was not able to flip a single congressional seat despite egregiously gerrymandered districts. Miami-Dade County went Democrat for the first time in years, and the three incumbent Cuban Republicans barely held their seats, with Florida District 27 going into a recount. Another interesting election data point from Florida: Doral, the city with the largest number of Venezuelan immigrants in the country, was the Miami-Dade city that turned the most against Trump.

Why? Largely because the Trump administration stripped protections, mainly Temporary Protected Status (TPS), from hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans, while arbitrarily denying their asylum claims, and then proceeded to hunt them like animals, separating families and destroying local businesses. At the start of Trump 2.0, Doral Mayor Christi Fraga and council members signed a 287(g) agreement.

In the past few months, a growing and relentless chorus of voices in Doral has been asking these officials to end that agreement. Yet Mayor Fraga has not taken action, choosing instead to attend a gala at Trump’s Doral Resort, where she took photos with a far-right influencer who is advocating for any Venezuelan who voted Democrat to be deported.

Mayor Fraga is one of many South Florida officials who have failed to act to curb the excesses and abuses of Trump 2.0. At the City of Miami, despite deteriorating conditions across the city and sustained community opposition to its ICE collaboration, city leadership has failed to rescind its own 287(g) agreement. This inaction is particularly concerning given Mayor Eileen Higgins’ campaign commitments on this issue. Elected late last year on a platform that included opposing Miami’s 287(g) agreement, Higgins has yet to meet with immigration advocacy organizations or take meaningful steps toward ending the city’s cooperation with ICE.

Meanwhile, despite repeated calls from residents and community organizations, thousands of Miami residents continue to face the consequences of increasingly aggressive and indiscriminate immigration enforcement. The growing disconnect between the mayor’s campaign promises and her actions in office has left immigrant communities and their allies waiting for the leadership they were promised.

The midterm election should be a bipartisan wake-up call to elected officials at all levels of government. While cost of living concerns and outrage at Trump’s illegal war drove voters to the polls in mass against MAGA, disgust at the immigration abuses we have seen was a huge motivator as well. People are tired of seeing their friends, neighbors, co-workers, family members, and loved ones racially profiled, questioned, assaulted, detained, and deported by masked ICE thugs who act with impunity. Despite this, Trump seems to signal that he is doubling down on aggressive enforcement by tapping Stephen Miller, the architect of his anti-immigrant policies, to replace Susie Wiles as his Chief of Staff.

There’s much work to be done in dismantling the enforcement infrastructure that the federal government has weaponized to terrorize communities and infringe upon the civil rights of Americans, but local governments can take one simple action across the state: ending 287(g) agreements and ensuring police departments don’t assist or cooperate with ICE.

text:
WASHINGTON – On November 9, Rony Alexander Gomez-Alberto, an illegal alien from Honduras, attempted to storm the cockpit of a United Airlines plane traveling from Newark, New Jersey to New Orleans, Louisiana, claiming to have a bomb. After the plane landed, he was taken into custody and charged with felony bomb threat, terroristic threats, and disorderly conduct. On November 10, ICE lodged a detainer with local authorities requesting they do not release this public safety threat without notifying ICE.

Rony Alexander Gomez-Alberto

After having previously been deported twice, he illegally entered the country a third time and claimed asylum. A judge granted him asylum after he claimed to be transgender, allowing him to stay in the country.

Gomez-Alberto's asylum application

“This criminal illegal alien attempted to storm the cockpit, hijack a plane, and claimed he had a bomb. Thanks to law enforcement, he is now behind bars. This twice-deported criminal illegal alien was allowed into our country because of a weak asylum system that allowed him to game the system,” said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “Under President Trump’s leadership, ICE has arrested 2,312 known or suspected terrorists and is strengthening our asylum system to put the safety of the American citizens first and crack down on fraudsters who try to game the system.”

From January 20, 2025, to November 10, 2026, ICE has arrested 2,312 known or suspected terrorists (KSTs), and has deported 2,157 KSTs.

Under the Trump Administration, DHS and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) have taken swift action to secure the asylum system and crack down on asylum fraud, so that dangerous illegal aliens like this cannot enter our country.

In May, DHS released a directive instructing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to take additional steps to crack down on fraudulent asylum claims. This includes developing anti-fraud policies that will further enforce 8 U.S.C. § 1324c(d), a law that establishes penalties for violations of document fraud. As a result of this directive, ICE attorneys have greater authority to enforce this law, including enforcement actions against immigration attorneys who file false asylum claims in an immigration court. In addition to 8 U.S.C. § 1324c(d), asylum fraud can also be prosecuted as a felony under both 18 U.S.C. § 1546 and 18 U.S.C. § 1001.

Recent cases of asylum fraud include:

On October 29, 2026, five Cuban aliens and one U.S. citizen were sentenced in Florida for their roles in an international conspiracy involving alien smuggling, asylum fraud, and money laundering schemes that brought thousands of aliens illegally into the United States. The U.S. Attorney General made the initial announcement last year of charges against 12 individuals in a superseding indictment for their roles in the conspiracy. According to court documents, the defendants operated a prolific alien smuggling operation that facilitated the unlawful entry of Cuban nationals into the United States by preparing visa applications, laundering millions of dollars in payment, and exploiting the immigration process. What began as a small operation grew into a commercial enterprise. As part of the enterprise, the defendants operated a sham immigration business, Asesoria Y Servicios Migratorios LLC, which promised asylum filings, work permits, and lawful permanent residency applications. The company churned out boilerplate asylum claims without clients’ knowledge or consent and even blocked them from accessing their own USCIS online accounts. Several other individuals have been convicted and sentenced because of this successful investigation.

Biqi “Ashley” Huang, 25, and Wentian Du, 35, were indicted in September 2026. Huang faces one count of making a false statement in a naturalization proceeding and one count of fraudulent acquisition of a firearm. Du faces one count of being an alien in possession of a firearm. According to court documents, Huang entered the U.S. on a student visa in 2023 and received lawful permanent resident status after misrepresenting the status of her marriage during a 2025 Green Card interview. Du entered the U.S. in 2022 on a B1/B2 nonimmigrant visa and applied for asylum about a year later. In June, Huang moved to New York and met Du. She then applied to join the U.S. Air Force, telling a recruiter that she wanted to enlist to obtain citizenship as soon as possible, divorce her current spouse, and marry Du.

Nazira Haji Zada, 47, an Afghan national previously residing in Fort Worth, Texas, was removed from the United States in September 2026 after conceding that she is an alien terrorist, in the first-ever case before the United States Alien Terrorist Removal Court (ATRC). Zada supported a plot to commit an ISIS-inspired mass shooting on Election Day in 2024 for which her son, Abdullah Haji Zada, and son-in-law, Nasir Ahmad Tawhedi, were previously arrested and convicted. Zada is now permanently inadmissible to the U.S.

Yuniel Lima-Santos, 31, of Tampa, Florida, pleaded guilty in August 2026 to alien smuggling, asylum fraud, and money laundering. Lima-Santos conspired with others to operate an alien smuggling organization that encouraged thousands of Cuban aliens to enter the United States using fraudulent Electronic System for Travel Authorization (ESTA) applications and visa waivers. The defendants advertised their smuggling services and bogus visa services across multiple social media platforms to solicit Cuban nationals and other aliens to attempt to illegally enter the U.S. and fraudulently obtain lawful status. Lima-Santos furthered the conspiracy by helping move aliens from their countries of origin, including Cuba, into the U.S. This included purchasing international and domestic flights to transport aliens into and throughout the United States.

Jose Gregorio Sosa Cardona, a suburban Chicago businessman, was sentenced in May 2026 to nine years in prison for immigration fraud, possessing child pornography, and committing tax fraud. Sosa Cardona operated Delta Global Solutions, Inc., which assisted individuals applying for asylum, immigrant visas, lawful permanent residence cards, and other immigration benefits. From 2020 to 2024, Sosa Cardona conspired with two employees of his firm and others to knowingly provide false and fraudulent information to USCIS for his foreign national clients who were seeking benefits. Sosa Cardona was accused of fabricating foreign law enforcement reports and foreign political party membership letters to falsely corroborate his clients’ asylum claims.

USCIS screening and vetting also helps identify individuals who may pose public-safety or national-security concerns.

title: Toronto Star: America is Not Safe. Canada Must Pause the Safe Third Country Agreement.
description:
This summer, a Haitian family in the United States attempted to seek asylum in Canada.
The policy is premised on the United States being a safe country for refugees and committed to sharing responsibility for protecting them.
Prime Minister Carney must pause the STCA until the United States is truly “safe” for asylum seekers.
Indeed, arbitrariness and coercion are pervasive throughout the U.S. asylum system, rendering it fundamentally unfair.
Now is the time for Prime Minister Carney to act: pause the STCA until the United States can show that it is actually a “safe” country for asylum seekers.
text:
This piece was originally published by the Toronto Star.

This summer, a Haitian family in the United States attempted to seek asylum in Canada. They had been stripped of their Temporary Protected Status by the Trump administration and feared they would be detained by ICE and deported to Haiti.

Instead of allowing them to seek safety, Canadian authorities made their greatest fears a reality. In an interview with Human Rights Watch, the father, Marc, recounted, “We went to Canada to seek asylum. Three days later, Canadian authorities sent us back to the United States and handed us over to ICE.” On August 27, 2026, the family was deported to Haiti, including their two sons, ages 5 and 3, one of whom is a U.S. citizen.

Canada turned this family away under the Safe Third Country Agreement [STCA], which allows Canada to, with some exceptions, turn away asylum-seekers at the Canada-U.S. border without hearing their cases. The policy is premised on the United States being a safe country for refugees and committed to sharing responsibility for protecting them.

This week, as Canada’s Federal Court hears arguments on the legality of the STCA, more than one hundred and thirty U.S.-based immigrant-serving organizations and experts issued a rare joint statement: The United States is not safe for asylum seekers.

The situation is clear. Prime Minister Carney must pause the STCA until the United States is truly “safe” for asylum seekers.

Our organizations maintain databases that catalogue U.S. human rights abuses against people seeking safety. One such database tracks third country deportations: the Trump administration’s cruel policy that deports asylum seekers and refugees to unsafe countries where they have never been, including the Central African Republic and Honduras. The other database tracks brutality and neglect in ICE detention, where deaths have nearly doubled in the past year. This includes Johnny Noviello, a Canadian citizen with U.S. permanent residency who died in ICE custody in a manner experts say was preventable.

The Canadian government claims that conditions in the United States are continually monitored, and “only countries that respect human rights and offer a “high degree of protection to asylum-seekers” may be designated as safe third countries.” When Canada’s highest court considered the legality of the STCA three years ago, it found that “a degree of difference as between the legal schemes applicable in the two countries can be tolerated, so long as the American system is not fundamentally unfair.”

However, the overall U.S. asylum grant rate has reached a record low of below 6 percent (in contrast to Canada’s over 60 percent) and the U.S. Attorney General has declared most people seeking asylum because of gender violence “generally” ineligible. Gay people deemed refugees by U.S. immigration judges are being deported to third countries where gay people are persecuted. This is why advocates are arguing in court that the STCA violates the guarantee of equal rights in Canada’s Charter.

On a recent trip to Haiti, we interviewed deportees who, while in U.S. immigration detention, had their claims of fear of return to Haiti ignored and were deprived of vital medical care. Their only escape from death in detention was accepting return to Haiti. Indeed, arbitrariness and coercion are pervasive throughout the U.S. asylum system, rendering it fundamentally unfair. When ICE detained the Haitian family turned back by Canadian authorities, it did not allow Marc to contact a lawyer about his asylum application. ICE told Marc: “Your [U.S. citizen] son can stay, but the state will take custody of him, and you will lose him.”

Asylum seekers facing detention, deportation, and even death cannot wait for a ruling from Canada’s court. Now is the time for Prime Minister Carney to act: pause the STCA until the United States can show that it is actually a “safe” country for asylum seekers.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, American Oversight filed suit against the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) demanding the agencies release records about USCIS’s “Unlawful Voter Initiative,” a secretive effort in which, according to a whistleblower, USCIS officers were diverted from their regular duties to comb through voter data in search of supposed noncitizen voters and were instructed to misrepresent themselves to gain access to state voter records. The lawsuit comes on the heels of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s Election Day pledge to review voting logs from last week’s election in search of noncitizen voting.

The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, asks the court to order the agencies to expedite six Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests and release records on the initiative’s quotas, training, data sources, and communications with state election officials. The records could shed light on how the administration is investigating alleged noncitizen voting, what safeguards exist to protect eligible voters, and whether these efforts could be used to cast doubt on legitimate election results.

“The election may be over, but the Trump administration’s efforts to cast suspicion on American voters is far from finished,” said Chioma Chukwu, Executive Director of American Oversight. “As Americans showed up to the polls, Secretary Mullin announced plans to comb through voting records in pursuit of a noncitizen voting problem the evidence shows doesn’t exist. That promise is especially troubling given what a whistleblower has already alleged about the administration’s effort to investigate purported noncitizen voters: aggressive quotas, data of unclear origin, and instructions to misrepresent themselves to gain access to state voter systems. That’s a recipe for eligible citizens to be wrongly flagged and investigated, while potentially casting doubt on legitimate election results. The public deserves to see the rules, the data, and the quotas behind this operation and know what safeguards are in place to protect eligible voters. We’re going to court to demand those answers.”

In September, Sens. Alex Padilla and Chuck Schumer sent a letter to DHS and USCIS that included a whistleblower disclosure about the initiative. The whistleblower alleged that officers in USCIS’s Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate (FDNS) were diverted to review data to identify supposed “unlawful voters,” and that USCIS instructed employees to misrepresent themselves to gain access to state voter records. Advocates indicate such false representations “would likely violate relevant state law,” and that officers faced a quota of at least five subjects per hour and 40 per day, leaving about 12 minutes to determine whether a person was a citizen or an unlawful voter. Those quotas — according to the whistleblower — left too little time to thoroughly review each case, increasing the risk of error, and officers did not know the source of the DHS voter data they were reviewing.

The initiative comes amid the Trump administration’s repeated statements that large numbers of noncitizens are voting in U.S. elections — claims that are unsupported by evidence.

American Oversight’s lawsuit concerns six FOIA requests filed on Sept. 16. They seek emails from top DHS officials — including Mullin, Deputy Secretary Troy Edgar, and Senior Counselor Heather Honey — and from Joseph Edlow and other senior USCIS leaders containing terms such as “unlawful voter,” “voter fraud,” “state voter,” “voter record,” “FDNS enhancement,” and “overtime”; training materials given to FDNS personnel, including a video shown to them on or around Aug. 21; records of any quotas or targets for the number of people officers were expected to review; USCIS communications since July 1 with election offices in 19 states and the District of Columbia; and records identifying the sources and types of data provided to officers, along with any matching or data-mining software used in the initiative. American Oversight is not seeking the voter data itself.

Given the urgency of the issue, American Oversight asked both agencies to expedite its requests. DHS did not acknowledge our request until Oct. 17 — a month after it was filed — when it denied expedited processing and claimed an extension to respond. It has not communicated with American Oversight since. USCIS has not responded to any of the five requests submitted to it, including the requests for expedited processing. Neither agency has produced any records.

text:
Canada is violating its own constitution by turning asylum seekers away at the border with the United States, where they face serious threats under U.S. President Donald Trump, Canadian legal experts and rights advocates say.

Amnesty International Canada, the Canadian Council for Refugees, and the Canadian Council of Churches are in court this week to challenge a decades-old pact that allows Canadian officials to summarily send most refugees back at the U.S. border.

People rallied in Toronto and Montreal, the two largest cities in Canada, on Monday to show support for the case and call on the Canadian government to rip up the Safe Third Country Agreement (STCA).

In Montreal, dozens of protesters held posters that read, “Canada must protect, not send back” and “Humanity has no borders.”

“If Canadians don’t feel safe in the United States, we can be sure that refugees aren’t safe either,” Lauren Lallemand, co-executive director of the Canadian Council for Refugees, told the crowd.

“The asylum system in the U.S. is failing, and those who flee in search of safety deserve to be protected.”

The Agreement

The Safe Third Country Agreement, which came into force in 2004, is premised on the idea that Canada and the U.S. each offer people access to a robust refugee protection system.

In practice, it means that asylum seekers can seek protection in the first country they arrive in, but not both: someone in the U.S. cannot apply for asylum in Canada, or vice versa.

For years, the restriction applied to asylum claims made at official crossings along the border.

But if people entered Canada irregularly between ports of entry (via farmers’ fields or rural roads, for example), they could circumvent the pact — and as Trump began to crack down on immigration during his first term, tens of thousands of people made dangerous crossings into Canada to request protection.

In 2023, amid public and political pressure to crack down on immigration, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and President Joe Biden closed the loophole, extending the Safe Third Country Agreement to the entire 5,525-mile border.

Now, only people who meet specific conditions — such as unaccompanied minors or individuals with relatives who are already in Canada — are exempt from being turned away under the Safe Third Country Agreement.

“Extremely Urgent, Harmful”

The lawsuit being heard in Federal Court in Toronto this week argues that the Safe Third Country Agreement violates equality rights under Section 15 of Canada’s constitution, known as the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

According to the complainants, that’s because the pact disproportionately harms racialized asylum seekers, including women fleeing gender-based violence, children, and members of the LGBTQ+ community.

Julia Sande, a lawyer at Amnesty International Canada, explained that Section 15 applies to everyone who is physically in the country, including refugee claimants.

“Canada cannot deport people to face torture, harm [and] persecution in another country,” she said. “It would be a violation of their Charter rights, even if it’s another country doing the harm, because it’s Canada’s decision to send them out … [and] to put them in [harm’s way] when harm is reasonably foreseeable.”

While conditions for asylum seekers and refugees in the U.S. have been concerning for a long time, Sande said the situation has deteriorated dramatically under the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump.

She pointed to the expansion of immigration detention as one example. “Things are obviously extremely urgent and extremely harmful,” she said.

“We all act in horror at what’s unfolding in the United States. You hear Canadian citizens talking about being afraid to go there, being afraid of ICE,” she told Truthout.

“I have a hard time believing that you could find anyone here who would say, ‘Yeah I’d really like my government to hand a child over to ICE to be thrown in detention … and ultimately sent back to a country where they fled gang violence.’”

Government Defends Pact

Canada’s federal immigration ministry — Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada — told Truthout in an email that it can’t comment on matters before the courts.

But it said the Safe Third Country Agreement “is designed to keep the Canada–U.S. border safe and well-managed,” adding: “It helps avoid sudden spikes in asylum claims that could overwhelm border crossings, housing, and processing systems. This means Canada can keep the border orderly while continuing to offer protection to people who need it.”

The government also says on its website that, “only countries that respect human rights and offer a high degree of protection to asylum seekers may be designated as safe third countries.”

But Yael Schacher, head of the Americas program at humanitarian group Refugees International, said the U.S. “absolutely” does not meet that threshold.

“The U.S. does not have fair procedures for asylum seekers anymore,” she said.

“We have a situation here where people that — by Canadian standards — should be entitled to asylum, entitled to protection, are having their rights violated all the time in the United States in many, many ways.”

“Canada Should Be Thinking Twice”

Schacher told Truthout that the Trump administration is not effectively screening asylum seekers for harm they would face should they be deported from the U.S. It also has purged judges who may have been favorable to asylum cases from U.S. immigration courts, effectively transforming them into “deportation courts.”

At the same time, the U.S. government is detaining people in dire conditions as it pushes to deport them to their home countries or to third countries where they face myriad dangers, including torture and imprisonment.

She described a recent case in which a Haitian man agreed to be deported to Haiti’s capital Port-au-Prince — which has been ravaged by deadly gang-related violence — after eight months in U.S. detention because he could not get sufficient insulin to manage his diabetes.

“He gave up his right to an asylum hearing on the merits because he couldn’t take the detention conditions anymore. He was afraid he was going to die,” Schacher said.

She said there have been cases in which people handed over to U.S. immigration authorities by Canada at the border have been detained and deported without a fair assessment of their asylum claims.

“‘Turning away’ is a way too euphemistic way of describing what Canada is doing, which is giving people to the U.S. immigration authorities, who are then putting them in prison and deporting them,” Schacher said, adding that Canada needs to rethink the STCA altogether.

“The U.S. doesn’t provide asylum anymore, and Canada — like Mexico — needs to rethink how it relates to the United States as a result.”

That was echoed by Sande at Amnesty International Canada, who said that while she expects the legal challenge to the Safe Third Country Agreement to be a long process, the Canadian government “has the power to end this at any time.”

“If you survey people on the street and ask them, based on what you’ve seen unfolding in the United States, do you think the United States is safe for refugees? I think most people would say no,” Sande said.

“A government does not need a court to tell them what is abundantly obvious. They could stop sending people back to the U.S. today.”

text:
In the year of our lord 2026, a federal judge getting real frustrated at a Trump administration lawyer is practically its own genre. On Monday, U.S. District Judge Sanket Bulsara of the Eastern District of New York added the latest entry, barring Assistant U.S. Attorney Thomas Price from ever appearing again in Benitez v. Department of Homeland Security. (That’s the suit alleging that federal immigration officers in New York arrest people based on their ethnicity and without the warrants the law requires.)

I need a moment for the harshness of the judge’s punishment — honestly, it’s cold as ice.

The problem was a November 4 letter with Price’s name on it. The letter told the court that an injunction in a related case covered only the one petitioner in that case. The injunction came from U.S. District Judge Gary Brown, a Trump appointee, in Sanchez Alfaro v. Mullin. That case was about ICE’s warrantless arrest of a Long Island man with Special Immigrant Juvenile status, and officers later admitted they’d grabbed the wrong guy. Brown had already called the government’s arguments “both factually incorrect and legally spurious.” And his injunction also wasn’t about one guy, it reads: “Before effecting a civil immigration arrest in this judicial district, ICE shall obtain a valid warrant of arrest in advance.” (There’s an exception for people likely to flee.)

“In this judicial district”… it’s right there in the text.

You can’t even write this off as a sloppy read because Price had also filed briefs in Sanchez Alfaro arguing that the district-wide warrant requirement would be hard to comply with. He knew exactly how big the order was, hell, he’d complained about how big it was! Then he signed a letter to another judge in the same courthouse saying it was tiny.

Bulsara wasn’t confused about what happened. From the bench, he said Price’s letter was written in “bad faith, a deliberate attempt to mislead the Court, perpetuate a fraud on the tribunal, and violate[s] obligations under Rule 11.” He said “the only conclusion that can be drawn from these statements is that they’re made in bad faith.” He also said this wasn’t a one-off but “a pattern of dissembling, obfuscation, and frankly outright misrepresentation that bled from Alfaro into this case.”

He also sounded a little hurt, because he thought he’d been doing the government a favor:

When I issued the order that I issued in this case, I actually did it fully expecting I was giving a gift horse to the respondents. … I was flabbergasted by the response.

Turns out you can look a gift horse in the mouth, you just shouldn’t lie to the judge about what you saw.

The minute order Bulsara entered after the hearing is drier, but it’s no gentler:

As stated on the record, the Court has found prima facie Rule 11 violations based on the contents of Defendants’ November 4 letter 111. AUSA Price is barred from continuing appearances in this case and must file a notice of withdrawal no later than November 13, 2026.

The order also gives the office’s line attorneys a chaperone:

Every future filing in this docket must be signed by Richard Hayes, Chief of the Civil Division of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of New York, or someone at his supervisory level or higher.

In other words, nothing gets filed in this case without a grown-up’s signature on it.

The office as a whole is also on the hook. Under Rule 11(c)(3), it has to show cause “why Rule 11 sanctions should not be imposed or imposed pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1927 or the Court’s inherent power.” That’s three separate grounds for sanctions in a single sentence. Two other AUSAs whose names appear in the letter’s signature block have until November 16, the same deadline as the show-cause response, to file sworn declarations explaining how much they wrote, edited, or supervised the letter. Bulsara indicated he’ll likely disqualify them too unless they can show they weren’t involved. He told Hayes to think about pulling Price from his other cases before the court as well, adding: “Your office is on notice.” Hayes didn’t address the misconduct allegations at the hearing and asked for time to review the transcript.

Then there’s the threat that really matters:

The Court has issued a warning about the consequence should the Court discover any future misrepresentation or false statement (either by counsel or any witness or declarant): after an opportunity to be heard, should preliminary findings be confirmed, the Court will enter a default judgment in this case in favor of Plaintiffs, with the only issue for resolution to be remedies to be imposed.

It’s also part of a pattern. In Florida, Judge Roy Dalton put DOJ lawyers on blast for pretending inconvenient law doesn’t exist. In New Jersey, Judge Zahid Quraishi tossed a supervisory AUSA out of his courtroom while trying to figure out who’s even running the office. In Rhode Island, Judge Mary McElroy nuked the department for an “appalling lack of candor” over its subpoena campaign. In Minnesota, Chief Judge Patrick Schiltz ran out of patience with ICE treating court orders as optional. And the Comey prosecution got the benchslap treatment before it ever got near a jury. The judges are Bush appointees, Trump appointees, Obama appointees, and Biden appointees. They keep reaching the same conclusion.

For decades the Justice Department walked into court with the presumption of regularity: judges took its word because its word was usually good. Price’s office is now on notice that it’s lost that presumption, and at this point it’s hard to argue any other office is in a different position.

WASHINGTON ― A day after Minneapolis resident Aliya Rahman sued the U.S. government for abuse by federal immigration enforcement agents, HuffPost got a Wednesday tip about something curious: Immigration and Customs Enforcement has deleted at least two posts from its official X account that previously defended its agents’ violent arrest of Rahman.

Rahman, a Bangladeshi American software engineer who is autistic and has physical disabilities, was on her way to a doctor’s appointment on Jan. 13 when ICE agents surrounded her car, smashed in her window and dragged her out. They locked her up in a federal detention center for hours, where Rahman alleges she experienced severe medical neglect and violence at the hands of ICE officers, requiring hospitalization.

Advertisement

An eyewitness captured her arrest on film, and footage of Rahman’s brutal encounter with ICE went viral. She testified to Congress about it on Feb. 3, and on Tuesday, filed a lawsuit against the government on eight counts, including assault, false arrest and negligence.

The Department of Homeland Security and ICE, which is part of the department, have repeatedly used X to try to dismiss Rahman’s allegations. On Feb. 6, a few days after she appeared before Congress, the agency scoffed at media coverage of her testimony.

“Unfortunately for the media, we have the receipts,” ICE posted on X, where it has more than 3 million followers. It claimed Rahman refused to get out of the way of ICE officers that day, thereby impeding their work, and she “found out the hard way” she couldn’t do that.

Advertisement

That post is gone now. An archived version is here.

On March 4, ICE accused Rep. Zoe Lofgren (D-Calif.) of spreading lies about its agents being abusive toward Rahman. That was the day Lofgren grilled then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem about Rahman’s assault in a House Judiciary Committee hearing, telling her, “She wasn’t protesting anything. She was on her way to a doctor’s appointment.”

“Rep. Lofgren is pushing a lie that’s already been debunked,” the agency posted on X, repeating its claim that Rahman “continued to impede our officers” in January by not moving her car, and finding out “the hard way” that she isn’t allowed to do that.

Advertisement

That post is now missing, too. An archive version is here.

It’s not clear why, or when, DHS deleted these posts. It’s also not clear if DHS has deleted other posts about Rahman, or if it was even legal to do this. Federal agencies are generally required to preserve all official records, including social media posts, for archival purposes.

“Agencies cannot delete records from a social media platform or from a recordkeeping system without a disposition provided by a NARA-approved records schedule,” reads a November 2022 guidance to senior agency officials from the National Archives and Records Administration.

Advertisement

A DHS spokesperson declined to answer any of these questions. Instead, they provided the same statement they gave on Tuesday in response to Rahman suing the U.S. government: “We are aware of the lawsuit and look forward to vigorously defending ourselves in court.”

DHS still has other X posts up dismissing Rahman’s claims. One, posted on the day of her arrest, quotes then-White House Homeland Security advisor Stephen Miller telling ICE officers they have immunity as they carry out their jobs. DHS posted on X again two days later about Rahman being an “agitator” who ignored police commands to move her car.

Rahman’s attorneys don’t know what to make of the disappearing posts. They’ve been demanding for months that DHS and ICE retract false statements about Rahman from their social media accounts. They sent cease and desist messages to both agencies in late June, via mail and email. They never heard back.

Advertisement

Those now-deleted posts were up for “many, many months, and the harm has been done,” said Jessica Gingold, senior counsel at MacArthur Justice Center and one of Rahman’s attorneys. “It’s not like taking them down without also putting up ‘we were wrong’ is sufficient.”

More broadly, it raises questions about DHS officials potentially trying to dodge accountability for things they’ve done as they start getting called out in lawsuits, she said. There have been at least six federal lawsuits filed against the Trump administration this year, including Rahman’s, relating to potentially illegal actions by federal immigration enforcement officers.

“The lawsuits are coming,” Gingold said.

text:
Residents of federally funded public housing will be required to show proof of U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status under a new rule published Thursday by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.

The measure could displace nearly 80,000 people, including tens of thousands of citizens in mixed-status families, from their homes, according to the Center for Budget and Policy Priorities, a nonpartisan research and policy institute.

Since 1995, mixed-status families have been permitted to live together in HUD-funded housing as long as federal subsidies covered only eligible household members. The new rule may force these families to decide whether to remain together in nonpublic housing or split up their households.

"This is tearing apart families and sowing division," said Marie Claire Tran-Leung, director of the Evictions Initiative Project and managing attorney at the National Housing Law Project.

The rule's prior status, which allowed mixed-status families to live together, worked well for all parties, Tran-Leung said. Mixed-status households often paid a higher share of rent because their subsidies were prorated, experts say. If those families are forced to leave public housing, HUD will likely face financial shortfalls, Tran-Leung said.

About 20,000 mixed-status families, or 80,000 people, could be affected by the rule, CBPP's data shows. About 37,000 of those are children, mostly U.S. citizens, CBPP said.

The rule is scheduled to take effect on Dec. 14.

"President Trump warned that the days of illegal aliens and ineligible noncitizens exploiting government-funded welfare programs would be over," HUD Secretary Scott Turner said in a statement. "It's unacceptable that America's homeless veterans, disabled, elderly, and victims of domestic violence languish on waitlists while illegals and ineligibles scam our system. American taxpayers will no longer foot the bill. Promises made, promises kept."

Turner's statement said a recent audit identified nearly 200,000 tenants with incomplete or unverified eligibility status. Currently, HUD-funded housing serves only a quarter of eligible households in need.

Families in all 50 states will be affected, with the largest concentration in New York, California and Texas. The rule would impact more than 7,000 mixed-status households in California and 2,500 mixed-status households in New York, according to a coalition of 22 state attorneys general who opposed the rule.

They wrote in an April letter that it "would inflict significant economic costs on the States and exacerbate the affordable housing crisis."

CBS News reached out to housing authorities in California, New York and Texas to learn how the rule would be implemented and enforced locally.

During the first Trump administration in 2019, HUD attempted to revise the longstanding provision, but the proposed change was withdrawn in 2021. In February 2026, the agency reintroduced the proposed rule, drawing more than 11,000 public comments from individuals, advocacy groups and members of Congress during the three-month comment period.

Reactions also came from individual members of the public.

Claire Stanley, a senior living in public housing in Auburn, Washington, wrote: "There is no justification for this rule — it won't save money because the increase in homelessness will cost more than just allowing families to stay together."

Another commenter, Mark Smith of Oconto Falls, Wisconsin, urged in March: "Please withdraw the proposal and think about what Jesus would do."

text:
On September 14, 2026, a federal court issued an injunction against the new Duration of Status (D/S) rule, one day before its scheduled implementation. The previous D/S rules will remain in effect until further notice. Additionally, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued a new rule regarding OPT fees, with the comment period ending on November 9, 2026.

Background

On July 17, 2026, DHS issued a final rule changing the Duration of Status. The rule would have required the following:

Students on F-1 and J-1 visas would have their admission limited to 4 years.

I visa holders would be limited to a 240 day admission.

Extensions of stay would require an application to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS).

The rule also restricted changing schools, objectives, or adding degrees.

On August 18, 2026, a group of schools and labor organizations sued DHS in the US District Court for the District of Massachusetts. Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV issued a nationwide preliminary injunction on September 14. The government appealed to the First Circuit Court of Appeals on September 30 and, on November 3, requested a 30-day stay of the appeal while the district court considers a final ruling.

Approximately 22,000 comments were submitted on the proposed rule, addressing concerns such as:

How this rule would affect international student numbers.

Ability to finish academic programs.

USCIS backlog.

Reliance on current Duration of Status.

Freedom of the press.

OPT Fees

On October 8, 2026, DHS proposed a rule requiring schools to pay $70,000 when recommending a student for OPT and an additional $30,000 for a STEM OPT extension. Schools may pass these costs to the student or employer. The comment period ended on November 9.

What does this mean for international students?

International students on F-1 and J-1 visas continue to be admitted for the duration of status. No new rules for OPT or STEM OPT are currently in effect, and the proposed fees do not apply at this time. DHS will review all comments and issue a final rule. Once issued, the fee will take effect after 60 days. If the government prevails in the D/S lawsuit, that rule will also take effect.
