text:
Months after the unprecedented immigration crackdown in the state during Operation Metro Surge, federal agents arrested a man in Robbinsdale, Minnesota, on Wednesday whose family says he is going through the process to obtain legal status.

The arrest was captured on video by his daughter, Chelsea Bernal, and neighbors. The altercation lasted several minutes before Jose Ruelas Viorato, 45, was taken into an unmarked black SUV. Records show he is currently detained in a Sherburne County facility after being transferred from the federal Whipple Building at Fort Snelling.

Court records show he has several parking tickets, but has not been charged or convicted of any violent crime.

In the video — shared widely online — Ruelas appears to struggle and at times resist arrest. He wraps his hand around one agent's leg as he is on the ground when the other agent tells that other officer to "strike to the face," punching Ruelas.

Bernal described being awoken to screams around 7 a.m.

"I was awakened to him screaming really loud this morning, and I got scared because I've never heard my dad scream that way," she said. "So I ran downstairs to my mom also yelling inside the house, and I came out and ICE agents were detaining my dad on a pole that he was holding on to for dear life."

Bernal and her brother, Andres Ruelas, are American citizens and said their father has been working through the immigration system to obtain legal status for years and that he is currently on a waiting list — and has been since 1999. WCCO could not confirm where he stands in that process as of today.

At one point in the video, Bernal tells the agents he is "in the process of getting papers," and one of the agents replies "if you're in the process you shouldn't have any issues, right?"

A spokesperson for U.S. Customs and Immigration Enforcement did not respond to a request for comment on the incident or an inquiry about the use-of-force policy for the agency.

The arrest underscores a shift in the federal government's approach to immigration enforcement compared to recent years, said Ana Pottratz Acosta, an associate professor at the Mitchell Hamline School of Law who practiced immigration law for years.

Under prior administrations, people with violent criminal histories and more recent arrivals were the priority, whereas people who entered without proper documents or overstayed a visa and had been living in the United States awhile were at the "bottom of the priority list."

Metro Surge yielded an unprecedented number of arrests, she said, but while that operation has ended, ICE arrests are still at higher levels than in previous years.

"The number of people being apprehended or arrested by ICE here in Minnesota, looking at it right now or over the past three or four months compared to, let's say, two or three years ago — it's much, much higher," she said.

"Arrests are continuing to happen of immigrants in our communities in Minnesota. And a lot of the time, the people who are being targeted or arrested are people who are trying to go through the process the right way — attending their hearings, going to an appointment as part of the process to apply for permanent residence," she added. "So those are really kind of the general trends that we're seeing."

Bernal and Andres Ruelas received a call from their father saying that he is OK, but they didn't get many other details and are awaiting more information about what led up to the arrest. They said he had left their home to go to a nearby grocery store for breakfast and he was detained right when he got back.

"I just think it's sad to see that ICE is getting people that aren't criminals, that aren't doing bad to this world, and they're just trying to provide for their families," Andres said.

A Northern California nurse and professor remains in a federal immigration detention center nearly two months after her arrest.

For 19 years, Ann Lawani, 39, built a life in the U.S. as a nurse, professor and caregiver. Then, earlier this year, federal immigration agents arrested her outside her Northern California home and sent her thousands of miles away to Louisiana, leaving her attorney struggling to find her in a federal detention system gone dark.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

On the morning of Sept. 16, Lawani, a longtime University of San Francisco professor who holds a Ph.D. in nursing, heard noises outside the home in Lodi she shares with her 83-year-old father, who has cancer, according to a Tuesday report by the New York Times. Still in pajamas and flip-flops, she opened her garage after spotting officers on her security camera, only to be arrested by Immigration Customs and Enforcement, reportedly without explanation or a warrant when she requested one.

Over the course of the next few days, ICE agents transferred her through four facilities, starting from Bakersfield, having shackled her ankles, waist and hands, the outlet reported. The whole time, ICE failed to notify her attorney of her whereabouts, according to federal court records reviewed by SFGATE.

“As a habeas attorney, the first step that I need to take is to find out where my client is. The first question that a family has for me is: Where is my relative?” Natalia Vieira Santanna, Lawani’s attorney, told SFGATE. “Her location did not show up the day she was detained. It did not show up the next day or the following day.”

Lawani’s attorney learned she was being detained in Louisiana after the federal government filed a motion on Sept. 23 to transfer her habeas corpus case there.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Nearly two months after being taken, Lawani remains at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center, yet her name was still missing from ICE’s online detainee locator when SFGATE checked Thursday. The database, which previously allowed families and attorneys to find people in federal immigration custody, stopped displaying the whereabouts of most detainees with final removal orders following a Sept. 15 policy change.

The change has effectively removed more than 20,000 people, about 32% of ICE’s detained population, from public searches, according to an Oct. 28 federal lawsuit filed in Massachusetts by four legal aid organizations. The groups contend that the policy unlawfully obstructs access to attorneys and prevents detainees from challenging their confinement or deportation before they are removed from the country.

“It just makes it so much harder,” Santanna said. “It delays everything for the client, and every delay causes another day in detention.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Lawani arrived in the United States as a teenager on a visitor visa in 2007 and applied for asylum within a year, her attorney said. In 2013, an immigration judge denied her asylum request but granted her protection from deportation to Nigeria, finding she would likely face persecution there.

Although the ruling did not cancel her removal order, Lawani remained in the U.S., complied with immigration requirements and maintained a work permit valid through 2029. She has no criminal history.

In a statement to SFGATE, the Department of Homeland Security defended her arrest, citing her expired visitor visa and a final removal order issued Aug. 6, 2013. The agency did not address the court-ordered protection against deportation to Nigeria.

“To be clear: work authorization does not confer legal status in the U.S.,” DHS said. “She will remain in ICE custody pending removal from the United States.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Santanna argued that Lawani’s detention violated her constitutional rights and challenged it in a Sept. 18 habeas petition. DHS has not disclosed whether it intends to deport her to a third country, which her 2013 order does not categorically prohibit.

On Sept. 29, U.S. District Judge Daniel Calabretta rejected the government’s attempt to move the case to Louisiana, finding that “no diligent attorney could have known” Lawani’s whereabouts when the petition was filed. Calabretta also barred federal officials from deporting Lawani while her petition remained pending and ordered the government to explain why she should not be released.

Lawani’s detention has also disrupted the University of San Francisco’s nursing program, where she oversees approximately 230 students, coordinates 51 faculty members and manages partnerships with 38 clinical sites, according to an Oct. 20 letter California Rep. Josh Harder sent to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. She also works as a nurse at John Muir Health and specializes in caring for critically ill and terminal patients.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“Her continued absence causes real and mounting harm to the students and faculty who rely on her mentorship,” Eileen Fry-Bowers, dean of USF’s School of Nursing and Health Professions, told SFGATE in a statement, citing disruptions to curriculum development and community health partnerships. The university helped Lawani’s family secure legal counsel and has joined efforts to bring her home.

Harder renewed his demand Tuesday for ICE to release Lawani under supervision and return her to California, an effort supported by Sen. Adam Schiff and Rep. Kevin Mullin, USF said in a statement.

“Given her longstanding compliance, lack of criminal history, and substantial community ties, there is no apparent public safety justification for keeping Dr. Lawani detained thousands of miles from home while her case proceeds,” Harder wrote in the Oct. 20 letter.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Lawani’s brother, Samuel Lawani, condemned her detention and cross-country transfer in a statement released by Harder’s office.

“For someone that vital to the community to be tracked, abruptly vacuumed into an abyss and moved across the country, is simply EVIL and consequential,” Samuel said. “My family and I want to see my sister returned home safely and as soon as possible.”

text:
The Supreme Court cleared the way Monday for the Trump administration to resume border wall construction in the Big Bend region of Texas, a blow to bipartisan opponents who had argued the project is a waste of money that threatens the unique landscape.

The border wall is a signature project of President Donald Trump, who has long vowed to build a wall from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico.

Landowners and business owners in the Big Bend region, environmentalists and others who’ve opposed the construction project were bitterly disappointed with the court’s decision.

“This horrific decision clears the way for contractors to bulldoze pristine desert and dynamite canyon walls before the courts have even decided whether this destruction is legal,” said Laiken Jordahl, national public lands advocate at the Center for Biological Diversity, one of the groups that sued to stop the construction. “They’re signing off on the permanent destruction of the wildest place in Texas, and the theft of a great American river from all of us.”

Republicans in Congress last summer funded the project with $46 billion, and Customs and Border Protection has been rapidly erecting 12 miles of barriers a week across the entire border with a goal of eventually covering the entire 2,000-mile border with a mixture of 30-foot-tall steel walls, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology designed to stop illegal immigration and smuggling.

The government has pushed forward by issuing sweeping waivers to bypass regulations. Those rules are aimed at protecting the environment, but have historically slowed down major construction projects.

Big Bend residents of both parties oppose the project

In Texas’s Big Bend region, bipartisan opposition has rallied to fight back against the project, which would include 30-foot-tall steel walls in some areas as well as vehicle barriers and new roads.

They’ve argued that the barriers are a waste of money that threaten the local economy and lifestyle in an area of historically low illegal immigration. They say the job could be better done using only surveillance technology like drones.

A judge in Texas sided with opponents, finding that Congress likely had not clearly authorized such broad waivers for an area with the southern border’s lowest rate of migrant apprehensions. She ordered an immediate stop to all construction-related activity in the area, which includes Big Bend National Park as well as land up and down river in state and private hands.

The Trump administration filed an emergency appeal, saying there are illegal border crossings and drug seizures in Big Bend. More traffic could also be funneled there if there’s a gap in the wall, federal attorneys argued.

Customs and Border Protection head Rodney Scott said in an interview with The Associated Press that if the Big Bend area were left without a wall or other border infrastructure while other areas along the border get those fortifications, he’s convinced it would be swiftly overrun by cartels.

The Supreme Court agreed that the law sharply limits judges’ powers to intervene when the federal government decides speedy border barrier construction is necessary. The majority paused the lower court decision as the case plays out. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.

CBP did not immediately respond to questions about how swiftly construction could restart. The agency started building an initial section of border wall in one area of the roughly 500-mile stretch that makes up the Big Bend region, but that was stopped with the judge’s order.

Construction activity in national park sparked outrage

The agency has encountered intense opposition from landowners up and down the region when it comes to getting permissions to enter their land to survey and build.

The Center for Biological Diversity sued over the construction, along with Friends of the Ruidosa Church and a river guide in the Big Bend area. Jordahl said it was the first time the government had waived a broad set of environmental laws inside a national park.

David Keller lives in the Big Bend region, is a member of the board of Conserve Big Bend and is a plaintiff in a separate lawsuit of landowners opposing the border wall projects.

He called the court’s decision devastating: “Everything is on the line again.”

Keller called the border infrastructure projects the “industrialization of one of the last best open undeveloped wild places in the lower 48 states.”

“We can’t afford to lose any more. Not an ounce. Not an acre,” he said. “We need wild country to be who we are, to be fully human, to be American I would say.”

The projects have drawn criticism from both Democrats and Republicans, including outgoing Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas, who wrote an op-ed arguing against the project published Monday in the San Antonio Express-News hours before the court’s decision.

“A combination of modern technology, adequate staffing, and meaningful cooperation with local officials and landowners offers a more sensible and effective path forward than indiscriminate construction of unnecessary barriers,” Cornyn wrote.

The government in August paused construction activity in Big Bend National Park that sparked outrage when bulldozers were spotted breaking ground in the park.

The government has repeatedly said no steel walls are planned for the national park. Initial plans included a new road as well as some vehicle barriers in the park. CBP has said in court filings that it will come forward with a finalized plan for what it intends to build in the national park but so far hasn’t done so while the case was at the Supreme Court.
