Illustrative volumes for those on non-Work routes

Those on non-work routes follow a range of pathways – the position of much of this cohort remains uncertain.

People on Family routes who have met the core requirements (have not needed to rely on exceptional circumstances) and are sponsored by a British Citizen have an unchanged residence requirement for settlement. Any of the 223,000 people sponsored by a British Citizen and arrived on a Family route that meet the core requirements will continue to be able to settle after 5 years.

The remaining 39,000 people who arrived on a family visa not sponsored by a British citizen will move to a longer pathway to settlement.

There are 105,000 main applicants and 26,000 associated dependants on other routes whose pathway would depend on individual circumstances, some of which may be outside of the Earned Settlement framework.

Illustrative volumes for refugees

There are 133,000 people whose first non-visit grant of leave was due to an asylum claim and 3,000 associated dependants who are expected to settle between 2026-2030. These refugees, as well as those who come in the future, will settle as detailed in Table 2: Refugee Pathways to Settlement. Aside from refugees admitted through the UK Resettlement Scheme and other designated resettlement or sponsorship routes, this cohort will therefore have a minimum 10 years residence requirement.

Some migrants who reach settlement via other routes will also be affected. Migrants who reach settlement via asylum, following entrance on a non-visit visa route, are included within the settlement forecasts for the other initial routes set out in this Annex. It is not possible to disaggregate these; however, this cohort will also have a minimum 10 years residence requirement.

There are 4,000 people on resettlement schemes (not including Afghan schemes) expected to settle between 2026-2030. This cohort would settle in 5 years subject to requirements as outlined in Table 2: Refugee Pathways to Settlement.

Illustrative volumes for those outside Earned Settlement

Outside the scope for Earned Settlement, there are:

117,000 BN(O) main applicant visa holders expected to settle along with 78,000 BN(O) dependant visa holders.

49,000 main visa holders who arrived on other out of scope routes, such as direct to settlement and Afghan schemes, and 22,000 associated dependants.

Annex B: The economic case for change

The Earned Settlement Framework requires migrants to make a genuine contribution to the UK. The reformed system will reward individuals who have made a sustained and measurable contribution to the UK, on the principle that any accelerated path to settlement should be earned through active participation in the economy.

At a minimum, individuals are required to make a genuine contribution to the UK by having annual earnings above £12,571 for a minimum of three years, in line with 2026/27 thresholds for paying National Insurance Contributions (NICs). Accelerated pathways to settlement are available for those who make a further sustained contribution either by earning over the higher tax rate threshold in England (£50,271) for a 5-year path or, the additional tax rate in England (£125,141) for a 3-year path. In addition, those who have made an active contribution in other ways, for example through working in a public sector occupation, will be on a 5-year path.

The fiscal contribution of migrants over a lifetime

Settlement confers the right to remain in the UK indefinitely, and it is therefore appropriate to consider the impact migrants with different economic characteristics make over their lifetime.

The Migration Advisory Committee (MAC) developed a modelling framework, set out in their 2025 publication The Fiscal Impact of Immigration: Static and Dynamic Estimates for the UK, which estimates the net fiscal impact of an individual over their lifetime. It compares the government revenue associated with an individual with the public expenditure allocated to them in each future year they are expected to remain in the UK.

The Home Office has undertaken analysis of the Earned Settlement framework using the MAC fiscal modelling framework to set out the case for change. The Home Office has made updates to the data and assumptions used in applying the framework which are set out at the end of this Annex. The resulting outputs are therefore Home Office estimates and responsibility for the analysis rests with the Home Office rather than the MAC.

Fiscal modelling – baseline contribution

The Earned Settlement framework will encourage migrants on non-sponsored routes to enter employment before applying for settlement, and reward those employed at higher salaries for their increased contribution. Home Office modelling illustrates the fiscal difference between the current Skilled Worker general salary threshold and the two earnings levels set out in this framework that lead to reduced settlement pathways.

An individual earning £41,700, the current Skilled Worker general salary threshold, is estimated to have a lifetime net fiscal impact of around £347,000.

An individual earning £50,271, the minimum to qualify for Settlement after 5 years, is estimated to have a lifetime net fiscal impact of around £456,000, around £109,000 higher than an individual earning £41,700.

An individual earning £125,141, the minimum to qualify for settlement after 3 years, is estimated to have a lifetime net fiscal impact of around £1.53m, around £1.08m higher than an individual earning £50,271.

Figure B1: Cumulative lifetime fiscal impacts of Skilled Workers by salary threshold and years since arrival

The examples above focus on the fiscal impact of the main applicant. However, the overall fiscal impact associated with migration also depends on any accompanying dependants. Therefore, a family level assessment needs to consider the fiscal contribution of the main applicant, alongside the revenues and public expenditure associated with adult and child dependants.

Adult dependants can contribute through employment and taxation, although their earnings and employment profiles may differ from those of the main applicant. Child dependants primarily accrue public expenditure costs while they are children, particularly through education and health care. As a result, a main applicant can have a strongly positive net fiscal impact while the fiscal contribution of the family as a whole is lower once dependants are included. The number and type of dependants is therefore an important part of the overall fiscal assessment.

Fiscal modelling – Impact of Earned Settlement

Earned Settlement has an impact through four primary channels:

For those on a path to settlement of 10 years:

Individuals could wait the additional 5 years to settle. In practice, this has a fiscally positive impact as it would result in delaying access to public funds for five years. There is a further ambiguous impact, as in one direction individuals are required to remain employed over this period, while in the other, evidence suggests removing sponsorship conditions when settled can lead to an increase in salary by allowing greater labour market flexibility.

Individuals could attempt to change their employment to a different occupation or employer to achieve settlement more quickly. In practice, for those that are able, this has a fiscally positive impact.

Individuals could choose to leave the UK, or future inflows could be deterred from coming. In practice this could have either a fiscally positive or a fiscally negative impact depending on salary and number of dependants.

For those on a path to settlement of 3 years:

Additional future inflows with an exceptionally high salary could be incentivised to come to the UK. In practice this has a significantly fiscally positive impact.

Individuals on the 5-year pathway will not be impacted by the introduction of Earned Settlement and will remain on the current path to settlement of 5 years.

The magnitude of the impact of Earned Settlement will depend on the behaviour of the individuals in each of the respective pathways, set out in Annex A.

Recognising the importance of drawing out these impacts thoroughly, a full Impact Assessment will be prepared to accompany the implementation of Earned Settlement, drawing on the results of the Consultation and Targeted Research that have been published alongside this response.

Further detail on fiscal methodology

The dynamic fiscal model estimates the fiscal impact of migrants over the time they are expected to remain in the UK. It starts with information on characteristics such as age, earnings, employment and visa route, then projects how employment and earnings change over the lifecycle. These determine the government revenues associated with each individual, including Income Tax, National Insurance, indirect taxes and other revenues.

The model also estimates the public expenditure associated with that individual over time. This includes benefits where eligible, health care, education, public services, social care and State Pension expenditure. Combining these revenues and expenditures gives the net fiscal impact in each year. The lifetime estimate brings these annual impacts together, while allowing for the probability that an individual remains in the UK and survives to each future year. The model also applies growth and discounting assumptions.

Differences between the MAC and Home Office estimates

The Home Office’s analysis retains the broad structure of the MAC’s dynamic fiscal model, while updating some of the underlying evidence and assumptions to reflect more recent or refined data. This includes revised Home Office and HMRC data on migrant employment and earnings and, use of DWP RAPID data to better reflect migrants’ benefit receipts. Evidence on the likelihood of Health and Care Workers remaining in the UK has also been updated, resulting in a central settlement assumption of around 85% remaining, compared with around 67% previously. The updates affect the earnings, tax, benefit and population profiles captured over time and, consequently, the resulting lifetime fiscal estimates.

Lifetime fiscal impact: illustrative example for Skilled Workers

The three examples below illustrate how the different elements of the model combine to produce a lifetime net fiscal impact. During the main working years, earnings are associated with Income Tax and National Insurance contributions, as well as indirect taxes and other government revenues. These revenues are generally greater than the public expenditure attributed to the individual during this part of the lifecycle, so cumulative net fiscal impact rises over time.

As individuals become older, the balance gradually changes. Employment and earnings fall, reducing tax revenues, while expenditure on areas such as health care, social care and State Pension increases. The annual fiscal contribution becomes smaller and can turn negative later in life, causing cumulative net fiscal impact to flatten or decline.

Across the three examples, higher earnings are associated with stronger positive fiscal contributions over the working life, because they result in higher direct and indirect tax revenues. While all individuals face increasing public expenditure later in life, the larger working life contributions of higher earners mean that they retain a substantially higher positive lifetime net fiscal impact overall.

Elections change who holds power. Racial justice depends on how that power is used—and whether communities can hold officials accountable. This week brought breakthroughs in Black, Native, Latino, and Muslim representation, alongside decisions affecting voting access, immigration enforcement, and civil rights.

Communities must now press elected officials to enforce civil rights, fund essential services, and end discriminatory practices. Historic victories deserve recognition. They also require scrutiny: representation does not relieve any official of responsibility for challenging discrimination.

The immediate action deadline is November 13, when comments are due on the federal rule shortening refugees’ time to respond to proposed termination of their status.

1. Census: Disability Advocates Challenge Proposed Changes

Disability-rights organizations submitted comments November 2 opposing proposed Census changes and calling for a disability-impact assessment and direct consultation.

The coalition requested a further extension. The published deadline remained November 2.

Why it matters:

Black, Indigenous, and other people of color with disabilities need to be counted accurately. Government cannot meet their needs while making their communities harder to measure. Census decisions must account for the combined effects of racial discrimination, disability barriers, and inadequate public services.

2. Asian American and Pacific Islander Voters: Affordability, Immigration, and Rising Hate

Asian Americans Advancing Justice–AAJC and APIAVote presented November 5 findings examining AAPI voters’ priorities. The briefing addressed living costs, immigration, voting rights, and concerns about hate and discrimination.

Why it matters:

AAPI communities deserve political attention that extends beyond election-season outreach. Officials must address economic insecurity and discrimination together. They must also recognize differences among communities rather than treating Asian American and Pacific Islander voters as a single, uniform constituency.

Source

Asian Americans Advancing Justice–AAJC, “2026 Midterm Election Voter Poll Shows What Moved AAPI Voters in 2026: Cost of Living, Immigration, and Voting Rights; Highlights AAPI Voters’ Concerns about Rising Hate and Discrimination,” November 5, 2026.

3. Black Families: Advocates Demand Healthcare Relief

Word In Black reported that family advocates are pressing incoming congressional leaders to address health coverage losses, food-assistance cuts, and threats to maternal healthcare. Mothering Justice called attention to the consequences for mothers and caregivers of color.

Why it matters:

Black families need accessible healthcare, adequate food assistance, and maternal care that addresses racial disparities. Judge officials by whether Black families can obtain care and afford necessities—not by promises of support.

Source

Jennifer Porter Gore, “Angry Voters Put Health Care on the Agenda. Now Comes the Repair Work,” Word In Black, November 6, 2026.

4. Black and Latino Communities (North Carolina): Voters Oust Sheriff Accused of Racial Profiling

Alamance County voters elected Shannon Long, a Black pastor and former school resource officer, over longtime Sheriff Terry Johnson. Long campaigned against racial profiling. Johnson had faced longstanding allegations concerning the treatment of Latino residents.

Why it matters:

Long’s victory creates an opportunity to confront racial profiling and rebuild trust with Black and Latino residents. The sheriff’s office should establish accessible complaint procedures, publish information about stops and enforcement, and provide independent review of alleged misconduct.

Source

Jacob Biba, “A Pro-ICE Sheriff, Once Investigated for Racist Slurs, Is Ousted in North Carolina,” Bolts, November 5, 2026.

5. Black Political Representation: Historic Gubernatorial Victories

Election reporting identified victories for Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia, Byron Donalds in Florida, David Crowley in Wisconsin, Aaron Ford in Nevada, and Wes Moore’s reelection in Maryland.

Bottoms’ victory marks the first election of a Black woman as governor of a U.S. state. The results expand Black representation across party lines.

Why it matters:

Black representation matters. Governors should use their authority to confront discrimination in education, housing, healthcare, and the criminal legal system. Black communities should demand specific commitments and track whether budgets, appointments, and enforcement decisions fulfill them.

Source

Beatrice Peterson, “Black Candidates from Both Parties Made History in Midterm Elections,” ABC News, November 4, 2026.

6. Civil Rights Ballot Measures: Equal Protection, Immigration, and Indigenous and Two-Spirit Communities

Vermont voters approved an equal-protection amendment covering race and other protected characteristics. Colorado voters rejected a proposal requiring certain cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

Underscore Native News and ICT also examined measures affecting Native communities, including restrictions on transgender people and New Mexico’s approval of legislative salaries.

Why it matters:

Ballot measures can expand rights while other measures restrict them. Native transgender and Two-Spirit people must be included in assessments of racial justice. Paying legislators also raises a representation question: who can afford to serve, and whose experiences government excludes when service requires financial sacrifice?

Sources

7. Direct Democracy: Voters Protect Citizen-Led Ballot Initiatives

Voters in Missouri and Montana approved constitutional protections for citizen-led ballot initiatives. Voters in California, Idaho, North Dakota, South Dakota, and Utah rejected proposals restricting aspects of the initiative process, according to Bolts.

Why it matters:

Communities need ways to pursue change when elected lawmakers refuse to act. Protecting ballot initiatives preserves one route for organizing around healthcare, criminal justice, and other public needs. That route must remain accessible to communities with fewer financial and political resources.

Source

Pascal Sabino, “In Seven States, Voters Side with Direct Democracy,” Bolts, November 5, 2026.

8. Educational Equity: Civil Rights Groups Challenge IRS Proposal Affecting Private Schools

A coalition including the ACLU, Legal Defense Fund, and Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law opposed an IRS proposal November 3. The groups argue that it would permit politically driven decisions about schools’ tax exemptions and threaten lawful programs supporting educational equity.

Why it matters:

Schools should not be pressured to abandon lawful efforts to remove barriers facing Black students and other students of color. Federal enforcement must follow civil rights law and clear standards, rather than political hostility toward equity programs.

Source

9. Election Administration: Voters Change Who Oversees Voting

Election results changed control of secretary-of-state offices in Georgia, Indiana, and Ohio, according to Bolts. In Georgia, Penny Brown Reynolds won the office responsible for overseeing the state’s elections.

Why it matters:

Election administrators should make registration accessible, maintain accurate voter rolls, and ensure that eligible voters can cast counted ballots. Communities should track polling-place access, registration problems, ballot rejections, and how officials resolve complaints.

10. Fair Housing: Funding Disruptions Weaken Enforcement

A November 1 National Housing Conference summary highlighted findings from the National Fair Housing Alliance’s annual report. Funding disruptions reduced some organizations’ ability to investigate discrimination and assist households. Missing federal data also limited comparisons of complaint totals.

Fewer recorded complaints should not be presented as proof that discrimination declined.

Why it matters:

Fair housing rights mean little when organizations investigating discrimination lack resources to act. Reduced enforcement leaves Black and Latino households, people with disabilities, and others confronting discrimination with fewer places to turn.

11. Immigrant Communities (Maryland): Voters Defeat Sheriff Known for ICE Cooperation

Frederick County voters elected Karl Bickel over longtime Sheriff Chuck Jenkins. Bolts reported that Bickel pledged to end cooperation with ICE and monitor the agency’s activities. Immigrant residents described fear associated with Jenkins’s enforcement practices.

Why it matters:

Bickel’s commitments should become written limits on cooperation with ICE, clear instructions for deputies, and public reporting on enforcement practices. Immigrant families need policies they can rely on when seeking help, reporting crimes, and participating in community life.

12. Latina Political Representation (Texas): Gina Hinojosa Elected Governor

Gina Hinojosa defeated Greg Abbott to become Texas’ first Latina governor-elect. Her campaign emphasized public education, living costs, and concerns about data centers, according to election reporting.

Why it matters:

Hinojosa’s victory opens a door long closed to Latinas in Texas government. Texans should demand stronger public schools, enforcement of civil rights, and action on the economic and environmental burdens facing underserved communities.

13. Latino Voters: Economic Pressure and Immigration Enforcement Drive Priorities

UnidosUS and the Latino Community Foundation released survey findings November 4 identifying economic pressure and opposition to immigration overreach as important concerns among Latino voters. The survey asked voters about their experiences and priorities, rather than treating party preference as a complete explanation.

Why it matters:

Latino communities should not be reduced to a campaign talking point. Their demands concern wages, living costs, family security, and equal treatment. Officials must address those priorities and remain accountable after the votes are counted.

Source

14. Muslim Civil Rights (Florida): Organizations Suspend Operations and Plan Appeal

CAIR and CAIR-Florida announced an appeal after a federal court declined to block Florida’s designation of the organizations as “terrorist.” Their November 5 statement reported that advocacy operations in Florida were being suspended.

The court provided limited protection for legal representation of the groups. It did not resolve the entire case or make factual findings establishing Florida’s allegations.

Why it matters:

When the state shuts down a civil rights organization, the harm reaches people who depend on it to challenge discrimination. Muslim communities must retain meaningful access to legal assistance and the freedom to organize.

Source

American Civil Liberties Union, “CAIR and CAIR-Florida Will Appeal Federal Court Decision Denying Relief from Florida’s Unconstitutional ‘Terrorist’ Designation Regime,” November 5, 2026.

15. Muslim Political Representation (Michigan): Abdul El-Sayed Elected to U.S. Senate

Abdul El-Sayed’s election marks the first time an American Muslim has been elected to the U.S. Senate. CAIR and its Michigan chapter celebrated his victory while condemning anti-Muslim rhetoric directed at him during the campaign.

Why it matters:

Muslim Americans have the same right to seek and hold public office as everyone else. This victory breaks a barrier. The responsibility now is to defend that equal belonging and hold the incoming senator accountable for protecting civil rights for all constituents.

Source

Council on American-Islamic Relations, “CAIR, CAIR-MI Congratulate Sen-Elect Abdul El-Sayed on Defeating the ‘Politics of Hate’ to Become First Muslim Senator,” November 4, 2026.

16. Native (Alaska): Voting Access, Ballot Counting, and the Senate Contest

The Native American Rights Fund sent legal volunteers to Alaska communities to help protect Native voting access and document barriers.

Subsequent development, November 10: Alaska Public Media reported that Mary Peltola led Dan Sullivan while counting continued. The race remained unresolved. Alaska’s published election schedule identifies November 18 for required ranked-choice tabulation and November 25 as the target certification date.

Why it matters:

Alaska Native voters should not have to overcome inadequate election services to exercise a right other voters take for granted. Their ballots must receive a complete, lawful count. An unfinished count is not evidence of misconduct.

name: Litigation
title: Stephen Miller-founded law firm stacks up legal wins | CNN Politics
authors: Rob Kuznia, Majlie de Puy Kamp
description:

text:
When he left the White House after the 2020 election, immigration firebrand Stephen Miller founded an upstart legal group to take his war against the left to the courts. His outsider firm, America First Legal, sued aggressively to overturn liberal initiatives in his quest to create MAGA’s answer to the ACLU.

With Miller now back in the White House, first as a top adviser to President Trump and now as his chief of staff, AFL isn’t an outsider any longer.

A CNN investigation has found an extraordinary overlap between leadership and policy from Trump’s administration and the group founded by Miller – a quiet collaboration that has made an outsized mark on American institutions and federal policies.

In the process, AFL has pushed the ethical boundaries of the ties between an advocacy group and the White House.

As AFL’s top leaders have taken senior government jobs under Trump or worked as the president’s personal attorney, the administration has acted as a friendly partner in more than a dozen AFL lawsuits – roughly 40% of AFL’s caseload in Trump’s second term. The administration has filed supportive documents in cases brought by AFL, settled AFL cases against federal agencies, and granted requests for probes into private groups at AFL’s request.

In one extraordinary case, an AFL attorney who filed a lawsuit against the State Department later joined the agency as its top attorney before it resolved the case favorably for AFL. In another, the Department of Justice reached a settlement with AFL and Texas’s attorney general on the very same day their complaint was filed in court.

The litigation coordination between AFL and the Trump administration has led to significant legal outcomes. These include the cancellation of aid to the Palestinian Authority, reversal of gender identity policies at school districts around the country, the stripping away of corporate DEI rules and the successful legal defense of sheriffs who helped Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

While many administrations have had friendly relationships with advocacy groups, the overlap between AFL and Trump’s White House far exceeds the norm, some legal and ethics experts said.

“The extent of the overlap between this organization and the federal government’s position seems significantly higher” than with other advocacy groups, said Leah Litman, a professor of law at the University of Michigan Law School.

In a statement to CNN, an AFL spokesperson said that shared politics explain the White House’s collaborative approach to many of its cases – “not because of who at AFL was involved.” The spokesperson added that it stands to reason that “an America First administration has similar priorities and policies to an organization called America First Legal.”

AFL did not respond to detailed questions for this story, but said that its employees followed all rules requiring staffers and former staffers to recuse from cases they previously worked on and to avoid lobbying agencies they’ve recently left. The spokesperson said “everyone involved understood their ethical and legal obligations and complied with them.”

CNN’s investigation found no evidence that those regulations regarding official recusals or lobbying were broken.

Trump has also ditched an ethics pledge nearly every president enforced for the past 30 years, which bans banning appointees from conflicts of interest. And he rescinded a Biden executive order that could have further restricted the actions of AFL’s leaders.

Miller did not respond to requests for comment. A White House spokeswoman said Miller is no longer affiliated with AFL.

“The real story is the multibillion-dollar network of leftist NGOs, like the ACLU, that have waged unrelenting lawfare against the Trump Administration,” said Lauren Bis. “It’s not newsworthy that ‘America First Legal’ is providing pro bono support to America First causes and clients.”

A thorn in Biden’s side

Weeks after President Joe Biden took office, Miller, who is not a lawyer, launched AFL, calling it “the long-awaited answer to the ACLU” – a MAGA advocacy group that explicitly aimed to use the courts to advance Trump’s priorities while he was out of office.

Miller co-founded the group with Gene Hamilton, another hardliner who had helped craft the first Trump administration’s family separation policy. The group started with little money or staff, but a board of well-known Trump acolytes.

AFL started slowly, raising $6.3 million in donations in its first year, and filing about a dozen cases. But it soon notched impressive wins against Biden’s White House, including halting a policy that put White restaurant owners at the back of the line for pandemic relief and killing a loan forgiveness program that excluded White farmers.

AFL built on that early success by taking on school districts, state governments, corporations and universities on culture war issues like gender identity and DEI policies.

Many of those challenges failed. AFL lost a slew of cases in 2022, including many over transgender policies in schools.

But AFL’s fundraising soared, driven by Miller’s high-profile advocacy. In 2024, it pulled in $32 million, according to the latest publicly available tax records. That catapulted the firm past the annual revenues for most other rightwing legal advocacy groups.

The group continued to be a thorn in the Biden administration’s side through the end of his term – suing over the federal vaccine mandate, Hunter Biden’s recovered laptop, and the expansion of Title IX protections to include “gender identity.”

When Trump won a second term, though, both Miller and the group he co-founded quickly shifted from nettlesome DC outsiders to ultimate insiders.

The revolving door

On Inauguration Day last year, Miller left AFL to become Trump’s deputy chief of staff, and the most influential staffer in organizing Trump’s mass deportation plans. Hamilton, then AFL’s executive director, followed suit, taking a job as deputy White House counsel.

This kicked off a striking period of overlap between the small firm’s leadership and the White House. At the same time, Trump skipped an ethics pledge signed by every president since George W. Bush that generally required federal employees to promise to avoid conflicts of interest and to refrain from post-government employment connected to their work. He also rescinded former President Biden’s executive order strengthening bans on government employees working on matters related to previous or future private-sector work.

Other top AFL leaders soon followed Miller, including Hamilton’s No. 2 at AFL, Reed Rubinstein, who became the top lawyer in the State Department. AFL vice president Daniel Epstein stayed at AFL – but also signed on as a personal attorney to Trump. A number of lower-ranking AFL staffers joined the administration, including at least two attorneys who took DOJ jobs.

In one case, an AFL leader took a job in the Trump administration while a lawsuit he’d filed was still ongoing against the very agency he was joining as its top attorney.

When Rubinstein jumped to the State Department, the agency was still battling a case he had filed more than two years earlier at AFL, seeking to block humanitarian funding that could benefit the Palestinian Authority. Less than a year later, the State Department gave in. The agency agreed to abide by a 2018 law signed by Trump to cut financial aid to the West Bank and Gaza that benefited the Palestinian Authority until it stopped sending payments to families of Palestinians killed, injured or imprisoned by Israeli authorities, including those who carried out acts of terror.

A State Department spokesman told CNN that Rubinstein formally recused himself from the case.

AFL and the White House appeared to cooperate on at least four cases while Hamilton worked as a top attorney under Trump, CNN found.

Hamilton’s specific duties as deputy White House counsel aren’t public. But in the private sector, he worked deeply on DOJ-related projects, including authoring the DOJ chapter for Project 2025, the conservative blueprint for a second Trump term published by the Heritage Foundation.

During Hamilton’s White House tenure, the administration launched probes into five school districts that AFL had lodged complaints about, supported sheriffs defended by AFL for working with ICE, and opened a federal investigation into a California law about gender identity school policies as AFL sued over the same policy.

As DOJ also cracked down on companies with DEI policies getting federal funds, the agency’s first target was IBM – a company Hamilton’s firm had twice sued during the Biden administration for anti-White discrimination.

Hamilton left his White House position after five months, returning to AFL as its president in June 2025. Shortly after his return, AFL brought a third suit challenging DEI policies at IBM; Hamilton was quoted in a Fox News story about the case. Less than a year later, the DOJ announced the penalty against IBM: $17 million for its “illegal DEI practices.”

Federal law barred Hamilton from seeking to influence the White House as AFL’s leader before a cooling-off period expired this summer, or to ever work on any matters at AFL that he directly worked on in the administration.

AFL said Hamilton followed all those rules in his official role at the White House – and since returning to the legal group.

But both AFL and Hamilton failed to address one key detail related to his White House job, CNN found.

Despite indicating in ethics documents that he ended his AFL job in January 2025, AFL’s DC corporate filings effectively continued to identify Hamilton holding a formal role. Its February 2024 filing listed Hamilton as the only “Authorized Person” and a January 2026 filing listed him as the nonprofit’s sole disclosed “beneficial owner.”

The filings are required every two years, but are supposed to be updated if there are changes in leadership, according to a spokesperson for the DC Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection. The spokesperson confirmed no other records were filed by AFL.

An AFL spokesperson said in a statement to CNN that the group believed it only had to file paperwork with DC every two years and that the titles listed on those forms did not correspond to his actual role with the group.

“Hamilton does not, nor did he, own America First Legal,” the spokesperson said. “Moreover, he had no formal agreement with America First Legal to return after his government service ended.”

Rubinstein, too, has now returned to AFL – as its senior vice president – after his yearlong stint in the Trump administration.

The firm has yet to file tax records showing which executives received compensation in 2025. In 2024, Hamilton earned more than $600,000 from AFL, according to tax records. Miller made more than $500,000 from AFL that same year.

Even one AFL leader who didn’t join the administration has helped Trump with some of his most contentious legal efforts. Epstein, in his role as Trump’s personal attorney, signed a settlement with the IRS that would have created a nearly $1.8 billion fund to compensate those Trump said were unfairly targeted by the government.

Critics pounced on the fund as a way for Trump to pay off his allies, and it was scuttled under Republican pressure. Epstein, meanwhile, was sanctioned by a federal judge for his role in the settlement, which the judge found was collusive and “had no viable basis in law or fact.”

He’s barred now for a year from appearing in federal court in the Southern District of Florida, where he lives and serves as interim dean of the Florida International University College of Law. A federal appeals court recently denied his request to pause the sanction.

Because Epstein works for Trump personally, and not in the Trump White House, he is not subject to the same ethics rules by which Hamilton, Rubinstein and Miller are bound.

Epstein, who left AFL in August according to his LinkedIn account, did not respond to requests to comment for this story.

Close legal partners

Soon after Trump’s second term began, AFL, which employs about 10 staff attorneys compared to the ACLU’s 500, began punching far above its weight – with help from the administration.

On February 3, 2025, AFL sent a complaint to the Department of Education about five Virginia school districts that allowed students to use bathrooms and locker rooms consistent with their gender identity. Just 11 days later, the department opened a probe – an unusually swift response, experts said. It concluded that all five districts had indeed violated the federal civil rights law.

When AFL sued one of those districts over similar policies, the DOJ attempted to file a motion of support, though it was blocked by a judge. The case was settled in February.

More significant victories soon followed – often with an assist from the White House.

In the first half of 2025, four large organizations targeted by AFL for DEI policies – IBM, CBS Broadcasting, Texas Tech and Ohio Northern University – capitulated after prolonged legal fights as they faced new federal pressure to drop the rules.

In Texas in June, the AFL teamed up with Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton to challenge a Biden-era rule that allowed immigration judges to close deportation cases for undocumented immigrants who were eligible to apply for legal status – a suit the DOJ had invited via an internal memo, obtained by CNN, that said it would not defend the rule in court.

The DOJ then agreed to a consent judgment on the same day the suit was filed. AFL swiftly celebrated the win, saying it killed an illegal “backdoor amnesty program.”

Legal observers said the same-day suit was not a typical use of the courts.

“That’s not really litigation,” said Ben Wizner, a deputy legal director at the ACLU. “There’s no case or controversy.”

Attorneys representing the cities of Baltimore, Columbus, Ohio, and New Haven, Connecticut, also objected, calling it collusive and saying it would trigger a rise in deportations of people who pay city taxes. “Texas did not even have to serve its lawsuit,” the attorneys said in their emergency motion to intervene. “DOJ was ready and waiting.”

The DOJ’s press office did not respond to CNN’s questions about the case.

AFL has had several other notable wins with aid from a Supreme Court stocked with Trump’s picks.

After a 6-3 conservative majority Supreme Court ruling this spring revived challenges against laws forbidding schools from disclosing students’ sexual orientation or gender identities to parents, AFL won appeals in two cases against Democratic states.

And this summer, the Supreme Court agreed to hear a case that AFL had lost twice in the lower courts seeking to challenge a Washington law that could allow minors to receive gender identity care without their parents’ consent.

How AFL is different

The Trump administration didn’t invent the concept of working with sympathetic legal advocacy groups to achieve its own policy goals, experts told CNN.

Both the Obama and Biden White Houses settled with environmental groups and supported cases brought by left-leaning groups. However, both also aggressively fought at-times friendly groups like the ACLU or Sierra Club when they challenged administration policies.

Other right-leaning legal advocacy groups have actually taken on Trump. Last year, New Civil Liberties Alliance and the Liberty Justice Center separately sued the administration over tariffs, with the Supreme Court ruling in their favor.

AFL rarely if ever genuinely breaks ranks with the Trump administration.

But it is the Trump administration’s softening of ethics rules – and the AFL’s close ties to the administration – that most concerns experts and watchdog groups.

Cynthia Brown, a senior ethics counsel at the Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, said all Americans should be concerned if the new norm is for outside groups and presidential administrations to operate as partners in lock step using the full weight of government against organizations “on their bad side.”

“It’s majority rule with rights for the minority,” she said, referring to a core tenet of American democracy. “It’s important to make sure that we’re treating all citizens fairly and keeping the justice system’s integrity, so that we can all trust that it’s working in our interest regardless of whether the leadership is who we voted for.”

text:
The San Francisco Chronicle has obtained internal ICE investigations into the deaths of dozens of people in its custody during the first year of President Donald Trump’s second term, finding that 23 of the 29 individuals died after a lack of proper medical care.

Guards, medical providers, and staff at Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facilities failed to provide emergency care, failed to send individuals to the emergency room, or ignored other critical warning signs, the report indicates. According to ICE’s own investigations, deficient medical care directly contributed to 20 of 23 of the deaths. The six other individuals who died in 2025 had received care within sufficient limits, the agency claims.

The Chronicle acquired the reports through a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request. The findings contradict the Department of Homeland Security (DHS)’s claim that its immigration jails provide “timely and appropriate medical care” and that “the medical care in ICE detention is the best care” that many immigrants “have received in their entire lives.”

The Chronicle previously reported on 48 deaths in ICE custody since Trump’s second term began, finding that delayed medical care and failure to provide critical care contributed to 17 of these deaths and that there was not enough information on at least 15 cases. This report, from April, came before the outlet obtained ICE’s own investigations into the 2025 deaths, which reported an even larger number directly caused by medical neglect.

At least 62 people have died in ICE custody since the start of Trump’s second term, more than double the amount of deaths from the first Trump administration and the highest rate in over a decade.

ICE has not investigated all of the deaths caused by the agency and its immigration jails. For example, Prisciliano Trejo Ricano died shortly after ICE released him from custody while he was in a coma; his name has not been counted among those who died in custody after the agency changed its policy in June to no longer report and investigate deaths of individuals who died within 30 days of release. Similarly, at least two disabled people died in 2026 shortly after ICE released them into freezing weather, and were not counted among ICE’s official death count.

In the second half of October alone, three people died in ICE detention: Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias, a 56-year-old permanent resident from Mexico who died on October 17 at the Rio Grande Processing Center in Laredo, Texas, whose family reported that he was denied medication and care; Luis Sandoval, a 48-year-old Salvadoran who died on October 23 in ICE detention in Georgia and, according to DHS, died by suicide; and Roberto Jimenez Gutierrez, a 43-year-old Guatemalan who was found unresponsive on October 24.

In some cases, prison staff mocked individuals who called for help and who later died after their neglect. In others — like the deaths at Camp East Montana in Texas, which have been referred to as suicides — conditions included medical neglect, solitary confinement, and physical and sexual violence.

text:
Video obtained by NBC Connecticut shows U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents arresting a man in downtown New Haven on Tuesday.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) identified the man as 18-year-old Jaime Enrique Diaz-Perez, of Guatemala, and said he was taken into custody during a targeted enforcement operation by ICE.

DHS said that Diaz-Perez "refused lawful commands to exit his vehicle and kicked ICE officers. He was placed under arrest without further incident. A passenger in Diaz-Perez’s vehicle attempted to physically interfere with the arrest."

Watch the video, provided by the New Haven Police Department, below:

Diaz-Perez was previously arrested by New Haven police on Aug. 30 and was charged with assault in the first degree, felony evading, and interfering with an officer, New Haven police said.

According to New Haven police, officers responded to East Shore Park on Woodward Avenue around 3:39 a.m. for a report of a pedestrian who had been struck by a vehicle and had severe injuries.

Police said a group of people had gathered at the park after leaving downtown, and several vehicles were performing donuts and other stunts in the parking lot.

During the stunts, police said Diaz-Perez struck a pedestrian who was filming the stunts and fled the scene.

The pedestrian, identified as a 30-year-old New Haven man, suffered life-threatening injuries, according to police. Diaz-Perez's bond was set at $350,000.

New Haven Mayor Justin Elicker released the following statement on the arrest:

"Mr. Diaz-Perez is accused of committing very serious crimes that nearly cost someone their life and he must be held accountable for his actions. At the same time, when someone is accused of a crime, they are entitled to due process and their day in court. The Trump Administration and ICE continue to show complete disregard for our judicial process, and the reports of ICE’s aggressive tactics yesterday are deeply concerning. As we have said time and time again, no one wants violent criminals in our community — and we hold people accountable regardless of their documentation status. However, it’s also important that all parties follow the law — and that includes ICE officers and our federal government.”

DHS also said Diaz-Perez had previously been apprehended by Border Patrol in January 2022 after entering the United States near Hidalgo, Texas.

"Diaz-Perez will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings," a DHS spokesperson said.

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials deliberately kept certain detainees out of a public database to make them harder to find.

The New York Timesreports that tens of thousands of people with final deportation orders have been hidden from the database since September, confirming earlier media reports. This policy change has made it almost impossible for lawyers and family members to find their loved ones’ locations, and ICE’s contractors were given a script to use on callers informing them that the detainees’ locations were no longer available.

ICE’s detention system encompasses over 300 facilities and was already chaotic before the change. Detained immigrants are quickly sent from one facility to another, and if their lawyers don’t know where they are, legal help is severely hindered. It’s a boon to the Trump administration’s efforts to deport large numbers of immigrants quickly without the obstacles of habeas petitions and other forms of due process.

If lawyers know where their clients are being held, they can fight their deportation orders and try to secure their release. But those options are almost wiped out after a person is deported, and if they’re missing from ICE’s system, they are almost doomed. Detainees could also be prevented from making phone calls or buying essential personal items like toiletries because someone on the outside can’t deposit money into their commissary account without knowing which facility they’re in.

One immigrant that the Times highlights is University of San Francisco nurse and professor Ann Lawani, who was detained in her pajamas from her home in Lodi, California, on September 16. Even after calling her family from a holding facility that day, her attorney and siblings still couldn’t figure out where she was.

“It was the worst time of my life, knowing she had been siphoned into an abyss and there was nothing I could do about it,” her brother, U.S. citizen Sam Lawani, told the Times.

When her lawyer, Natalia Vieira Santanna, tried to file a habeas petition, she did so in California, Lawani’s last known location. But DHS tried to get her petition transferred to Louisiana, where they had moved her, which would have restarted Lawani’s case and required a new lawyer. Vieira opposed that effort, pointing out that Lawani’s location was kept secret, and the judge in the case agreed, finding that “no diligent attorney could have known” where Lawani was.

The judge also blocked the federal government from deporting Lawani while her habeas petition was in progress, and ordered officials to explain why she shouldn’t be released. While she is in the country right now, Lawani’s location still isn’t in the public database, and other detainees have not been fortunate enough to have her resources and support.

The Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who fatally shot a Colombian man in Maine earlier this year had a history of making vehemently racist remarks.

Four years before he joined ICE, David Brouillette ranted against his sister over her relationship with a 37-year-old Colombian Ph.D. student, with whom she had two children.

“He can takes his non citizen ass back to his country and enjoy his third world luxuries,” Brouillette wrote in a 2021 email thread, which was shared with The New York Times by his sister, Elizabeth Emen. The emails were sent to Emen and other family members, and were confirmed by a friend whom Emen discussed the messages with and a family representative.

“David had no basis for saying that my partner was undocumented,” Emen, a licensed therapist in Maryland, told the Times. “It was about how he saw him based on his race.”

Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, age 25, who was shot and killed by Brouillette during a traffic stop in July, was in the United States legally, like Emen’s partner. ICE quietly admitted that it had a warrant for a different person and that Guerrero was never a target.

In the emails, Brouillette claimed that his sister’s boyfriend’s “bloodline knows nothing about what it takes to earn and then CHERISH the freedom America offers.”

“He does not emulate what it means to be an American” but “rather he emulates what it’s like to be entitled and think he has a seat” at a table “that has no room for his (or your ignorance),” Brouillette wrote.

Brouillette’s family said that he never attempted to hide his sentiments about immigrants. His relatives previously revealed that he had a history of violent and abusive behavior, including attacks on the women and girls in his life. But after President Donald Trump’s sweeping mandate to increase the number of deportations, ICE relaxed its vetting process in order to enlist thousands of new so-called “homeland defenders,” which allowed many unqualified candidates—even some with criminal records—to join the federal agency’s ranks.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has been going to college football games on the taxpayer’s dime.

The Washington Post reports that Rubio almost never misses a University of Florida Gators football game, as his son Anthony is a walk-on running back for the team. Since taking office in 2025, Rubio has flown to at least 10 football games on government planes, including a military C-37 jet earlier this month, landing at Gainesville Regional Airport in the Sunshine State before being met by security officers in unmarked SUVs. Anthony Rubio, a senior, has only played in four games in four years.

The elder Rubio, a UF alumnus, traveled to Gainesville’s airport on government aircraft at least 23 times as a Cabinet official, 15 of which the State Department classified as solely personal. The flights have cost taxpayers more than $1.2 million, according to a Post review of the Defense Department’s published costs. Former department officials told the newspaper that Rubio takes personal trips much more often than previous secretaries of state.

Rubio is barred from taking commercial flights in his position for security reasons, just like the defense secretary, attorney general, and heads of the CIA and FBI. He is required to reimburse the government the cost of an economy-class plane ticket for every personal trip he takes. Those reimbursements are rarely made public and only cover a small part of the true cost of a government flight, according to the Post.

When contacted by the newspaper, neither Rubio nor the State Department disclosed how much he has paid back to the government. In a statement, Rubio said, “I have and will continue to try and make it to as many events that are important to me personally and to my family as possible.”

Assistant Secretary of State Dylan Johnson told the Post that Rubio takes military planes to “ensure continuity of operations, continuity of government and access to secure communications at all times. And he will continue to do so.”

While Rubio’s government flight habits are less egregious than those of FBI Director Kash Patel, who tends to look for any exotic locale where he can party, they do raise questions about misusing taxpayer funds. As the country’s top diplomat, Rubio’s plane trips are supposed to mostly be to represent the U.S. and its interests overseas. According to the Post, he should be paying the government back anywhere from $18,000 to upward of $30,000 for his personal excursions to Florida alone.

“I’ve been a Democrat my whole life. I grew up in a far-left environment. I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir—all of our products are essentially progressive,” Karp said in an interview where he used the word “progressive” eight times to describe himself.

This is a pretty significant shift from just eight months ago, when the CEO appeared desperate to align his technology with GOP political strategy as a method to sap political capital away from the Trump administration’s enemies.

“This technology disrupts humanities-trained—largely Democratic—voters, and makes their economic power less, and increases the economic power of vocationally trained, working-class, often male, working-class voters,” Karp said in March, admitting that his technology was “dangerous societally” but would allow us to “be American” in the future.

Now Karp claims that his company is chiefly concerned with “economic justice” and that he believes that Trump’s immigration policies “went too far.” Of course, Palantir’s technologies were essential in implementing the Trump administration’s sweeping deportation agenda. The company even developed an app that provided ICE agents with a digital map populated by potential deportation targets.

The technocrat’s self-proclaimed “anti-woke” company reaped billions of dollars in federal contracts during the second Trump administration. The company just hired former Republican Senator Jon Tester as an adviser ahead of likely congressional investigations.

“My giving is equal Democrat, Republican,” Karp told Politico. “I can tell you, without going into things I’m not going to disclose, I’m very balanced, and everyone in the political arena knows it. And I’ll tell you what, I’m also not the village idiot.”

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer is losing support from even moderate members of the Democratic caucus.

Virginia Senator Mark Warner is not committing to supporting Schumer for majority leader next year, the Virginia Scope reports, telling the publication: “We got to reflect in leadership the real talents.” Warner’s new comments follow his praise for Schumer on Tuesday for raising an “enormous” amount of money for Democrats in the midterms and for recruiting many of the winners this election.

Warner’s stance follows Senator Bernie Sanders, who said in a press conference on Tuesday, “Nobody works harder than Chuck Schumer, but in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader.”

Other senators and senators-elect refusing to commit to Schumer include Elissa Slotkin, Abdul El-Sayed, Richard Blumenthal, Juliana Stratton, Peggy Flanagan, Adam Hamilton, Troy Jackson, Chris Pappas, Annie Andrews, and James Talarico.

The alternative candidate gaining steam is Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who is open to the idea and criticized Schumer and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee for siding “with the crypto industry” and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee in a press conference on Tuesday.

“I am listening to all the people from around the country that were calling for big change,” Van Hollen said, noting that two of the Democrats’ incoming senators, El-Sayed and Flanagan, didn’t receive support from Schumer and the DSCC. “I am in the process right now of calling my colleagues.”

Trump gives 'credit' to Scott Colom for coming to his Mississippi rally and mingling with the president's supporters

Trump weighed in on Sen.-elect Scott Colom's historic win in Mississippi's Senate race last week, saying he gives him credit for campaigning at the line for Trump's Oct. 26 rally in Corinth, Miss.

“I had a rally there, and we had lines that went 10 miles long, and he campaigned on that line telling everybody in the line what a good job he did. I give him a lot of credit for that,” Trump told sports commentator Stephen A. Smith in a White House interview for his podcast “Straight Shooter."

Video of Colom working the line went viral, and he went on to defeat incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, flipping a deep-red seat for Democrats.

GOP committee chairs give Jensen Huang, Nvidia a Friday deadline to commit to closed-door testimony

The GOP chairs of the House Select Committee on China, Foreign Affairs Committee and Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence sent Jensen Huang and a lawyer for Nvidia letters today demanding they agree by tomorrow evening to give closed-door testimony.

Reps. John Moolenaar of Michigan, Brian Mast of Florida and Rick Crawford of Arkansas asked Huang, who resigned as CEO of Nvidia earlier today over reports that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese agent, and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter to appear before Congress in early December.

"As reports continue to come to light regarding Jensen Huang, NVIDIA, and MegaSpeed, there are clear national security concerns that need to be addressed immediately,” Mast, Moolenaar and Crawford wrote. “We need to know the full extent to which our national security has been put at risk.'

They added: "This situation is a prime example of why Congress must immediately pass the AI OVERWATCH Act, Chip Security Act, MATCH Act, and Remote Access Security Act in the NDAA.”

Mast also asked Jeff Kessler, undersecretary for industry and security at the Department of Commerce, to appear before the Foreign Affairs Committee.

Mast told NBC News earlier today that Huang agreed to brief lawmakers, though the date and venue were still being negotiated. The letter to Huang this evening asks that he appear before the committee on Dec. 1 for a “closed-door, transcribed interview,” adding that a subpoena would be issued if Huang did not confirm the interview by tomorrow evening.

Similar letters were sent to Teter and Kessler, who were asked to appear on Dec. 2 and Dec. 3, respectively. Teter was also warned that a subpoena would be sent if he does not confirm the interview by tomorrow evening.

Howard Lutnick agrees to testify as bipartisan pressure grows over Nvidia scandal

Facing bipartisan pressure, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick agreed tonight to testify before Congress over national security concerns regarding the expanding Nvidia scandal.

The announcement comes after Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., chair of the Senate Banking Committee, sent letters today to Lutnick and Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s CEO earlier in the day after reports that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

“Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions,” Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., announced tonight he will run for Senate majority leader, becoming the first to challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for the position.

“In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies — but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen said in a statement.

Van Hollen’s move follows attempts by grassroots progressives — and some newly elected Democratic senators — to draft him for the position as some seek an alternative to Schumer.

“It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person — it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader,” he added.

Trump’s FDA pick faces Republican doubts as confirmation deadline nears

The Food and Drug Administration is set to finish its safety review of the abortion pill mifepristone in March, setting up one of the most politically charged decisions the agency has faced in years. And yet it may not have a permanent leader to oversee it.

Dr. Heidi Overton, Trump’s pick to run the agency, faces a vote next week before the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, but key Republicans whose support she needs remain uncommitted, with only weeks before Democrats take control of the Senate.

“I have not taken a position,” said Sen. Susan Collins of Maine in a brief interview on Capitol Hill on Thursday, adding that she needed “to get some answers on various things.” Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska declined to say how she’d vote. During her confirmation hearing in September, Murkowski asked Overton about political pressure surrounding access to mifepristone.

Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, the health committee’s chairman, also declined to comment. Asked about his decision, he said, “I’m a last-second sort of guy,” laughing as he moonwalked away from reporters.

54 protesters arrested outside Sen. Chuck Schumer's office, officials say

U.S. Capitol Police said this evening that 54 protesters were arrested outside of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer's personal office in the Hart Senate Office building.

Police said that the protesters were arrested for crowding, obstructing and incommoding outside of the New York senator's office.

The protesters, who were wearing “GREEN NEW DEAL” shirts, were chanting “Hey hey, ho ho, Chuck Schumer has got to go,” and holding a sign that read, “Schumer: Step up or step aside.”

Schumer, who is angling to take over as majority leader when the Democrats take charge of Congress next term, has faced opposition from some members of his party that say Americans want change.

While no competitor has launched an official bid for the role, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., has earned support from some colleagues, including Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., as him name as been floated.

As he heads to the Senate, James Talarico says Democrats 'have a mandate the size of Texas'

Sen.-elect James Talarico said this evening that after a remarkable sweep by Democrats in deep-red Texas, lawmakers now have responsibility to deliver those promises to voters.

“In Texas, we go big or we go home, and that’s exactly what we did last week," Talarico said at Majority Democrats' "What's Next" conference. "We won big. We ended the longest losing streak in American politics, and we did it by double digits."

Talarico added: "We went up against the richest man in the world, and we won," referencing Elon Musk, who made at least $168 million in campaign donations to keep Texas in Republican control this fall.

Talarico touted Democrats' victories "all the way down the ballot" in Texas, where the party won every statewide office on the ballot, flipped the state house and the state board of education and elected four new members of the Texas Supreme Court.

"It was a win the size of Texas, and now we have a mandate the size of Texas," he said.

Talarico added that Democrats must work with Trump, a notion he's repeated since his victory last week, in order to make progress for voters.

"If President Trump wants the same plaques and portraits and busts as L.B.J., we can help make that a reality," Talarico said. "We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history."

DOJ has no ‘investigations into words’ of Democrats, Todd Blanche says

Attorney General Todd Blanche said today there were no criminal investigations by the Justice Department into words spoken by senators or members of Congress, the same day that Trump once again called for six Democrats to be prosecuted over a social media video they posted last year.

“There’s no ongoing investigations, criminal investigations, into words that incoming senators or congressmen have said,” Blanche said at a news conference at the Justice Department.

Blanche’s comments came hours after Trump called for six sitting members of Congress to be charged over their speech in a social media video in which they told members of the intelligence and military communities not to obey unlawful orders. The Trump administration attempted to indict the the lawmakers earlier this year, but a federal grand jury in Washington unanimously rejected the charges.

“Will the Seditious Six ever be prosecuted? What they did was a great violation to our Country and its Constitution!” Trump posted on his social media website on Thursday morning.

Democrat Cindy Holscher defeats Republican Ty Masterson in Kansas governor’s race

Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher has narrowly won Kansas’ race for governor, NBC News projected today, extending the party’s hold on the office in the red state.

Holscher defeated Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson, who was backed by President Donald Trump, to succeed two-term Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly.

While Trump carried Kansas — a state where registered Republicans outnumber registered Democrats nearly 2 to 1 — by double digits in the latest three presidential elections, polling had shown a close race down the stretch due mostly to voter frustrations with Trump and his handling of the economy. Democrats also benefited from increased attention on the traditionally conservative state as its Senate race tightened.

Holscher’s victory came despite a nearly 3-to-1 Republican ad spending advantage in the general election, according to ad-tracking firm AdImpact.
