Montana senators say they'll fight Trump admin plan to sell public lands

After the Department of the Interior released a new strategic plan to sell public lands to states, localities and tribes, Sen. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., announced on X that his office was not consulted on the plan.

“I will not allow ONE ACRE of Montana land to be sold,” Sheehy wrote.

On his way to the Senate floor this afternoon, Montana’s senior Sen. Steve Daines, a Republican who plans to retire once his term ends early next year, told NBC News that he was not consulted by the Trump Administration either.

“Public lands belong in public hands,” said Daines.

“I don’t support it,” Daines said of the plan. “We need to understand what they’re thinking at the moment.”

Daines added that preventing the sale of public lands “is a battle we’ve been fighting for years out west, and I’m concerned.”

Annie Andrews poses with Sen. Darline Graham after unseating her in stunning victory

Sen.-elect Annie Andrews thanked Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C, for her service to South Carolina today, meeting with her in Washington after winning over the seat in a major upset to Republicans last week.

"Campaigns are tough but anyone willing to step up and fight for the people of South Carolina will always earn my respect and thanks," Andrews wrote in a post on X, which included a photo of the pair smiling beside each other.

Andrews thanked Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, for her "commitment to a smooth transition, advice on strong constituent services, and for you and your family’s service to our state and nation."

In her own post about the meeting, Graham that she is "committed to ensuring a smooth transition, and I wish her and her team the best."

The posts follow a similar show of bipartisanship earlier this week by GOP Sen. John Cornyn and Sen.-elect James Talarico, whose victory marks the first Democrat to take over the Texas seat in over three decades.

"Good meeting with Senator-elect @jamestalarico today as he prepares to serve Texans in the U.S. Senate next Congress," Cornyn wrote in a post on X on Monday alongside a photo of him and Talarico shaking hands.

Talarico wrote in his own post that Cornyn, whom he did not run against but whose seat he will take over, "has served our state honorably, and I’m grateful for his advice and guidance."

"Now is the time for us to come together — Democrats and Republicans — to deliver for Texas," he added.

Senators call on Howard Lutnick to answer Nvidia questions before Congress

Republican and Democratic senators today called for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify about what he knew about the Nvidia scandal and when — and to do so soon.

"Come here before Thanksgiving. Give us the facts," Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters, referring to Lutnick and concerns the Commerce Department did not quickly act upon intelligence reports showing the company's head was involved with a suspected Chinese agent.

The CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned this morning. The company Alice Huang, the alleged agent worked for, Megaspeed, is under U.S. criminal investigation for allegedly smuggling American-made AI chips into China in defiance of U.S. export controls.

Tillis suggested it would be smart for Lutnick to answer questions now, before Democrats take over Congress in January.

The secretary "should recognize right now he’s got a lot of Republicans that are pulling for him. I’m not one of them, but he does. So it would seem to me that he would do himself a favor by getting in a room with Republicans, whether it’s a committee hearing or not, and lay out the facts so that he’s got a group of people that are generally going to take at face value what he says," Tillis said.

“If there’s a storyline that’s credible that he can present that way, I’d get it done before a turkey is served,” he added.

Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., said in an interview with Fox News "I would like for Secretary Lutnick ASAP to come testify before the Senate Banking Committee because we have a lot of bipartisan questions and concerns about what's happened over the last year," including chips being exported that should not have.

The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., noted that Nvidia had donated $25 million to the president's ballroom project.

“Were export controls relaxed?” Blumenthal asked. “Did Donald Trump order the intelligence community to scuttle investigative efforts because of that $25 million donation to his ballroom?”

He said he thinks Lutnick should appear voluntarily, and if he doesn't, "He may need to be subpoenaed."

The White House has said the president “maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history.”

Tony Salisbury promoted to replace Stephen Miller as Trump's homeland security adviser

Tony Salisbury, who previously served as deputy homeland security adviser at the White House, has been promoted to homeland security adviser, according to two administration officials and two sources familiar with an internal announcement.

Stephen Miller previously served in the role until he was promoted to White House chief of staff last week. Miller also served as deputy chief of staff for policy, a position that is now filled by Caleb Orr.

In his previous role, Salisbury often ensured that the Department of Homeland Security was carrying out Miller’s ideas by communicating with officials and giving directives on how to carry out policies, including the targeting of foreign students, expanding immigration detention and the deportation of immigrants to Guantanamo Bay.

Trump redefined the role of homeland security adviser upon taking office in his second term, allowing the person in the role to convene the National Security Council as the Homeland Security Council on certain topic areas, including immigration.

Salisbury’s appointment signals that Trump and Miller want to stay the course on immigration policy following the midterms, the two sources familiar with the appointment said.

Hakeem Jeffries pledges to support proxy voting for expecting mothers, new parents

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said today that he is in favor of a rule change allowing proxy voting for expectant mothers and new parents as Democrats are poised to take control of Congress in January.

Jeffries, who is expected to take over as speaker of the House, did not offer specifics on what that new process would look like, but said he would "continue to support" Reps. Brittany Pettersen of Colorado and Sara Jacobs California as they pursue the policy change after a failed 2025 push.

"I'm thankful for the leadership of Brittany Pettersen and Sara Jacobs and other members of the House Democratic Caucus in this regard, to support proxy voting for expectant mothers and for new parents," Jeffries said at a press conference.

At the beginning of every Congress, House members must adopt a rules package that governs the lawmaking process. The change to proxy voting could be included in that package.

The potential for the new Democratic majority to push through such a rule change comes after the idea faced pushback from House Republicans last year, when they blocked a bipartisan effort that would have allowed lawmakers who had just given birth to vote remotely via a proxy for up to 12 weeks.

That resolution, brought by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla., was blocked by House Republicans in April 2025 after it faced opposition from Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., and the far-right House Freedom Caucus. At the time, Jeffries called the move "a very strange hill for them to die on.”

Pettersen, who worked on the 2025 resolution with Luna, said in a statement in September that she was "reupping her push to allow new parents to vote by proxy in the House" and would pursue it in January whether or not Democrats won the majority.

DOJ charged Somali man to try to get information on Ilhan Omar, lawyer says

Justice Department officials brought a felony case this spring against a man who briefly served as security for Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., in an attempt to get incriminating information about the congresswoman, an attorney for the man said.

Omar, a longtime political opponent of Trump who is under federal investigation in an immigration-related case, had her home searched and phone seized last month. Her attorneys have filed a sealed request for the return of the items taken, which the Trump administration has opposed. She has not been charged, and she has denied any wrongdoing.

Read the full story here.

How Amy Acton overcame big money and a vicious attack ad to make history in Ohio

Amy Acton’s running mate saw the ad first.

Shortly after 8:30 p.m. on a Monday night in mid-October, David Pepper was entertaining local Democrats over dinner at the Old Canal Smoke House in Chillicothe, Ohio, when he peeked at his phone. There in Pepper’s X feed was Acton’s long-estranged mother, in a 60-second video, calling her daughter a liar and urging Ohioans not to vote for her to be the state’s next governor.

To Acton and her advisers, the possibility that Republican Vivek Ramaswamy would enlist the help of Donna Arthur — a woman she had not seen or spoken to since her stepfather was charged with raping her as a young child — was revolting. But it was a scenario they had braced for, based on Arthur’s previous public criticism of Acton and on their low opinion of Ramaswamy’s principles. Fifteen days before Election Day, it had arrived.

Read the full story here.

Democratic super PAC launches effort opposing Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer

A Democratic super PAC is hitting the airwaves with a new effort to encourage Democrats to oppose naming Rep. Hakeem Jeffries and Sen. Chuck Schumer as their party's leaders in the next Congress.

The group, called "A Fight Worth Having," is launching tomorrow a TV ad effort along with print ads and ads on trucks targeting Democrats attending new member orientation. So far, the group has spent nearly $15,000 on an ad buy on national cable networks, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact.

“We’re trying to make sure that the freshman class knows that the American people are behind standing against Hakeem Jeffries as leader. We’re trying to make sure they know that Jeffries and Schumer are less popular than Donald Trump,” Democratic strategist Corbin Trent, who founded the super PAC, told NBC News. Trent said the effort could reach into "six figures."

Trent said the group is also helping fundraise for incoming lawmakers who said they would oppose Jeffries as the next House speaker, including Ohio Rep.-elect Don Leonard and California Rep.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres.

"We're doing everything that we can to show support for bravery and reward people that understand that this election was about a rejection of the status quo,” Trent said.

Trent acknowledged that denying Jeffries and Schumer their leadership spots is an uphill climb, giving it a "10% chance" of success. So far, no other Democrats have said they are also running for the top posts. But Trent noted that he was less confident that Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., could win her first race when he worked for her successful 2018 campaign.

"You don’t take on fights because you’re sure they’re going to win," Trent said. "That’s not a fight. You take on a fight because it’s something worth fighting for."

Republican Paul LePage flips Maine's 2nd District, NBC News projects

Former Gov. Paul LePage, a Republican, has defeated Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap in Maine's 2nd Congressional District, NBC News projects.

The result marks the only seat Republicans have flipped this year that wasn't a result of the party drawing more favorable lines through redistricting ahead of the midterms.

The race to replace retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden moved to ranked choice tabulation after no candidate received a majority of the vote on the first ballot. LePage won 51% to 49% after the ranked choice tally.

Even though Trump won the 2nd District by almost 10 points in the 2024 presidential election, it will be one of the bluest seats Republicans hold in the next Congress after the party experienced a wipeout in this month's elections.

Iran-linked plots come into focus in the U.K. as U.S. pulls jets from British bases

Since World War II, the rolling green hills of Britain’s countryside have been home to American air bases — hosting the fighter planes that have projected Washington’s power from Kosovo to Iraq.

The American military presence is rarely remarked on and often unnoticed by British residents, but a flurry of incidents this week has brought this relationship into sharp focus.

Read the full story here.

Pete Hegseth awards medal to soldier who reprimanded him at Arlington National Cemetery

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth today awarded a commendation to the Army sentinel who reprimanded him and his guests for their behavior at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Veterans Day.

“We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist,” Hegseth wrote in a post on X with a picture of him awarding Army Specialist Thomas Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for his action while guarding the site.

Read the full story here.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang agrees to appear before lawmakers

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., told NBC News that outgoing Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang agreed last night to appear before lawmakers.

"As of right now, we don’t have to subpoena because he came back last night and agreed to come in," Mast said.

The congressman said he expects to receive a briefing from Huang “certainly before we depart for Thanksgiving.” He did not have an exact day yet.

Mast, Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford sent a letter to Huang last week requesting that he brief lawmakers on his interactions with Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy. Mast did not share further about the details of the outgoing CEO's response.

Separately, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said that Huang was right to resign from Nvidia.

“It was the right thing to do,” Jeffries said during a press conference. “Now we have to get to the bottom of whether America’s national security has been compromised.”

Jeffries also called for a classified briefing on the situation for members of Congress.

“The American people deserve answers, and we’re going to work to make sure that happens,” he said.

Huang resigned from the tech giant after reportedly having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The New York Times also reported yesterday that Huang engaged in a relationship with an Nvidia executive.

Democrats ask top Trump fundraiser to retain records on White House ballroom and other projects

Three incoming Democratic Committee chairs have sent a letter to Meredith O’Rourke, a National Park Foundation board member and top fundraiser for Trump, asking her to retain relevant documents, communications, and materials related to fundraising for the White House ballroom and other projects.

“We write to request information concerning your role in soliciting and coordinating over $800 million in large corporate contributions to President Trump’s White House Golden Ballroom project, presidential library, Freedom 250 celebrations, Garden of Heroes, MAGA Super PAC, and other vanity projects,” the letter said.

The letter, signed by Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., asked O’Rourke a series of questions about her formal relationship with the president, how she goes about raising money for the various projects, and whether she ever mentioned policy matters to companies when soliciting donations from them.

"We are considering the efficacy of current federal ethics and anti-corruptions laws, and whether they adequately apply to executive branch employees,” the lawmakers wrote.

"To the extent these fundraising efforts implicate federal bribery law, responsible officials could be subject to criminal penalties as well as civil forfeiture of any property 'which constitutes or is derived from proceeds traceable to” the violation,'" they added.

Speaker Johnson says he found out about Jensen Huang allegations 'when everyone else did'

Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters this morning he learned about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s alleged affairs “when everyone else did in the media.”

Nvidia said today that Huang had resigned after reported extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected agent of China.

Asked if he was concerned that Trump may have been compromised by his dealings with Huang, Johnson said “I’m not.” He added that he would leave the issue to the White House.

Johnson said he would “withhold judgment” on whether Huang did anything wrong, adding that there are some House members who are interested in having Huang testify before Congress. “It is my understanding the Department of Justice has an investigation going, and there are some members of Congress who are interested in that,” Johnson told reporters.

“It sounds like there’s a lot of facts that need to come out, so I’m going to withhold judgment on all that until we get all the answers,” he said.

U.S. attorney demands Sen. Blumenthal preserve documents from his White House ballroom inquiry

A Justice Department official called on Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., yesterday to preserve documents related to what he claims is harassment of citizens during Blumenthal’s investigation into White House ballroom donors, threatening “significant legal consequences” if he does not comply.

The U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, Aaron Reitz, alleged in a letter to Blumenthal that his investigation equated to threatening “citizens for associating themselves with the President and other public officials.” The White House warned congressional Democrats on yesterday that efforts to investigate the administration could be a crime.

In a post on X with a copy of the letter attached, Reitz equated Blumenthal’s investigation examining anonymous donors for the roughly $400 million project on White House grounds with wielding Congress as a “weapon” against Americans.

Read the full story here.

Trump questions when 'seditious six' Democratic lawmakers will be prosecuted

In a post on Truth Social this morning, the president asked when the “seditious six" will be prosecuted — an apparent reference to Democratic lawmakers who made a video in November 2025 urging U.S. service members not to comply with illegal orders.

“Will the Seditious Six ever be prosecuted? What they did was a great violation to our Country and its Constitution!,” Trump wrote.

The lawmakers included Sens. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan and Mark Kelly of Arizona. In February, a grand jury declined to indict them.

Ukraine says it’s facing new restrictions to the Starshield network, as Trump envoys meet with Putin

Hours after an American delegation touched down in Moscow for peace talks, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country’s military had experienced a renewed wave of “significant disruptions” to the Starshield satellite internet service, hampering its ability to defend itself against Russia.

“These are not random errors but systematic speed restrictions,” he said in a Telegram post. “For us, this primarily means a significant complication in intercepting Russian jet-powered drones.”

His comments came as U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, arrived in the Russian capital for peace talks with President Vladimir Putin, a day after trilateral talks aimed at ending the war were held in the United Arab Emirates.

Read the full story here.

Trump says that Apple executive chairman Tim Cook should lead Nvidia

Trump says that Apple executive chairman Tim Cook should take over as Nvidia's CEO after Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the tech giant this morning.

"NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place — TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!" Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Cook stepped down in August as Apple's CEO after serving in the role since 2011. He then took over as executive chairman.

Johnson calls Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia 'a big and shocking development'

House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., answered questions from reporters this morning following the announcement that Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia.

“It’s a big and shocking development,” Johnson said. “You know, that’s a very important company, not only in the U.S. economy but for national security purposes. ... We’re certainly hopeful that the right person is chosen and selected to lead because it’s critically important for all of us.”

When asked about the impact Huang's departure could have on legislation, Johnson noted that export controls on chips to China are a big issue on Capitol Hill.

“I’m in favor of that of limiting those exports, and I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that that is an important position to take, especially given in the light of recent developments, it makes sense,” Johnson said. “So, we’ll see where that where that goes. I think it might change a few minds around.”

Johnson also said members of Congress are interested in questioning Huang, adding, “If that’s the will of the body, that’s what will happen.”

Bessent moves to a military base amid Iranian threats

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent moved to a military base following threats from Iran, according to a source familiar with the situation.

The move, first reported by The New York Times, marks the latest instance of a Cabinet official reportedly moving to military housing.

Read the full story here.

Jensen Huang agrees to brief Congress on relationship with alleged spy, lawmaker says

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has agreed to brief lawmakers on his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and the global chip behemoth’s security protocols, according to Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich.

Huang is “in discussions to find a date that works and in the right form,” Moolenaar said Thursday morning. Moolenaar, along with Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., and Rep. Eric Crawford, R-Ark., had requested the tech leader brief Congress in a letter sent Nov. 4.

Read the full story here.

Megaspeed, chip firm at center of Nvidia scandal, pledges to cooperate with U.S. investigation

Megaspeed, the tech company at the center of the Chinese spy scandal engulfing Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, said today that it will cooperate with U.S. government investigations.

Megaspeed’s statement came as Nvidia’s board met to decide whether Huang, one of the leaders of the AI boom, will remain at the helm of the American chipmaker he co-founded and helped build into the world’s second most valuable company.

Read the full story here.

Newly elected members of Congress pose for class photo outside the Capitol

Newly elected members of the House of Representatives gathered outside the Capitol this morning to pose for their first group photo.

Trump threatens to double Mexico tariffs over alleged 'caravans'

Trump this morning threatened to double U.S. tariffs on Mexico, claiming without evidence that an "INVASION of our Country is taking place again" in the wake of the midterm elections.

"Huge CARAVANS are forming and beginning their illegal march through Mexico. Many of the people in these Caravans are those that various countries don’t want — 'Send them to America,' they say — But they will not be accepted!" he wrote in a Truth Social post.

Trump wrote in mostly all caps that Mexico has to "stop them" and warned that if it doesn't take such action then "the Tariffs on Mexico will be IMMEDIATELY DOUBLED."

He claimed that Mexico, the current GOP governor of Texas and the incoming Democratic governor of Texas, Border Patrol and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement "HAVE BEEN SO INFORMED."

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum responded to Trump's post by pointing out during a news conference that "no caravan has reached the northern border" since Trump has been back in office.

"There are currently two caravans," Sheinbaum said. "One is in Arriaga, Chiapas, which initially consisted of around 500 people, or 600, and now fewer than 100 remain. How do we do this? We informed the people traveling with the caravan that it is very difficult to enter the United States."

"There is another caravan that has formed, coming from Honduras, and the approach is the same,” she said.

Trump says U.S. doesn't need a deal with Iran

Trump said in a Truth Social post this morning that the U.S. doesn't need a deal with Iran despite repeatedly stating there would be one in the run-up to the midterm elections.

"We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!" he wrote in a post saying he wants Vice President JD Vance to focus on corruption and crime in "Democrat run Cities and States."

The president had said numerous times before the elections last week that there would likely be an agreement with Iran to resolve the conflict with the U.S. in the near future.

Both the president and Vance, to varying extents, have blamed GOP losses on the ongoing war.

Read the full story here.

Democrats ask administration to preserve documents related to Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy

Senate Democrats sent a letter last night asking Trump administration officials to preserve documents related to Nvidia’s exports of advanced AI chips to China and related national security risks.

Sens. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts — the top Democrat on the Banking Committee — and Chris Coons of Delaware made the request over reports that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy and is being investigated by the FBI.

They asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State and national security adviser Marco Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller to preserve all materials related to the operation and to brief Congress about potential national security risks.

While Democrats’ power to compel the administration officials may be limited now, they will have the Senate majority, and the power to subpoena, next year.

“This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” Warren and Coons wrote.

“Reports suggest that officials within the government — including at the White House, State Department, and Commerce Department — were aware of concerns about Nvidia, its relationship with Megaspeed, and the suspected Chinese intelligence operation, yet did not move to block the continued flow of advanced AI chips to Megaspeed or other companies affiliated with the suspected operative,” they added.

Rubio circulated a memo to Trump administration officials in the spring outlining Huang’s relationship to Alice Huang, a business executive who is alleged to be an asset of China’s spy service, a person familiar with Nvidia and a former national security official with knowledge of the matter confirmed to NBC News.

China has denied the allegation, calling it “purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China.”

Trump said at a news conference this week that he had known about Huang’s affair but had not learned about it “too long ago.”

Nvidia’s board is meeting this evening to discuss Huang’s future at the company, a source familiar with the matter said, adding that the White House is aware of the meeting.

Democrats gather in Denver to discuss plans for what's next

Democrats are gathering in Denver today to debrief on the midterms and talk about what comes next as the party looks to 2028.

The conference, called "What's Next," is presented by Majority Democrats, a group that works to elect Democrats.

The gathering includes several Democrats who are considered potential 2028 contenders, such as Sens. Raphael Warnock of Georgia and Ruben Gallego of Arizona, Rep. Ro Khanna of California, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.

Several high-profile incoming members of Congress will also deliver remarks, including Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas and Gov.-elect Rob Sand and Sen.-elect Josh Turek, both of Iowa.

The event kicks off today and runs through tomorrow.

Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate race, breaking the GOP’s grip on the state

Scott Colom has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi, NBC News projects, capping a string of Democratic victories by flipping the reddest seat yet in this year’s midterms.

Mississippi last elected a Democrat to the Senate 44 years ago, just a few weeks before Colom was born in 1982. Colom, a district attorney, will become Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era.

The historic win comes after days of uncertainty in the race, with Colom holding a razor-thin lead over Hyde-Smith as more votes continued to be counted. Colom remained confident throughout the vote counting that he would prevail.

In the next Congress, no Democratic senator will represent a redder state than Colom. Trump carried Mississippi by 23 percentage points in 2024. Colom’s victory also underscores the Trump administration’s broad unpopularity with voters just two years after that presidential election, even in parts of the ruby red Deep South.

Read the full story here.

Alaska judge rules a request by Peltola campaign for ballot data in Senate race is ‘not reasonable’

An Alaska judge ruled yesterday that a request by Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign for a list of absentee voters whose ballots have been rejected is “not reasonable,” particularly given the time crunch election officials face as they continue counting ballots from last week’s election.

Ballots are still being tallied in the ranked vote election, in which Peltola and two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan are the main contenders. Alaska’s is the only Senate race in the country that remained too early to call.

The state accepts ballots up to 15 days after general elections from overseas voters, making Nov. 18 the final day to receive them. That date is also the Division of Elections’ target for conducting ranked vote tabulations if no candidate wins more than 50% of the first-choice votes.

Attorneys for Peltola’s campaign sued state elections officials Friday ,seeking a list of voters whose absentee ballots have been rejected and the reasons for the rejections. They said their intention was to ensure that all qualified voters’ ballots are counted.

Read the full story here.

Republicans tiptoe around Trump as they process defeat in the 2026 elections

Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va., didn’t mince words when he was asked what happened to Republicans in the midterm election.

“We forgot those people out there are hurting, and they vote,” said Justice, a former governor who is in his first term in the Senate. “We got our ever-loving butt handed to us.”

Read the full story here.

WASHINGTON – The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) released the following statement announcing that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested an illegal alien who intentionally struck an ICE officer with his vehicle in Chicago, sending the officer to the hospital.

On November 10, ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) Chicago pulled over Jose Juan Garnica-Naranjo, an illegal alien from Mexico, during a targeted enforcement operation in Chicago Heights. His criminal history includes prior arrests for assault and domestic violence.

Image

Jose Juan Garnica-Naranjo

When officers ordered Garnica-Naranjo to shut off his engine, he refused to comply. As officers then attempted to remove him from the vehicle, he sped away while an ICE officer was still partially inside the vehicle through the driver-side door. After Garnica-Naranjo drove over a median, the officer was thrown from the vehicle before being struck by the vehicle as Garnica-Naranjo fled the scene.

Image

The injuries sustained by the officer

The officer was sent to the hospital with a leg injury but has since been released. ICE officers apprehended Garnica-Naranjo later the same day.

“This illegal alien used his vehicle to assault one of our ICE officers, hospitalizing the officer,” said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “Thankfully, the officer has since been released from the hospital. This illegal alien’s prior criminal history includes assault and domestic violence. This is just the latest example of the staggering rise in anti-ICE violence, with our officers facing a more than 1,600% increase in assaults against them. This is the result of anti-ICE rhetoric from sanctuary politicians like Illinois Governor J.B. Pritzker. DHS is calling on Governor Pritzker and all other sanctuary politicians to knock off this violent rhetoric and start cooperating with ICE before any more officers are injured in the line of duty.”

text:
Press Releases

Attorney General Tong Opposes Trump Administration’s Attempt to Impose Unlawful $100,000 Tax on International Students

(Hartford, CT) —Attorney General William Tong today joined a multistate coalition in submitting a comment letter opposing the Trump Administration’s proposed rule that would require colleges and universities to pay up to $100,000 for each international student seeking to participate in Optional Practical Training (OPT). OPT allows international students to gain practical work experience in their fields of study following graduation, strengthening Connecticut’s workforce and economy. The proposed rule would impose significant financial burdens on institutions of higher education, discourage international student enrollment, and jeopardize the economic and educational contributions of international students. In the comment letter, Attorney General Tong and the coalition argue that the proposed rule exceeds the Trump Administration’s legal authority, imposes an unconstitutional tax, and fails to adequately consider the substantial harms to states and educational institutions.

“Donald Trump is once again putting his anti-immigrant agenda ahead of common sense and the law. Connecticut’s world class colleges and universities attract some of the brightest students from around the world, driving innovation and creating opportunities. This unlawful $100,000 fee punishes our universities, drives away talent, and threatens our economy. We’re fighting back,” said Attorney General Tong.

BACKGROUND

OPT allows international students studying in the United States on F-1 visas to gain practical work experience related to their fields of study. Students are generally eligible for 12 months of OPT, with qualifying graduates in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields eligible for an additional 24-month extension. On October 8, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) published a proposed rule that would require institutions of higher education to pay $70,000 for each international student they initially recommend for OPT and an additional $30,000 for a subsequent recommendation, including a STEM OPT extension. Although the proposed rule would allow institutions to seek reimbursement from students or employers, it would require institutions to transmit the payments to DHS.

The proposed rule is the latest in a series of Trump Administration efforts to impose extraordinary taxes on immigration and employment programs. Rather than targeting corporations that could abuse these programs, the Trump Administration’s efforts create significant financial burdens on public institutions and employers.

In the comment letter, Attorney General Tong and the coalition urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule, arguing that the proposed rule would:

Impose extraordinary financial burdens on colleges and universities: With more than 294,000 students participating in OPT nationwide during the 2024-2025 academic year, maintaining current participation levels could cost institutions $12.9 billion annually, effectively forcing many to stop recommending students for OPT.

Harm Connecticut’s educational institutions and economy: By discouraging international student enrollment, the rule would threaten billions in economic contributions, reduce tuition revenue, weaken the diversity of academic environments, and deprive our communities of individuals who contribute to research, innovation, and economic growth.

Exceeds DHS’s legal authority and imposes an unconstitutional tax: DHS incorrectly characterizes the proposed payment as a fee when it is, in fact, a tax that Congress has not authorized under the Immigration and Nationality Act. As with the Administration’s previously invalidated $100,000 H-1B tax, the proposed payment exceeds DHS’s fee-setting authority and unlawfully intrudes on Congress’ taxing power.

Violates the Administrative Procedure Act: DHS fails to adequately consider the financial and economic consequences for states and educational institutions, disregards the benefits of OPT participation, and fails to consider less harmful alternatives.

DHS has failed to provide sufficient time for public comment: Despite the sweeping consequences of a proposal estimated to require institutions to pay billions of dollars annually, DHS provided only 30 days for public review and comment without adequate justification.

In filing the comment letter, Attorney General Tong joins the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Nevada, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, and Wisconsin.

text:
United States President Donald Trump has warned Mexico that it must stop a group of migrants travelling through the country towards the US border or face a doubling of tariffs.

“Huge CARAVANS are forming and beginning their illegal march through Mexico. Many of the people in these Caravans are those that various countries don’t want,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday. The president said that a “perceived loss” by his Republican Party in last week’s midterm elections had emboldened the migrants, and that he was putting the incoming Democratic governor of the border state of Texas on notice about the issue.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

list 1 of 3Democrats win control of House and Senate: Key US midterms takeaways

list 2 of 3What’s next for US Republicans and Trumpism?

list 3 of 3IBM’s biggest division ends most US foreign worker sponsorships

end of list

Republicans lost control of the House of Representatives and the Senate in the midterm elections, with Democrats flipping multiple seats in both chambers of Congress.

More than a thousand migrants began marching on Tuesday through southern Mexico in a caravan, encouraged by last week’s Democratic victory in the elections, as Mexican authorities blocked a second, smaller group from trying to reach the US.

The caravan, called “God With Us”, was en route on Wednesday after setting off the day before from Tapachula, near the Guatemalan border, according to the Reuters news agency.

A Chiapas state government source estimated about 1,500 people were taking part, including many families, with parents carrying small children in their arms, in strollers or on their shoulders.

The migrants, mostly from Central America, said they aim first to reach Mexico City, more than 1,000km (621 miles) away, a journey likely to take at least several weeks, to seek help from the Mexican government and protection from detention.

Tapachula is a key transit point for migrants heading to the US, and thousands have become stranded there because of US entry restrictions and deportations, with few jobs, little healthcare and limited access to schools.

Caravans are common, but many migrants said the Democrats’ victory in congressional elections, in which voters delivered a rebuke of President Trump in part for his immigration policies, gave them new hope.

Among the unusual victories by Democrats was the governorship of Texas, which went to Gina Hinojosa, a woman of Mexican-American descent, and the first Latina to lead the state.

“There might be a light at the end of the tunnel, a way for us to get in,” said Cesar Sandoval, a 47-year-old Nicaraguan who was deported from the US a few months ago. “We believe the Democrats will help us,” he added.

Second group blocked

Local news footage showed officers positioned across a road, and the migrants ran as they were surrounded. About 40 were detained, according to reports from Tapachula.

The larger group of about 1,000 had crossed on Sunday evening without resistance. It is the third caravan to try to reach the US since September, the AFP said. The other two were broken up before leaving Chiapas, and their members were given temporary stay permits.

“As long as Trump remains president, the deportations will not stop,” said Ivan Porraz, a researcher at the College of the Southern Border.

text:
Following the Democratic gains in Congress on November 3, questions have arisen about whether the administration’s immigration policies are likely to change.

We do not anticipate significant changes to U.S. immigration policy affecting the business community or the issuance of nonimmigrant and immigrant visas. The executive branch that oversees and directs the Department of Homeland Security and its policy directives are likely to remain largely unchanged.

Key Takeaways from Our Immigration Team

The current climate should serve as the planning baseline for employers or foreign national employees for the remainder of this term. Organizations that build procedures for timelines, documentation, and contingency planning around today's stricter standards will be better positioned than those waiting for a policy shift.

Changes to Immigration Policy Under Trump Administration

Since President Trump’s inauguration in January 2025, the administration’s guidance has resulted in increased denial rates across visa, immigration, and adjustment of status cases. A substantial shift in policy interpretation appears unlikely. Major changes during this administration have included travel bans, pauses in immigrant visa processing, wage-weighted H-1B lottery regulations, four-year limits on student visas, the termination of many longstanding TPS programs, and stricter public charge rules.

USCIS has also issued policy memoranda establishing shorter response periods for requests for additional evidence and asserting its authority to deny cases without first seeking further clarification of the submissions.

In January, when Congress reconvenes with a majority of democrats in the House and Senate, we may see bills put forward for comprehensive legalization on the immigration agenda. It would remain to be seen if these bills might pass both houses and actually materialize.

title: DV-2027 Registration at a Standstill: What the Ninth Circuit's Stay Means | JD Supra
description:
DV-2027 registration remains unopened.
Importantly, the panel did not determine whether the Department of State acted lawfully by failing to open DV-2027 registration.
It suspends the district court’s registration timetable during the appeal, but does not establish that the Department’s failure to open registration is lawful or permanent.
What the Stay Means for DV-2027 For now, the practical outcome is straightforward: DV-2027 registration remains unopened.
Red Eagle Law was not an individual seeking to enter the Diversity Visa lottery, but rather an immigration law firm.
text:
DV-2027 registration remains unopened. On October 29, 2026, in Red Eagle Law, L.C. v. Rubio, No. 26-6943 (9th Cir. Oct 29, 2026) (Order), the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit stayed a district court order that would have required the Department of State to open registration for the DV-2027 program. The stay suspended the court-ordered timetable for registration, but it did not reach the issue of whether the Department may lawfully leave registration unopened.

Instead, the court focused on a threshold issue: whether the plaintiff bringing the challenge had a sufficient legal basis to pursue it. The panel concluded that the plaintiff, Red Eagle Law, L.C., was unlikely to establish that its interests fell within the zone of interests protected by the relevant statute and therefore that it lacked a viable cause of action.

However, the Ninth Circuit did not rule that the Department of State had acted lawfully by suspending the registration process. Nor did it order the Department to keep the program closed. Rather, it temporarily suspended the effect of the district court's order while the government's appeal proceeds.

For prospective entrants, the result is that, as of November 11, 2026, DV-2027 registration is not open and the Department has not announced an opening date. Whether and when registration will open remains uncertain. For immigration practitioners, the case illustrates how identifying a plaintiff that has interests sufficiently affected by agency action remains crucial to ensuring that a court may reach the substance of a challenge to agency action.

The District Court's October 14 Order

Red Eagle Law, L.C., an immigration law firm whose practice includes representing Diversity Visa selectees, filed suit in August 2026 to challenge the Department of State’s failure to open registration for the DV-2027 lottery. According to the Ninth Circuit's order, the Department had neither opened the registration period for Fiscal Year 2027 nor provided an explanation for the delay.

On October 14, 2026, U.S. District Judge Jinsook Ohta of the Southern District of California granted Red Eagle Law a preliminary injunction. As modified at the parties' joint request, the injunction directed the Department of State to announce the DV-2027 registration period by October 29, open a 30-day registration period by November 1, and notify selected entrants by December 3, 2026.

Thus, the order went beyond addressing the Department's delay. It required the agency to resume the registration process according to a specific timeline.

Had the injunction remained in effect, registration would have opened by November 1. However, the Ninth Circuit's subsequent intervention prevented that timeline from taking effect, leaving prospective applicants without a registration date.

Why the Ninth Circuit Granted the Stay

On October 29, 2026, a three-judge panel of the Ninth Circuit granted the government's request for an emergency stay. This stay suspends the district court's preliminary injunction while the appeal moves forward.

Importantly, the panel did not determine whether the Department of State acted lawfully by failing to open DV-2027 registration. It also did not decide whether the statutory framework established by Congress allows the Department to keep the program paused. Those substantive questions remain unresolved.

Instead, the court concentrated on whether Red Eagle Law could assert the claim in the first place. It found that the government had made a strong showing of likely success because the firm had not demonstrated that its interests arguably fell within the statutory zone of interests. The panel therefore concluded that the firm lacked a cause of action under the Administrative Procedure Act because its economic interests were not sufficiently within the zone of interests protected by the Diversity Visa statute.

These conclusions provided the panel’s stated grounds for staying the district court’s order pending appeal. In other words, the decision turned on the legal basis for bringing the challenge, not on whether the Department's conduct was justified.

The Legal Questions Behind the Decision

The central issue the panel addressed was whether Red Eagle Law could assert a viable cause of action under the Administrative Procedure Act. Under federal administrative law, establishing that an agency may have acted unlawfully is not enough; a plaintiff must also fall within the “zone of interests.” This requirement means that the plaintiff must be among those protected or regulated by the statute.

The Ninth Circuit concluded that Red Eagle was unlikely to satisfy this standard: the court determined that the law firm’s asserted economic interest in representing future lottery selectees was outside the statute’s purpose, which was enacted to encourage immigration from underrepresented countries, not to generate legal fees for law firms. Because Red Eagle falls outside the statute’s zone of interests, the court concluded that it lacks a cause of action under the APA to challenge the Department’s delay.

A separate concurrence by Judge N. Randy Smith addressed whether Red Eagle could establish standing under Article III. While the per curiam order did not reach constitutional standing, Judge Smith concluded that Red Eagle failed to establish an injury-in-fact. The concurrence reasoned that the law firm’s claim of lost revenue from hypothetical future clients was speculative and dependent on the independent choices of unrepresented third parties. Because the firm could not show a concrete injury or a causal connection to the government’s action, he reasoned that it was unnecessary to reach redressability, noting that federal courts are not an open forum to challenge government conduct without a direct, particularized injury.

What the Court Did Not Decide

The scope of the Ninth Circuit's ruling is just as important as its immediate effect.

The court did not hold that the Department of State has the authority to cancel the Diversity Visa program. It did not determine whether the failure to open registration violated the Immigration and Nationality Act. Nor did it decide whether Congress's direction that Diversity Visas be made available each fiscal year requires the Department to open a registration period, although the per curiam order described the Department as "required to implement an annual program" and stated, "We do not endorse the Department's failure to open the lottery registration period."

The court's reasoning was specific to Red Eagle as plaintiff. The per curiam order noted that Red Eagle neither joined prospective applicants to the suit nor claimed to presently represent them, and it did not address whether a different plaintiff could establish standing and a cause of action.

Consequently, the stay should not be interpreted as a final endorsement of the Department's handling of DV-2027. It suspends the district court’s registration timetable during the appeal, but does not establish that the Department’s failure to open registration is lawful or permanent. Further judicial review remains possible.

What the Stay Means for DV-2027

For now, the practical outcome is straightforward: DV-2027 registration remains unopened.

The district court's deadlines are stayed while the appeal proceeds. The Department of State is no longer bound by the injunction’s deadlines. As of November 11, 2026, the official entry site says that entries are not being accepted, and the Department has not announced DV-2027 registration dates.

This situation leaves prospective applicants uncertain about whether they will have an opportunity to enter the lottery. It also complicates planning for immigration practitioners advising clients who may be eligible to participate. Without an announced registration period, practitioners cannot provide clients with a confirmed opening date or assurance that the lottery will proceed.

The absence of registration should not be confused with repeal of the statutory program. The litigation is ongoing, and the Department could announce a registration period or a court could order further relief.

Neither an imminent opening nor permanent closure can be assumed.

Why the Identity of the Plaintiff Matters

Beyond the immediate implications for DV-2027, the case raises a question about who can challenge an agency’s failure to administer a federal program.

Red Eagle Law was not an individual seeking to enter the Diversity Visa lottery, but rather an immigration law firm. The per curiam order identified Red Eagle as the sole plaintiff and noted that it had not joined or claimed to presently represent any prospective applicants.

The Ninth Circuit found that Red Eagle Law’s economic interest in representing Diversity Visa selectees was not “more than marginally related” to the program’s purposes, noting that the program “was enacted to encourage immigration, not generate revenue for law firms.” The order may create additional obstacles for similarly situated organizations seeking to compel the Department of State to open future registration periods.

The statutory language also shaped the court’s analysis. Red Eagle relied on E. Bay Sanctuary Covenant v. Trump, 932 F.3d 742 (9th Cir. 2018), in which the Ninth Circuit held that nonprofit organizations providing legal representation to asylum seekers fell within the zone of interests protected by the asylum statute. The panel distinguished that case because the asylum statute expressly contemplated access to pro bono legal services, whereas the Diversity Visa statute contains no provisions concerning legal services for applicants or selectees.

That does not mean an individual applicant or another organization could never bring a successful challenge. Their legal position would depend on whether their interests fall within the zone of interests protected by the relevant statute.

The case therefore highlights how both the plaintiff’s circumstances and the statute at issue can shape the viability of litigation involving federal immigration programs.

What Prospective Applicants Should Know

For individuals interested in participating in the Diversity Visa program, the most important consideration is the continued inability to register.

As of November 11, 2026, there is no DV-2027 registration window. Individuals cannot submit an entry, or be selected from entries, unless the Department of State opens registration and conducts the selection. Prospective applicants should also exercise caution when dealing with third-party services that claim to offer access to a lottery that has not yet opened.

The situation remains subject to change. If a court orders further relief or the Department independently opens registration, an entry period could be announced. Until then, applicants should not make plans based on an assumed opening date.

The most reliable approach is to follow official Department of State announcements and developments in the ongoing litigation. Neither a reopening nor a permanent closure should be treated as certain at this stage.

Looking Ahead

Further developments could come in the Ninth Circuit appeal or a new Department of State announcement. In granting the stay, the Ninth Circuit indicated that Red Eagle Law falls outside the Diversity Visa statute’s zone of interests and therefore lacks a cause of action. Although the stay order is not a final decision on the appeal, the panel found that the government had made a strong showing of likely success on the merits.

If the Ninth Circuit ultimately concludes that Red Eagle cannot pursue its claim, this lawsuit would not provide a path to compel registration.

text:
A Lodi nurse and University of San Francisco professor who was arrested by federal immigration agents at her home in September has spent nearly two months in detention, as colleagues and elected officials push for her release.

Dr. Ann Lawani, 39, has been transferred from California to Texas and then Louisiana, according to her colleague at USF, Dr. Eileen Fry-Bowers.

Fry-Bowers said she first learned of Lawani's detention through a message from her colleague.

"I turn my phone on and there were a bunch of messages including a call to text message from Ann saying that she had been detained by immigration enforcement and that she didn't know what was going on," Fry-Bowers said.

Lawani has spent years caring for patients and teaching future nurses. Fry-Bowers said colleagues decided to speak publicly about her detention because they believe advocacy could help bring her home.

"We decided to take it public because we believe in the power of public advocacy. I certainly believe in the power of nurses," Fry-Bowers said.

The case has drawn attention from state Sen. Jerry McNerney, who said he intends to push federal officials to intervene.

"We are going to do everything we can to pressure the federal level to put a stop to this," McNerney said.

Rep. Josh Harder has also called for Lawani's release, sending a letter to the Department of Homeland Security.

In the letter, Harder said an immigration judge granted Lawani protection from removal to Nigeria after finding she would likely face persecution there. The letter also says a federal judge blocked her removal.

Harder argued that, given Lawani's clean record, there was no apparent public safety justification for her continued detention.

"I think this case is the perfect example of ICE breaking their mandate and breaking the law," Harder said.

Lawani had been authorized to work in the United States. However, the Department of Homeland Security says that authorization does not change her immigration history.

In a statement to CBS News San Francisco, the DHS said Lawani overstayed her admission in 2007 and was issued a final order of removal in 2013. The department said she will remain in custody pending removal.

Those advocating for Lawani's release say they are not giving up.

Fry-Bowers described her colleague as highly educated and respected, saying she believes Lawani belongs in the community.

"I mean if there was anyone that we would want to have as a part of our community, Ann is that person," Fry-Bowers said.

She called Lawani's detention "an injustice."

The DHS has not provided a timeline for Lawani's removal. In its statement, the department said: "Being in detention is a choice. We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure."

text:
The Trump administration doubled down on its criticism of the financially embattled UN refugee agency this week at the UN General Assembly, accusing it of overstepping its mandate.

On Wednesday, the United States, the UN refugee agency’s biggest contributor, voted against a resolution at the UN General Assembly that warned of persistently high numbers of displaced people and the need to share the cost of hosting them, in a politically charged statement rejecting its international duties toward asylum seekers.

The report of the Office of the High Commissioner for Refugees is meant to reiterate states’ political endorsement of the agency’s mandate.

A delegate, Yaryna Ferencevych, told the assembly her country rejected any scheme that would “infringe on its sovereign rights of who enters our country” and demands for “blank check funding”. The US representative stressed that the resolution, presented by a group of 41 countries, mostly European, conflicted directly with Washington’s “sovereign” migration policies.

The US also rejected the text’s references to climate change and to delivering health care and food aid to affected populations, saying the organisation needed to focus on core principles enshrined in the 1951 refugee convention and its 1967 protocol. “Strike this language entirely,” the delegate demanded. “UNHCR is not the WHO [World Health Organization], it is not the World Food Programme, and it certainly has no business masquerading as a global public health agency.”

The resolution still passed overwhelmingly, with 173 member states in favour, four opposed – Argentina, Israel, Paraguay and the US – and five abstentions.

Funding and principles

The US statement comes as the relations between Washington and the UN organisation could hardly be chillier. UNHCR, one of the hardest-hit agencies by US funding cuts since early last year, announced further major budget reductions this year. In October, Barham Salih, UNHCR’s high commissioner, warned its executive committee about the limits of what the agency could achieve in responding to the needs of displaced people worldwide, numbering over 117 million.

The White House has refused to work with Tressa Rae Finerty, a US diplomat, appointed earlier this year as deputy high commissioner after Salih and UN chief António Guterres rejected a Trump nominee for the job. In July, media reports suggested that the US was even considering cutting ties with the refugee agency.

Read more: UN refugee chief says aid organisations ‘asked to do the impossible’ amid drastic funding shortfalls

Salih, a former Kurdish exile and refugee who fled Iraq, has largely avoided criticising the US government and ICE’s heavy-handed practices in detaining and deporting migrants, including asylum seekers.

In late 2025, the US already made its position clear on international duties toward refugees when deputy secretary of state Christopher Landau told diplomats at an event held on the sidelines of the UN Geneva Assembly that the “asylum system has become a huge loophole in our migration laws”.

In this week’s statements at the General Assembly’s third committee, responsible for humanitarian and human rights issues, the US also rejected the Global Compact on Refugees adopted by states in 2018 and other international initiatives aimed at protecting refugees, calling them “vehicles of ongoing commitment creep”.

Following Trump’s recent appointment of Stephen Miller – a key architect of the administration’s hardline approach to migration – as chief of staff, Eugene Chen, a UN analyst at the International Peace Institute, expects the administration to double down ideologically on this issue, while disassociating itself from multilateralism.

text:
Fiscal Year 2026 alone dwarfed deportation and arrest numbers from the entirety of the Biden Administration

WASHINGTON – The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) broke the record for the highest number of deportations and arrests in any fiscal year in Fiscal Year 2026 (FY26), with more than 491,000 immigration arrests and more than 483,000 deportations.

In FY26, ICE carried out 483,200 deportations, which broke the record for the highest number of deportations in the agency’s history. This surpasses the previous record held by FY25, which saw 442,640 deportations.

Image

FY26’s deportation total is almost the same as all three full fiscal years under the Biden Administration (FY22, FY23, and FY24) combined, at 486,000. FY26’s total is also more than eight times the number of deportations in Biden’s first fiscal year, as FY21 saw just over 59,000 deportations.

FY26's arrest total includes nearly 475,000 administrative arrests, which is by far the highest total in ICE’s history.

Image

FY26’s arrest total is greater than the entirety of the three full fiscal years under the Biden Administration (FY22, FY23, and FY24) combined, at less than 427,000. It is also more than six times the number of arrests in Biden’s first fiscal year, as FY21 saw just over 74,000 arrests.

In the month of September, ICE carried out more than 48,000 arrests, as well as 44,000 removals. This arrest total represents a more than 300% increase over the average September during the Biden Administration.

This follows several record-breaking months, with August shattering the record for the most illegal aliens arrested by ICE in a single month, at 50,925. This broke the previous record held by July 2026, which saw 50,208 illegal aliens arrested. The record prior to July was held by June 2026, when 43,900 illegal aliens were arrested.

“I couldn’t be prouder of the brave men and women of ICE, who just broke more historic records,” said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “Fiscal Year 2026 saw the highest number of ICE deportations and arrests for any year in ICE’s history. September 2026 was the best September in ICE’s history in terms of arrests. The total number of ICE arrests in Fiscal Year 2026 was more than all three full fiscal years under Biden combined, as the patriots of ICE work around the clock to make America safe again. Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, ICE has been unleashed to target and remove illegal aliens so that we can save American lives.”

Under President Trump’s leadership, more than 3 million migrants have left the U.S. As of October, we have now deported nearly 1.2 million illegal aliens and arrested over 1.25 million illegal aliens.

Below are some examples of the worst illegal aliens arrested by ICE during FY26:

Image

Raul Genesis Ortiz Moran, an illegal alien from Mexico, arrested by ICE in July 2026. He has been charged with second-degree murder and aggravated sexual battery after he allegedly sexually assaulted and murdered a 2-year-old girl in Louisa County, Virginia. Following his initial arrest by the Louisa County Sheriff’s Department, local authorities cooperated with federal law enforcement and turned him over to ICE custody.

Image

Tou Lue Vang, an illegal alien from Laos, arrested by ICE on December 10, 2025. His criminal history includes a conviction for first-degree criminal sexual conduct in 2006 after he repeatedly assaulted a girl between 2002 and 2004. In June 2026, Governor Tim Walz’s Minnesota Clemency Review Commission voted to grant Vang a pardon. ICE deported Vang in July 2026.

Image

Josue David Carranza-Castellon, an illegal alien from Honduras, arrested by ICE in June 2026 at Newark International Airport in New Jersey. He was attempting to flee the country due to being wanted on charges of homicide – negligent manslaughter with a vehicle in Maryland. His criminal history includes a prior conviction for fourth-degree sex offense and an arrest for lewd or lascivious acts with a minor.

“[The president] should be focused on lowering our costs and ending this illegal war, not deporting our best and brightest students,” said U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md. “I am working tirelessly with my team to do everything in our power to locate Maria and her mother and bring them home safely.”

Flores Garcia joined her mom, Mirna Aracely Garcia Cabrera, at a scheduled immigration check-in in Baltimore last week when Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained them.

The Prince George’s County residents are in a detention center in Louisiana under threat of deportation to Mexico.

“The situation in the cells is horrible," Flores Garcia's best friend told News4. "t"There’s sickness going around and there's no medicine being provided for any of the women in there. And the food ... they barely get fed.”

Flores Garcia, who came to the U.S. when she was 9 years old, was valedictorian at Parkdale High School just last May.

"Congratulations, class of 2026, and remember that dreams don't have limits or borders," she said in her speech.

“Maria and her mother did everything the government asked of them,” said Justice Haynes, counsel for Flores Garcia and Garcia Cabrera. “Mirna showed up for her ICE check-ins. Maria worked, graduated first in her class, and started college. They both had a court order protecting them from being sent back to El Salvador. Flores Garcia illegally entered the U.S. in 2016, She was placed in removal proceedings and released.

In 2021, an immigration judge issued a final order of removal, according to a statement from the Department of Homeland Security.

“She will remain in ICE custody pending her removal from the United States. This administration will not ignore the rule of law,” the DHS statement said, in part.

Flores Garcia’s long-term boyfriend spearheaded efforts to bring attention to her case, raising more than $35,000 for her defense fund and securing legal representation

“The Latino community is not very highly represented here at the University of Maryland. text:
This week, multiple organizations and States have filed amicus briefs with the U.S. Supreme Court in Peter K. Navarro v. United States, supporting America First Legal’s (AFL) client Dr. Peter Navarro. The briefs urge the Court to review Dr. Navarro’s contempt of Congress conviction.

In October 2026, AFL, in partnership with Holtzman Vogel PLLC, filed a petition for a writ of certiorari with the Supreme Court, challenging the D.C. Circuit’s interpretation of the word “willfully” in the federal contempt statute. AFL’s petition argues that the government must prove a defendant knew his conduct was unlawful and that Dr. Navarro’s good-faith belief that he was complying with the President’s assertion of executive privilege precluded any finding of “willfulness.”

AFL’s petition has been supported by:

The States of Alabama, Florida, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, South Carolina, Texas, and West Virginia, led by the State of Oklahoma. The States argue that the Circuit Court adopted a definition of “willfully” that Congress never enacted and that the Supreme Court’s decision will have significant implications for state law.

Former U.S. Secretary of the Department of the Interior David Bernhardt, represented by the America First Policy Institute, who emphasizes the vital need for free, candid advice from presidential advisors and the importance of the protections afforded by executive privilege.

The Oversight Project, which argues that the Circuit Court’s interpretation of “willfully” is incorrect, that a senior presidential advisor’s assertion of executive privilege differs fundamentally from an ordinary person’s refusal to comply with a subpoena, and that the issue at hand is extremely important for the separation of powers.

Citizens United, Citizens United Foundation, and The Presidential Coalition, LLC, argue that Dr. Navarro’s assertion of executive privilege negated the “willful” element and that the Circuit Court erred in disregarding the January 6 Committee’s failure to negotiate with President Trump.

The Article III Project warns that denying a good-faith defense would undermine the longstanding accommodations process between Congress and the Executive Branch and may also empower Congress to weaponize subpoenas.

The briefs underscore the national importance of Dr. Navarro’s case and its implications for executive privilege, the separation of powers, and the rule of law.

“We are grateful for the strong support of these organizations and States for our client, Dr. Peter Navarro,” said Gene Hamilton, President of America First Legal. “A weaponized Department of Justice punished a political opponent for honoring what he believed was the President’s claim of executive privilege. The Supreme Court should take this case, reverse the conviction, and restore the proper meaning of ‘willfully.’”

Read AFL’s petition for a writ of certiorari here.

title: ICE dropping off released detainees in unfamiliar cities with no support, advocates say
description:
Perez said ICE agents arrested him in August while he was working as a landscaper in Miami.
The group has been putting recently released detainees up in hotels and helping them finalize arrangements for their travels home.
They began hosting released detainees in October, and since then more than 100 people have slept in their building, which used to be a convent for the church.
ICE agents arrested Bautista and four co-workers after a local sheriff’s deputy had pulled them over on suspicion of speeding.
Although the Otay Mesa Detention Center is technically not a jail — immigration detention is administrative civil detention — Bautista said he felt imprisoned.
text:
Immigrant advocates said it’s the latest in a long line of controversial ICE tactics.

Over the last few months, federal agents have dumped people who judges have ordered released from the Otay Mesa Detention Center onto the streets of San Ysidro late at night. Oftentimes they are left without charged phones, money, food, or any help getting home, according to human rights volunteers trying to help this vulnerable population.

Perez, a Guatemalan national released from Otay Mesa Tuesday night, described the treatment he endured to KPBS. Despite that a federal judge had ordered their release, he said he and other detainees were handcuffed, loaded into a van and left at the San Ysidro Transit Center around 10 p.m.

“They just stopped the bus and threw us out into the street,” Perez said in Spanish. He asked KPBS not to use his first name because of a pending deportation case.

Perez did not have a working phone or any money. And while other detainees were able to call friends and relatives to pick them up, Perez doesn’t know anyone in San Diego. Even if he had a phone, he wouldn’t know who to ask for help.

“I’m from Florida, so I don’t know anyone here,” he said.

An ICE spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Perez said ICE agents arrested him in August while he was working as a landscaper in Miami. After spending more than three months in detention, a cold and tired Perez was stranded in San Ysidro on Tuesday. Then he was saved by a volunteer from Detention Resistance, a San Diego-based advocacy group.

The group has been putting recently released detainees up in hotels and helping them finalize arrangements for their travels home.

On Tuesday night, a Detention Resistance volunteer took Perez and three other released detainees to Our Lady of Guadalupe Church in Logan Heights, which operates the Pope Francis Center.

The center serves as a resource hub for immigrant families. Connecting them with legal aid and hosting know-your-rights workshops. They began hosting released detainees in October, and since then more than 100 people have slept in their building, which used to be a convent for the church.

Brinkley Johnson, who manages the Pope Francis Center, said it was cruel and unnecessary to release people late at night without offering any aid.

“The process and protocols that the government takes are deliberate but they are not inevitable,” Johnson said. “And it’s important to recognize that. We could do this completely differently. We could treat people with dignity."

Despite President Donald Trump’s claims that his mass deportation campaign targets “the worst of the worst” criminals, Johnson said roughly nine out of 10 people who go through the center are working-class people with families.

“They are fathers, they are workers, they are uncles, they are good people,” Johnson said. “They are God-fearing people. They go to church, they help their neighbors and they’re often picked up while they’re working.”

That’s what happened to another man who slept in the church Tuesday night. He said federal agents arrested him in July near Orlando as he was coming home from a construction job.

“I was two miles away from home,” said the man, who identified himself as Bautista, in Spanish.

ICE agents arrested Bautista and four co-workers after a local sheriff’s deputy had pulled them over on suspicion of speeding. The local deputies called federal immigration agents after the stop. Bautista said ICE agents arrested him even though he wasn’t driving or committing any other crimes.

This kind of collaboration between local law enforcement and federal agents is common in Florida, where every county has a 287(g) agreement. The agreements, which are honored in 38 states, essentially deputize local police to enforce federal immigration law. The agreements are illegal in California.

While in detention, ICE transferred Bautista to Louisiana and then Texas before finally taking him to Otay Mesa, where he spent four months.

Although the Otay Mesa Detention Center is technically not a jail — immigration detention is administrative civil detention — Bautista said he felt imprisoned. Guards tell him where to go, what to do and when to do it.

“It’s horrible,” he said. “You don’t have any liberties.”

Bautista said he felt particularly bad for the detainees who had no money for simple luxuries like a cup of soup, coffee or bag of potato chips. That’s because their families could not afford to deposit money into their commissary accounts. People desperate enough for those things worked custodial jobs for $1 a day.

“Three days working to buy a bag of Doritos,” Bautista said.

Life in detention was among the topics of conversation among Bautista, Perez and other detainees at the Pope Francis Center Wednesday morning over coffee and breakfast. They all felt refreshed after sleeping in a clean bed and showering.

The men bonded over their families. Both teared up when asked about their children — Perez has two boys and Bautista has a daughter.

Perez cried when sharing that one of his son’s birthdays was Monday. He missed the celebration because he was detained. But now that he’s been released, he’s free to attend his other son’s birthday next week.

description:
