text:
The American publisher Crucial Comix has released a collection of political comics documenting the impact of immigration enforcement in the United States. Among the 25 contributions is a two-page comic about Minneapolis, written by Italian journalist Laura Cappon and illustrated by Gianluca Costantini.

In January 2026, Minneapolis became the center of a national confrontation over immigration enforcement, civil liberties, and the use of federal power. As immigration agents carried out raids across Minnesota, residents organized protests, documented arrests, and mobilized networks of solidarity. Journalists followed events on the streets, while artists began searching for another way to record what was happening.

Among them were three Minneapolis-based cartoonists, K. Woodman-Maynard, Jason Walz, and Trung Le Nguyen, who launched an artistic initiative called Cartoonists Against ICE. Their idea was to invite cartoonists to document the human consequences of the operations conducted by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and other federal immigration authorities.

What began as an online call for solidarity grew into an international artistic response. In autumn 2026, the independent American publisher Crucial Comix transformed part of that collective effort into a printed anthology, bringing together 25 cartoonists whose work explores fear, resistance, solidarity, and the lives of communities affected by immigration enforcement.

Among the contributions is a two-page comic about Minneapolis, written by Italian journalist Laura Cappon and drawn by Gianluca Costantini, the artist and founder of ChannelDraw.

The collaboration brings together two forms of storytelling: journalism, which investigates and documents events, and comics, which can give those events a visual narrative. Their contribution connects the experiences of Minneapolis to a wider international discussion about immigration, state power, and the responsibilities of those who witness injustice.

The context in which the comic was created was especially dramatic.

On January 7, 2026, Renée Nicole Good, a 37-year-old Minneapolis resident and mother of three, was fatally shot by an ICE officer. Her death provoked widespread protests and intensified scrutiny of federal immigration operations in the city.

Seventeen days later, on January 24, another Minneapolis resident, 37-year-old intensive care nurse Alex Jeffrey Pretti, was shot and killed by a U.S. Border Patrol officer during a federal immigration enforcement operation. Pretti worked at a hospital serving military veterans. His death further escalated the confrontation between federal authorities, local communities, and demonstrators.

The two killings became defining moments in a broader crisis that raised serious questions about the use of force, the monitoring of federal agents, and the right of residents to document government operations.

For Laura Cappon, Minneapolis was not simply a distant news story.

As a journalist working for the Italian public broadcaster Rai, she traveled to Minnesota to report on the immigration crackdown for the television program In Mezz’ora. Together with her colleague Daniele Babbo, she accompanied local volunteers who monitored the movements of federal immigration officers and alerted communities to their presence.

On January 25, 2026, while the journalists were traveling in a vehicle with one of these volunteers, federal agents intercepted their car.

In footage broadcast by Rai, officers can be heard threatening to break the vehicle’s window and forcibly remove its occupants if they continued following and recording them. The journalists identified themselves as members of the press.

The incident attracted attention in Italy, where journalists’ organizations expressed concern about the treatment of reporters covering the operations.

It also revealed something about the atmosphere in Minneapolis: journalists documenting public events could themselves become targets of intimidation.

Cappon’s experience gives particular significance to her collaboration with Costantini. The two-page comic belongs to a form of visual journalism in which written accounts and drawings work together to preserve events that might otherwise be reduced to fleeting images in the news cycle.

For Costantini, whose work has long explored political repression, migration, freedom of expression, and human rights, the collaboration continues a sustained investigation into the relationship between drawing and contemporary history.

His approach is rooted in the belief that comics can do more than illustrate information. They can connect political events to individual experiences, make distant situations more immediate, and encourage readers to examine what lies behind the headlines.

The artistic collaboration with Laura Cappon also has an earlier history. In a 2024 interview published on ChannelDraw, Costantini discussed the importance of working with journalists and writers and mentioned a children’s publishing project he was developing with Cappon. The Minneapolis comic represents another expression of that dialogue between reporting and drawing, this time within an international collective publication.

The origins of Cartoonists Against ICE are closely connected to the experiences of artists living in Minnesota.

In January, Woodman-Maynard, Walz, and Nguyen created a recognizable visual template dominated by icy blue tones. They encouraged artists to produce short, personal comics about immigration enforcement in their communities and share them on social media using the hashtag #ICEOUTCOMICS.

The initiative was deliberately accessible. Artists did not need to produce long graphic narratives or follow an established editorial structure. A few panels could be enough to describe an encounter, document a frightening incident, express solidarity, or explain how a community was responding.

The project also emphasized the importance of individual testimony. Rather than attempting to construct a single comprehensive account of the immigration crackdown, it invited hundreds of artists to contribute their own observations and perspectives.

The result was a growing visual archive of experiences from Minneapolis and other American cities.

Cartoonists Against ICE Zine

Published by Crucial Comix, this anthology brings together work by 25 cartoonists across the United States documenting how the 2026 ICE raids affected people and their communities.

Buy from Crucial Comix

In an interview published by Crucial Comix in January 2026, Trung Le Nguyen described the fear that had entered his daily life, even though he was an American citizen. Living near George Floyd Square, he explained how the increased federal presence had changed something as ordinary as taking his dog outside.

His contribution illustrated how immigration enforcement could affect not only people facing deportation but also the wider communities around them.

The campaign soon attracted artists from across the United States and beyond. Among the cartoonists associated with the project and its publication are Lucy Knisley, Aubrey Hirsch, Rosemary Mosco, Jason Walz, K. Woodman-Maynard, and Trung Le Nguyen.

Their works move between personal testimony, documentary observation, political criticism, and reflections on solidarity.

The printed anthology published by Crucial Comix brings together 25 contributions in a 50-page zine measuring 5.5 by 8.5 inches. Priced at $12, the publication is designed to remain accessible while helping sustain independent comics and the communities represented in its pages.

The publisher has announced that all profits from the zine will be donated to the Minnesota Immigrant Rights Action Committee (MIRAC), an organization involved in defending immigrant rights and supporting community mobilization.

The publication therefore serves a dual purpose: it documents the events of 2026 while also raising money for people organizing in response to immigration enforcement.

Crucial Comix is an independent, cartoonist-run publisher founded in 2024, specializing in nonfiction comics and zines. Its editorial approach emphasizes collaboration, personal narratives, and the ability of comics to address subjects often overlooked by mainstream publishing.

The choice of a small printed zine is itself significant. In an age when political images circulate rapidly through social media before disappearing into constantly changing feeds, a physical publication offers another form of preservation.

The drawings become pages that can be kept, shared, circulated through bookstores, and revisited years after the events that inspired them.

That is particularly important for stories about immigration enforcement, where public attention frequently focuses on spectacular confrontations while neglecting the everyday experiences of people living under uncertainty.

Cartoonists Against ICE brings these experiences into a shared visual space. Its value lies not in offering a single interpretation, but in gathering different perspectives through the language of comics.

The contribution by Laura Cappon and Gianluca Costantini is part of that broader effort.

Two pages cannot tell the entire story of Minneapolis. But they can connect the work of a journalist who documented events in the city with the visual language of an artist who has spent decades portraying political struggles and defending human rights.

The project also connects with Costantini’s wider artistic research, including ICE: Faces Against Erasure, a ChannelDraw initiative exploring how portraits and drawings can confront the human consequences of immigration enforcement.

The Minneapolis story demonstrates that graphic journalism does not need to be monumental to be meaningful. Sometimes a short narrative is enough to preserve a testimony, draw attention to an injustice, or connect people separated by geography.

In Cartoonists Against ICE, the individual voices of journalists and artists become part of a collective record.

What began in Minneapolis as an urgent response to events on the streets has become a publication that carries those stories beyond the city, beyond the United States, and beyond the immediacy of the news.

And among its pages, the words of Laura Cappon and the drawings of Gianluca Costantini contribute to that memory.

Cartoonists Against ICE is published by Crucial Comix and is available through the publisher’s official website.

text:
WHEN DONALD TRUMP discussed his party’s historic defeat on 60 Minutes over the weekend, he was uncharacteristically conciliatory about immigration. “I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out. But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally,” he told interviewer Ross Douthat.

Most remarkably, Trump suggested that a grand immigration deal may be “doable” in the next Congress, adding that Democrats “have already called me” to begin discussions.

But within twenty-four hours of the interview’s airing, he’d already started backtracking.

“Somebody suggested, will there be amnesty? No,” he said at an impromptu White House press conference on Monday. “They came in. They knew the law.” He went on to add: “My policy hasn’t changed.”

The quick reversal didn’t surprise longtime Trump observers, who saw his initial comments to 60 Minutes more as post-election salve than anything else. But it has created a lot of hamfisted spin and cleanup, including from members of his cabinet.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, for starters, affirmed that Democrats have been reaching out to make a deal on immigration with Trump. He even said that he would be comfortable with one centered around DACA recipients. But Mullin botched the basic categories of what a deal could be, confusing “citizen” and “legal permanent resident” all while insisting that nothing could result in “amnesty.”

The haphazard nature of his and Trump’s remarks has left even the administration’s ideological allies befuddled and wondering

text:
The Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer accused of fatally shooting a Colombian national in July made what his sister considers anti-immigrant statements more than five years earlier, a copy of the emails shared with ABC News shows.

Relatives have previously identified David Brouillette as the ICE officer who fatally shot Johan Sebastián Duran Guerrero during an immigration enforcement operation in Biddeford, Maine, on July 13.

In an email dated Jan. 5, 2021, Elizabeth Emen, Brouillette's sister, invited him to record a video wishing her child a happy birthday.

Two days later, Brouillette responded, "you said that '[REDACTED] doesn't need a racist uncle in his life.'"

"Now you would like me to send your son a video for his birthday to be a part of that memory. YOUR choices affects YOUR kids," Brouillette added, according to one of the emails shared with ABC News.

Emen said Brouillette was referring to previous comments he had allegedly made about her former partner, a Colombian national, who was living in the country legally and with whom she has two children. The partner was a graduate student pursuing a Ph.D and at the time and had been dating Emen for five years, Emen said.

Emen shared the emails with ABC News. Names are redacted and they contain several typos. The emails were first reported by the New York Times.

According to one email, Emen responded that Brouillette had made "racist/xenophobic" comments about her partner "not being a citizen."

In a response dated Jan. 11, 2021, Brouillette said that the partner "can takes his non citizen ass back to his country and enjoy his third world luxuries."

"He does not emulate what it means to be an American..rather he emulates what it's like to be entitled and think he has a seat at a table that has no room for his (or your ignorance)," Brouillette wrote, according to the email.

Brouillette added that the partner's "bloodline knows nothing about what it takes to earn and then CHERISH the freedom America offers. He sure doesn't have a problem with freeloading off of our country, not claiming to be part of it..and then criticizing it," according to the email provided by Emen.

A friend of Emen's told ABC News they recalled speaking to her about her brother's comments soon after the exchange.

ABC News has been unable to reach David Brouillette for comment. A number belonging to him appears to have been disconnected. He did not respond to a request for comment sent to his last known email address.

Emen said that exchange ended her relationship with her brother.

"That was a very overt and excessive expression of his beliefs," she told ABC News in an interview. "When I saw his actions on July 13, I just couldn't believe that it had been allowed to get to that point. I can't believe that he was onboarded into a federal agency and provided a weapon."

At the time of the shooting, an ICE spokesperson said the agency was in Biddeford "conducting targeted surveillance on the last known address of an illegal alien with a final order of removal," and when an "illegal alien departed the residence in a vehicle," ICE agents "attempted to conduct a vehicle stop."

"The vehicle attempted to flee the scene and fearing for public safety an officer discharged his weapon," ICE said.

Maine Sen. Angus King told reporters Duran Guerrero was not the target of the operation.

Emen, a licensed therapist, said she grew up with her brother until she moved away to college. Most of their adult relationship was long distance through phone and video calls up until 2021, she said.

She first learned her brother was an ICE agent when she recognized him from a photo in an article about the shooting, she said. She's now calling the agency's hiring practices into question.

"If it was rigorous, I imagine they might have talked to the people close to him about his behavior, about his motivation to join, and whether or not he could do what was asked of him and use the least amount of force possible in his role," she said.

The Maine Attorney General's Office is investigating the shooting. Brouillette has not been charged with a crime.

In a social media post earlier Wednesday, Democratic lawmakers on the House Homeland Security said they will investigate the emails.

"Democrats will investigate who approved this hire and why ICE ignored the serious red flags," the lawmakers said.

DHS has not identified the officer. A spokesperson said the agency "will never confirm or deny attempts to dox our law enforcement officers."

In a statement, a DHS spokesperson did not identify the officer and defended the agency's hiring practices.

"Incoming ICE officers, many already with years of law enforcement experience, are onboarded in accordance with applicable policies and standards. Any claims of substandard training or vetting are FALSE. This administration is preserving ICE's reputation as one of the most elite law enforcement agencies not only in the U.S., but the entire world," the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson did not comment on Brouillette's alleged remarks.

In a statement, an attorney representing Duran Guerrero's family said his death was the result of the "government's failure to properly screen" ICE agents.

"David Brouillette is the poster child for what happens when our government chooses to recruit agents to carry out a campaign of hate against immigrants, hires those agents without adequate screening and places them on the street without basic training," attorney Sean P. Murphy said.

Emen says she's now coming forward about her brother in an attempt to seek justice and support for Duran Guerrero's family.

"I've watched their speaking out after learning about my brother's actions and repeatedly my thoughts and prayers have been with them and I'll do what I can to support an investigation," she said.

text:
WASHINGTON — Democrats and business leaders publicly lobbied the Trump administration Wednesday to prioritize work permits and other protections for long-term immigrants during the lame-duck session of Congress and beyond.

Citing the midterm elections, when Democrats flipped the U.S House and Senate, and President Donald Trump’s recent admission that his immigration crackdown hurt Republicans at the ballot box, Democratic lawmakers argued that voters were clear about wanting immigration reform before the start of the next Congress.

Congress has a lengthy to-do-list for the lame-duck session, possibly including government funding, the annual defense policy bill, the farm bill, a measure to regulate the college sports landscape and permitting reform to ease regulation on large construction projects.

“We owe it to these families to try anything, and I’m willing to try anything,” Arizona Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego said.

He was joined by American Business Immigration Coalition Action, which lobbies for work permits and legal pathways for long-term immigrants, and the South Texas Builders Association, a local trade group that represents the construction industry that has a workforce that is 30% immigrant nationwide, and Democratic U.S. House members from Texas.

Asked how receptive the White House would be to work permits for immigrants, which the administration has vigorously worked to limit, Gallego didn’t directly answer.

Trump’s mixed signals

The administration has revoked millions of immigrants’ work permits in the last two years. Many were workers in hospitality, healthcare and the construction industries.

But shortly after the midterm elections, the president said he was open to making a deal on work permits in certain industries.

At the same time, though, he elevated Stephen Miller, an official who has crafted some of the president’s harshest immigration policies, to White House chief of staff.

“I think right now the best thing the White House could do is to actually try to send some type of signal, besides talk, that they’re serious about this, and the way to do that is to have some reforms already at (Immigration and Customs Enforcement),” Gallego said.

“Whether it’s shutting down the detention centers, giving (a) certain level of protections, whether to veterans so they don’t get deported, to maybe parents of U.S. students so they don’t get deported, something to show that it’s not just talk, and this isn’t going to be a policy that’s led by Stephen Miller,” he added.

The vice chair of South Texas Builders Association, Benny Melendez, had a pointed message for Miller.

“If you want to continue harassing our communities, prepare yourself not only to lose your job, but … these same communities you are now harassing will make sure you lose the White House” in 2028, he said.

Next Congress

If lawmakers are unable to get any major reforms through the crowded end-of-year session, Democrats are looking ahead to when they control both chambers next year.

House Republicans on Tuesday elected Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan, a staunch Trump supporter who has not supported immigration reform, to lead them in the minority.

Texas Democratic Rep. Henry Cuellar, the incoming chair on the subcommittee that handles government funding for the Department of Homeland Security, said he’s not worried about Jordan because Democrats will have a majority in January.

Cuellar, whom Trump pardoned after he and his wife were indicted on charges of bribery, money laundering and conspiracy, said he’s going to use his subcommittee gavel to add guardrails on ICE and clear the backlog at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, which processes legal immigrants.

Gallego said he thinks the Senate will be able to get to 60 votes on some type of immigration reform legislation in the 120th Congress, when Democrats will have at least 54 and up to 56 seats depending on races that are still too close to call.

Whether that overhaul is in one bill or a series of increments is up for debate, Gallego said.

“If we can pass a big, beautiful conference immigration reform bill, the Trump immigration reform bill, and if that gets them on our side or not, then let’s do that,” Gallego said. “But if that doesn’t work, then I do think incremental passes to start protecting different communities I think is also an option. We should not avoid that either.”

text:
U.S. bishops urged the Senate to pass legislation extending immigration protections for Haitians, arguing that escalating violence and instability in Haiti make deportations unsafe and calling for broader immigration reforms to provide a pathway to more permanent legal status.

The Nov. 10 letter sent to every U.S. senator urged passage of a bill, S. 4814, that would designate temporary protected status (TPS) for Haitians through April 20, 2029. It would allow TPS recipients, including more than 330,000 Haitians, to remain and work legally in the United States during that period.

TPS is an immigration status granted to eligible foreign nationals from designated countries that are deemed unsafe to return to due to ongoing conflict, environmental disasters, or other extraordinary conditions.

The Trump administration has moved to end TPS for people from more than a dozen countries since 2025, and Lebanon TPS is set to end Nov. 27. TPS for Haiti ended July 27, after a Supreme Court decision allowed the termination to take effect.

In April, the Republican-controlled U.S. House passed legislation, H.R. 1689, that would extend TPS for Haitians for three more years. No legislative efforts have gained traction in the Senate.

The letter was signed by Bishop-designate Brendan Cahill of Joliet, Illinois, chair of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops' (USCCB) Committee on Migration, and Bishop A. Elias Zaidan of the Maronite Eparchy of Our Lady of Lebanon, chair of the Committee on International Justice and Peace.

Cahill and Zaidan wrote that they “pray that, in its remaining weeks, the current Congress, along with the incoming 120th Congress, will devote more attention to the situation facing both Haitian families in the United States, especially those who have recently been stripped of their legal protections, and the human tragedies unfolding in Haiti itself.”

“Finally, we reiterate the need for all of Congress to work in a bipartisan manner, together with the Administration, to pursue broader reforms that provide expanded opportunities for longtime residents of American communities, such as Haitians and others with TPS, to achieve a more durable legal status, something President Trump expressed openness to in the last few days,” they wrote.

Trump told CBS’ “60 Minutes” on Nov. 8 that he would “love to do something on immigration” with congressional Democrats, who will hold the majority in the House and Senate starting in 2027.

Crisis in Haiti

The bishops said Haitiʼs worsening violence, kidnappings, and institutional collapse make it unsafe to return large numbers of people to the country.

In a September appeal to Trump, Oklahoma City Archbishop Paul Coakley, USCCB president, referenced a mass killing in Haiti that left 47 people dead and dozens abducted, including children. The bishops’ Nov. 10 letter also cited that attack, which Pope Leo XIV later called a “grave massacre,” as evidence of the countryʼs ongoing security crisis.

The attack and “the lack of any justice in its wake, and its existence as one of many such tragedies in recent months, help to demonstrate why it is unacceptable and untenable to forcibly repatriate hundreds of thousands of Haitians at this time,” the bishops continued.

“This conclusion is bolstered by the absence of an orderly reception system and the lack of coordination needed to safely receive large numbers of repatriated families,” Cahill and Zaidan wrote to the senators. “Under these circumstances, we are deeply troubled by the deportation flights that have been departing for Haiti on a weekly basis since August.”

title: Democrats are ready to fight Trump on immigration. But how much can they achieve?
description:

text:
By Julia Harte, Kristina Cooke and Richard Cowan

Nov 11 (Reuters) – Democratic lawmakers are gearing up to fight President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown when in control of Congress next year, targeting ICE tactics and expanding paths to legal status despite limits on how much they can achieve.

Democrats handily won control of both chambers of Congress last week, fueled in part by voters’ dissatisfaction with Trump’s aggressive arrest and deportation campaign. But lawmakers from both parties expect Stephen Miller, the architect of that campaign and Trump’s new chief of staff, to go on driving immigration policy.

House and Senate ​staffers told Reuters they expect the president to veto any legislation that would curb immigration enforcement or expand pathways to legal residency and citizenship.

Trump’s immigration crackdown has become a political vulnerability, with his ‌approval on the issue falling to 38% from 50% at the start of his presidency, based on Reuters/Ipsos polling, and Latino voters swinging sharply back to Democrats in the midterms after tilting Republican in 2024.

In a Friday interview with CBS’ “60 Minutes,” Trump acknowledged his deportation strategy may have been “too tough.” Asked about that by reporters on Monday, Trump responded: “My policy has not changed.”

Democrats will have more latitude on oversight. They have already drawn up a list of investigative targets at the Department of Homeland Security, the parent agency of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, according to staffers, including detention center conditions, fatal use of force by federal agents and the 2025 deportation of Venezuelans to a Salvadoran megaprison.

“We will investigate the administration weaponizing DHS against Americans (and) its out of control immigration policies,” US Representative Bennie ‌Thompson, a ​Mississippi Democrat and the soon-to-be chair of the House Homeland Security Committee, told Reuters in a statement.

The party also plans to push for greater transparency ⁠into how DHS is spending the more than $100 billion allocated by ⁠Congress since last year, staffers said, speaking on condition of anonymity.

At a Wednesday press conference at the US Capitol with House members and newly elected representatives from southwestern border states, Henry Cuellar, a centrist Texas Democrat, said he had already had conversations with Trump officials about focusing deportation efforts on criminals.

“We’re not going to be extreme,” Cuellar said, nodding to conservative voters across the United States who cast their votes for Democrats.

Asked for a response to this story, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told Reuters in a statement: “The Democrats are colossally misreading the electorate if they think the American people want an extremist, anti-American immigration agenda.”

The ​Department of Homeland Security in a statement said claims the agency had been weaponized against Americans were “absurd and false.”

The Democratic Party is in a “whole new world when it comes to their immigration agenda,” said Sarah Pierce, social policy director at the center-left Third Way think tank.

“They’ve clearly broken from the policy that we saw under the Biden administration, but they have yet to offer a proactive vision for what immigration should look like.”

Democrat Joe Biden, ⁠president from 2021 to 2025, initially rolled back some of the restrictive immigration policies of Trump’s first four-year term before taking a ⁠tougher approach to the border late in his presidency.

REINING IN ICE

Some Democrats emerged from last week’s midterm elections ready for battle.

“We will rip ICE apart,” Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan ​said while celebrating her triumph in Minnesota, where federal immigration agents shot dead two US citizens during an enforcement surge in January.

US Representative Pramila Jayapal, a Washington state Democrat and the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee’s immigration subcommittee, ​pledged to summon “every single one of these corrupt people that kidnapped and detained and deported and killed people in the streets.”

Just the specter of having to testify on Capitol ‌Hill could change the behavior of federal officials, a Democratic congressional staffer said.

In a statement to Reuters, Josh Gottheimer, a moderate Democratic representative from New Jersey, highlighted the ICE Standards Act, which he introduced in March.

“Agents need real training and body cameras,” he said. “They need to wear clear identification unless they are on an undercover operation. They must coordinate with state and local law enforcement.”

Republicans counter that they have already provided ICE with funding to purchase body cameras and have resisted Democratic attempts to place further guardrails on the agency.

On the campaign trail in 2024, Trump made no secret of his plans for an immigration crackdown. But the tactics of masked, armed federal agents, first in Minneapolis and ⁠then across the country, generated widespread outrage.

REFORMING THE SYSTEM

Jose Parra, a former US Senate aide with knowledge of current congressional discussions on immigration, said “voters moved the goal posts” last week, potentially opening the way for some stalled bills to advance.

He pointed to the Dignity Act, a bipartisan bill that would create a path to legal residence for workers while tightening border security and reforming visa programs.

Another bill likely to gain traction, Parra said, is the ⁠Dream and Promise Act, which would open a pathway to US citizenship for immigrants ‌who arrived as children, known as “Dreamers.”

Despite Gallup polling that shows more than 80% of Americans support a legal pathway for Dreamers, even that legislation might be difficult ⁠to advance, according to a senior Senate Republican aide, who said any serious attempt would likely come closer to the next presidential election.

Parra agreed with that ​assessment, saying Republicans might ‌want to “take that off the table and not let it be a messaging cudgel against them in 2028.”

Trump’s veto power will likely be an insurmountable ​barrier to enacting comprehensive ⁠immigration reform or clawing back the tens of billions of dollars already appropriated to ICE.

“Congress has ceded so much of its authority and so much of its power to the executive,” said Claire Trickler-McNulty, a former senior ICE official. “There are real limitations on how much Congress can do.”

Still, she said, lawmakers could use funding deadlines and Senate confirmation votes as leverage. And they could pass measures redirecting ICE funding to popular programs like healthcare or school lunches, even if the bills die on Trump’s desk.

At Wednesday’s press conference, US Senator Ruben Gallego, Democrat of Arizona, said his party will have to cut deals with Trump, and that members were already discussing how to move forward with a Dreamers bill by the end of 2026.

“Republicans have been saying we will have immigration reform as soon as we have a safe, secure border,” Gallego said. “We have that right now.”

(Reporting by Julia Harte in New York, Kristina Cooke in San Francisco and Richard ​Cowan in Washington. Editing by Jesse Mesner-Hage and Howard Goller)

text:
Jean d’Aspremont’s recent mind-expanding book ‘The Epistemology of the Secret: International Law as Revelation’ argues that international law, like any serious epistemological project, proceeds on the assumption that the world is a continuous stream of hidden knowledge which the discipline is duty-bound to reveal – except that, in the very act of revealing, international law also creates the hidden knowledge it purports merely to uncover, unveiling some truths while suppressing others. International legal texts, on this account, are not neutral repositories awaiting discovery: the act of ‘revelation’ is itself an act of ‘ordering’ – of determining what can be said, thought, perceived and actioned through the discipline.

In state responsibility, the role of causation in determining the availability, form and extent of reparations for wrongful conduct is a strikingly apt illustration of this dynamic. The Articles on State Responsibility for Internationally Wrongful Acts (ARSIWA) present causation as though it were simply there, waiting to be applied – a settled criterion, cursorily stated in Arts. 31, 34 and 36 ARSIWA, that adjudicators need only ‘reveal’ in each case. Yet, as this blog post will show, the practice of international courts and tribunals suggests the opposite: in choosing between multiple tests of ‘but for’, ‘directness’, ‘proximity’ or ‘foreseeability’, international judicial bodies are not excavating a pre-existing legal fact so much as constructing – case by case, and often without acknowledging that they are doing so – the very causal reality they claim only to identify. The kaleidoscope image in the post’s title seeks to stress precisely that: not only does the picture shift depending on which international judicial body one asks, but each forum’s ‘revelation’ of the applicable causal standard is itself a creative act, quietly foreclosing other ways the causal link could have been drawn in the given context.

Applicability of ARSIWA – and its Reparation Rules – to Human RightsViolations

As well known, state responsibility extends to human rights violations. Although ARSIWA is formally ‘without prejudice to any right’ arising from the breach of obligations owed to individuals under international law (Art. 33(2)), international judicial practice strongly suggests that the obligation to make reparation – i.e. restitution, compensation and satisfaction (Arts. 34-37 ARSIWA) – governs human rights violations too, by force of the customary rule of full reparation. That premise traces back to the PCIJ’s iconic pronouncement in Factory at Chorzów, which was later codified in Art. 31 ARSIWA, and also confirmed by the ICJ as applying equally to injuries suffered by individuals.

When international courts and tribunals decide on reparations as a consequence of state responsibility, no reparation can be awarded without causation, i.e. without a link between the wrongful conduct and the injury occurred (Lanovoy, p. 2). Art. 31(1) ARSIWA is explicit: full reparation is due ‘for the injury caused by the internationally wrongful act’ – and the same causal language recurs in Arts. 34 and 36(1) ARSIWA. Causation between the breach of law and the harm (here: a human rights violation) is therefore the hinge on which the availability, form and extent of reparation turn. Causation’s function is, thus, protective. It wards off speculative claims from injured parties, while barring punitive damages against the wrongdoing State, a form of relief that remains impermissible in light of the practice of international (quasi) judicial bodies.

Unlawful Expulsion of Non-Nationals: A Valuable Setting for Testing Causation in Reparation

To examine how this causal inquiry actually operates in the context of reparation, this post uses a high-stakes subject-matter as a microcosm: the unlawful expulsion of non-nationals. Expulsion affects millions of people every year, and a wrongful expulsion can trigger drastic, sometimes irreversible, consequences for an individual’s life and family. Such a measure is squarely an internationally wrongful act within the meaning of Art. 2 ARSIWA, and it happens to be one of the most heavily litigated corners of international human rights law – having generated a dense, albeit scattered, body of case law from multiple universal and regional (quasi-)judicial bodies. Given the laconic nature of ARSIWA and its Commentaries on causation, this jurisprudence – as ‘subsidiary means for the determination of rules of [international] law’ under Art. 38(1)(d) of the ICJ Statute – constitutes a rich and helpful pool of legal arguments on the subject, and, on d’Aspremont’s reading, a valuable setting for observing the discipline’s revelatory posture at work.

Before causation in the specific reparation context can even be considered, wrongfulness must be established. Expulsion of a non-national typically becomes unlawful under international law in one of three ways: 1) it breaches a substantive human right, e.g. the prohibition of refoulement or collective expulsion, or the right to family life; 2) it fails to respect procedural safeguards, such as those in Art. 13 ICCPR or Art. 1 of Protocol No7 to the ECHR; or 3) when it is enforced unlawfully – through excessive force, means of restraint, or otherwise abusive physical conduct during removal (for more, see Molnár).

Where any of these occurs, the coercive act of the host State’s immigration authorities not only triggers state responsibility but also activates the full panoply of reparation under ARSIWA and beyond. The ILC’s 2014 Draft Articles on the Expulsion of Aliens confirm that. Seen through a purely human rights lens, the UN Human Rights Committee’s General Comment No 31 (2004) states that reparation for ICCPR violations ‘can involve restitution, rehabilitation and measures of satisfaction’ as appropriate, while the 2005 UNGA Basic Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Remedy and Reparation add rehabilitation and guarantees of non-repetition to the classic ARSIWA triad. That reparation is applicable in expulsion cases is clear. The practical difficulty lies elsewhere: in figuring out which injuries are close enough to the wrongful acts to actually be repaired.

The Elusive Concept of ‘Injury’– and its Causal Tether

Art. 32 ARSIWA defines ‘injury’ expansively, as encompassing ‘any damage, whether material or moral’, caused by the wrongful conduct. In the wrongful expulsion cases, injury can flow either from the unlawful expulsion order itself, or from the substandard manner in which removal was carried out – and it can ripple outward into secondary harms: loss of employment, disrupted schooling for children, family separation, psychological trauma, etc.

But only injury that is caused by, and ascribable to, the wrongful act qualifies for reparation. Not every consequence flowing from it does (ARSIWA, Commentary to Art. 31, para 9). As international law draws a line between injury resulting from the breach and injury merely following it in time, the question is: what test to employ to draw that line?

The Plurality of Causation Tests: A Kaleidoscope, Not a Single Lens

Remarkably, causation – so central to the entire reparations edifice – remains comparatively under-theorised. And international judicial practice offers no single formula either. The common starting point is the ‘but for’ (conditio sine qua non) test: a factual causation mechanism asking whether the injury would have occurred absent the wrongful act. If it had happened regardless, no reparation is due. Yet, the ‘but for’ test, standing alone, is not sufficient in itself – it does not filter out injuries that are technically consequential but legally too remote.

To do that filtering, international adjudicators reach for supplementary tests: ‘directness’, ‘unbroken causal link’, ‘proximity’ and ‘foreseeability’. These borrow from the old Roman-law maxim injure causa proxima, non remota, inspicitur. Still, in judicial practice, almost every move is allowed on the dancefloor of causal inquiry, given that ‘[n]o specific test of causation is prescribed by international law’ (Guiding Principles on Shared Responsibility in International Law). Not only do the plethora of these tests in judicial pronouncements explain the situation that ‘causation’ and ‘remoteness’ resist generalisation (Wittich, para 17), but some substantive regimes even prescribe their own bespoke causation standards (see e.g. UN Security Council Resolution 687 (1991) on Gulf War reparations).

ARSIWA and its Commentaries treat the topic cursorily: symptomatic is the minimalistic wording in Arts. 31, 34 and 36, without elaboration. One explanation is that causation standards are inherently context-dependent and resist a one-size-fits-all formula (Wittich, para 17). But other scholars (e.g. Shelton, 846; Crawford, 492; and Lanovoy, 38) caution that this deceptively simple language masks a series of complex legal issues stemming from causation. Even the ILC itself essentially raised its hands and concluded in the Commentary to Art. 31 that the precise standard of causation must be determined on a case-by-case basis, in light of the relevant primary obligations (substantive rules).

Mapping International Judicial Practice: AFertile but Fragmented Field

Given the ILC’s own indetermined position and the increasing caseload on expulsion-related matters before regional human rights courts (and also beyond), this jurisprudence offers a fertile ground to understand better how causal inquiry works in reparation cases. The following draws on rulings from judicial bodies as varied as the ICJ (most notably Diallo), the ECtHR, the IACtHR, the AfCtHPR, the Iran–US Claims Tribunal, the Eritrea–Ethiopia Claims Commission, and the UN Compensation Commission. Most recently, the CJEU has entered the fray with the Grand Chamber ruling in WS and Others v Frontex, offering fresh insights into how a supranational court approaches causation in expulsion-related cases (albeit with respect to the human rights responsibility of an organ of a (supranational) international organization, Frontex).

One important caveat: expulsion-related reparation claims pursued through diplomatic protection and inter-state mechanisms exhibit different procedural features and evidentiary requirements than those brought by individual petitions before regional human rights courts. Even so, the causation methodologies developed by the latter exercise a gravitational pull on other adjudicators, at least to some degree – making cross-fertilisation, however imperfect, a real phenomenon.

Discernible Trends and Blurred Lines

Surveying this scattered international jurisprudence reveals several distinct – and not entirely reconcilable – tendencies.

A recurrent feature is applying the ‘directness’ or ‘proximity’ standards in expulsion cases. The ICJ requires a ‘sufficiently direct and certain causal nexus’ (Diallo, para 14), whereas the ECtHR tends to apply a ‘proximity’ standard, setting a comparatively high threshold for awarding pecuniary damages for both material and non-material harm in expulsion cases (Pusztai, 148-152). At the same time, the African Court requires directness in relation to loss of income but accepts an indirect connection as sufficient for moral prejudice (Anudo).

The IACtHR, by contrast, adopts a markedly more lenient approach, often simply asserting that a causal link exists without ever articulating the standard it is applying – a methodological opacity that makes its jurisprudence hard to systematise or predict (Pusztai, 123, 152).

Unlike regional human rights courts, the Iran–US Claims Tribunal has historically shown less appetite for a relaxed ‘but for’ test, adhering instead to a stricter approach to the causal chain. On multiple causation more specifically, the Tribunal has rejected ‘parallel causation’ arguments. In the Yeager and Leach cases, the Tribunal denied compensation for lost income on the ground that the claimants’ employment would have been terminated by their employer regardless of the expulsion, severing the causal chain the claimants sought to establish.

The CJEU, interestingly, appears to be context-specifically relaxing the causation test for the EU’s non-contractual liability – which is ‘directness’ by default (Katsoni) – in those expulsion cases where vulnerable asylum seekers are involved and under specific circumstances, particularly in scenarios of overdetermined refoulement, such as in WS and Others (paras 154-161). It should be added that what was at stake here was not the responsibility of a State, but that of an international organization, namely the EU.

A further recurring pattern is that international judicial bodies, the ICJ included, frequently dispose of causation questions simply by finding that the expelled individual failed to prove causation, without ever clarifying what standard was applied or how it was applied to the facts. The ICJ’s insistence on the ‘directness’ test across very different areas of law stands in stark contrast with the ILC’s own (and several scholars’) preferred view that causation standards would be highly dependent on the primary rules breached and the type of injury suffered, rather than being imported wholesale from one area of law into another.

Also, a strict directness standard, applied indiscriminately, risks undercutting both the restorative function of state responsibility (by denying reparation for genuinely connected harms) and its deterrent function – without making it punitive – by reducing the practical cost of States’ engagement in unlawful expulsion practices. The ECtHR’s demanding proximity threshold is an illustrative example: such a standard may sit uneasily with the normative function of reparation ‘to wipe out all the consequences’, as far as possible, of the wrongful act (PCIJ, Factory at Chorzów, 47; ICJ, Diallo, para 24).

The Conundrum and a Proposed Way Through It

All this, however, reveals a deeper structural difficulty. Set the causation bar too high (directness, strict proximity), and responsibility is unlikely to result in full reparation – the wrongfully expelled individual is left under-compensated. Set the bar too low (as arguably the IACtHR’s practice risks doing), and reparation drifts toward something functionally indistinguishable from punitive damages – a result international law expressly disavows (see similarly, Lanovoy, 62).

A more conceptually defensible middle path, inspired by Pusztai, runs as follows: notwithstanding that the wrongful act may be a conditio sine qua non of a given harm, the State should bear no duty to repair that harm if it could not reasonably have been anticipated by the wrongdoer. That is a foreseeability standard, calibrated specifically to the purpose of the primary obligation breached (be it the prohibitions of refoulement, collective expulsion, or arbitrary pre-removal detention) and to the gravity of the particular factual circumstances constituting that breach.

Several reasons underpin adopting Pusztai’s refinements in expulsion cases. It is faithful to the ILC’s own choice that the primary norm should shape the applicable causation standard, rather than employing an across-the-board test. It allows foreseeability to be assessed in light of the specifics of each expulsion-related breach, while maintaining a coherent general framework that takes account of the concrete primary obligations involved. It also aligns with an objective regime of State responsibility, since what matters is not the mens rea of the State agents, but the objectively discernible purpose behind the primary obligation and the factual matrix of the breach (Pusztai, 163).

FinalThoughts – Looking Ahead

A more conceptually robust approach to causal inquiry in expulsion cases would help ensure that any reparation ordered is objective, principled and legally sound rather than seemingly arbitrary. It would enhance the predictability of outcomes and – perhaps most importantly for a field with already fragmented judicial practice – it would foster greater comparability of expulsion-related reparation decisions across adjudicative bodies confronting materially similar facts.

Circling back, finally, to d’Aspremont’s opening thoughts: perhaps the most candid lesson of this brief survey is that causation in reparation is not a secret waiting passively to be revealed by the right adjudicator or the right test. Rather, it is a standard that each judicial body actively constructs, and in doing so, oftentimes forecloses alternative approaches. Recognising causation as a matter of construction, rather than discovery, may be the first step toward building a more coherent framework that expulsion-related cases still lack. The ILC’s new focus area, ‘Compensation for the damage caused by internationally wrongful acts’, which addresses, inter alia, questions of causation, will most likely provide further impetus for academic reflection and doctrinal refinement in this field – and for courts to keep a close eye on these as well.

text:
The first detainees have arrived at a new western Minnesota immigration detention center. Observers and lawyers say the center in Appleton, opened earlier this week.

Immigrations and Customs Enforcement has not added the facility to its public list of detention centers or responded to requests for comment.

MPR News immigration reporter Estelle Timar-Wilcox went to Appleton Tuesday and joined Minnesota Now to share what she learned.

Then, MPR News host Nina Moini spoke with Immigrant Law Center of Minnesota legal director Tracy Roy for her perspective on the facility.

Use the audio player above to listen to the full conversation.

Subscribe to the Minnesota Now podcast on Apple Podcasts, Spotify or wherever you get your podcasts.

We attempt to make transcripts for Minnesota Now available the next business day after a broadcast. When ready they will appear here.

Turn Up Your Support

MPR News helps you turn down the noise and build shared understanding. Turn up your support for this public resource and keep trusted journalism accessible to all.

Audio transcript

[MUSIC PLAYING] NINA MOINI: The first detainees have now arrived at a new Western Minnesota immigration detention center. Observers and lawyers say the center in Appleton, Minnesota, opened earlier this week. And Estelle Timar-Wilcox was in Appleton all day yesterday and joins us now. Thanks for being with us, Estelle.

ESTELLE TIMAR-WILCOX: Thanks, Nina.

NINA MOINI: What do you know about who is being held at this facility in Appleton so far?

ESTELLE TIMAR-WILCOX: Well, a spokesperson at the ACLU told me that they can confirm at least one person is being held there. And observers in Appleton told me they saw vans come by and drop off detainees earlier this week. ICE has not yet added this facility to its own public list of detention centers, and they haven't answered messages from MPR News asking if the site is open. So we don't know exactly who is detained there or how many people.

NINA MOINI: What do you know so far about the conditions at this detention center?

ESTELLE TIMAR-WILCOX: Well, since it's just opening up, we know very little as of now. And local attorneys and advocates told me that no one's been able to go in except staff, construction workers, and now apparently detainees. I spoke with John Boehler, the policy counsel for ACLU Minnesota. He told me he's worried about the conditions in the building and a potential lack of oversight, since it's owned by the federal government and operated by a private company.

JOHN BOEHLER: I think what we've seen in the past two years is that the executive branch, the federal legislative branch, DHS, ICE, and their private partners have all been working in lockstep. So there hasn't been a true oversight of these facilities.

ESTELLE TIMAR-WILCOX: Boehler said congressional representatives are also legally allowed to see the site, so he's waiting to see if any of them are able to visit, as well as attorneys who are allowed to go in and see their clients.

NINA MOINI: And we mentioned you were out in Appleton yesterday. What were you hearing from just people who live in the area?

ESTELLE TIMAR-WILCOX: Yeah, well, residents there have been pretty divided about this. Some of them say the town can use the economic boost of jobs at this facility. But there's also lots of opponents. I talked to Brian Radulovic, who's been protesting the site. He and other advocates are now trying to figure out what will happen to anyone who's released from there.

BRIAN RADULOVIC: We've been really concerned about what is already proven to happen in the Whipple building, where they just dumped people when they release them. They just put them out on the street, even on blizzard winter days.

ESTELLE TIMAR-WILCOX: And I should note, this facility is in a really small town. It's about three hours west of the Twin Cities, and it's set off of a two-lane highway. It's mostly surrounded by private farmland. So it's really not easy to get to and also not easy to get out of for anyone who might be released from there.

NINA MOINI: Are you getting a sense at all, Estelle, for how ICE plans to use the site once it's fully up and running? Because it can hold a lot of people.

ESTELLE TIMAR-WILCOX: Yeah, up to 1,600 people. They'll likely be flown and bussed in from other states. It's what we've seen happen at similar ICE facilities around the country. For context, Boehler told me that 1,600 people number. That's about twice the number of detainees in the state compared to the highest number we saw during Operation Metro Surge. And he said that could put a strain on resources like attorneys and community aid groups.

JOHN BOEHLER: Those resources were strained to the breaking point through Metro Surge. And so to take that and multiply it by three or four times and to put them instead of at Whipple, put them three hours outside the metro, where there are very few attorneys, let alone specialized immigration attorneys, you're going to make it quite difficult for these individuals to get adequate representation.

ESTELLE TIMAR-WILCOX: And as far as what we know about operations here, the company CoreCivic will be operating the site. They owned that facility up until earlier this year, when they sold it to the US government for almost $500 million. And CoreCivic will still run the site. Their revenue will be partly tied to the number of detainees held there. That's on top of a fixed monthly payment that they'll get. And in all, they expect to make about $75 million a year in revenue from this center.

NINA MOINI: Thanks so much for your reporting, Estelle.

ESTELLE TIMAR-WILCOX: You're welcome.

NINA MOINI: That's MPR Newsday reporter Estelle Timar-Wilcox. We're going to bring in Tracy Roy now, who's the legal director at Immigrant Law Center of Minnesota. Tracy, thanks for your time today as well.

TRACY ROY: Thank you for having me, Nina.

NINA MOINI: I'm sure you were able to listen to Estelle's reporting before we talked. And we're so glad to have you here to put even more context around this. What information do you have about just how many people are at Appleton at this moment? And can you tell us about how information is traveling, given that there is no information really coming from the federal government?

TRACY ROY: Yeah. So as Estelle said, we are expecting 1,600 beds at this facility. And the performance work statement that was on sam.gov about the Appleton facility shared that they were planning to have 150 detainees the first week and ramp up to 250 each week after that. And so we are working on getting access to the facility, ramping up our detainee rights program, because our top priority is to make sure that these folks have access to accurate legal information, information about their rights, and legal advice about any forms of relief that may be available to them. So we are planning to be there on the ground at the detention center. And we also have our detention line for folks who are detained to be able to contact us as well.

NINA MOINI: Kind of building off what you're saying, Estelle was mentioning this is in a more rural area surrounded by farmland, three hours west of the Twin Cities. And the attorneys we were hearing from were concerned about just this infrastructure of being able to help all the clients that will need representation. How are you working around that? You just mentioned the vigilance with which you're moving forward, but how is that realistically going to work?

TRACY ROY: Yeah, that is a great question. The size of the Appleton facility, the number of beds is many times more than the current facilities are running now. And so we are ramping up by expanding our detention team. So we are expanding the number of attorneys, legal assistants.

We're also not doing this alone. We can't do this alone. And we don't do this alone. So we're working with community partners, legal aid partners, to make sure that we are able to get access, be near the facility, have people actually going to the facility and be there on the ground because that's the best way to be able to reach folks is if we can actually see it.

And so there are some offices near-- some of our partners have offices near to the facility that are able to be closer. And we are, like I said, working with community partners, legal aid partners, to make sure that we're able to get there and continue to ramp up. Right now, we're ramping up internal staffing. This could expand to more pro-bono support, things like that.

So taking what we already have in place for our detention centers across the state and just building upon that. We have a really great solid structure, where we're able to reach detainees. We're able to get folks advice building upon what we already have.

NINA MOINI: Tracy can you describe a little bit about how attorneys and lawyers figure out where their clients are when it comes to these detention facilities? DHS owns this Appleton facility. It's going to be operated by CoreCivic, which is a private company, which makes it the first privately run detention center in Minnesota.

Can you talk about the differences just on access and information? If it's like a county jail, you can look people up. How does it work? Is there secrecy around it? Are people going to have to work extra hard to figure out where their clients are, like we've seen at some facilities across the country?

TRACY ROY: Yeah, this is definitely a different type of facility. All of our other facilities are state owned and run by counties, and so we are able to work directly with the county jails in order to get access and get information. There are different ways that we learn about people being detained, one, through our detention line. And that's open Monday through Thursday from 1:00 to 3:00 PM. And so detainees or their loved ones are able to call and let us know where they're at.

The ICE detention locator is another way. If somebody has an A number, then we're able to look up where somebody is being held. And that is the most common way to find out where someone is at. Otherwise, again, getting on the ground into the facilities is another way. Sometimes our partners, sometimes community partners are going to facilities and they're meeting folks and they're learning, OK, you're working with this person. I'll connect that person to make sure that where you are. So there are a lot of different ways that we are able to connect with folks in those ways.

NINA MOINI: And Tracy, just lastly, are you expecting, or have you had any conversations or learned of anything just related to gaining access to the Appleton facility? Estelle's reporting folks were mentioning members of Congress should be able to go in there and then take a look when they're able to do that. They were turned away from some other facilities in the past, including the Whipple at different times. So what is your plan or your sense for just the level of access to be able to make sure that conditions inside of this facility are up to par?

TRACY ROY: Like I said, we have a lot of practice working with different facilities. They were run differently. So we're going to have to be talking to different people than we have before. But we are working-- like I said, our top priority is to be able to get in there and get access to folks so that way they have access to legal support while they are detained, and to make sure that conditions are sufficient to be able to support folks.

NINA MOINI: And as we know, the facility is expected to be fully up and running by mid 2027. So we hope that you'll continue to check in with us, Tracy, and let us how things are going. Thank you for your time.

TRACY ROY: Yes, thank you, Nina.

NINA MOINI: Tracy Roy is legal director at Immigrant Law Center of Minnesota.

SAN FRANCISCO (KGO) -- University of San Francisco nursing professor Dr. Ann Lawani remains in federal immigration custody nearly two months after agents arrested her outside her home in Lodi in Northern California, despite a federal judge's order protecting her from deportation to her native Nigeria.

"One of the worst days of my life was September 16," said Dr. Eileen Fry-Bowers, dean of the University of San Francisco School of Nursing and Health Professions, recalling the moment she learned Lawani had been detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Fry-Bowers said the arrest marked the beginning of what colleagues, students and supporters describe as an eight-week ordeal.

According to Fry-Bowers, Lawani texted her shortly after the arrest, writing: "I was coming out of my house this morning and got picked up by immigration for whatever reason, no warrant, no nothing. I haven't committed any crime. I don't know what's going on."

MORE: ICE releases San Francisco assemblymember's aide on bond after 15 days in detention

Supporters say Lawani, a longtime nursing educator with no criminal history, was transferred through multiple detention facilities before being moved to a processing center in Louisiana, where she is believed to remain in custody.

In response, Fry-Bowers launched a petition and GoFundMe campaign, drawing support from students, faculty and community members.

The Department of Homeland Security defended the detention in a statement, saying Lawani entered the United States legally on June 7, 2007, on a temporary visa, but remained in the country after her authorized stay expired on July 6, 2007.

MORE: Rally held in support of Concord mother, nurse detained by ICE in Louisiana

The case has also drawn attention from Rep. Josh Harder, who recently called on Homeland Security officials to release Lawani.

Harder argued the case raises questions about the agency's stated focus on removing violent offenders.

MORE: Judge orders UC Berkeley student released from ICE custody after SFO arrest

"She's a nurse, a university professor at USF, a caregiver to her 83-year-old father," Harder said. "This goes to all the rhetoric used by ICE over the past two years when they say they are targeting violent criminals."

Lawani's supporters maintain she came to the United States on a valid visa, has no criminal record and should be released while her immigration case proceeds.

text:
Saying it hopes to "carry out the American people’s mandate for mass deportations," the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has confirmed it has begun operating at the site of a former private prison in Appleton, Minnesota.

ICE facility opens in Appleton

What we know:

DHS says that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) had previously been exploring the location, which has been vacant since 2010, as a site to expand its operations involving federal immigration enforcement.

Officials with ICE have previously said they had hoped the facility would be running by mid-2027, with a potential capacity of up to 1,600 detainees.

Dig deeper:

The center will be operated by CoreCivic, a company that sold the property to the U.S. government earlier this year for $495.6 million.

CoreCivic has said the company expects to make a $75 million return in revenue from the Appleton site annually, under its five-year contract.

After reports that CoreCivic previously offered to buy the prison from the state of Minnesota for a reported $75 million, the company has since released a statement providing further details on the sale.

The company says, in part, that the reported figure was never intended to be a purchase offer.

"It's important to understand that the reported $75 million figure and the federal purchase price measure two different things at vastly different points in a valuation process. The earlier figure was never an appraisal or a replacement cost and was never intended to be. It was a preliminary number dating back to 2015, which was an unsuccessful attempt to engage the MN DOC in a discussion of future use of the Prairie facility," a statement reads. "The federal purchase price reflects what it would cost to build a facility of equivalent square footage and security at today’s construction prices, less depreciation."

What they're saying:

A statement provided to FOX 9 from a DHS spokesperson confirms that the location is now operational and in use.

"DHS opened the Appleton Detention Facility on November 9 to strengthen America’s ability to enforce its immigration laws and carry out the American people’s mandate for mass deportations," the statement says. "The site gives ICE immediate capacity to detain and remove those who have no legal right to remain, protecting American communities and restoring the integrity of our borders without waiting years for new construction.

"Every day, DHS is conducting law enforcement activities across the country to keep Americans safe. It should not come as news that ICE will be making arrests in states across the U.S. and ensuring we have resources to carry out President Trump’s mission."

Big picture view:

Appleton is located in far western Minnesota, just about 20 miles east of the South Dakota border. The prison is located on the south side of the city off of Highway 119.

text:
LODI, Calif. —

Dr. Ann Lawani, a nurse and educator living in Lodi, has been detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement for nearly two months, leading her family, attorney and Congressman Josh Harder to call for her release.

"To simply put it, she is a lifesaver," said her brother, Sam Lawani. He described his sister as someone who "lives, breathes, and exudes just health care."

In addition to her work overseeing 230 nursing students, coordinating 51 faculty members and managing partnerships with 38 clinical sites for the University of San Francisco, Dr. Lawani is also a nurse at John Muir Health and a caregiver for her 83-year-old father.

Nearly two months ago, Dr. Lawani was arrested by ICE at her home in Lodi and transferred across multiple states to a detention facility in Louisiana.

"That's just beyond comprehension that this can happen to such a person," Sam Lawani said.

During her transfer, Sam said her location was not reflected in ICE's online detainee locator, and he only learned where she was after she called him three days later.

Her attorney, Natalia Vieira Santanna, said Dr. Lawani came to the U.S. legally in 2007 on a visitor visa from Nigeria and applied for asylum within a year. In August of 2013, a federal immigration judge denied her asylum and entered a removal order but granted her withholding of removal in the same order, according to Vieira Santanna.

"What that means is that first, there was a finding that she would be more likely than not to suffer persecution in Nigeria, her country of origin, and second, also that the government could not remove her to Nigeria," Santanna said.

Vieira Santanna said the withholding grant protects Dr. Lawani from deportation and allows her to have a work permit in the U.S., which she holds and is valid through April 2029.

KCRA 3 reached out to the Department of Homeland Security. A spokesperson did not acknowledge the withholding grant, but sent a statement reading in part, "She received due process and was issued a final order of removal on August 6, 2013. She will remain in ICE custody pending removal from the United States." DHS added, "Work authorization does not confer legal status in the U.S."

Congressman Josh Harder has joined the effort to secure Dr. Lawani's release, sending a letter to DHS urging the agency to return her to California. He said she does not have a criminal record and has spent years serving her community.

"I think this is another example of ICE not actually prioritizing threats to public safety. They say they're going after folks with a criminal record. This is exactly the opposite," Harder said. “It's absolutely heart-wrenching, and it has huge ripple effects across Lodi and our entire community.”

Sam Lawani expressed his determination to see his sister released.

"I will move the earth if possible to make sure she gets out of there," he said.

Dr. Lawani’s attorney said her case includes a pending petition requesting her immediate release, alleging constitutional violations in her detention.

text:
On Wednesday, November 11, 2026, the House of Representatives raised a grave alarm over the escalating crisis of human trafficking across the nation, describing it as a devastating violation of human rights and a transnational emergency.

Acting on a motion brought forward by Hon. Dominic Okafor, the House underscored that vulnerable demographics, particularly women and children, are increasingly subjected to commercial sexual exploitation, forced labor, domestic servitude, forced begging, and illicit organ harvesting.

Legislators noted that compounding socioeconomic challenges, including widespread poverty, unemployment, insecurity, displacement, and irregular migration, have left citizens heavily exposed to sophisticated criminal syndicates. These networks frequently prey on victims using false promises of foreign employment, education, marriage, and overseas opportunities, only to subject them to severe physical abuse, psychological trauma, and, in tragic cases, death.

The House expressed deep concern that porous state and national borders, coupled with inadequate public awareness and weak inter-agency coordination, continue to fuel the operations of these criminal networks.

While acknowledging the vital contributions of the National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP), the Nigeria Police Force, and the Nigeria Immigration Service, the parliament stressed the urgent necessity of bolstering their operational capacity, intelligence-sharing mechanisms, and funding under the Trafficking in Persons (Prohibition) Enforcement and Administration Act, 2015.

Key Resolutions Adopted by the House:

Urged the Federal Government to ramp up nationwide efforts to combat trafficking through stringent enforcement of existing laws, intelligence-led investigations, and the decisive prosecution of offenders and their collaborators.

Mandated the strengthening of victim identification, rescue, rehabilitation, psychosocial support, legal aid, and reintegration frameworks, with specialized focus on women and children.

Called for targeted policies to tackle the underlying drivers of vulnerability, such as poverty, joblessness, lack of educational access, and the plight of displaced persons.

Directed NAPTIP and security agencies to scale up cross-border and inter-state surveillance and intelligence coordination.

Urged the Federal Ministry of Education, state ministries, local governments, civil society organizations, and community leaders to aggressively educate the public on deceptive recruitment tactics and the dangers of irregular migration.

The House Committees on Human Rights, Interior, and Police Affairs have been officially mandated to thoroughly investigate the current scale and patterns of human trafficking, assess enforcement measures, and identify institutional challenges, reporting back within four weeks for further legislative action.

text:
An ICE agent who fatally shot a Colombian migrant in Maine had previously spewed racist abuse about his sister's Colombian partner in a series of vile emails.

David Brouillette, 38, called his sister Elizabeth Emen's longtime partner—a Colombian-born graduate student who was living legally in the U.S. and with whom she shared two children—a "non citizen" who should return to his "third world" country in a 2021 exchange obtained by The New York Times.

He also attacked his "bloodline" and accused him of failing to embody American values.

"He can takes his non citizen a-- back to his country and enjoy his third world luxuries," Brouillette wrote in one email, riddled with typos.

In another, he attacked the man's "bloodline," claiming it knew nothing about what it took to "earn and then CHERISH the freedom America offers."

"He does not emulate what it means to be an American" but "rather he emulates what it's like to be entitled and think he has a seat" at a table "that has no room for his (or your ignorance)," he wrote.

He added that the man's "bloodline knows nothing about what it takes to earn and then CHERISH the freedom America offers."

Emen, who shared the emails with The Times, said her brother's attacks had nothing to do with her partner's immigration status, but rather his ethnicity.

"David had no basis for saying that my partner was undocumented," she told The New York Times. "It was about how he saw him based on his race."

Emen said the exchange began after she invited relatives to celebrate her son's birthday.

Brouillette responded by condemning her relationship and accusing her partner of harboring "anti-American ideologies."

He then turned his fury on his sister, telling her she had effectively lost him as a brother.

"Your choices have cost you a brother. I am so so so ashamed of you," he wrote. "You're dead to me Liz. Enjoy it. Dead to me. DEAD."

Four years later, Brouillette fatally shot 25-year-old Colombian migrant Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero during an attempted traffic stop in Biddeford, Maine.

Guerrero was struck four times in the face and neck, the New York Times reported. He was killed in front of his wife and 3-year-old daughter, who stood crying in the street dressed in Bluey pajamas.

His wife was on her knees next to their daughter, screaming out in what one onlooker described as an agonizing howl.

"I heard agony," resident Mary Hayes told The New York Times. "I heard a howl that came from your soul, that your whole life had just changed and it was never going to be the same."

Guerrero was driving to work when ICE agents rammed his car while attempting to execute a warrant for a final order of removal.

The Department of Homeland Security claimed "the vehicle attempted to flee" and that Brouillette opened fire because he feared for public safety.

But evidence substantiating the department's account has yet to emerge.

DHS initially claimed Guerrero had entered the country illegally, a statement it subsequently retracted, according to the office of Senator Angus King of Maine.

The Guerrero family's lawyer said he was authorized to work in the U.S. and was not the subject of ICE's investigation.

The shooting provoked widespread outrage in Biddeford, with elected officials from both parties criticizing ICE.

Republican Senator Susan Collins called on the agency to halt all non-urgent vehicle stops.

The shooting is now being investigated, and Brouillette's emails could prove to be an important part of the investigation.

Michael Gennaco, a former federal prosecutor in California, told The New York Times that the emails could help support an argument that an officer used excessive force.

"Federal statute doesn't require a prosecutor to prove racial animus, but such bias could support the idea that the officer used excessive force," Gennaco said.

The Daily Beast has contacted DHS for comment.
