text:
A car traveling south on State Street approaches Court Street as three unmarked vehicles — one with law-enforcement lights flashing — box it in, forcing the car to stop and blocking a lane of traffic.

Four federal immigration agents emerge. They’re all wearing vests. At least one is wearing a face mask. Another unmarked car and more Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents soon show up.

Eventually, the ICE agents open the car’s rear driver’s side door and pull out the man they had been looking for — 18-year-old New Havener Jaime Diaz-Perez. They secure his hands behind his back while he’s on the ground.

Another man, Diaz-Perez’s father, opens the front passenger’s side door and steps out of the car, only to be pushed back inside by an ICE agent.

The ICE agents walk Diaz-Perez, with his hands secured behind his back, over to one of the unmarked vehicles. They put him in the back seat and drive away, leaving the car they had stopped behind.

All of this plays out in less than three minutes.

That scene is included in newly released video footage documenting Tuesday morning’s ICE arrest on State Street. The video was recorded by one of the New Haven Police Department’s (NHPD) Milestone cameras.

The NHPD provided that video to the Independent a day after federal immigration agents arrested Diaz-Perez in the middle of the day on the downtown corridor. Diaz-Perez had just left the latest hearing in his ongoing criminal case at a courthouse a few blocks away.

Meanwhile, Diaz-Perez has since been transferred to Plymouth County Correctional Facility in Plymouth, Mass., according to ICE’s online detainee locator.

In a statement sent to the Independent on Wednesday, an anonymous DHS spokesperson said ICE arrested Diaz-Perez “during a targeted operation in New Haven” on Tuesday.

The spokesperson described Diaz-Perez as a “criminal illegal alien from Guatemala” and noted that he had been arrested by city police on Aug. 30 on various charges, including aggravated assault.

The DHS spokesperson said that ICE “lodged a detainer for Diaz-Perez” on Sept. 3, “but the Connecticut Department of Corrections released him back into the community.”

The DHS spokesperson also wrote that, during Tuesday’s arrest, Diaz-Perez “refused lawful commands to exit his vehicle.” They also said that a “passenger in Diaz-Perez’s vehicle attempted to physically interfere with the arrest.”

That account differs from the one given by the driver, Catherine John, an organizer with Black and Brown United in Action. She said agents boxed in her car on State Street near Court Street around 11:30 a.m. Tuesday, broke a rear window, and dragged Diaz-Perez out of the car. When Diaz-Perez’s father got out to ask what was happening, John said, an agent grabbed him and threw him, hurting his head in the process.

The DHS statement did not address the car’s broken window nor the allegations that an agent struck Diaz-Perez’s father. The NHPD video does not show the side of John’s vehicle with the broken window. It’s unclear from the video when the window is broken.

Instead, the DHS statement said ICE officers are “trained to use the minimum amount of force necessary to resolve dangerous situations to prioritize the safety of the public and our officers.”

Both Catherine John and John Lugo of Unidad Latina en Accion (ULA) disputed ICE’s written account.

“That is not true,” Lugo said. “You can see in the video, his father didn’t physically interfere with ICE,” Lugo said in reference to a video taken by a bystander. The NHPD video does show Diaz-Perez’s father exiting the vehicle, but it does not appear to show him interfering with the ICE agents. Instead, it shows him being pushed back into the car.

“It is wild that they could say something like this,” said Catherine John.

Lugo said that Diaz-Perez’s father, who went to the hospital after the encounter with ICE, was in stable condition as of Wednesday.

Lugo also said Diaz-Perez told him that, after the arrest, he was denied medical attention for his injuries until Tuesday evening.

ICE did not respond to a question about Diaz-Perez’s medical status.

New Haven police spokesperson Officer Christian Bruckhart said police first learned of the ICE arrest when a city police officer stopped Catherine John shortly afterward as she was using her phone while driving Diaz-Perez’s father to the hospital and she told him what happened.

Catherine John said that the officer called a supervisor and documented the incident.

DHS’s statement also laid out Diaz-Perez’s immigration history.

The agency said Border Patrol arrested him in January 2022, when he was roughly 14 years old, after he illegally entered the country near Hidalgo, Texas, “and the Biden administration RELEASED him into the country.”

Lugo said Diaz-Perez was in the process of obtaining legal status. DHS’s statement said that “work authorization does not confer legal status in the U.S.”

Diaz-Perez’s immigration attorney, Yasmin Rodriguez, could not be reached for comment at the time of publication.

Diaz-Perez was at the courthouse at 121 Elm St. on Tuesday for a hearing in a pending criminal case – not an immigration matter.

According to court records, New Haven police arrested him on Aug. 30 and charged him with first-degree assault, interfering with an officer and evading responsibility in a crash that caused serious injury. He was released after posting a $200,000 bond and has not entered a plea.

The Connecticut constitution says that every person facing a pending criminal charge has a constitutional right to have bail or release conditions set.

Mayor Justin Elicker said that regardless of the charges against Diaz-Perez, he “still deserves due process.”

ICE described the interfering charge as a felony; court records list it as a misdemeanor.

The arrest came about 10 months after ICE arrested a man inside the 121 Elm St. courthouse in January. A state law passed in November 2025 restricts civil immigration arrests on courthouse grounds and expands the area around courthouses where people are shielded from such arrests.

Rhonda Hebert, a Judicial Branch spokesperson, said the area near State and Court streets where Tuesday’s arrest took place “is not considered court grounds,” so ICE was not required to notify the court.

She said marshals and court staff were not aware of ICE agents near the courthouse that morning and the Judicial Branch had no comment on the arrest.

DHS said Diaz-Perez will “receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.”

Other audience members were sharply critical of the “crowd control” response by Morristown police on that morning of Oct. 29, 2026, suggesting it gave the appearance of police cooperation with ICE, prohibited by state law.

The mayor, police chief and public safety director vigorously maintained that police were only there to protect the public — called to the scene by a Morris County dispatcher, according to the mayor, in a testy exchange with speakers who were cut short by the council’s three-minute limit on public statements.

“If ICE is there without a warrant, they need to bring their own crowd control. (Morristown’s police presence) is breaking public trust with police,” Joseph Bellomo insisted to Morristown Green.

The Morris Plains resident, a retired social studies teacher, had gotten wind of an ICE vehicle near a school bus stop at Abbett and Lincoln Street on that October morning and helped escort children onto school buses, he said, to reassure them. Then he heard about the enforcement action and joined other bystanders there.

Trink Prinz, a former member of Morristown’s now-defunct EMT squad, told the council that she found videos appearing to show collaboration of Morristown police with ICE “deeply disturbing.”

Adam McGovern, of the Project NINJA group opposing an ICE detention center in Roxbury, called for “more proactive noncooperation” with ICE.

Citing a recent Washington Post investigation revealing the checkered pasts of some ICE hires, and a Prison Policy Initiative report contending New Jersey’s “wishy washy compromises” have failed to slow aggressive ICE enforcement, McGovern challenged local police to show “the same courage” as Renee Good and Alex Pretti — activists killed by ICE agents in Minnesota.

“Why are officers only treating ICE intruders as the ones needing protection? Are they asking to see a judicial warrant, or even an ID, so they know if these guys are even who they say they are, and not committing a crime themselves?” asked McGovern, who described ICE agents as “thugs.”

Calling claims of collaboration “not factual,” Mayor Tim Dougherty asked Police Chief Darnell Richardson and Public Safety Director Michael Corcoran Jr. to explain what happened.

Richardson said police did not know ICE was coming, and responded to a request from the county dispatcher for help managing the crowd. “There was no collaboration… We kept control of the crowd… That was our own agenda: Keep the peace between the public and the ICE agent.”

The chief told Morristown Green that his officer at the scene did not observe an assault on Brown, who did not file a complaint. Brown, a 44-year-old retired pediatrician, was uninjured. She said she was not comfortable filing a complaint against the federal Department of Homeland Security. She stood by her video, which she said was unedited.

Corcoran said police would not do anything to jeopardize their “outstanding relationship” with Morristown’s sizable Latino community, nor would they violate the state law that bans assisting ICE in most circumstances.

“We act in the interest of public safety,” Corcoran said. “ICE … doesn’t give us information that they’re coming. They just show up. We have to respond and react to the situation at hand and maintain public safety. And that’s our role. We follow the Immigrant Trust Act as codified, and we always will.”

The Department of Homeland Security, which declined to identify the ICE officer who confronted Brown, has denied her assault accusation as “categorically FALSE.”

In a statement after the incident, DHS said it had been conducting a targeted enforcement operation to arrest a “criminal illegal alien from El Salvador and MS-13 gang member” when an “anti-ICE agitator refused to observe officers’ lawful commands.” DHS asserted its officers are the ones who need protection from a “coordinated campaign of violence” and rising death threats.

Morristown has been the target of a series of ICE sweeps this year. Dougherty predicted raids will intensify, citing President Trump’s promotion of Stephen Miller — architect of the administration’s mass deportation policy — to his chief of staff in the wake of Democrats’ huge wins in this month’s congressional midterm elections.

ICE officers are “a bunch of cowboys on the street,” untrained and inhumane, Dougherty said. “I wish they would stay out of Morristown, but they don’t… Our hands are kind of tied. ”

IN OTHER BUSINESS…

The council unanimously introduced measures to extend hours for the town’s lone cannabis shop, and adjust liquor serving hours for bars and restaurants.

If it passes muster with the planning board, the council next month is likely to extend cannabis dispensary and retailer hours to 7:00 a.m. to midnight Monday through Saturday and noon to midnight on Sundays. Currently Uma Flowers operates from 9 am to 10 pm Monday through Saturday, and noon to 10 pm on Sunday.

Councilman David Silva questioned the change but voted for its introduction. Council President Steve Pylypchuk said he had heard no negative reports and called the increase insignificant.

The other ordinance amendment seeks to create a uniform 10 am start for alcohol service at licensed establishments, benefiting the Sunday brunch scene. Presently, noon is the Sunday start, with 7 am starts the rest of the week. Pylypchuk noted the 7 am start for alcohol service on Saint Patrick’s Parade day is preserved in the ordinance and New Year’s Eve extended service from 2 a.m. to 3 a.m. remains unchanged.

The council also adopted an ordinance moving forward plans for a linear park and preservation of a 19th century site of a school house for Black children. The plans were part of the approvals for a redevelopment scheduled to bring 150 residential units, including 30 designated as affordable, to Spring Street.

Todd Cohen, who lost his father to pancreatic cancer, shared grim statistics after accepting a mayoral proclamation for National Pancreatic Cancer Awareness Month. Cohen has appeared annually since 2015 urging public support for research.

On a lighter note, Councilman Nathan Umbriac noted after the meeting that the unbeaten 7th and 8th grade Junior Colonials football teams will play at Morristown High School this Sunday at 1:30 pm and 3 pm, respectively, for Super Bowl championships. They’re facing Hunterdon Central from Flemington. Go Colonials!

And council members applauded Vice President Chris Russo, who last week became the first Democrat in 53 years elected to the Morris County Board of Commissioners. The mayor said it was “bittersweet” losing him from the council, but good to gain an ally at the county level.

“It’s been a pleasure working with all of you. I see you not only as colleagues but friends,” said Russo, a protege of Dougherty’s in his first term representing the Fourth Ward.

Umbriac, who chairs the town’s Democratic committee, said the organization is looking for three candidates to present to the council in January to fill Russo’s unexpired term. Russo, who also must step down from the planning board, will be sworn in to his county post on Jan. 6, 2027.

title: More Than 30% of All Immigrants Detained in ICE Jails Now Have Their Location Hidden ...
description:

The change targets people with administratively final removal orders.

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is withholding the detention locations of thousands of immigrants with final deportation orders, a policy that has removed an estimated 30% of detainees from its public tracking system and drawn a federal lawsuit over access to lawyers and families.

The New York Times reported that a Department of Homeland Security document announcing the change included a script for contractors answering inquiries about detainees. Callers seeking the whereabouts of affected immigrants were to be told that the information was not public.

The change targets people with administratively final removal orders. According to a complaint filed Oct. 28 in federal court in Massachusetts, ICE began excluding those detainees from its Online Detainee Locator System around Sept. 15, with exceptions for four facilities. The complaint also alleges that officers were instructed to refuse location information requested by relatives or attorneys.

The widely circulated figure of 30% is an estimate, rather than a verified count of everyone currently missing from the locator. The plaintiffs cited July detention data showing an average daily population of 66,904, including 21,700 people with final removal orders, approximately 32%. They estimated that more than 20,000 people were affected when the policy began.

One case illustrating the consequences involves Ann Lawani, a Nigerian nurse and University of San Francisco nursing professor detained at her home in Lodi, California, in September.

Rep. Josh Harder, D-Calif., has demanded her return to California, saying she has judicial protection allowing her to remain in the United States. Her exclusion from the locator left relatives and her attorney struggling to track her after she was transferred to Louisiana, KQED reported.

"ICE has also reportedly pursued her removal to an undisclosed third country without providing her or her attorney with the relevant documentation," Harder wrote in an Oct. 20 letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

For immigration lawyers, locating someone in custody is often the first step toward arranging a confidential conversation, reviewing documents, or seeking emergency court intervention.

The National Immigration Project says people with final removal orders can still have legal options, including seeking to reopen immigration proceedings, challenging detention in federal court or obtaining help with medical care and mistreatment. Its attorneys say the policy has forced legal organizations to spend hours calling detention centers and relatives, while some prospective clients have never been located.

DHS has argued that immigrants with final removal orders have already received due process, according to the AP. Immigration advocates counter that an order does not eliminate every available legal remedy or the need to communicate with counsel.

The lawsuit was brought by Greater Boston Legal Services, Rian Immigrant Center, Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project and Amica Center for Immigrant Rights.

Their challenge alleges violations of the Administrative Procedure Act and the First Amendment. It also includes claims that the government violated the Freedom of Information Act by failing to publish the policy.

The organizations are asking the court to set aside the restrictions and require disclosure of the policy. They argue that withholding detainees' locations obstructs communication at the moment legal assistance can be most urgent, before a transfer or deportation makes reaching a client even harder.

text:
A University of Maryland student who was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents alongside her mother last week is speaking out from an immigration detention facility in Louisiana.

Maria Flores Garcia, a former valedictorian at Parkdale High School in Prince George's County, was taken into custody during a routine immigration check-in with her mother at an ICE office in Baltimore.

Flores Garcia, who is originally from El Salvador, came to the United States when she was 9 years old.

"I'm here with my mom, so that's nice," Flores Garcia told WUSA9, the CBS affiliate in Washington, D.C. "But you look at your surroundings and you're like, 'Oh my God, nobody deserves to be here. Especially me.'"

From high school valedictorian to immigration detention

Flores Garcia was the 2026 valedictorian at Parkdale High School before receiving a full scholarship to the University of Maryland.

During her high school graduation, she spoke about the challenges she and her family faced after coming to Maryland from El Salvador. She said those experiences motivated her to excel academically and show that anything is possible.

Flores Garcia was accompanying her mother to the immigration check-in. When ICE agents moved to take her mother into custody, Flores Garcia chose to remain with her.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said Flores Garcia and her mother entered the United States illegally and were arrested in the Rio Grande Valley of Texas in 2016.

DHS said they were placed in removal proceedings but released into the country. An immigration judge issued a final order of removal on Feb. 23, 2021, according to the agency.

"She will remain in ICE custody pending her removal from the United States. This administration will not ignore the rule of law," the DHS spokesperson said.

"My life outside is on pause"

"I keep thinking, 'Oh, I should be doing this in my math class, or going to my class,'" Flores Garcia told WUSA9.

Flores Garcia said she is not alone in the facility, describing other detainees who have no criminal records and have built lives in the United States.

"Sadly, I'm not the only person that has no criminal record, that has made a life in the United States without hurting anybody that's in here," Flores Garcia said. "There's millions and millions of stories in the cell. Everybody here misses their family."

She described conditions inside the detention facility as "devastating."

"It's just a big room. You can hear the people coughing. It smells in here," she said.

In an interview with CBS News Baltimore, Flores Garcia said she is trying to remain positive and support others around her.

"I'm definitely trying to keep my essence and stay true to myself as much as I can," she said. "There's obviously times where I break down because it's devastating being here, knowing that my life outside is on pause. That I didn't do anything to be here."

Gov. Wes Moore voices support

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore voiced his support for Flores Garcia in a social media post Wednesday.

"Maria Flores Garcia should be home with her family today," Moore said. "Instead, President Trump's ICE agents detained Maria – a Marylander, high school valedictorian, and University of Maryland student – as she accompanied her mother to an immigration check-in last week."

Moore criticized the administration's immigration enforcement, saying ICE was not targeting only people with serious criminal records.

"ICE isn't rounding up 'the worst of the worst.' This is just pure cruelty for cruelty's sake," Moore said. "If the President is actually serious about wanting to work with the incoming Democratic majority on an immigration deal, he must end ICE's attacks on our communities and our people like Maria."

title: St. Johns school custodian denied bond, remains detained in New Mexico after federal court battle
description:
An immigration judge denied him a bond hearing in August.
On Nov. 1, U.S. District granted the petition and ordered that Linares receive a bond hearing within seven days.
The Immigration Judge denied bond, ruling that Linares was a flight risk, according to the bond denial order.
Linares remains detained at the Cibola County Correctional Center in New Mexico, according to his attorney and family.
A habeas ruling that orders a bond hearing does not itself guarantee release.
text:
ST. JOHNS COUNTY. Fla. – Leonel Armando Bolivar Linares, a 29-year-old Venezuelan, was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Aug. 6, 2026, while on his way to work in St. Johns County.

At the time, Linares had an approved work permit and a pending asylum case, according to his family and attorney. An immigration judge denied him a bond hearing in August. His attorney filed a habeas corpus petition in federal court on Aug. 17, challenging his continued detention.

On Nov. 1, U.S. District granted the petition and ordered that Linares receive a bond hearing within seven days. The hearing took place Nov. 5. The Immigration Judge denied bond, ruling that Linares was a flight risk, according to the bond denial order.

The order rejected four proposed sponsors, all U.S. citizens, individually by name. One of the sponsors, Gregory Gonzalez, said the family expected Linares to be released.

“We were set to pick him up at the airport on Saturday because we thought he was going to get out,” Gonzalez said. When we got the news that he wasn’t coming home, we were devastated.

Linares remains detained at the Cibola County Correctional Center in New Mexico, according to his attorney and family. The facility is roughly 1,500 miles from St. Johns County.

His parents said the bond decision was unfair.

“It’s not fair. It’s not what they’re doing with Leo,” they said. Leo has no criminal record and they are violating his human rights."

They also criticized the hearing, saying it lasted about five minutes.

“It was a trial that lasted five minutes. You can’t know if a person is good or bad in five minutes,” his parents said. “We arrived in this country for humanitarian reasons. We didn’t enter this country illegally.”

Gonzalez said the judge’s assessment of the sponsors offended him.

“We’ve been just trying to do the right thing. And for some guy to just go up there five minutes later and say your sponsor can hide you or whatever — I found that offensive, because you don’t know anything about me or my character,” he said.

Linares’ asylum application was denied Oct. 5, and an appeal was filed with the Board of Immigration Appeals on Oct. 30, according to his attorney.

A habeas ruling that orders a bond hearing does not itself guarantee release. Lasnetski Gihon Law said that after an immigration judge denies bond, a person may return to the district court and argue that the hearing was a sham and request immediate release. The firm said district courts often deny such requests because immigration judges’ discretionary bond decisions generally are not reviewable there. If there is a factual basis for the denial, the firm said, an appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals may be the only recourse; the board is part of the executive branch.

In August, the Department of Homeland Security said Linares entered the United States lawfully through Miami International Airport on Feb. 3, 2023. DHS said the U.S. Supreme Court upheld the termination of Venezuela’s 2023 Temporary Protected Status designation, and said Linares “does not have legal authorization to remain in the United States.” The agency said he would remain in ICE custody for immigration proceedings.

Until then, his sponsors, along with his family, say they will do everything they can within the legal proceedings to bring him home.

“Leo and his family have our support, and hopefully this can get this resolved, and they go back to living their lives here and get what everybody calls the American dream,” said Gonzalez.

ICE and DHS have not responded to News4JAX’s follow-up request for comment on the court ruling, bond denial, or Linares’ current detention. This is a developing story; News4JAX will provide updates as more information becomes available.

text:
Rep. Josh Harder (D-Stockton) is calling for the release of a nurse who was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents and sent across the country, 1,700 miles from home.

Nurse detained by ICE

What we know:

ICE agents arrested Ann Lawani in September in Lodi, Calif., where she lives and cares for her elderly father. Lawani has professional ties to both the University of San Francisco and John Muir Health in the Bay Area.

According to the Department of Homeland Security, Lawani entered the U.S. legally on a temporary basis from Nigeria in 2007, but overstayed that admittance. She is currently being detained in Louisiana.

In late October,Harder sent a letter to DHS demanding her supervised release and immediate return to California while her immigration case remains pending.

"ICE has also reportedly pursued her removal to an undisclosed third country without providing her or her attorney with the relevant documentation," Harder wrote. "These circumstances raise serious concerns about due process, transparency, and the justification for her continued detention."

On Wednesday, California Sen. Jerry McNerney (D-Stockton) also condemned ICE.

"Ann Lawani is a highly respected and beloved nurse and professor who lives in my Senate district," McNerney said in a statement. "ICE disappearing her from her home is an absolute outrage. It’s even more outrageous that ICE essentially kidnapped Professor Lawani, shackled her at the ankles, waist and hands, and secreted her to Louisiana, without notifying her family, her attorney, or the public – despite the fact that she has a valid federal work permit to stay in the U.S.."

To date, ICE "has disappeared" an estimated 20,000 people throughout the nation, effectively denying them their right to due process, McNerney added.

No comment

What we don't know:

ICE did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday on Lawani's transfers or her absence from the agency's detainee locator.

Lawani's brother, Samuel Lawani, described his sister as a caring medical professional who was dedicated to helping her father, patients, and students with equal attention.

"My sister is an amazing caregiver, healthcare leader, and educator in our community, and I was devastated not just at her unacceptable arrest, but the decision to send her across the country and detain her unnecessarily," he said in a statement provided by Harder's office. "Not only is Dr. Ann a scholar in her profession, but an extremely skilled nurse with unmatched dedication to her patients and students alike. She gives everything she has, daily, to save lives and train the nurses of the future to be as trained, ready and dedicated as she is."

As the program director for University of San Francisco's master's in nursing degree, Lawani also oversees the nursing education of about 230 students.

Absence causes harm: USF

What they're saying:

Eileen Fry-Bowers, dean of the School of Nursing and Health Professions at USF, said in a statement shared by Harder that Lawani's absence was being acutely felt by students and colleagues.

"Her continued absence causes real and mounting harm to the students and faculty who rely on her mentorship, to our accreditation-mandated curriculum work, and to the safety-net partnerships she has built," Fry-Bowers said.

Harder said in his letter that Lawani had complied with all previous requirements placed on her by immigration authorities, so there was no reason not to allow her to remain free while any potential immigration proceedings play out.

He added that what happened to Lawani raises broad questions about the department’s priorities, such as why significant taxpayer resources are used to target and transport people like Lawani.

"Her case illustrates the troubling consequences of an enforcement approach that fails to adequately distinguish between individuals who threaten our communities and those who help sustain them," Harder wrote.

text:
The transcript version of our weekly Q&A for corporate immigration professionals. Join our Immigration News Digest Newsletter for more immigration updates.

By Kimberley Best Robidoux & Miki Kawashima Matrician

🎧 Available on YouTube & Spotify

In this edition of Rapid-Fire Wednesdays, WR Immigration attorneys Kimberley Best Robidoux and Miki Kawashima Matrician discuss what the 2026 midterm election results could mean for U.S. immigration policy and employers. With Democrats gaining control of both chambers of Congress and flipping several traditionally Republican governorships, the election results could bring significant changes to immigration oversight, enforcement funding, and state-level policy. Topics include congressional oversight of immigration agencies, appropriations restrictions on ICE, the prospects for immigration legislation, anticipated regulatory changes, the Congressional Review Act, and the role of state governors and attorneys general in challenging federal immigration policies. Discover what employers, HR teams, and Global Mobility professionals should be watching as the immigration landscape evolves.

Question 1: How could Democratic control of Congress change immigration oversight?

Response: Democratic control of both chambers of Congress gives the new majority control over committee leadership, hearings, investigations, and the legislative agenda. One of Congress’s most significant tools is its oversight authority. Committee chairs can call agency officials to testify, request documents, issue subpoenas, and investigate federal agencies involved in immigration, including ICE, USCIS, CBP, the Department of State, and the Department of Labor. Congress can also ask the Government Accountability Office and agency inspectors general to review worksite enforcement, processing delays, adjudication holds, and agency spending. These efforts could produce more public information about agency practices and increase pressure on agencies to streamline adjudications. Congress also has authority to inspect immigration detention facilities, providing another avenue for oversight of DHS operations.

Question 2: What can Congress do through its power of the purse to influence immigration enforcement?

Response: Congress can use appropriations legislation to place conditions on how ICE and other federal agencies spend their funding. Potential measures include restricting funding for certain enforcement practices, limiting transfers between agency accounts, imposing reporting requirements, requiring access to detention facilities, and setting conditions on private detention contracts. Congress could also decline to fund new enforcement initiatives. These appropriations provisions can create leverage in negotiations with the administration, particularly regarding ICE enforcement, detention spending, workplace actions, and the use of private contractors. On the other hand, Congress could direct additional funding toward USCIS processing, immigration courts, asylum adjudications, legal orientation programs, and agency oversight. Employers should watch how funding decisions affect agency resources, enforcement priorities, and immigration processing.

Question 3: Does Democratic control of Congress make comprehensive immigration reform more likely?

Response: Comprehensive immigration reform remains unlikely without support from the White House or a significant bipartisan coalition. Although Democrats will control both chambers, President Trump retains veto authority, and the new majority is not expected to have the two-thirds support in both chambers necessary to override a veto. Large legislative packages addressing legalization, asylum, family-based immigration, and employment-based immigration will therefore face significant obstacles. However, more targeted bipartisan legislation may have a path forward, particularly when attached to must-pass bills. Potential areas include visa number recapture, protections for certain long-term residents, targeted workforce programs, and agency funding. President Trump has also indicated a willingness to negotiate with Democrats on immigration, although the appointment of Stephen Miller as Chief of Staff suggests that disagreements between Congress and the Executive Branch will likely continue.

Question 4: Could the election results accelerate pending immigration regulations?

Response: The administration may try to finalize pending immigration regulations before the new Congress takes office and begins its oversight work. Several proposals are already in the pipeline involving employment-based immigration, student work authorization, grace periods, and public charge. Finalizing a regulation before the new Congress convenes could put the policy in a stronger position than leaving it as a proposal. However, moving quickly also creates litigation risks. Agencies must comply with the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), including responding to public comments, explaining their decisions, and assessing costs and reliance interests. Failure to follow required procedures could expose finalized regulations to legal challenges. Employers should continue monitoring pending proposals and be prepared for potential changes.

Question 5: How does the Congressional Review Act allow Congress to challenge recently issued regulations?

Response: The Congressional Review Act (CRA) allows Congress to pass a joint resolution invalidating a recently issued final rule. If the resolution becomes law, the rule is invalidated, and the agency generally cannot issue another substantially similar rule unless Congress subsequently authorizes it. The CRA includes expedited procedures, and certain rules issued late in a congressional session may receive an additional review period when the next Congress convenes. The exact lookback period depends on the congressional calendar. However, the CRA has an important limitation: the joint resolution must be presented to the President. President Trump could veto a resolution disapproving a regulation issued by his own administration. Without the two-thirds majority needed to override that veto, Democratic control of Congress alone may not be enough to overturn recently finalized regulations through the CRA.

Question 6: How could newly elected Democratic governors influence immigration policy?

Response: Although immigration is primarily governed by federal law, states have authority over their own agencies and how state resources are used. Governors cannot grant immigration status, issue visas, or prevent federal immigration enforcement. However, they can influence state policies involving information sharing, cooperation with federal enforcement, access to state services, workplace notice requirements, and professional licensing. State responses to federal enforcement activity may also become an important area of focus. Employers should remember that governors do not necessarily control their state’s attorney general. In states where the attorney general is independently elected, the two officials may take different positions on immigration matters. Employers should therefore monitor both offices when evaluating a state’s immigration posture.

Question 7: How might states challenge federal immigration regulations and executive actions?

Response: Democratic governors and state attorneys general may work together to challenge federal immigration policies through litigation, as occurred with challenges to the 2019 public charge rule. States can argue that the federal government exceeded its statutory authority, violated the APA, failed to consider the impact of its actions on states, or violated constitutional protections. For example, a coalition led by California, New York, and Illinois has challenged the administration’s 2026 public charge rule, arguing that the rule exceeds DHS’s authority and is arbitrary and capricious. These lawsuits may provide an important check on federal immigration policy. However, litigation outcomes and timelines are unpredictable. A court must issue an injunction, stay, or vacatur before implementation of a challenged policy is legally blocked.

Question 8: What should employers and Global Mobility teams watch following the 2026 midterm elections?

Response: Employers should monitor developments across Congress, federal agencies, state governments, and the courts. Congressional oversight could generate greater transparency into agency practices and enforcement priorities, while appropriations legislation could affect agency resources and operations. Targeted immigration legislation may advance even if comprehensive reform remains unlikely. At the same time, pending regulations could be finalized before the new Congress takes office, creating potential compliance changes and litigation risks. State governors and attorneys general may also take a more active role in challenging federal immigration policies. HR, Legal, and Global Mobility teams should stay informed about legislative developments, regulatory changes, court decisions, and new agency guidance to anticipate potential impacts on immigration sponsorship, workforce planning, and employer compliance.

About the Authors

Kimberley Best Robidoux is a Partner in WR Immigration’s San Diego office with 25+ years of experience advising employers and individuals on business immigration, immigration compliance, and I-9 and E-Verify matters. She currently serves as the Chair of the American Immigration Lawyers Association’s Verification and Documentation Committee and has been recognized by The Best Lawyers in America®, Super Lawyers®, Who’s Who Legal: Corporate Immigration, Lawdragon and other leading publications.

text:
Evidence mounts that some of the people who answered the call to become Immigration and Custom Enforcement agents over the past two years aren’t very good guys. Who’d have thought, right?

The Washington Post was able to infiltrate the blackout curtains our federal government has drawn around the ICE employee directory, a move the administration has defended as a way to protect the masked force from harassment.

Too bad. Hackers busted into a Department of Homeland Security database in October and named names of about 1,500 agents. The Washington Post ran background checks on 300 of them, and found public documentation proving that at least 19 of those have no business going out in public with guns.

Per the Washington Post:

“The Post found at least 19 officers who had faced past allegations of misconduct or criminal charges, or had other employment red flags. At least five involved use-of-force incidents, and five officers were named in lawsuits that resulted in settlements. In at least six cases, the officers had been fired or decertified, or resigned under threat of dismissal. The leaked information represents a small fraction of the 12,000 officers DHS said it had hired as of January.”

Arkansan Dnae Reo Blow made this list of shame, having been fired from the Springdale police force in 2016 after allegedly threatening a supervisor and then fired from the Lowell force in 2018 for insubordination. ICE hired Blow in 2025, per the WaPo report.

How many more guys has ICE sent out there with anger issues and electrocution gloves?

The Department of Homeland Security hired 12,000 new troops through 2025 and into 2026 as ICE actions surged across the country, perhaps most famously in Minneapolis, where masked marauders fatally shot U.S. citizens Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti. Federal immigration agents have shot scores more people during President Donald Trump’s second administration. And dozens have died in ICE custody.

On the bright side, voters look to be rejecting the government’s kidnapping of innocent people, including hundreds of U.S. citizens.

That roughly 70% of people detained by ICE have no criminal record doesn’t appear to matter much to President Trump, who doubled down last week by elevating Stephen Miller, the reputed architect of the recent deadly raids and purges, to be his chief of staff.

Arkansas Gov. Sarah Sanders, long a cheerleader for family separation for brown people, applauded Miller’s ascension during an appearance on “The View” Monday, where she was touting her new book, “Unapologetic: Clarity and Conviction in a World Gone Crazy.”

name: Policy
title: Democrats push to rein in Trump on immigration after voter backlash to ICE raids
description:
“I have very aspirational dreams and hopes for immigration reform.
There was no detailed talk on Wednesday of how to abolish or even significantly reform Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) despite it being a hot topic during the election campaign.
“We all can agree that the immigration system is broken.
Separately, the Dignity Act is the only bipartisan, comprehensive immigration reform bill introduced in over a decade, with 35 Democratic and 20 Republican sponsors.
“We need to bring sanity back to the immigration system.
text:
A group of congressional Democrats on Wednesday pushed for immediate efforts to rein in the Trump administration’s sweeping immigration enforcement operation and “bring sanity” to an immigration system that Donald Trump said, after his party’s midterm drubbing, had been “too tough” in certain aspects.

Just over a week after the midterm elections in which the US president’s harsh crackdown on immigration fueled a voter backlash against Republicans, some sitting and newly elected Democrats gathered outside the US Capitol in Washington to advocate for a bipartisan approach to reforms – even as they gear up to take control of both legislative chambers next year.

“I have very aspirational dreams and hopes for immigration reform. But I am also a pragmatist. And as we have – as we continue to have – Donald Trump in the White House, and without a supermajority in the Senate, we need Republican support. So any comprehensive immigration reform must be bipartisan,” said congresswoman Veronica Escobar, a Democrat from Texas whose district includes El Paso on the US-Mexico border.

The group’s press conference included progressive as well as moderate Democrats from the Senate and House, in a show of unity. Many attendees held signs saying “legal pathways for long-term immigrants”.

The one Republican lawmaker slated to attend, congresswoman Maria Salazar of Florida, who has taken jabs at the president over immigration that are rare from his side of the aisle, did not appear.

“There is time still this session for a deal,” said US senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona. “We should try to work, even if we can’t get something this session, next session for a deal. We owe it to this country. We owe it to our friends.”

He added: “Republicans have been saying we will have immigration reform as soon as we have a safe, secure border. We have that right now. We did the job. Now let’s figure out how to right-size our immigration issue. Let’s figure out how to keep families together.”

The remarks followed Trump’s aggressive mass deportation campaign and ruthless moves that dramatically slowed crossings at the border, beginning as soon as he re-entered the White House in January 2025. His Democratic predecessor Joe Biden saw significantly elevated levels of migration at the border, and despite his at times harsh approach, the subject of migration became a high-risk political topic for Democrats, who gained a reputation as being too soft on the issue.

Since then, Trump’s second term has also seen US citizens and immigrants killed by immigration enforcement agents, record numbers of people held in often squalid detention conditions and highly visible, violent tactics in the country’s interior that led many voters to sour on some of his policies or at least how they are carried out.

The president’s mixed messages post-midterms included a tentative offer to make a deal with Democrats to help longstanding and law-abiding undocumented immigrants in the US avoid his crackdown. But that contrasted sharply with his actions so far, and shortly after the comments were recorded for TV he named Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff despite him being the architect and orchestrator of Trump’s most draconian, white nationalist immigration policies.

Trump has also signaled that he intends to use his presidential veto power often to block Democratic-supported legislation if it passes Congress.

At the same time, experts expect a barrage of investigations and oversight hearings from Democrats next year in an effort to bring accountability.

But lawmakers on Wednesday said they did not want to wait that long to begin improving the immigration system, highlighting two existing bipartisan bills they believe could be a practical starting point. There was no detailed talk on Wednesday of how to abolish or even significantly reform Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) despite it being a hot topic during the election campaign.

The first highlighted by the lawmakers who spoke on Wednesday, the American Dream and Promise Act, focuses on providing legal pathways to a green card for undocumented immigrants brought stateside as children, colloquially known as “Dreamers”, as well as people with temporary protections to remain in the US while their country of origin experiences serious turmoil.

Not only has Trump not offered such a path, his administration stopped recognizing many temporary legal statuses awarded under past Democratic administrations and has been deporting or trying to deport many who have papers or long-term legal options.

Lawmakers on Wednesday pitched the proposed legislation as an opportunity to act even before the new Democratically-controlled Congress is sworn in come January, asking for Trump’s help in getting it past the finish line.

“We all can agree that the immigration system is broken. But we can start today on a path to build a foundation with the Dream and Promise Act, and to move forward next year when we take over to make even more reforms,” said representative Sylvia Garcia of Texas.

Separately, the Dignity Act is the only bipartisan, comprehensive immigration reform bill introduced in over a decade, with 35 Democratic and 20 Republican sponsors. It couples strict border security measures with some protections for undocumented people.

Salazar is the bill’s lead sponsor. But Escobar, one of the Dignity Act’s fiercest champions and its co-author, said that she and her colleagues planned to reshape it over the next few weeks before reintroducing it next legislative session.

“If we can get this passed this upcoming Congress, we can do even more in 2028 to grow and expand what we can do for immigrants, immigrant families, and our economy and our communities,” she said. “We need to bring sanity back to the immigration system. We can do this. We will do this.”

Meanwhile, representative Henry Cuellar, another Texas border-area Democrat, expects to chair the House appropriations homeland security subcommittee in the new year – and thus control the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) funding.

text:
While detained at Michigan’s North Lake Processing Center, Lucia learned she was pregnant—a nightmare scenario for her and many other women who are held in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody while pregnant.

“I prayed every day for God to take care of my little angel,” said Lucia, who is using a pseudonym for fear of retaliation and harm.

Originally from Venezuela, Lucia left the political turmoil of her home country in 2022 as the COVID-19 pandemic also abruptly ended her ability to study nursing.

“I left because I was looking for a better future,” she said.

She was in the U.S. for three years before the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) rescinded Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for multiple countries, including Venezuela, in February 2025. An ICE traffic stop that year in Detroit landed Lucia in detention, just weeks after her partner was also detained by ICE.

Lucia was transferred to four different detention centers before arriving at the South Louisiana Processing Center in Basile, Louisiana. She described her time there as “horrible.”

“I saw many high-risk pregnancies,” Lucia said.

Her own pregnancy was classified as high-risk due to a previous miscarriage. Lucia told Prism that she met dozens of pregnant women while in detention.

“I saw a woman who gave birth,” she said. “I saw her in a wheelchair with her newborn crying, and a nurse was taking her somewhere. I never saw her or her baby again.”

A recent investigation from The Guardian corroborated Lucia’s claims. ICE is arresting a record number of pregnant women and teenagers who cannot access the medical care they need, according to the reporting. At the same time, the agency appears to have lost count of how many people had miscarriages after October 2025.

In an emailed statement to Prism, a DHS representative said that “being in detention is a choice” and that “pregnancy in ICE detention is exceedingly rare.” The spokesperson also alleged that pregnant women receive regular prenatal visits, mental health services, and nutritional support.

“Claims that there are subprime conditions at ICE detention centers are false,” the representative said. “For many illegal aliens this is the best healthcare they have received their entire lives.”

According to experts and advocates, the racist cruelty and abusive immigration policies women in ICE detention face are built on a legacy of eugenics, an ideology that aimed to “improve” the human population based on white supremacy.

An alarming escalation

Often referred to as “Basile,” the South Louisiana Processing Center is the single women-only immigrant detention center in the state. In July, videos created by women detained at the facility went viral, exposing inhumane conditions and alleging sexual abuse.

Basile is located in rural Louisiana and has an extensive history of denying migrants access to food, interpreters, and medical care. The facility is 1 of 10 ICE detention centers in Louisiana, known as the “incarceration capital” of the U.S. for having the county’s highest rates of incarceration.

Documents from DHS released earlier this year further corroborated Lucia’s account of meeting a large number of pregnant women in detention.

According to government records, ICE detained approximately 498 pregnant, postpartum, or nursing immigrants between Jan. 1, 2025, and Feb. 16, 2026. The detention of pregnant people shows an alarming shift away from Biden-era policies that required their immediate release from federal custody.

Louisiana is often at the center of allegations of reproductive injustice in detention. Over the last year alone, detained women in the state have made serious allegations of medical neglect and sexual abuse. This includes the case of a Jane Doe, who alleged last year that she was sexually abused and threatened by Manuel Reyes, Basile’s former assistant warden. Trans immigrants have also alleged that Reyes “ran an off-the-books late-night work scheme” that coerced them into “physically and psychologically painful labor.”

For women detained at Basile, it can be difficult to separate fact from fiction, due to ICE’s extensive history of malpractice and dishonesty.

Lucia told Prism that this reality, paired with the everyday mistreatment of detained immigrants, has fueled an environment that is full of medical mistrust. As an example, when she was first detained at Basile, she said that women inside instructed her not to accept any vaccines or medications from the medical staff because they would “make you miscarry.” Because Prism would not reveal Lucia’s identity to DHS, the agency said it could not comment on any of her claims.

Allegations of medical abuse have been documented at other detention centers. For example, in 2020 at the Irwin County Detention Center, ICE contracted an OB-GYN named Mahendra Amin to provide care to detained women. He was later found to have carried out invasive and unnecessary gynecological procedures on detained women without their full and informed consent.

The mistreatment of pregnant people in detention was a daily reality that also shaped the views of women inside, according to Lucia. She said she once witnessed guards push a pregnant woman into solitary confinement, where she remained for several days.

“She was crying and telling me to please talk to an officer. She had gone three days without food,” Lucia recalled.

ICE did not respond to requests for comment and neither did GEO Group, the private prison company in charge of Basile.

GEO Group profits tremendously from overseeing a vast network of ICE’s detention centers. In August, GEO Group reported total revenues of up to $732.1 million—an increase of nearly $96 million—over the same period last year. President Donald Trump owns stock in GEO Group and other private prison companies financially benefiting from his immigration policies. A GEO Group subsidiary even donated more than $1.4 million to Trump’s political operation in July after his administration awarded the company detention contracts amounting to $165 million a year.

The money flowing from the detention system does not improve the healthcare detained migrants receive, according to Lucia and immigrant rights advocates.

Lucia said she was allowed just one prenatal medical visit during the four months she was detained in Louisiana. Medical services for pregnant people are typically accessed off-site, as detention centers do not employ OB-GYNs as staffers. According to Denáe Hebert, a medical advocacy program volunteer with the grassroots organization Louisiana Advocates for Immigrants in Detention, healthcare providers at nearby hospitals told her that a guard must be present during all appointments with detained immigrants. This is one of the detention system’s many overlaps with the carceral system.

In both settings, Hebert said having a guard in the exam room obliterates any possibility of confidentiality between the patient and their medical provider. Even more troubling, Hebert said, is that detained people likely don’t receive even a fraction of the healthcare they need. Hebert told Prism that she’d heard rumors from people detained in Basile that ICE has refused to pay for at least one person’s surgery.

Last year, DHS left thousands of medical claims unpaid when the agency abruptly ended its payment processing system for outside providers. Hebert and other advocates fear that this has delayed critical medical services for detained immigrants. An investigation from the Los Angeles Times detailed 2,267 unpaid DHS and ICE medical claims from last year, most of them related to pregnancy and maternal care.

“These are for-profit detention facilities,” Hebert said. “When you create an environment where that is the structure, it necessitates poor treatment. The primary objective is saving and making money, not doing what is best for the people within those facilities.”

“Nativism and eugenics co-created each other”

A system that allows private prison companies to financially benefit from detention, and detains immigrants in remote areas with little outside oversight, is poised to usher in human rights abuses, said Alexandra Minna Stern, the author of “Eugenic Nation: Faults and Frontiers of Better Breeding in Modern America” and UCLA’s dean of the humanities.

The eugenics movement began in the 19th century with British scientist Francis Galton, who believed the burgeoning field of heredity should be used to control human populations so that they could “be better,” Stern said. What constituted “better,” according to Stern, was based on ableism and racial hierarchies.

By the 20th century, the eugenics movement was global. The U.S. eugenics movement shaped sterilization campaigns and immigration laws. However, as Public Health Post reported, forced sterilization is “not a relic of our distant past.” California, a trailblazer in the eugenics movement, forcibly sterilized 150 incarcerated women between 2006 and 2010. Stern’s Sterilization and Social Justice Lab, which for 10 years studied eugenic sterilization in the U.S. during the 20th century, informed the historic California reparations bill that compensated survivors.

Immigrants’ legitimate mistrust of healthcare providers and institutions speaks to broader, historical reproductive injustices against Black and brown communities, according to advocates.

For centuries, women of color have been the target of eugenics. This includes enslavers’ reproductive violence against African women during the early colonial period until chattel slavery was abolished in 1865, the mass sterilization of Puerto Ricans through the 1960s, and eugenics policies that sterilized Mexican women in California and Indigenous women nationwide through the 1970s.

Women who were detained at Basile while pregnant told Prism that they were regularly berated by guards; forced to wear shackles on their wrists, hands, belly, and feet; and were made to eat inedible food that, in Lucia’s case, made her vomit. They also reported a lack of language access, adding to their isolation.

Experts have long said that detention is dangerous for women’s health, especially for those who are pregnant. Not only can psychological stress affect health during pregnancy, but ICE has a documented practice of subjecting women to unsafe conditions and denying prenatal care.

We would talk, and we would touch each other’s belly. She lost her baby, and it was her first pregnancy at 22 years old.

Lucia, formerly in ICE detention

Lucia still remembers comforting a friend who miscarried while detained.

“She slept in the same block as I did. We would talk, and we would touch each other’s belly,” Lucia recalled. “She lost her baby, and it was her first pregnancy at 22 years old.”

Miriam, who is using a pseudonym for fear of retaliation, is a Nicaraguan doula and organizer with Louisiana’s Southeast Dignity Not Detention Coalition (SEDND Coalition) that supports people impacted by detention. She told Prism that she has witnessed abuse and eugenic harm—and not only in detention.

Lucia was in her 20s and still pregnant when she was released from ICE custody. For the remainder of her pregnancy, Miriam supported her as a doula and interpreter. This included several instances when Miriam said she had to intervene during medical appointments because staff at the local public hospital repeatedly asked Lucia if she wanted a tubal ligation, even after she said no. Miriam said that medical staff again brought up the procedure after Lucia gave birth.

“I thought: Are you offering this to any of your white patients, or is this just because she’s a younger, brown woman?” Miriam said.

According to Lucia, being an immigrant and monolingual Spanish speaker from a Latin American country only seemed to worsen the treatment women received in healthcare settings. This was especially true in the detention system, she said.

“I remember a woman who needed a translator being berated by an officer for not eating fast enough. He threatened to throw her plate in anger,” Lucia said.

According to Stern, the eugenics movement has always operated in lockstep with immigration law. The professor attributed “nativist” restrictive immigration policy in the early 20th century to eugenic ideals of racial purity in the U.S. However, Stern noted, “nativist” is a misnomer because white Anglo-Saxon elites were not native to the U.S.

“Nativism and eugenics co-created each other, and they worked hand in hand,” Stern said, citing the 1917 Immigration Act as a policy directly shaped by eugenic goals. The law distinguished between “classes of aliens” who were “defective” and thus, should be excluded from admission to the U.S.

In “Eugenic Nation,” Stern also characterizes the earliest forms of border enforcement, carried out by the U.S. Public Health Service (USPHS), as a “eugenic endeavor.” In 1917, this included harsh quarantine measures such as kerosene baths that USPHS forced upon Mexican migrants traversing the Texas-Mexico border. Under the guise of “defending Texas” from “infected and disease-ridden Mexicans,” USPHS officials also enforced physical examinations and brandings with permanent ink. Today, medical examinations are still required as part of immigration proceedings.

Fatima Khan, a New Orleans-based immigration lawyer who previously represented detained immigrants in Louisiana, cites the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 as another example of anti-immigrant policies operating in unison with eugenic projects. For a time, the law banned Chinese migration to the U.S.

“The underlying tone was that the people who were coming to America really did want to control the makeup of the society, and it went down to race, but also religion, values, and land ownership,” Khan explained.

Like many before her, Khan traces the origins of laws related to racial superiority and migration to the trafficking of enslaved Africans.

“We can’t deny that this is baked into it,” Khan said. “We know that the criminal legal systems, especially in the South, developed from slave patrols.” Today, criminal and immigration law are so enmeshed, there’s a phrase for it: crimmigration. The overlap in these systems is perhaps most apparent in the hundreds of 287(g) agreements local law enforcement agencies have entered into with ICE, allowing them to carry out immigration enforcement.

Today, eugenics rhetoric is easy to spot in immigration discourse at the highest levels of government.

For example, Trump continues to challenge birthright citizenship and has publicly stated that immigrants are “coming in with bad genes.” Khan said these racist and xenophobic dog whistles are the same as those perpetuated by eugenics and racist movements focused on racial purity.

Over hundreds of years, eugenics transformed into policy, practice, and law, as illustrated by today’s immigration quotas, surveillance systems, detention centers, and instances of modern-day slavery.

Over hundreds of years, eugenics transformed into policy, practice, and law, as illustrated by today’s immigration quotas, surveillance systems, detention centers, and instances of modern-day slavery.

Hebert told Prism that detention centers, along with the policies and laws that shape immigration enforcement and mass incarceration, are “inherently eugenicist.”

“Folks are demonized solely because they weren’t born here, and they don’t have whatever paperwork the current administration deems that they should have,” the volunteer said.

“I never wish this on anyone”

With no human rights framework guiding their treatment, women in detention have found ways to affirm their humanity and show care for each other.

Lucia said that in detention, women were given a meager amount of toiletries intended to last the whole month but were never enough. The women often banded together to buy hygiene items they could share, and they combed and styled each other’s hair.

These are just small examples of solidarity between detained women, moments that were plentiful and brave in the face of cruelty and dehumanization.

Hebert told Prism that volunteers routinely see women translating for each other during visitation or when filling out forms, writing letters, or talking to officers.

“We’ve seen cases where folks are so ill or in so much pain that they’re not able to care of themselves … and folks who are detained with them will assist them, walking them to the bathroom and helping them shower or bringing them food,” Hebert said.

Similarly, when Miriam visits detention centers in Louisiana and Mississippi as a representative of the SEDND Coalition, she routinely encounters detained people who ask for help for those they’ve become friends with inside. More broadly, detained people show each other care by sharing resources, being a listening ear, forming networks, organizing hunger strikes, and even helping their friends inside who are struggling with suicidal ideation.

In an immigration system structured to divide people and destroy their care for each other, detained women such as Lucia banding together and taking care of each other can be an act of courage and a vision for the future.

It’s easier for Lucia to be joyful now that she is free from the literal and figurative shackles of detention.

“When I got out, I felt so happy because I had my son in my belly, and I thank God that I am out of that detention center. I never wish this on anyone, I never want to go back,” said Lucia. During an interview in February, the young mother smiled as she sat at her dining room table with her giggling 8-month-old son, the two of them now far removed from the harm they endured.

After her release from detention when she was seven months pregnant, Lucia gave birth in Louisiana and has since raised her child in the state. However, at the time of publication, she was making arrangements to return to Venezuela with her American citizen son. Many of the friends she made at Basile remain detained.

Louisiana remains the center of detention and incarceration systems in the U.S. An investigation from the New Orleans-based nonprofit newsroom The Lens found that ICE apprehensions in Louisiana are at an all-time high. And in the deportation hub of Alexandria, a family detention center was recently approved to move forward on contaminated land. The SEDND Coalition and other groups are fighting the project while providing support to people currently detained in the state.

Louisiana’s newly approved family detention center, which will detain mothers alongside their young children, brings eugenics to the forefront once again.

Miriam, who is organizing against the family detention center, said that after centuries of eugenics, any hope for justice requires dismantling the idea that immigrant families and women of color’s reproductive choices are problems “that need to be managed.”

For families such as Lucia’s who have survived these systems, it’s perhaps more difficult to envision the long arc of justice. She can think only of the pregnant women who remain locked behind bars and the freedom they desperately yearn for.

”They have to have faith that they will get out,” she said, “that all women everywhere get to be free. … That is what is important.”

text:
Right-leaning pro-Israel groups hailed President Donald Trump’s appointment of Stephen Miller as the next White House chief of staff, welcoming the Jewish aide’s appointment as a safeguard against antisemitism in an era marked by an increase in attacks on Jews and Israel. Liberal Jewish groups expressed alarm, saying his hardline politics endangered the community.

In a letter congratulating Miller, groups including the Combat Antisemitism Movement, the Louis D. Brandeis Center for Human Rights Under Law, the Zionist Organization of America expressed an interest in working with Miller to “hold institutions accountable when they fail to protect Jewish Americans from discrimination and harassment.”

The writers, who also included the American Association of Jewish Lawyers and Jurists, the Coalition for Jewish Values and the Israeli-American Civic Action Network, described Miller’s appointment as “a meaningful reflection of the longstanding contributions of Jewish Americans to public service.”

Just days after the Republican Party incurred massive losses in the midterm elections, Trump announced that he was replacing former chief of staff Susie Wiles with Miller, who had previously served as her deputy. In a Truth Social post, he described Miller as one of his “most trusted advisors.”

The chief of staff holds one of the most powerful White House positions, acting as a gatekeeper to the president and helping to shape his daily agenda.

Liberal Jewish voices warned that Trump’s promotion of Stephen Miller to the role of White House chief of staff could make Jewish communities more vulnerable.

“We expect this appointment to only reinforce some of the most dangerous ways the administration has normalized antisemitism and broader extremism,” Amy Spitalnick, CEO of the Jewish Council for Public Affairs, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, noting Miller’s embrace of anti-immigrant rhetoric popular on the far right.

Spitalnick said there is a throughline between the hard-line immigration policies Miller has shaped as a longtime confidant to Trump and the flourishing of antisemitism in recent years.

“At the core of the anti-immigrant agenda Miller has spearheaded are deeply antisemitic conspiracy theories about ‘replacement’ and ‘invasion’ that have already fueled a cycle of deadly violence targeting Jews and others,” she said.

The dueling sentiments from across the Jewish political spectrum were a signal of how divided the community has become during the second Trump term over the best means of combating antisemitism: Through aggressive policing of elite institutions, which Trump favors, or through opposition to what liberal groups say is the president’s systematic corrosion of civil rights protections.

The groups on the right that welcomed Miller’s appointment have generally been pleased by the steps Trump has taken to counter antisemitism on the left. In January 2025, Trump issued an executive order requiring new measures for combatting antisemitism. The Justice Department then launched a multi-agency Task Force to Combat Anti-Semitism. This past May, the department announced the formation of an Advisory Committee on Anti-Semitism, while emphasizing a “commitment to protecting Americans from unlawful discrimination and antisemitic threats.” Much of the focus has been on allegations of antisemitic harassment on university campuses.

While it’s unclear what Miller will do on these specific issues, his supporters see his key role as likely to strengthen such efforts.

Miller has longstanding links to Trump, including on a personal level. Miller’s wedding officiant at the Trump D.C. hotel was Rabbi Aryeh Lightstone, who was involved with the administration’s Abraham Accords to establish peaceful relations between Israel and several Arab neighbors.

But Miller’s critics have pointed out that he, along with Trump and other top Republicans have embraced troubling conspiracy theories that can be linked to Jews. Namely, that Democrats want to flood America with immigrants who are likely to vote against Republicans. At Trump’s October 2024 campaign rally at Madison Square Garden, Miller declared, “America is for Americans and Americans only.”

A more extreme version of the conspiracy theory, which blames Jews for organizing an “invasion” of people of color to replace whites, fueled a number of deadly attacks over the past decade, including the massacre at the Tree of Life synagogue in Pittsburgh in 2018.

The White House press office, which fields media communications for the chief of staff, did not respond to requests for comment.

Spitalnick also slammed the current administration for failing to “protect the civil rights of Jewish – and all – people,” by rolling back programs aimed at countering hate, including at the Office for Civil Rights in the Department of Education and extremism prevention programs at the Department of Homeland Security.

Spitalnick also referred to a 2019 letter sent by Jewish Democratic members of Congress urging Trump to dismiss Miller, who was his senior adviser at the time. The lawmakers argued that his “support for white nationalist and virulently anti-immigrant tropes is wholly unacceptable and disqualifying for a government employee.”

Regarding the current appointment, Spitalnick warned that Miller’s role could “make Jewish and so many other vulnerable communities less safe, instead of advancing the civil rights and pro-democracy policies we know are inherent to our security.”

“As the president and vice president are now seemingly pinning the U.S. election results on Israel, we should be concerned about further scapegoating of the Jewish and Israeli American communities,” she added.

The liberal pro-Israel lobby J Street, meanwhile, posted a Haaretz analysis that likened Miller to Itamar Ben-Gvir, a far-right minister in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition known for his extreme nationalistic rhetoric.

“Stephen Miller and Itamar Ben-Gvir both owe their prominence and access to power to their enablers – Trump and Netanyahu – and both traffic in racism and nativism to attempt to build power and incite fear,” the J Street post stated.

Robert Reich, U.S. secretary of labor in the Clinton administration, wrote in a Facebook post that Miller’s appointment was “not a positive development for anyone interested in mending our government or healing our nation.” Reich, who is Jewish and also served in the Ford and Carter administrations, expressed concern that Miller would have outsized influence on the president’s decisions.

“Miller is bigoted, xenophobic, and vicious — the architect and chief advocate of Trump’s loathsome immigration policy,” Reich stated, accusing him of conducting a “brutal Kristallnacht against undocumented immigrants.” Kristallnacht refers to the wave of deadly anti-Jewish violence in parts of Nazi-occupied Europe in 1938.

Katie Miller, who is also Jewish and married to Stephen Miller, defended her husband this weekend, after Michigan Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed called him a “broken man” on ABC’s “This Week with George Stephanopoulos.”
