text:
By VALERIE GONZALEZ and TIM SULLIVAN

It’s business as usual for President Donald Trump’s deportation offensive despite the Republican wipeout in the midterm elections.

In Los Angeles, masked immigration officers in body armor blocked a hospital emergency room driveway in a heavily Latino neighborhood early Saturday. In central Alabama, twin 19-year-old brothers from Venezuela were arrested while driving back to college a day after the election.

Advocates reported arrests from California to Michigan to Massachusetts. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has not released numbers.

After Democrats trounced the GOP and won control of the next Congress, Trump said his immigration crackdown may have been “too tough” and suggested it was time to sit down with the rival party.

“I’d love to do something on immigration,” he said in an interview with CBS “60 Minutes” recorded Friday.

Hours later, he named Stephen Miller, the architect of his hard-line immigration agenda, as his new chief of staff. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, meanwhile, said his orders have not changed.

“Deportations will continue,” Mullin wrote in an online post the day after the election, warning that ICE takes no days off and that “this includes on Thanksgiving, Christmas, and Election Day.”

María Bilbao, a campaign coordinator for the American Friends Service Committee in Miami, said she has received at least one call a day from someone detained in South Florida since the election.

“Everything remains exactly the same. The arrests have not ceased at all,” Bilbao said.

Florida Highway Patrol officers and ICE agents have detained people in their cars, as well as places including supermarkets, pharmacies and gas stations. Immigrants under supervision have also been arrested when they showed up at ICE’s Miami office for their appointments.

Officers assembled outside a Los Angeles hospital

Erick Gasca, 31, got home Friday night after an evening playing board games with friends. He lives near Adventist Health White Memorial Medical Center in Los Angeles.

An “unprecedented” number of vehicles with tinted windows and no license plates were parked near the hospital’s emergency room entrance, he said.

“I thought they were going to raid the hospital or something,” he recalled.

The Department of Homeland Security declined to explain the officers’ presence there, though Bill Essayli, the top Justice Department prosecutor in Los Angeles, said they were bringing a detainee for medical treatment. Essayli said two people were arrested for assaulting federal agents.

“ICE does not target hospitals, schools, or churches,” DHS said in a statement.

The agents’ presence attracted some 30 residents and passersby. Footage shot by Gasca’s cousin, Michelle Rivera, shows protesters shouting and officers pinning down someone.

The hospital said it wasn’t involved.

“White Memorial does not participate in immigration enforcement,” hospital president Daniel Fontoura said in a statement, adding it would not let such activities “compromise our commitment to patient care and safety.”

A couple is arrested at the Phoenix airport

A married couple from Orlando, Florida, was arrested Saturday at the airport in Phoenix while traveling to a funeral.

Gustavo Romanello and Agustin Baccega, both from Argentina, have work permits while they seek asylum after entering the United States about six years ago, according to Jonathan Batchelor, a family friend.

Batchelor was on the phone with them at the time. A mutual friend died Friday and the couple was visiting for the funeral Saturday. As the couple left the airport, two casually dressed officers asked if one was Agustin Baccega. Batchelor heard the officer say, “Asylum seekers are not in the United States legally.”

Batchelor said he could hear Romanello walking alongside his husband during the arrest and asking the officers how to collect his things. Batchelor said they then asked what his name was, “and then the guard said, ‘Oh, do you have another set of handcuffs? This is another one.’”

The voices grew distant, and the call then ended.

Both men remain in detention centers. They worked as acrobats in Florida and had no criminal record, Batchelor said.

“This is just taking good people who have been following the rules out of their lives and out of the lives of those who rely upon them and care about them,” Batchelor said.

DHS said the couple legally entered the country in 2020 but overstayed. In a statement, the agency said both men were arrested “during a targeted enforcement operation in Phoenix, Arizona. They will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.”

Twin brothers seized while driving back to college

The brothers were headed back to college after visiting their parents when they were stopped in a small city in central Alabama.

Luis and Carlos Orta-Santoro, 19-year-olds born in Venezuela and living in the U.S. for four years, are soccer players at Wallace State Community College in Hanceville, Alabama.

Relatives say they have pending asylum applications, valid work permits, and no criminal records. Both are now in an immigration detention facility.

“Our family is devastated,” said their aunt, Carolina Orta.

DHS said that while they had entered the country legally, they had “overstayed in defiance of our laws,” and their case would be heard by an immigration judge. It said pending asylum applications do not confer legal status in the U.S.

The school said in a statement, “Both young men are valued members of the Wallace State community, and our thoughts are with them during this difficult time. We sincerely hope for a positive resolution to their situation.”

A Haitian boy is taken into custody, drawing protests in San Diego

An 8-year-old Haitian boy had been living with his uncle in San Diego since his father was deported last year. The uncle, who is not a legal guardian, took him to an ICE office when the boy was summoned Nov. 4 and taken into custody.

That left the boy “without the support of their family, community and their school,” according to a letter to top administration officials from San Diego Unified School District Superintendent Fabi Bagula and school board members.

“Children should not lose access to education simply because of circumstances unfolding around them,” they wrote.

ICE has defended its actions.

Johny Oxeda, pastor of the Fairmount Haitian Community Church, which helped get legal representation for the boy, said he’ll ultimately benefit by going through legal channels.

Activists, though, were furious.

“This is not child protection,” said Guerline Jozef of Haitian Bridge Alliance, adding, “this is state-inflicted trauma.”

Associated Press reporters Gisela Salomon in Miami and Elliot Spagat in San Diego contributed.

The Senate should pass a bill, S. 4814, that would designate temporary protected status (TPS) for Haitians through April 20, 2029, the bishops said.

U.S. bishops urged the Senate to pass legislation extending immigration protections for Haitians, arguing that escalating violence and instability in Haiti make deportations unsafe and calling for broader immigration reforms to provide a pathway to more permanent legal status.

The Nov. 10 letter sent to every U.S. senator urged passage of a bill, S. 4814, that would designate temporary protected status (TPS) for Haitians through April 20, 2029. It would allow TPS recipients, including more than 330,000 Haitians, to remain and work legally in the United States during that period.

TPS is an immigration status granted to eligible foreign nationals from designated countries that are deemed unsafe to return to due to ongoing conflict, environmental disasters, or other extraordinary conditions.

The Trump administration has moved to end TPS for people from more than a dozen countries since 2025, and Lebanon TPS is set to end Nov. 27. TPS for Haiti ended July 27, after a Supreme Court decision allowed the termination to take effect.

In April, the Republican-controlled U.S. House passed legislation, H.R. 1689, that would extend TPS for Haitians for three more years. No legislative efforts have gained traction in the Senate.

The letter was signed by Bishop-designate Brendan Cahill of Joliet, Illinois, chair of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops’ (USCCB) Committee on Migration, and Bishop A. Elias Zaidan of the Maronite Eparchy of Our Lady of Lebanon, chair of the Committee on International Justice and Peace.

Cahill and Zaidan wrote that they “pray that, in its remaining weeks, the current Congress, along with the incoming 120th Congress, will devote more attention to the situation facing both Haitian families in the United States, especially those who have recently been stripped of their legal protections, and the human tragedies unfolding in Haiti itself.”

“Finally, we reiterate the need for all of Congress to work in a bipartisan manner, together with the Administration, to pursue broader reforms that provide expanded opportunities for longtime residents of American communities, such as Haitians and others with TPS, to achieve a more durable legal status, something President Trump expressed openness to in the last few days,” they wrote.

Trump told CBS’ “60 Minutes” on Nov. 8 that he would “love to do something on immigration” with congressional Democrats, who will hold the majority in the House and Senate starting in 2027.

Crisis in Haiti

The bishops said Haitiʼs worsening violence, kidnappings, and institutional collapse make it unsafe to return large numbers of people to the country.

In a September appeal to Trump, Oklahoma City Archbishop Paul Coakley, USCCB president, referenced a mass killing in Haiti that left 47 people dead and dozens abducted, including children. The bishops’ Nov. 10 letter also cited that attack, which Pope Leo XIV later called a “grave massacre,” as evidence of the countryʼs ongoing security crisis.

The attack and “the lack of any justice in its wake, and its existence as one of many such tragedies in recent months, help to demonstrate why it is unacceptable and untenable to forcibly repatriate hundreds of thousands of Haitians at this time,” the bishops continued.

“This conclusion is bolstered by the absence of an orderly reception system and the lack of coordination needed to safely receive large numbers of repatriated families,” Cahill and Zaidan wrote to the senators. “Under these circumstances, we are deeply troubled by the deportation flights that have been departing for Haiti on a weekly basis since August.”

text:
NYT reporter Katie Benner joined us this morning to discuss her new reporting, which is headlined, “ICE Officer Involved in Maine Shooting Expressed Anti-Immigrant Hatred.” She discussed the new information she obtained and read an email the ICE agent who shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero sent to a family member several years earlier where he expressed those views. If you’re outraged by how the Trump administration has deployed ICE and ignored the use of force against people on American streets, this case will be especially interesting to you, because as Katie explains, accountability is a possibility here.

The rookie ICE enforcement officer who shot him, David Brouillette, was hired during a period when ICE appears to have relaxed its hiring standards, although the agency denies doing so. Katie and her colleague were pursuing that story when they came across information, which hasn’t been published before, that shows anti-immigrant animus, specifically against Colombians. Brouillette’s victim was Colombian.

You should read the full report in The New York Times. Gift link here. One key part:

“Mr. Brouillette’s family said he didn’t hide his sentiments about immigrants. Those views, along with publicly accessible court records documenting claims of abuse, mental health challenges and workplace struggles underscore concerns about the federal government’s hiring of Mr. Brouillette, who applied for a job with ICE as the agency relaxed its vetting process and added thousands of new officers.” He struggled with mental health issues that the report suggests would normally be disqualifying for someone seeking a job in federal law enforcement.

In an exchange of texts with The Times, Brouillette’s mother wrote, “He is dangerous and should not have weapons… Believe his victims, not him.”

The DHS inspector general appears to be investigating whether Brouillette used excessive force. He shot Durán Guerrero in the face four times. Katie explained that no video of the shooting itself has surfaced. Her reporting includes the Department of Homeland Security’s official version of what happened: “the vehicle attempted to flee’ and the officer, ‘fearing for public safety,’ fired his weapon.”

Federal prosecutors would normally investigate a case like this to determine whether an excessive force or civil rights prosecution is warranted. It’s unclear whether that is happening. But Maine has a state statute it could use, depending on what its investigation reveals.

Katie explains that there is more to come, possibly on a short timeline. Maine’s current attorney general’s term ends on January 5. The legislature will select his successor, with a vote scheduled for early December. So it’s possible we could see some forward movement in the case by then.

If you missed us live, take a minute to watch the video now. The reporting is compelling, and Katie’s explanation of it is very helpful. You’ll want to hear her read Brouillette’s email to his sister, which is chilling. The government shouldn’t unleash people like this against American streets with authority over civilians. Accountability is essential.

If you value conversations like this that help us understand the news, subscribe to Civil Discourse.

We’re in this together,

Joyce

text:
Note: ICE officials are slated to visit Louisiana this week to mark the opening of a family and child detention center on a refurbished military base in Alexandria. You can read a recent Lens commentary by Tania Wolf of the National Immigration Project about the new shelter and potential toxins on that site. To reflect the impending opening of the shelter, we have also added local Lens reporting into this article, which was first published by KFF Health News.

One morning this summer, a 9-year-old girl from El Salvador picked through colorful markers at a Houston-area shelter for migrant children and crafted a letter to her mom.

“I want to be with you already,” the little girl, M.R., wrote in misspelled, unpunctuated Spanish, adding hearts, a rainbow, and a large “I love you” surrounded by pink and blue dots. “I miss you a lot, mami I love you a lot mami I want to be with you.”

The girl had begged to leave the government-run shelter where she had been held for more than seven months, an attorney for the child said. She’d become distraught, telling her mom on the phone that she felt sad and lonely, that she desperately wanted a hug, that she was getting nosebleeds and thought she had an infection.

Meanwhile, as her mother, Carmen, was going through the process to regain custody, federal immigration officials instead arrested her, sending her to a Louisiana detention center though she had a pending asylum case and no criminal record.

“Both of us are trapped,” Carmen said in a September interview from the detention center. “She’s just a helpless little girl. The process shouldn’t be like this.”

KFF Health News is using only the mother’s first name and daughter’s initials, because they fear government reprisal for sharing their story.

As of September, the 9-year-old was among almost 1,900 children being held at shelters overseen by the Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Refugee Resettlement, which was tasked by Congress over a decade ago with looking after unaccompanied children to separate their care from immigration enforcement.

Instead, the second Trump administration has reconfigured the resettlement office to aid its deportation campaign. This includes holding children rather than reuniting them with family in the United States, and often using them to ensnare family members, according to interviews with families, lawyers, and child advocates, as well as reviews of court documents. Many children in the office’s care are fleeing violence or abuse in their home countries.

Previously, the resettlement office attempted to prioritize the well-being of children in its care, said Jonathan White, a former federal health official who ran the office’s unaccompanied children program for part of President Donald Trump’s first term. The office is legally required to place children “in the least restrictive setting” and release them “without unnecessary delay,” usually to a vetted parent or other family member who is willing to care for them.

Now children in the office’s custody have become collateral damage as the administration seeks to advance its larger immigration policy goals, said White, a licensed clinical social worker. He said the administration is deliberately reshaping the nation’s shelter system for unaccompanied minors from a child welfare program into a detention program that encourages immigrants to leave the country.

Louisiana “staging center” designed for child deportations

A key part of the nation’s new child-detention program will be the new 528-bed facility called “Alexandria Family Staging Center” that is slated to open this week within former barracks in the England Airpark, the refurbished former Air Force base that houses the Alexandria International Airport, the departure site for roughly 30% of all United States deportation flights, according to the group Human Rights First. The tarmac already holds a different “short-term holding center” with a capacity of 400 adult men, though roughly 1,000 men pass through the center every week.

The South Texas Family Residential Center in Dilley, Texas is much larger, holding 2,400 non-citizen children and minor children. But the Alexandria facility would be the nation’s first to hold the unaccompanied minors who are usually held in shelters under the custody of the Department of Health and Human Services before deportation or release.

The facility’s daily operations will be handled by Anovaeon for Lasalle Family Foundation, now a for-profit company in its own right, as Verite reported, though it was initially labeled a division of the private prison company LaSalle Corrections.

ICE and Anovaeon officials have insisted that families will only be kept in the new facility for 72 hours, until they board a deportation flight. “This project right over here is not a detention center, it’s a staging center for families who are voluntarily departing this country, admittedly through pretty crappy circumstances on their end. I acknowledge that,” Anovaeon CEO Eric Fritz told the Airpark board of commissioners, as reported by ABC News.

But advocates note that if the families are not put on a flight within the allotted 72 hours, they will not be released, but will instead be transferred to another ICE detention facility. And despite the “short-term” label, advocates have litigated this issue with the other Alexandria Holding Facility and other “short-term” ICE facilities that have detained people for weeks.

ICE has also refused a request from the National Immigration Project and the ACLU of Louisiana to conduct “stakeholder tours” of the new facility, routine visits that would allow the advocates to understand the place and its conditions.

Kids not released to sponsors, lack legal guidance

Nationally, although fewer kids are now held in shelters run by the Office of Refugee Resettlement than in past years, those who remain often find themselves trapped for months with no clear way out other than to enter long-term foster care or return to the dangerous conditions they fled, attorneys said. That’s because their potential guardians get detained themselves or are afraid or unable to complete the sponsorship process. Often, attorneys said, the office refuses to release the children even when sponsorship requirements are met, and they have to sue for the kids’ release.

“When a child sees no way out of detention, ‘voluntary departure’ may no longer feel like a real choice,” U.S. Rep. Andrea Salinas (D-Ore.) said during an Oct. 1 news conference calling attention to the administration’s changes to the unaccompanied children program.

“Immigration courts are intentionally speeding up children’s cases,” she said, “while access to legal help has been disrupted.”

Without crucial legal help, unaccompanied minors are left alone to make life-changing decisions that could lead them to the new Alexandria facility, where ICE contends that everyone has chosen “voluntary departure.”

In recent years, unaccompanied children are less and less likely to have legal representation, leading to worse outcomes, according to the Vera Institute’s Immigration Court Legal Representation Dashboard, which found that roughly 84% of an unaccompanied children’s cases completed in August 2026 resulted in departures, a drastic increase from 54% in August 2025 and 33% in August 2024.

The Department of Homeland Security did not directly answer questions sent by KFF Health News but framed detentions of migrant children’s sponsors by Immigration and Customs Enforcement as part of an effort to prevent kids from being harmed. A federal watchdog in 2024 found that the resettlement office didn’t properly screen sponsors amid a surge of unaccompanied children during President Joe Biden’s term, and news reports have documented incidents of children being exploited after their release from the agency’s custody.

In an unsigned email, DHS reiterated previous statements that “ICE does not separate families” and that the administration is working to locate 450,000 unaccompanied children who arrived during the Biden administration. It said many of the children were placed with unvetted sponsors who were smugglers and sex traffickers, a claim that has been disputed. It provided a list of 16 cases in which sponsors were arrested in connection with serious crimes, including the rape of an unaccompanied child, drug trafficking, and homicide.

John Fabbricatore, a senior adviser with the Office of Refugee Resettlement, echoed DHS’ statements about the safety of migrant children. He said the office’s application processing and release times mirror those of the U.S. foster care system. “ORR is not slow,” he said in an emailed statement, “we are just more careful, as we should be: children’s lives are at stake.”

From child welfare to detention

M.R. spent about two weeks traveling to the U.S. late last year with her older sister, wading across the Rio Grande before being detained by Border Patrol officers in Texas, according to case documents. The sisters hoped to join their mother and a brother who had fled El Salvador a few years earlier and were living in Tennessee. Gang members murdered M.R.’s father, her uncle, and a pregnant cousin, according to Carmen, who feared for her daughter’s safety, too. M.R.’s maternal grandmother in El Salvador hit her and her sister with a belt and open hand while caring for them, M.R. later told a social worker.

Like others arriving in the U.S. alone and without legal status, the girl and her older sister landed in a shelter thinking they would be out in days. Before Trump’s second term, children typically waited in the resettlement office’s custody for about a month while federal officials screened their relatives or other sponsors. M.R.’s brother, who arrived in the U.S. in 2024, said he stayed in a shelter for 11 days.

The second Trump administration is arresting parents and other trusted caregivers who have come forward to get children released, has created onerous new requirements for sponsors, and has installed a former immigration official with experience in law enforcement as the head of the resettlement office. Average stays stretched to nearly six months, with some like M.R. staying much longer, even when they have qualified sponsors.

Alvaro Huerta of the Immigrant Defenders Law Center said during a July news briefing that a 3-year-old remained in the resettlement office’s custody for 300 days. A 6-year-old girl remained in custody for seven months, Huerta said, after her father was detained while being vetted as a sponsor and then deported. When the mother arrived at an appointment in March to reunite with the girl, he said, they were sent together to an immigration detention center in Dilley, Texas, that has drawn criticism from Democratic lawmakers, advocates, and families who have reported inhumane conditions.

Immigration lawyers say the administration has undermined legal protections for migrant kids while simultaneously fast-tracking deportation. Children, including some as young as 1, are appearing before immigration judges alone because of administration disruptions to legal services.

In some cases, immigration officials are detaining kids after they have been placed with sponsors and are already living in their communities. The administration has also offered children, including M.R., payments of at least $2,500 if they agree to return to their home countries voluntarily.

M.R.’s sister was released when she turned 18, three weeks after her arrival. Courts have blocked the Trump administration’s attempts to transfer to immigration detention people who turn 18 while in the resettlement office’s custody. That left young M.R. on her own in a new country, without her mom, her twin older siblings, or other close family.

Family separation

In April, Carmen went to a DNA test appointment, which she was told was the last step she needed to secure her daughter’s release. KFF Health News reviewed a text confirming the appointment at a DHS office. She thought she would soon be reunited with her youngest child. By then she had already presented her tax and salary information, submitted fingerprints, and been visited at home by a social worker. She and her teens prepared the little girl’s bedroom, adorning it with a Hello Kitty bed cover, Frozen curtains, and a lamp that projects stars and astronauts on the ceiling. They showed it to M.R. on a video call. She was excited, her brother said.

Without a warrant, immigration officers detained Carmen at the appointment. The resettlement office subsequently rejected her sponsorship application, citing the detention it had helped facilitate.

The girl was crushed.

“She doesn’t have an understanding of why she’s stuck there and why the government would detain her mom instead of reuniting them,” said Alexa Sendukas, managing attorney with the Galveston-Houston Immigrant Representation Project, which is representing the girl. “Our government has completely failed them and has treated them in a way no human being should ever be treated.”

DHS declined to comment on a description of the case of Carmen and her daughter. The agency said it could comment only if it had the names, dates of birth, and noncitizen identification numbers of the people involved.

“When the media refuses to give names, it makes it impossible to provide details on specific cases or even verify any of this even happened or that the people even exist. If you can’t do your job, we can’t do ours,” the agency’s press office responded, without providing the name of a spokesperson as requested.

Reports from the Houston-area shelter show that the girl received counseling. She was not diagnosed with any mental health conditions, though the therapist reported she was sad and cried while discussing her long shelter stay and missing her mom.

Carmen, who talked to her daughter on the phone about three times a week, said the child was struggling. The girl blamed herself, Sendukas said.

Every phone call, M.R. would ask her mom when she’d be released and when they’d be together again. She complained of feeling unwell. She lamented having no one to hug or comfort her, despite all the bad news she’d received, her mom said.

“I felt like the worst mother in the world, because I couldn’t explain to my daughter what was happening, what they’d done to me,” Carmen said.

Situations like M.R.’s are indicative of the resettlement office’s shift to prioritizing immigration enforcement over children’s well-being, White said.

“There is no scenario ever where it’s in the best interest of the child to tell them you’re going to release them to their mom, and prepare them for that, and then use their planned unification as a pretext to apprehend the mom,” he said.

Sural Shah, part of a team of physicians with the American Academy of Pediatrics who have visited several shelters for migrant children over the past year, said many are developing mental illnesses due to prolonged shelter stays.

“It’s heartbreaking,” Shah said, adding that kids are exhibiting anxiety, depression, and stress disorders, leading them to regress developmentally, act out, and harm themselves. Some wet their beds, experience chest pains, or cry out at night. Being stuck in a shelter for months can have long-term health effects like post-traumatic stress disorder, she added.

Some distressed children have also attempted suicide, said Mickey Donovan-Kaloust, legal services director at the Immigrant Defenders Law Center, which has offices across Southern California.

A teenage brother and sister from Venezuela who spent more than a year in a different federal shelter in Texas told KFF Health News that during their stay, they barely left the building and had to follow a rigid routine. The academic lessons they received at the shelter repeated every month, they said, and meals were the same each week. They also complained that they got reprimanded for small things like laughing too loud or having water fights.

When their father was detained during his sponsorship process, the girl stopped eating for days, she said. She showed symptoms of PTSD.

The boy said the experience wore him down mentally and emotionally.

“I was a broken kid,” he said. “I didn’t know whether to laugh when I got bad news, I didn’t know whether to cry.”

An excruciating choice

In detention, Carmen received a deportation order and faced an unthinkable choice: leave her youngest child behind in long-term foster care or return to potentially deadly conditions in El Salvador together, leaving her teens in the United States. Although gang violence is down in the country, Carmen said the people who killed her family members and threatened to kill her are still active in her old neighborhood.

It’s the kind of choice that immigrant families across the country are facing daily, said Jennifer Podkul, chief of global policy and advocacy at Kids in Need of Defense, a nonprofit that represents kids in Office of Refugee Resettlement custody.

In July, Carmen decided she could no longer bear her youngest daughter’s distress. They asked to leave together.

The mom could have appealed her deportation order but was worried about the mental health toll, Sendukas said. Carmen said her daughter told her: “I don’t want to feel alone again like I did at Christmas, like I did on Mother’s Day, and for your birthday. All of those days I’ve felt so alone. I don’t want to go on like this.”

In mid-September, three weeks before her 10th birthday and 281 days after she arrived in the U.S., the daughter was sent with her mother to El Salvador.

The child’s older siblings remain in the U.S. fighting their own asylum cases without their mother. The brother dropped out of high school in Tennessee and, along with his twin sister, moved to live with a relative.

“I just hope other people understand that we’re all fighting for something,” he said. “We were fighting to be together. It wasn’t a dream that hurt anyone.”

KFF Health News correspondent Jazmin Orozco Rodriguez contributed to this report. Katy Reckdahl added local reporting for The Lens.

description:

Is there any basis for the White House to be threatening members of Congress for their oversight?

text:
Amna Nawaz:

As Democrats gear up to take control of Congress, the White House is threatening them over planned investigations into the Trump administration.

In a letter this week, the top White House lawyer warned the likely incoming House Oversight chair, Robert Garcia, that aggressive oversight of the administration -- quote -- "may cross the line into blatant criminality."

It comes amid a wave of high-profile resignations within the Justice Department following last week's Democratic wins and reporting that there are more to come.

Here to discuss this is Devlin Barrett. He's a New York Times reporter who covers federal law enforcement.

Welcome back. Good to see you.

Devlin Barrett:

Thanks for having me.

Amna Nawaz:

Let's start with this letter. Is there any basis for the White House to be threatening members of Congress for their oversight?

Devlin Barrett:

Look, as a legal document, it doesn't mean very much. As a political document, it's quite important, because it's sending the message about how much the White House plans to fight these investigations.

We have already seen the administration fight even judicial inquiries about what the administration has done. So I take this letter to basically mean, we intend to fight every subpoena you send us.

Amna Nawaz:

Related to that, we saw the attorney general, Todd Blanche, over the weekend say that Democrats' talk about investigating some of the administration was akin to outright threats and that some of those could be considered a crime.

Do you see the attorney general launching probes into Democratic lawmakers who are engaged in oversight?

Devlin Barrett:

Well, we have already seen them launch probes into Democratic lawmakers for very shaky premises. For example, there was an attempt to get an indictment on lawmakers who made a video talking to military officers about not following illegal orders.

I don't think there's any reason to expect they will stop launching investigations of Democratic lawmakers. But I think, when it comes to this particular fight over investigations, they're going to be very hard-pressed to craft a sort of criminal theory of why a congressional investigation is in any way a crime.

They haven't articulated that certainly. The letter really doesn't, nor does Blanche in his comments.

Amna Nawaz:

Devlin, let's talk about some of those resignations, several high-profile folks leaving their jobs in the last week, and some were very strong enforcers of the president's agenda, among them Harmeet Dhillon, who was the president's former personal lawyer and led the Civil Rights Division to DOJ, Jason Quinones, who oversaw investigations into the president's opponents.

Brett Shumate was central in attacking DEI programs, and John Eisenberg oversaw national security at the Department of Justice. What do we know about why they're leaving and why now?

Devlin Barrett:

First of all, it's not completely out of the ordinary for senior DOJ officials to leave after an election, to leave after two years.

But, obviously, this is a very different type of Department of Justice in the Trump administration. And I think what you're seeing here in a lot of these cases is senior officials who, for very different reasons, each sort of unique to their own jobs, did not live up to some of the expectations that the White House set for them or even that Todd Blanche set for them, particularly when you look at the U.S. attorney in Miami, who's in charge of this grand conspiracy investigation of former officials.

There's been a lot of disappointment by the White House that that hasn't produced more in the way of criminal charges or accusations.

Amna Nawaz:

You think that they were forced out of these rules or asked to leave?

Devlin Barrett:

Our reporting shows that there is a significant amount of displeasure from senior officials with the U.S. attorney in Miami who just left. And there were significant disagreements in some of these other issues like national security, like civil rights.

Amna Nawaz:

Permanent replacements for those roles would require Senate confirmation. With the incoming Democratic majority, how do you see that playing out?

Devlin Barrett:

Well, that's why these departures are categorically different than many other administrations, because it's going to be extremely hard to confirm someone in these top jobs that the president would like to have in these top jobs.

So it may be that, for the people who stay in the Trump Justice Department, they may be in a sense locked in for a long -- for the rest of the ride.

Amna Nawaz:

There's also this reporting that the DOJ warned its field office leaders in a meeting earlier this week to prepare to be on -- quote -- "wartime footing" when Democrats take over or to leave if they couldn't do that.

When you hear that, combined with these resignations, what do you think we should expect to see from the Department of Justice?

Devlin Barrett:

So one thing is, this happened in the type of call where the person -- the senior official doing these calls does a lot of this sort of rhetoric. Like, to many of the career staff, it comes across as wild rhetoric.

But this kind of rhetoric is not that unusual for this senior official. But what's really interesting here is, the elections had consequences for the Justice Department. And one of those consequences is states like Texas are now going to be run by Democratic officials.

Until now, states like Texas have been very cooperative with the Trump administration on issues related to ICE and immigration. You have already seen local officials in Texas say they are going to cut back on that cooperation.

So I think what you're seeing in terms of statements like that is, you're seeing from Stephen Miller on down, this administration is preparing for more arguments and more fights with local officials, similar to the ones that they have had with officials, for example, in Minnesota. And, politically speaking, in some ways, Texas just became Minnesota.

Amna Nawaz:

The Democrats are also preparing their agenda for the when they assume the majority in both chambers of Congress.

The idea of impeaching Todd Blanche, attorney general, has also been raised by a couple of lawmakers, including Jamie Raskin, who's poised to become the chair of the House Judiciary Committee. How likely is that kind of move, based on your reporting, and how is that resonating within the Justice Department?

Devlin Barrett:

Todd Blanche has overseen a drastic set of changes at the Justice Department, causing mass departures, mass firings, and there is a tremendous morale problem within the rank and file of the department.

Nobody really, I think, has a great read on what Congress is going to do. I think we're now -- that letter we talked about earlier shows that everyone is sort of like drawing lines and talking tough.

But, at some point, Congress is going to have to show up and cast votes, and we will see then how much they are willing -- which officials they really want to go after. Obviously, Pete Hegseth is another important target at the Pentagon. The Democrats are going to have to make some decisions and make -- decide priorities about who they want to really go after.

Amna Nawaz:

We will be following your reporting, for sure.

Devlin Barrett of The New York Times, always great to see you. Thank you.

Devlin Barrett:

Thanks for having me.

text:
Today, Congresswoman Veronica Escobar (TX-16) joined fellow Democrats, the American Business Immigration Coalition Action (ABIC Action) and the South Texas Builders Association to discuss the future of immigration reform and solutions.

Below is a lightly edited transcript of her remarks. You can find video of her remarks here.

Congresswoman Escobar: Buenos dias! What a beautiful day on Capitol Hill. And we have been blessed with incredible advocates, with an amazing freshman class. We've turned the border blue, and we have a mandate from the American people.

As my colleagues have mentioned, today is Veteran's Day. I would be remiss if I didn't mention that there are hundreds of veterans who have been deported. Not just during this administration, but prior administrations. We need to get them home, and we need to address the broken system that has removed American heroes from American soil. It is incredibly unjust.

As Ashley - one of my personal heroes - has mentioned, I am the co-author of the Dignity Act. My colleague Maria Salazar could not be here with us. She just won her race. And she and I are deeply committed to continuing our effort at bipartisan, comprehensive immigration reform.

When we introduced the Dignity Act in 2023, we were subjected to a lot of criticism about the bipartisan effort that we - the journey - that we began together.

I am a progressive Democrat. I have very aspirational dreams and hopes for immigration reform. But I am also a pragmatist. And as we continue to have Donald Trump in the White House and without a super majority in the Senate, we need Republican support. So any comprehensive immigration reform must be bipartisan.

I am deeply committed to ensuring that the Dignity Act is reintroduced in 2027. To my incoming freshman colleagues: this is the only bipartisan, comprehensive immigration reform bill in the House in over a decade. This last Congress, we had 20 Republicans and 20 Democrats. We want to grow that number and get the bill out of the House, get it to the Senate - where I already have a bipartisan Senate duo very interested in the Dignity Act - and get this bill to the president's desk.

To Republicans and Democrats alike who did not like the Dignity Act because it didn't meet their goals: we are going to reshape it in the coming weeks. If you want to be a part of bipartisan, comprehensive immigration reform compromise so that we can get a bill to the president's desk in 2027, we welcome you with open arms. We welcome your ideas. We welcome your initiative. We want you at the table. And if we can get this passed this upcoming Congress, we can do even more in 2028 to grow and expand what we can do for immigrants, immigrant families, and our economy and our communities.

I know all of us never want to see another family separated ever again. We never want to see private prisons like those run in my district - Camp East Montana, a $1.24 billion facility, a profit-making enterprise that is essentially feeding its profits off of human misery - we need to bring that to an end. We need to bring sanity back to the immigration system. We can do this. We will do this. Thank you all.

Less than six months ago, University of Maryland student Maria Flores Garcia, 19, delivered her valedictorian speech at Parkdale High School’s graduation in Prince George’s County.

Today, she sits in ICE custody in Louisiana with her mother.

Flores Garcia and her mother drove to an annual immigration check-in in Baltimore last Thursday, an appointment that in the past has taken about 30 minutes, Flores Garcia’s boyfriend, Cesar Saavedra, said.

At the appointment, ICE officers asked Flores Garcia if she wanted to remain with her mother or leave, Saavedra said. Flores Garcia chose to stay and the two were taken into ICE custody. They’ve since been transported to a facility in Louisiana.

This story continues. Read the rest at The Banner.

A small-scale study from the advocacy group Environment America found evidence of microplastics throughout the Chesapeake Bay watershed, the group announced Tuesday. Using citizen scientists, the group collected several water samples at 15 different places throughout the watershed, including five sites in Maryland waterways. They found microplastics at every site, whether in the form of plastic fiber, film, beads or fragments. “Plastic pollution is pervasive, and it’s a danger that’s not just out there in some patch across the ocean. It’s right here. It’s knocking at our front door,” said Baltimore Harbor waterkeeper Alice Volpitta during a news conference Tuesday along the Baltimore waterfront. The results, according to several local environmental groups, are strong evidence that Maryland lawmakers should move forward with legislation this year to curb plastic pollution, including a bottle return program that would reimburse Marylanders who drop off plastic drink containers for recycling.

text:
A Nigerian born nursing professor whose work spans university education and patient care is at the center of a growing dispute over US immigration enforcement after being detained by federal agents and transferred from California to Louisiana.

Dr. Ann Lawani, 39, was taken into custody at her Lodi home on September 16. She is now being held at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center, prompting relatives, colleagues and California Congressman Josh Harder to demand her return.

NBC Bay Area’s Jodi Hernandez reported on November 10 that Lawani’s supporters say she has protection under a legal ruling known as withholding of removal, which prevents her deportation to Nigeria because of the risk of persecution. She also holds a work permit.

However, the Department of Homeland Security has told other news outlets that her detention stems from a final removal order issued in 2013. That distinction is important: withholding of removal protects someone from being sent to a particular country, but does not itself grant permanent immigration status.

Ann Lawani ICE detention raises questions over her transfer

Harder has written to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin seeking Lawani’s release and return to California while her case proceeds. In a November 10 statement, the congressman said her transfer to Louisiana raised concerns about due process and the justification for continued detention.

KQED reported that Harder also questioned why Lawani’s whereabouts were missing from ICE’s public detainee locator, leaving her family and lawyer struggling to find her. He further alleged that authorities had pursued removal to an undisclosed third country.

Lawani oversees nursing education at the University of San Francisco and also works at John Muir Health. Her colleagues say her absence is affecting students, faculty and the patients who depend on her clinical work.

The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to NBC Bay Area’s request for comment. The government’s stated basis for detention, however, remains part of the dispute.

Lawani’s case has drawn attention beyond her university, with her family and supporters continuing to press for her return.

On Nov. 2, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani threatened legal action against the Trump administration and Immigration and Customs Enforcement over the agency’s reported use of city-owned property in enforcement operations, in violation of a February resolution barring the federal agency from using city-owned property.

The announcement followed an Oct. 8 incident in which an ICE officer shot a man in the Bronx. Just over a week later, Mamdani and more than 100 state and federal elected officials sent a letter to owners of private parking lots and garages, asking them not to make their properties available to ICE.

In the Capital Region, Albany County adopted its own restrictions earlier this year. The County Legislature passed a resolution in March barring ICE and other agencies under the Department of Homeland Security from using county property as staging areas for enforcement operations. The policy also barred the county sheriff from directly cooperating with ICE or Border Patrol.

County Legislator Jeff Kuhn, who spearheaded the resolution, told the Times Union it was adopted in direct response to federal immigration operations taking place across the country, particularly in Minnesota at the beginning of the year.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“The principle was fairly straightforward,” Kuhn said. “Albany County would comply with federal immigration law, but we weren’t going to volunteer county law enforcement personnel or county property to facilitate federal civil immigration operations that we believed could undermine public safety.”

Since the resolution’s adoption, Kuhn said, he is not aware of any instances of county-owned property being used in ICE operations. But he said the county is prepared to take action, including going to federal court, if the resolution is violated.

A spokesperson for the state attorney general’s office confirmed that the Office of Immigrant Trust, which was established in July, has not received any complaints of ICE staging on public property in Albany County.

Kuhn noted that much of what the county outlined in its resolution was later adopted at the state level through the Local Cops, Local Crimes Act, which bars or strictly limits local law enforcement from collaborating with ICE and establishes guidelines intended to prevent the federal agency from conducting operations in sensitive locations, such as churches and schools.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The county’s resolution is set to expire Dec. 31, but at Monday’s legislature meeting, lawmakers introduced a resolution to extend the policy through noon on Jan. 20, 2029, which would mark the inauguration of the next president.

“Albany County was in the lead on this issue,” Kuhn said. “We took the initiative with a resolution that was designed to protect public safety, preserve county taxpayer resources and discourage mass ICE operations in our community.”

But the county resolution does not apply to city or state property within Albany County. Immigrant rights advocates have claimed that ICE has used public lots in the city of Albany as staging grounds for its operations, but the Times Union has not been able to verify those accounts.

A spokesperson for Albany Mayor Dorcey Applyrs said in a statement that the mayor is “committed to protecting the safety and dignity of all residents as it relates to ICE activity,” adding that the city continues to work with local partners to “strengthen city policies that expand protections for all residents.”

Albany Common Councilmember Tom Hoey, who represents District 15 and chairs the Public Safety Committee, said he would need to discuss the matter with Albany Police Chief Brendan Cox and the greater Common Council.

Common Councilmember Alfredo Balarin, who represents District 11, said he would support a move to adopt legislation similar to that of the county, placing additional guardrails to prevent ICE from using city property as a staging ground for operations. He said he has heard from concerned constituents about the federal agency conducting arrests in his district, particularly on the boundary of Central Avenue. He believes legislation would receive strong support from the body.

“Unfortunately, this is an issue residents are concerned with,” Balarin said. “We are limited in what we can do at the local level, but that doesn’t mean we can’t do anything. Making clear that our city property shouldn’t be used for these initiatives is something we should definitely push forward with.”

WASHINGTON (OSV News) — In the aftermath of Republicans losing control of both chambers of Congress in a Democratic landslide, President Donald Trump suggested he was open to working with Democrats on immigration policy, before his administration indicated its deportation policy would continue.

Initial exit polls of 2026 midterm voters conducted by NBC News in coordination with a group of other news organizations found 57% of voters said Trump’s immigration enforcement actions have gone too far.

In an interview on the CBS News program “60 Minutes” that aired Nov. 8, Trump appeared to acknowledge that data, saying the results suggested his administration’s immigration crackdown was “too tough” and that he could “work something out” with Democrats when they take control of Congress.

“I think ultimately that hurt me,” Trump said on immigration, adding, “I think it both helped and hurt. I think I got an A+ for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out. But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that — that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally.”

Trump leans into hardline deportation policy and elevates its architects

The interview was taped on the morning of Nov. 6. Hours later, Trump named Stephen Miller, previously his deputy chief of staff and senior policy adviser, as his new White House chief of staff after the departure of Susie Wiles. Miller is seen as a key architect of many of the Trump administration’s immigration policies.

On Nov. 9, Trump told reporters at the White House, “There won’t be amnesty.”

“Somebody suggested, ‘Will there be amnesty?’ No, but — they came in. They knew the law,” he said.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a Nov. 10 post on X, “Amnesty will NEVER be on the table.”

Kevin Appleby, senior fellow for policy and communications at the Center for Migration Studies of New York and the former director of migration policy for the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, told OSV News, “It’s important to note what policies the administration are implementing, not what the president says, to measure where they are on immigration.”

According to the Migration Policy Institute’s “Fact Sheet” report from October, domestic immigration-related arrests rose from 8,000 per month in the first three months of Trump’s term to 19,000 per month from May through July 2026. Of those deported by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, 61% had been in the U.S. at least two years and 15% had lived in the U.S. 10 years or more. Of these immigrants, 71% had never been convicted of a crime, and 61% of those in the U.S. 10 years or more had no criminal convictions.

Catholics impacted directly by mass deportation

A joint report issued last year by the USCCB’s Migration and Refugee Services, the Center for the Study of Global Christianity at Gordon-Conwell Theological Seminary, and World Relief, found that more than 10 million Christians living in the U.S. would be vulnerable to deportation under Trump administration policies implemented in 2025. A majority of them — 61% — were Catholic followed by a sizable number of evangelicals.

It also found more than 1 in 6 Catholics are either vulnerable to deportation themselves or could see a family member deported, barring law or policy changes.

“I don’t think there can be a real bipartisan conversation on immigration reform until the administration shows it has changed its approach and moderated its enforcement tactics, consistent with the protection of human dignity,” Appleby said.

Catholic social teaching on immigration balances three interrelated principles: the right of persons to migrate in order to sustain their lives and those of their families, the right of a country to regulate its borders and control immigration, and a nation’s duty to regulate its borders with justice and mercy.

Church’s voice needed in the immigration discourse

Dylan Corbett, executive director of the Hope Border Institute, a group that works to apply the perspective of Catholic social teaching in policy and practice to the U.S.-Mexico border region, told OSV News, “Even President Trump recognizes that an exclusively enforcement-driven approach to immigration remains fundamentally counterproductive and unsustainable.”

“He now possesses a pivotal opportunity to foster broad consensus by pairing meaningful legalization with addressing our nation’s critical labor needs — expanding lawful pathways for Dreamers, caregivers, and long-standing community members who have contributed to the fabric of our society for years, if not decades,” Corbett said. “A policy centered on mass deportation is not only morally indefensible and economically harmful, but also a demonstrable political liability. Now is the defining moment to champion substantive reform and for the Church to uphold the moral imperative at the heart of this discourse.”

Catholics, Appleby said, “should certainly engage the debate, but not be caught up in a race to the bottom, where we wind up with legislation which is more damaging than beneficial.”

“In other words, we must enter the dialogue with eyes wide open and not compromise our principles,” he said. “I expect that the next two years will set the parameters for the reform debate, which will happen under a new administration.”

US bishops call for Haitians to be shielded from mass deportation

Among the Trump administration immigration policies the U.S. bishops have criticized is its termination of Temporary Protected Status for Haiti earlier this year and subsequent mass deportations of Haitian nationals.

Temporary Protected Status grants the U.S. government the power to shield eligible migrants from deportation if they are from countries experiencing dangerous conditions such as war, disaster, or other unrest. The Trump administration has sought to end TPS for several countries, notably Haiti, which is racked by extreme levels of gang violence, but it also recently granted an extension to migrants from El Salvador.

In a Nov. 10 letter to members of the U.S. Senate, Bishop Brendan J. Cahill of Joliet, Illinois, chair of the USCCB’s Committee on Migration, and Bishop A. Elias Zaidan of the Maronite Eparchy of Our Lady of Lebanon, chair of its Committee on International Justice and Peace, reiterated the conference’s previous call for the extension of Haiti’s TPS status, writing, “We pray that, in its remaining weeks, the current Congress, along with the incoming 120th Congress, will devote more attention to the situation facing both Haitian families in the United States, especially those who have recently been stripped of their legal protections, and the human tragedies unfolding in Haiti itself.”

title: Report reveals troubling history of ICE agent in deadly Biddeford shooting - WGME
authors: Ariana St Pierre, WGME, Ariana St Pierre
description:
BIDDEFORD, Maine (WGME) -- The ICE agent accused of shooting and killing a young father in Biddeford had a record of workplace problems, alleged domestic abuse and mental health issues, according to the New York Times.
Officials said ICE Officer David Brouillette, a Gardiner native, fatally shot 25-year-old Colombian national Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero while serving as part of an ICE operation in Biddeford on July 13.
According to military records, Brouillette served in the Maine National Guard from 2007 to 2010 as a quartermaster and chemical equipment repairer.
ICE then put Mr. Brouillette on the street without sending him to the standard ICE training course, which would have trained him on, among other things, the standards that govern use of deadly force and shooting into moving vehicles.
I look forward to the results of the Maine Attorney General’s independent investigation into this shameful use of deadly force.
text:
BIDDEFORD, Maine (WGME) -- The ICE agent accused of shooting and killing a young father in Biddeford had a record of workplace problems, alleged domestic abuse and mental health issues, according to the New York Times.

Officials said ICE Officer David Brouillette, a Gardiner native, fatally shot 25-year-old Colombian national Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero while serving as part of an ICE operation in Biddeford on July 13.

At least four gunshots went through the windshield of a car, and Guerrero died at the scene.

The Department of Homeland Security said the vehicle tried to flee and that Brouillette fired because he feared for public safety.

In July, Ashley Brouillette, an ex-wife of Brouillette, spoke with CNN, and claimed her ex called her after the shooting and admitted to being the agent who shot Guerrero. She said he told her it was "justified" and done in self-defense.

Guerrero’s family said they shot and killed an innocent man who was in the country legally and had been issued a work permit and a Social Security number. Guerrero was a father to a young daughter, and his wife, Karolina Rojas Alvarez, said she and her husband dreamed of a long life together. He used to say until they were ‘little old people.’

Also read: Ex-wife of ICE agent allegedly involved in Maine shooting says he has pattern of violence

According to the New York Times, Brouillette had a record of workplace problems, alleged domestic abuse and mental health issues. The article also detailed anti-immigrant and anti-Colombian comments Brouillette made in emails to relatives in 2021.

Brouillette’s sister shared emails with the New York Times in which he reportedly disparaged her Colombian partner, who was living legally in the United States, telling her that her partner could take "his non-citizen a** back to his country and enjoy his third world luxuries."

Brouillette also told his sister that she was, “Dead to me. DEAD,” and her partner’s “bloodline” did not understand the value of American freedom.

His mother told the Times that he was dangerous and urged people to believe his alleged victims. His former wives accused him of physical abuse in court filings; he disputed those claims. His mother also said he had been diagnosed with bipolar disorder and hospitalized multiple times.

The article said Brouillette joined ICE in December 2025 during a major hiring surge, when the agency had reportedly relaxed parts of its vetting process.

According to the Times, he was cleared to start before the agency had reviewed his full background report, which remained in a backlog at the time of the shooting. He also skipped ICE’s full training course, completing a shorter online program because of prior law enforcement experience, according to the Times.

A DHS spokesperson responded to the report, saying in part:

"Incoming ICE officers, many already with years of law enforcement experience, are onboarded in accordance with applicable policies and standards. Any claims of substandard training or vetting are FALSE. This administration is preserving ICE’s reputation as one of the most elite law enforcement agencies not only in the U.S., but the entire world.

ICE maintains rigorous standards for all personnel. We ensure that every applicant is thoroughly assessed through mandatory pre-employment vetting protocols. All federal personnel must be found suitable for employment in accordance with 5 CFR Part 731 and, for those occupying national security positions, must be eligible based on Security Executive Agent Directive (SEAD) 4 guidelines and Executive Order 12968, as amended.

ICE continues to actively recruit and onboard personnel to ensure the agency reaches authorized staffing levels, accounting for natural attrition and retirements. While we saw a successful hiring surge last year made possible by President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill, our efforts to fill these positions in fulfillment of the President’s mandate continue.

Officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics. ICE law enforcement officers are trained to use the minimum amount of force necessary to resolve dangerous situations to prioritize the safety of the public and our officers."

When asked specifically about Brouillette's training and conduct, DHS said it "does not comment on matters regarding personnel who are no longer with the agency."

According to military records, Brouillette served in the Maine National Guard from 2007 to 2010 as a quartermaster and chemical equipment repairer. He received an honorable discharge with the rank of private first class.

He then enlisted in the U.S. Army, where a spokesperson confirmed he served from 2010 to 2015 as a human intelligence collector. During his military service, Brouillette completed a nine-month deployment to Afghanistan and left the Army with the rank of sergeant.

Also read: 'My daughter asks for Papa': Family of Maine man killed by ICE agent speaks to media

After leaving active duty, state employment records show Brouillette was hired as a corrections officer at the Maine Correctional Center in Windham in 2015. Records indicate he resigned approximately one year later.

In 2019, Brouillette joined the Maine Department of Health and Human Services as a human services enforcement agent with the Division of Support Enforcement Recovery. A department spokesperson confirmed he resigned voluntarily after a little more than seven months.

The CBS13 I-Team also confirmed Brouillette served as a volunteer firefighter with the Manchester Fire Department for about a year. Town officials said he left the department for undisclosed medical reasons in 2024.

According to the Times, a former volunteer fire chief called Brouillette a “loose cannon” and described an incident in which Brouillette, after a training injury, allegedly yelled and threatened to punch him.

Brouillette later sued the college where the injury occurred, saying it affected his memory and cognitive abilities; the case was settled, according to the Times.

Court records also indicate Brouillette worked as a federal police officer at the Togus VA Medical Center.

State licensing records show Brouillette was also licensed as a Maine real estate agent for a period of time before that license ended last year.

Also read: ICE agent who allegedly killed man in Maine had military background, past government jobs

He was also let go from a pest control job over behavioral issues, according to the Times.

A review of Maine criminal court records found Brouillette has no criminal record in the state other than a traffic violation from about a decade ago.

The I-Team also obtained hundreds of pages of civil and family court records, which include allegations of domestic violence made by former partners. Court records show petitions seeking protection from abuse orders were either denied or later dismissed. None of those cases resulted in criminal convictions.

Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey’s office is investigating the shooting, as is the DHS inspector general.

The Times reports that cooperation between federal and state investigators has been limited.

The Times also noted that any racial bias could be relevant to an excessive-force inquiry, though federal prosecutors do not have to prove racial animus to bring such a case.

Benjamin Gideon, the attorney representing Guerrero’s wife, released a statement following the Times’ report, saying in part:

“It is appalling that our government handed David Brouillette a badge and a gun. Mr. Brouillette's threats, rage, and instability, have been covered in previous reporting. Liz Emen is the fourth member of Mr. Brouillette’s immediately family to state that he was unfit to work in law enforcement in any capacity, something a local Maine police department figured out when they turned him down for a job for ‘too many red flags.’

Today’s report adds to the long list of Mr. Brouillette’s disqualifying conduct open hostility toward immigrants, generally, and toward people from Colombia, specifically. Any reasonable background investigation would have uncovered who this man was and sent him home. Instead, the New York Times ‘could not find any employer or family member’ who was contacted about Mr. Brouillette before he was ‘fast-tracked’ for hire during a surge in which ICE lowered standards to rush new recruits out onto our streets. ICE then put Mr. Brouillette on the street without sending him to the standard ICE training course, which would have trained him on, among other things, the standards that govern use of deadly force and shooting into moving vehicles.

David Brouillette is the poster child for what happens when our government chooses to recruit agents to carry out a campaign of hate against immigrants, hires those agents without adequate screening and places them on the street without basic training. Johan Sebastián’s death was not an inevitable accident. It was a natural and predictable choices of the policies of our government and its political leadership.”

According to Gideon, the federal government has yet to tell Guerrero’s family if Brouillette has been disciplined, whether anyone who hired, trained, or supervised him has been held accountable, or what any federal investigation has found.

Congresswoman Chellie Pingree is also responding to the Times' report, saying part:

"ICE handed David Brouillette a gun and sent him into Maine communities before anyone at the agency had reviewed his background check. The agency restricted his access to certain computer systems because he had not been fully cleared, yet apparently saw no problem trusting him with the power to take someone’s life. That is an unconscionable betrayal of the public’s trust.

I have demanded answers from DHS about training and background checks in the days following Johan Sebastián’s death. This reporting makes a full, independent investigation even more urgent. DHS must release Brouillette’s hiring, vetting, training, and deployment records and cooperate fully with independent investigators.

ICE must be abolished and that is what I will continue to fight for. But perfect can’t get in the way of better. Until we can abolish ICE, this agency needs serious, immediate reforms. I am working on legislation to ensure federal agents are never armed and deployed into our streets without being fully vetted. Our communities’ safety cannot depend on whether this administration finds basic safeguards convenient."

Senator-elect Troy Jackson issued a statement as well:

"Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero should still be alive. ICE put an armed officer on Maine’s streets without fully reviewing his background. Now we’re learning about his disturbing history of anti-immigrant hatred. His family deserves answers and justice. Those responsible must be held accountable. ICE must be abolished. This is exactly why."

Governor-elect Hannah Pingree issued a statement, saying in part:

"[Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero'] family and the people of Maine deserve justice and a full accounting. I look forward to the results of the Maine Attorney General’s independent investigation into this shameful use of deadly force. As Governor, I will ensure there is no state cooperation that aids ICE operations in our communities and work with our federal delegation to demand answers from the Trump Administration about ICE’s appalling hiring and training practices. I have long believed that ICE must be abolished, and this tragedy underscores why. Maine families deserve to be safe in our own neighborhoods."

text:
(11 Nov 2026) Case-by-case records current through August 24, 2026, obtained by TRAC through successful litigation under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) document that contrary to news reporting and public perception, the number of individuals removed from the United States actually declined after President Trump assumed office in January 2025.

These records are from the Department of Homeland Security’s Enforcement Integrated Database (EID) which Immigration and Customs Enforcement personnel manage. This is the official repository and most comprehensive source of immigration enforcement data covering not only actions by ICE, but also by Customs and Border Protection (CBP). Data are structured to follow each noncitizen from the initiation of their case to final outcome. Records cover the period from 2008 to the present, with some individuals’ immigration histories going back to the 1920s or earlier.

Despite the reassignment of personnel from other agencies to immigration enforcement, the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) and with it, a substantial increase in resources for immigration enforcement activities, the number of immigration removals conducted by DHS has actually declined. During the first full month of Trump’s second term, for example, a total of 30,893 removals were recorded by the agency. During July 2026, the last full month for which data are available, the number declined to 26,908 – a drop of 13 percent.

The Trump administration’s record has also lagged behind a number of past administrations. Analysis of these recently released case-by-case records systematically tracking all individuals DHS has sought to remove since 2008 documents that the greatest number of removals occurred in FY 2024, the final full fiscal year of the Biden administration. The number of removals during the last 12 months under President Trump is also less than in any fiscal year from FY 2008 to FY 2016 during the George W. Bush’s and Barack Obama’s administrations.

When ICE speaks about removals, in the fine print they usually include removals plus returns. Removals bar an individual from legally returning to the United States for a period of years. For returns, reentry is not legally barred. This broader measure (“deportations”) includes voluntary departures and voluntary returns along with removals. Even with voluntary departures and voluntary returns added to traditional removals, these EID records document that deportations are not as high or are about the same as the number of deportations twenty years ago. Documented deportations during the last two decades peaked at 489,251 in FY 2009 under former President Obama and were also about the same under the final year of President Bush’s administration in 2008.

In July 2026, under the second Trump administration, the number of monthly deportations reached 42,399 far above actual monthly removals of 26,908. Removals made up only 63 percent of total deportations in both July and August 2026. Voluntary departures had risen to 31 percent, while voluntary returns made up the remaining 6 percent. Voluntary departures ordered by Immigration Judges soared during FY 2026. This rise is likely attributable to a number of factors including the sharp rise in asylum denials, increased exigency with which removal proceedings are being conducted and the denial of bond for detained foreign nationals. The increase in voluntary returns may also reflect the use of a “stipulation” that waives an Immigration Court hearing and agrees to deportation, which ICE began using in the spring of 2025.

Further details on these findings and information about this initial court-ordered data release covering 19.9 million individuals are found in the full report.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement made five arrests Tuesday throughout San Mateo County, according to the county's Rapid Response Hotline and Office of Community Affairs.
